1791-09-10.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 1-2]
# ACCOUNT OF THE VOYAGE IN SEARCH OF LA PÉROUSE.

## CHAPTER THE FIRST.

*Departure from Brest. Arrival at Santa Cruz de Tenerife. Journey to the Peak. A sailor who had just been drowned is brought back to life. Bold thieves rob him of his clothes. Two naturalists seized with a spitting of blood which prevents them from reaching the summit of the Peak. English ships in the roadstead of Santa Cruz. Various results of observations made to determine the variation of the magnetic needle. New volcano to the south-west of the Peak.*

The fitting out of the two ships intended for the voyage we were about to undertake was well advanced towards the end of the month of August, when General Dentrecasteaux notified us to repair to Brest. I had the pleasure of making the journey with three persons belonging to the same expedition, Citizens Riche, Beaupré and Pierson.

[t. I, p. 2-3]
We arrived at Brest on the 10th of September. The finest ships in France, such as the Majestueux, the Etats de Bourgogne, the América, etc., were then in the harbour.

While the astronomers were busy with the observations that were to give them the rate of the timekeepers and marine clocks, the naturalists hastened to complete the articles needed for preparing the collections they proposed to make in the new countries we were about to visit.

As my intention was to devote myself chiefly to the observation of plants, I needed a great deal of paper, and I wished to find some of a very large size. I had much difficulty in procuring twenty-two reams, because almost all that remained in the storehouses had just been given over to the service of the artillery.

Part of the time at my disposal was spent in visiting the botanical garden, which is extremely well kept. In the same premises there is a small cabinet of natural history, in which one notices several anatomical preparations given by Citizen Joannet, surgeon-major of the Espérance.

1791-09-21.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 3-4]
The muster of the crews was held in the harbour on the 21st of September. Our ships were moved out into the roadstead on the 25th. There was then no foreign vessel there, and few French ones.

We were heavily laden. Accordingly, at the moment of our departure, our draught of water was four metres forty-six centimetres and a half aft, or thirteen feet nine inches; and four metres seventeen centimetres forward, or twelve feet ten inches.

There were on board the Recherche:

6 eight-pounder guns.

2 thirty-six-pounder carronades.

6 swivel guns of half a kilogramme.

12 swivel guns of two hectogrammes.

45 muskets.

*35 pistols.*

50 sabres.

30 boarding axes.

10 Espingards.

The Espérance had much the same means of defence, and this was enough to secure us against any attempt on the part of the savages.

Both ships were supplied with a great quantity of articles intended for distribution among the natives of the South Seas. Iron tools and stuffs of different colours, particularly of red, formed the basis of our articles of exchange.

1791-09-23.journal_labillardiere: (Labillardière's account for this day is given under 1791-09-21.)

1791-09-24.journal_labillardiere: (Labillardière's account for this day is given under 1791-09-21.)

1791-09-25.journal_labillardiere: (Labillardière's account for this day is given under 1791-09-21.)

1791-09-28.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 4]
Each of our ships carried for eighteen months' provisions. We waited only for a favourable wind to set sail. A fairly fresh easterly wind allowed us to get under way at about one o'clock in the afternoon, on the 28th of September. As soon as we were out of the roadstead, two sailors and a ship's boy were discovered who, burning with the desire to make this voyage and much vexed at not being included among the crews, had hidden themselves on board. As we had scarcely room enough left for those who were meant for this voyage, the general had the ship worked into the roadstead of Bertheaume, from where these three guests, on whom no one had reckoned, were sent ashore.

The Espérance had got well ahead of us, because she had kept on her course; but we rejoined her before nightfall, for we sailed a great deal better than she did.

Our point of departure at six o'clock in the evening was in latitude 48° 13' north, and 7° 15' west longitude.

We had the tower of Ushant bearing north 2° west by compass.

The Bec de la chèvre south-east 4° east.

The Bec du raz south 2° east.

Pointe Matthieu was then at a distance of one myriametre from us.

The course was set to the west-north-west; it was afterwards directed to the west towards midnight.

1791-09-29.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 4-6]
On the 29th, on opening dispatches which he was not to read until he was at sea, Commander Dentrecasteaux learned that Major Huon-Kermadec, commander of the Espérance, had just been given the rank of post-captain, and that he himself had been raised to the rank of rear-admiral. This news was at once passed to the Espérance by speaking-trumpet.

Our ensigns were immediately hoisted, with the distinguishing marks of the rank that had just been conferred on the general.

Two marines and a ship's boy who were not on the muster-roll were also discovered. These had kept themselves hidden until then. There was no longer any means of sending them back ashore, because we were too far from it; so the general allowed them to make the voyage.

As I had already made some sea voyages, I had imagined that I had grown sufficiently used to navigation to be no longer troubled by the motion of the ship; but this habit had long since been lost; and so I was seasick for the first three days after our departure from Brest. I had occasion to notice many times, in the course of the voyage I have just made, that a short stay on shore was enough to make me lose my habit of the sea; so that every time we set sail again, even after a very short port of call, I was for two or three days almost as ill as on leaving Brest. Seamen advise eating in such a case, in spite of the disgust caused by the nausea peculiar to this kind of complaint. It is hard to agree with this opinion; for, besides a great difficulty in swallowing, the presence of food in the stomach increases the nausea; and it is one more misery when it comes to bringing it up.

Diluent drinks, taken in small quantities at a time so as to spare the contractility of the stomach, always relieved me: lukewarm water, lightly sweetened, was the drink I then most commonly used, because it is the one most easily obtained on board a ship.

We had, however, several persons who, though they had never been to sea before, felt no effect whatever from the waves. Such a constitution is much to be desired when one undertakes long voyages; for it is difficult to express the distress caused by this spasmodic affection which, spreading to every part of the body, throws you into so great a dejection that you cling to life only because you glimpse an end to your sufferings.

1791-10-05.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 6-7]
The winds were light and variable from west to north from our departure until the 5th of October... They were then rather fresh, varying from north-east to north until our arrival at Tenerife. We were not without anxiety at this freshening of the wind, for in our situation it might have proved fatal to us. Cluttered on every side, with far too great a load above the waterline, we might have capsized in heavy weather; the stowage was very incomplete. It was in this disorder that we had sailed, although the National Assembly had decreed nearly eight months before that this voyage should take place.

1791-10-11.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 7]
On the 11th of October, at about fifty-five minutes past ten, there was an eclipse of the moon. It is very difficult to make use of the observation one can make of it at sea. Citizen Willaumez nevertheless deduced from his a longitude of 18° 59' 45" west.

1791-10-12.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 7]
The Espérance signalled land to us on the 12th at about eight o'clock in the morning.

Towards noon we reckoned ourselves fourteen myriametres from the Peak of Tenerife, which could be seen *to the south*-west by south, raising its head majestically above the clouds.

1791-10-13.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 7-9]
By nightfall we were no more than two myriametres from the north-east point of the island. We stood off and on under the topsails, going about every three hours while we waited for daylight. As soon as it began to appear we closed the coast, which we ran along at a distance of one kilometre.

The anchor was let go at about half past nine in the morning in the roadstead of Santa Cruz, on a bottom of muddy black sand, in two decametres and a half of water. Citizen Fonspertuis, the French consul, came at once to offer the general to do all he could to supply the needs of our expedition.

I went ashore in the afternoon in order to acquaint myself with the surroundings of the town. Although the season was already well advanced, the reflection of the sun's rays from the volcanic stones produced a heat all the more oppressive because the dead calm left them their full strength.

Among the plants that grow around Santa Cruz I noticed a woody balm, known to botanists by the name of *melissa fruticosa*, the *saccharum teneriffæ*, the *cacalia kleinia*, the *datura metel*, the *chrysanthemum frutescens*, etc.

The beautiful tree known by the name of poincillade, *poinciana pulcherrima*, was the ornament of some gardens.

That same evening Citizen Elie, struck by the odd attire of some of the women of the town, who, even in the season of the greatest heat, wear a kind of short cloak of very coarse wool, was busy pencilling a sketch of it when a sentry came and interrupted him, believing that he was taking a plan of the roadstead. In vain did he show him that it was only a matter of costume; the soldier would on no account let him finish his drawing.

We had anchored too close to a small vessel, and so in the afternoon an anchor was carried out towards the shore, by means of which we kept ourselves at a proper distance from her.

The bearings taken from this position gave us:

The redoubt to the north of the town, north by east 4° east.

The great tower standing towards the middle of the town, west-south-west.

1791-10-14.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 9]
At sunrise each of the forts returned with nine guns the salute we had fired with the same number. We had fired fifteen for the town, which returned them gun for gun towards noon.

*A* packet-boat arriving from Spain came to anchor in the roadstead.

We had planned to set out the very next day on the journey to the Peak, and to visit the high mountains of the *island* one after another. *T*he French consul readily procured us every facility in his power, and he gave us a letter of recommendation to M. de Cologant, a worthy merchant residing at Orotava.

1791-10-15.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 9-15]
At about four o'clock in the morning we made our way to the mole, eight of us in all; namely, Develle, one of the officers of our ship; Piron, Deschamps, Lahaye, three servants and myself: one of the servants knew enough Spanish to act as our interpreter. On the open ground bordering the sea we found some of the mules intended for us; but more than an hour passed before we could set off; for it was no easy matter to get together some of the muleteers, who, knowing full well that we would not leave without them, had no fear of keeping us waiting. As soon as they had arrived, we thought we could start on our way; but they had to hold a long discussion among themselves before loading the few effects we needed for this journey.

It is worth recalling that on board they had furnished us with provisions as if we were to travel in some savage country. Rossel, who was in charge of the officers' table, had ordered the cook to make us an excellent salmon pie. I would not have mentioned it were it not in singular contrast with the worm-eaten biscuit and the cheese with which we were regaled at most of the other ports of call we made afterwards.

M. de Cologant, informed by the French consul of our intended journey, sent to invite us to stay at his house at the port of Orotava. This place, which is only three myriametres and a half from Santa Cruz, is one of the best stations for going to the Peak; for it lies at the foot of the mountains nearest to it.

We took three hours to reach Laguna. This town is only one myriametre distant from Santa Cruz; but the road is not easy, because one must climb almost the whole way: the town is badly built and very thinly peopled. Convents are very numerous there. We were told that the monks made up at least half of its inhabitants.

Before reaching Laguna we had just crossed some barren mountains covered with a few succulent plants, among which we had noticed the Canary spurge (*euphorbia canariensis*), the *euphorbia dendroides* the *cacalia kleinia* and the kind of prickly pear to which botanists have given the name of *cactus opuntia*, etc. These plants, which live almost entirely at the expense of the atmosphere, adapt themselves fairly well to the sterility of these steep slopes. On reaching the little plain on which the town is built, we had the pleasure of seeing that the soil of the surrounding mountains had not been washed down by the rains to no purpose, since it had come to fertilise this small corner of land, where much wheat, maize, millet, etc., is harvested.

I gathered a species of *periploca* which I had already brought back from my journey to the Levant. I published it in my second decade of the plants of Syria, under the name of *periploca angustifolia*. Citizen Desfontaines had also brought back the same species from the coasts of Barbary.

All the stones we had found so far had undergone the action of fire. As these mountains, of middling height, are composed of great masses which, at the time of their fusion, must have kept a very high degree of heat for a very long time, I was fully prepared to find these lavas very compact. And so they are; their grain is very fine, and their commonest colour is a dark brown.

In the midst of this volcanic debris we suffered from great heat, which our guides bore much less well than we did; and so they used every means of persuasion to induce us to halt for the whole day, so as to travel only by night. They probably imagined that we had no other purpose than to see the summit of the Peak. This plan of travel had not displeased several of us. But it was not difficult to make them understand that such a nocturnal visit to the mountains could not suit naturalists.

The inhabitants of this island are surrounded from their birth by religious prejudices. Children came out of their houses to ask us whether we were of their religion: we confined ourselves to pitying these unfortunate people, over whom fanaticism and monkish intolerance hold their dangerous sway with so much power.

The pretty fern known by the name of *trichomanes canariense* covers most of the walls enclosing the gardens we came upon beyond Laguna.

We were descending by fairly gentle slopes as we drew near the port of Orotava; these were no longer the barren mountains around Santa Cruz, whose succulent plants proclaim their sterility, but charming hillsides covered with vines, which form the chief wealth of the island.

The shrub known by the name of *bosea yervamora* grew in the hollows.

It was five o'clock in the evening when we arrived at Orotava, where M. de Cologant received us as well as could possibly be.

Two ships, one Dutch and the other English, were then at anchor in the roadstead, taking in a cargo of wines. Landing there is even more difficult than at Santa Cruz. And so this roadstead is the least frequented.

M. de Cologant's cellar could not fail to arouse our curiosity; for the trade of this rich merchant is chiefly in the wines of the island.

Among the different qualities of wine to be found there, there are two quite distinct sorts; namely, the dry wine and that called malmsey, in the preparation of which care has been taken to concentrate the sugary part strongly.

A pipe of the best wine then cost a hundred and twenty piastres, and that of the lowest quality cost sixty. It should be noted that I speak only of the price at which it is sold to foreigners; for this same wine at sixty piastres is given to the inhabitants of the island for thirty-six. When the fermentation of these wines is well advanced, it is the custom to mix a great deal of brandy with them, so that they may keep. And so they are very heady. Many people cannot drink them, even in rather small quantities, without feeling on the nervous system the disagreeable effects that this mixture causes there.

We were assured that the island commonly yields thirty thousand pipes of wine a year.

As not enough corn grows there for the consumption of the inhabitants, part of the proceeds of the wines, which are sold abroad as Madeira wine, from which indeed they differ very little, is spent on the purchase of this prime necessity.

The olive tree, which thrives fairly well in this island, is nevertheless little cultivated there. The papaw and the date palm, which are grown in some gardens, are merely objects of curiosity there.

We had been assured, before leaving Santa Cruz, that snow covered the summit of the Peak. I had not wished to burden myself with a barometer; but we learned at Orotava that we had been misled, when I no longer had the means of procuring this instrument of observation[^014-1].

We were to set out very early the next day towards the Peak.

[^014-1]: (continued) the mercury had fallen there to 18 inches 4 lines, the thermometer then indicating 9° 3/10 above o; while at Santa Cruz the mercury in the barometer stood at the same moment at 28 inches 3 lines, the thermometer at the same place giving 24° 1/2.

1791-10-16.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 15-18]
But it was a feast day; and our guides would not have been willing to set out without having attended mass; some of them had even heard as many as three: as for us, we were waiting with the keenest impatience, when our anxiety was redoubled on learning that it was only as a very special favour that they were willing to set out on so great a day. They were, however, ready to start at about nine o'clock in the morning.

As soon as we were out of the town, we climbed by roads that were often very steep, from which we could see enormous heaps of mountains piled one upon another and rising in an amphitheatre up to the base of the Peak. Their ridges sometimes offered us fairly level places, which served us as so many resting points, where, after climbing by very steep paths, we would take breath for a moment, so as to attack the higher mountains with greater courage.

Our guides were astonished to see some of us make this road on foot, contrary to the custom of most travellers who come to visit the Peak, so much so that for a long time they kept urging us to mount the mules they had brought for us. After passing through fine plantations of vines, we found ourselves among chestnut trees, which grow in higher regions.

The ravines furnished me with the Virginian polypody (*polipodium Virginicum*), and several new species of laurel, among which one notices the one known by the name of Indian laurel (*laurus Indica*, Linn.)

Although this journey was not to last beyond a few days, we had been very rightly advised to take several pairs of shoes; for the best of them hold out only a short time against the lava on which one must walk continually.

It was scarcely noon when we had reached the clouds, which shed a heavy dew on the shrubs through which we had to pass.

The abundance of rain brought to these heights by the natural drift of the air[^016-1] ought to give rise to a great number of springs. They are nevertheless very rare there; for the soil is not fine enough to hold back the rain water, which, filtering through this volcanic debris, for the most part makes its way to the ocean without having formed any streams.

As soon as we had passed through these thick clouds, we enjoyed the finest spectacle it is possible to imagine. The clouds that were piling up below us merged in the distance with the waters of the sea, hiding the island from our view; we enjoyed the purest of skies; the peak then appeared like an island whose base seemed to plunge into a vast ocean.

Scarcely out of the clouds, I saw for a moment a phenomenon I had had occasion to observe several times during my stay in the high mountains of the Kesroan, in Asia Minor. It was with fresh surprise that I perceived the whole outline of my body traced in the beautiful colours of the rainbow on clouds which lay below me on the side opposite the sun.

The rays of the sun, which are decomposed in passing over the surface of bodies, give a very exact explanation of this brilliant phenomenon. It represents on a large scale the experiment known to natural philosophers, in which the rays that have just been made to pass over the surface of an opaque body placed at the opening of a window show the whole outline of that body in the colours of the rainbow, after being concentrated by means of a lens and then received on a sheet of white paper.

We had just crossed prodigious heaps of pumice stones, among which we noticed few plants, and even these were very sickly. A few *spartium* were the only shrubs that could put up with such an elevation.

We walked with some difficulty through this volcanic debris, for one sank into it up to mid-leg.

Blocks of pozzolana were scattered over it at fairly great distances from one another.

It was nine o'clock in the evening when we took up our quarters among the lavas, some large fragments of which were our only shelter against the east wind, which was then blowing fairly hard. The cold was very great at this height, where nature has not consulted the needs of travellers, for wood is very scarce there; and so the little fire we were able to make did not prevent us from spending a very bad night there.

[^016-1]: It is worth noting that when high mountains are strongly heated by the rays of the sun, they become a kind of hearth above which the surrounding air rises because of the expansion it undergoes; from which results an inflow of the more distant air, which, coming to replace that which rises, brings with it the clouds with which it is laden, as I had occasion to observe very often on Mount Lebanon, where this phenomenon never failed to occur at about five o'clock in the afternoon in the heats of the month of Fructidor, when too strong an agitation of the atmosphere did not counteract this natural drift. This is perhaps the only cause of the apparent attraction of clouds by mountains.

1791-10-17.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 18-23]
Day at last began to break.

We then left some of our guides with their mules at the place where we had just spent the night, and we took the road to the Peak, the summit of which we were soon to reach.

We went on for an hour over considerable heaps of fragments of greyish lava, among which were scattered here and there blocks of pozzolana and large masses of a very compact blackish glass, much resembling bottle glass. Although manufactured in the vast crucibles of these mountains at the time of their combustion, this glass would be no less fit to be useful in the arts, since, being wholly formed by nature, it would need only the firing necessary to melt it in order to become fit to receive from the hand of man every shape of which it is capable.

The cavern at the edge of which we arrived is called *la queve del ana*. Its opening is fully a metre and a half across. As it goes down more than two metres in an almost vertical direction, we could only reach the bottom by descending into it by means of a rope. We found water there, the surface of which, as we might well have expected at this elevation, was covered with ice nearly half a decimetre thick. It was broken at once, and we quenched our thirst with very good water. I felt no disagreeable sensation from it in my throat, as I had noticed so many times in the Alps of France when quenching my thirst with the water that wells up at the foot of the glaciers, although the water of this cavern was one degree colder than the water of glaciers commonly shows; for the thermometer I plunged into it fell to freezing point. It would seem, then, that the disagreeable pricking which water taken at the foot of glaciers causes inside the throat is due to the want of atmospheric air.

Flakes of nitre lined the inside of this grotto.

Piron had been unwell for several days: he felt too tired to come any farther; Deschamps thought fit not to go beyond the cavern, while we went on climbing towards the summit of the Peak.

Having reached its base, which forms the crown of the highest mountains, we saw it shoot up in the form of a cone to a prodigious height. From there our view soared above all the mountains, which form as it were so many steps that we had had to climb to reach this point.

The place called *la Ramblette*, lying towards the north-west, offered to our curiosity some openings in the rock, some a decimetre wide, others mere cracks, from which came an odourless watery vapour, although their edges were lined with crystals of sulphur resting on a very white earth that had every appearance of clay.

A mercury thermometer graduated on Réaumur's scale was introduced into some of these openings, where it showed, within the space of one minute, 43° above o. In several others the mercury rose only to 30°.

We had come to the most difficult part of the climb, for the Peak is very steep. When we had got to about a third of its height, although the surface of the ground was no warmer than one commonly finds at such an elevation, I took it into my head to dig in the soil a hole about two decimetres deep, from which there at once came an odourless watery vapour, in which the thermometer, plunged into it, gave 51° above o.

The *spartium supra nubium* was indeed the last shrub I found before reaching the foot of the cone; but there is a herbaceous plant which, in spite of its apparent delicacy, still grows at a greater height. It is a violet with somewhat elongated leaves, lightly toothed at the edges; its flower was already over: it grows very close to the summit of the Peak, which we soon reached. As the vapours of the atmosphere cannot rise to this height, the sky there shows itself in all its purity and shines with an azure more vivid and more brilliant than on the finest days of our climates: a few clouds scattered here and there, far below our feet, did not hide the neighbouring islands from our view.

This summit ends in a crest, the highest point of which is towards the north-west. To the south-west one notices a marked depression, which seems to have been produced by the subsidence of the ground.

Very close to its point one sees several openings of a decimetre at most in width, from which comes a very hot vapour that makes Réaumur's thermometer rise to 67° above o, producing a noise much like the humming of bees. When, late in the season, the snows come to whiten the summit of the Peak, those lying close to these openings do not long withstand such a degree of heat. Fine crystals of sulphur, most of them needle-shaped, among which some of regular form are to be seen, adorn the edges of these vents. The sulphuric acid, combined with water, has so altered the neighbouring volcanic products that one would take them for a very white clay, made very ductile by the moisture that constantly comes out of these openings. It is on this earth that the fine crystals of sulphur I have just spoken of are fixed.

The decomposition of the sulphur and of the volcanic products there yields an aluminous salt in extremely fine needles, which covers the surface of the ground.

The thermometer, observed in the shade for more than a quarter of an hour on the summit of the Peak, one metre above the ground, rose to 15° above o: it did not vary appreciably whether it was nearer to it or farther from it, even by two or three metres, which would lead me to believe that the internal heat of this ground, though very great, has little influence on that of the atmospheric air. Besides, the atmospheric air may well receive 15° of heat from the rays of the sun at this elevation, since a greater heat is often felt at the foot of our glaciers. The thermometer, taken up Mount Lebanon, quite close to the snows, often gave me 20° above o there.

The slope of the mountain favoured our return, and we came down much faster than we had gone up.

The day was drawing to its close when we reached the place where we had spent the previous night. The almost total want of sleep caused by the great cold we had felt there had taken away from us *the wish to* make it our resting place again.

1791-10-18.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 23-26]
We would gladly have set off at once, so as to seek a better shelter on some lower mountain; but as our guides would not stir before the moon rose, we had to stay there until about midnight, to wait for it to appear above the horizon. It was by the faint light of that orb that we came down through the pumice stones by a path not far from the one we had made for ourselves while climbing these high mountains.

After four hours' walking, the shrubs, which grew very close together, made the path difficult enough to oblige us to halt and wait for daylight. In this place we were no longer without wood, as we had been the night before; and so we made up for it amply with a great fire, which was lit at once. While we were warming ourselves very comfortably, the conversation turned on what remained for us to do. Most of us, tired by this laborious excursion, had no other wish than to get back to Santa Cruz by the shortest way. We had, however, agreed at Orotava that on our return we would follow the far side of these mountains. But we did not all have the same views; and so we let those who had nothing further to wish for go back on board, and we stayed behind, the gardener and I, with the intention of continuing our researches. All the guides wanted to follow those who were going back on board. I had great difficulty in persuading one of them to come with us.

I had the pleasure of finding, among the plants that clothed the slope of the rocks, the beautiful golden-flowered bellflower (*campanula aurea*), the *prenanthes pinnata*, the *adiantum reniforme*, and a species of *cétérac*, remarkable for foliage much larger than that of the European kind.

As water was very scarce on these heights, we turned our steps towards a small dwelling, near which we fully supposed some stream must flow. And indeed we found there a fine spring, whose water, as delicious as it was clear, sank into the ground after appearing for a moment at its surface.

Apple trees laden with fruit adorned the garden of these peaceable inhabitants: this fruit gave so much pleasure to a servant from the ship who was with us that, while we were busy exploring the surroundings of this little settlement, he took it into his head to make an exchange which gave us a very poor opinion of his foresight. He had just given away almost all our provisions of meat for apples, without troubling himself whether apples would be good victuals for roaming the mountains. We fully resolved to employ a more intelligent steward another time It is worth noting that ships' servants are generally little fit for any service on shore.

As night came on we were very far from any dwelling. It was nearly nine o'clock in the evening when we reached a village where hospitality is certainly not the favourite virtue of the inhabitants. It was only with the greatest difficulty that we found shelter there. As we did not understand the Spanish language, we could express ourselves only by signs, and at night above all this language is of little help; but our guide, who wished as much as we did to find somewhere to sleep, went knocking in vain at every door, when, after passing through almost the whole village, we met two good people who were kind enough to give us refuge.

A frugal meal was served to us at once, during which we were lighted in the manner of some of the inhabitants of our Alps: small splinters of very resinous fir wood, stuck into the wall, burned, giving a fair amount of light but far too much smoke. One of our hosts took care to replace these small pieces of wood as they burned away.

We had more need of sleep than of food; and so we soon gave ourselves up to a sleep all the sweeter for being no longer disturbed by the cold of the high mountains.

1791-10-19.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 26-34]
The next day, the 19th, I went back on board laden with volcanic products and some very pretty plants, among which were the *teucrium betonicum*, the *echium frutescens*, etc.

The birds called *canaries* are very common in the lower regions of these mountains; they are all brown mixed with various colours, and their plumage is not as fine as in the domesticated state. Travellers have asserted that a species of parrot native to the island is to be found there. I never met with one in any of our excursions, and several trustworthy inhabitants told me that this assertion was without foundation. That same day a very fresh wind had raised the sea so high that it threw ashore the Espérance's boat, moored near the landing-place, after capsizing it on top of a sailor who could only be freed after some minutes: he was already badly asphyxiated; but happily the means employed in such cases brought him back to life.

While expressing here my gratitude to the garrison of Santa Cruz for the eagerness with which they came to the help of this unfortunate man, I cannot pass over in silence a piece of roguery on the part of some of the inhabitants of the town.

The sailor's clothes had been put out to dry while he was being given assistance; none of us could have suspected what happened. Some people of the town, perhaps already taking him for dead, thought that his clothes ought to go to the benefit of the living; they were carried off without its being possible to discover the thieves.

Citizens Riche and Blavier had undertaken the journey to the Peak one day after us; but these two naturalists could not climb as far as the summit; they were still a long way from it when, their lungs being unable to cope with air that was too rarefied, they spat blood and were obliged to give up their undertaking.

The following days were spent in visiting the surroundings of Santa Cruz, where the countryside is generally very barren. The town, even in proportion to its small extent, has a rather scanty population, although its roadstead is the most frequented in the island. The Spaniards have brought their way of building there; the arrangement of the inside of their houses is the same as the one they have adopted in Europe, without any of the modifications that the difference of climate ought perhaps to have given rise to.

The governor-general of the Canaries usually resides at Santa Cruz.

There are several convents of men and of women. A parish church, in which gilding is spread about with all the profusion of bad taste, is also remarkable for the poor choice of its pictures.

In the public square there is a pretty fountain; the water is brought from a great distance across the mountains in wooden channels. The streets are badly paved: most of the windows have no glass; they are closed by lattice blinds, which the women very often raise when curiosity or some other motive leads them to let themselves be seen.

The rich women are dressed in the French fashion: the others cover their shoulders with a piece of coarse woollen stuff, which forms a kind of short cloak, very uncomfortable under a very hot sky; a black felt hat with a broad brim protects them from the rays of the sun: their complexion is darkened by mixture with the natives of the island, and their features are, in general, not very agreeable. The multitude of religious practices introduced among the inhabitants did not prevent several of these women from going, rosary in hand, to meet our sailors every time they came ashore: several of them had long cause to repent of having let themselves be seduced by so many charms.

The wine of Tenerife, which, as I have already remarked, is very heady, nearly proved fatal to one of our soldiers; in his drunkenness he committed a very serious offence against a sentry. Our consul used the credit he enjoyed with the officer commanding in the absence of the governor-general to stop all proceedings against this man, more to be pitied than blamed.

The discipline established on board English ships protects them from such mishaps.

The sloop Scorpion, of sixteen guns and a crew of a hundred men, commanded by Captain Benjamin Hallowell, had come to anchor in the roadstead on the 18th, in company with a small cutter, five days out of Madeira: they had left there a ship of fifty guns which was shortly to proceed to Tenerife. Commodore Englefield, who was aboard her, was in command of this small expedition, bound for the coast of Africa. These navigators, knowing the danger of a stay on shore for sailors, kept them on board. Only the service of the ship could induce the captain to let them go ashore. The commodore fully intended not to relax this rule during the whole of his station on the coast of Africa.

The variation of the magnetic needle observed on board, and deduced from sixteen observations, fourteen of them azimuths and two of them amplitudes at rising, was found to be 18° 7' 7" to the west.

The result of two observations made on shore, on the terrace of one of the houses of the town, by Citizen Bertrand, one of the astronomers of the expedition, was 21° 33' west.

Another observation, made on the mole with an azimuth compass, gave a variation of 23° 43' west. So great a difference over such small distances is probably due only to the quantity of ferruginous matter unevenly distributed in these volcanic mountains.

Of these observations, those made on board seem the more deserving of confidence, since they agree with the progressive decrease of the declination observed since our departure from Brest, and with what has long been observed by many other navigators.

The dip of the magnetic needle (it was a flat needle) was 62° 25'. The same needle had given a dip of 71° 30' at Brest, and 72° 56' at Paris.

28° 29' 35" north latitude and 18° 36' west longitude were the position of our anchorage in the roadstead of Tenerife.

The thermometer and the barometer, observed on board towards noon, varied little during this port of call; the first did not exceed 20° 2/10, and the second 28p 2l.

Water, which is very good at Santa Cruz, is easily taken in there when the swell is not heavy.

This port of call is excellent for the ease with which all the vegetables of Europe can be obtained there in abundance, with the exception of cabbages, which, though very small, are very dear there. Generally speaking, all the fruits of Europe are found there, and the same domestic animals as in our French ports.

Experience taught us that their sheep do not stand being on board ship as well as ours; the pure air they breathe on the mountains where they go in search of pasture makes them little fit to bear the foul air of a between-decks.

Fish preserved by drying can be obtained at Tenerife; there is a particularly large trade there in the species known by the name of *bonito*.

The parts of the island that it has been possible to bring under cultivation are very fertile; this is characteristic of volcanic islands. The internal heat of such soils draws up to their surface part of the water with which they are soaked by the rains, and so gives vegetation an uncommon vigour. The too slow decomposition of some of these volcanic stones and the dryness of some of the mountains are so many causes that make many other places little fit for cultivation: the action of fire, which has fallen in succession, at periods very remote from one another, on the various parts of the island, as the historical records and the preservation of the plants peculiar to it attest, has delayed in these different places the completion of a decomposition without which vegetation cannot take place.

There had been no volcanic eruption on the island of Tenerife for ninety-two years when, in the month of Prairial in the year VI, a new volcano opened to the south-west of the Peak, as I was told by Citizen Gicquel, a naval officer, who put in at Santa Cruz on his return from the Isle of France [Mauritius] in the frigate Régénérée.

Here is the account of it given to him by Citizen le Gros, consul of the French Republic:

"It was on the 21st of Prairial in the year VI that the inhabitants of Santa Cruz heard dull, repeated reports, rather like the sound of cannon heard from afar; in the night there was a slight earthquake, and the next day it was learned that a volcano had opened to the south-west of the Peak. As many as fifteen mouths were counted in the first days of the eruption; they were soon reduced to twelve, and at the end of a month only two were to be seen, from which large rocks continually issued, which, hurled out with the lava, followed their upward flight, often for fifteen seconds, before falling back to the ground."

We had been so crowded until our arrival at this port of call that it had not been possible to find proper room for all the men of the crew.

## CHAPTER II.

*Departure from Tenerife for the Cape of Good Hope. Various observations. Brilliant phenomenon of a sea singularly phosphorescent. Experiment which showed me the most usual cause of the phosphorescence of sea water. Four of the Tenerife sheep thrown overboard, and why. Slight degree of heat quite close to the Line. Much greater variation of the compass south of the equator than north of it. Very easy means used to purify fresh water that had just gone bad. Very thick fog which caused the mercury to rise in the barometer. Lunar rainbow. Arrival at the Cape of Good Hope.*

A very heavy swell had prevented us for nearly two days from getting our provisions on board.

1791-10-23.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 34-36]
We were not ready to sail until the 23rd of October. Work began very early in the morning on getting under way. All the boats had been hoisted in the day before, after we had unmoored; for we had to try to take advantage of the land breeze, which seldom fails to make itself felt every morning. It was besides advisable to get ahead of the flood tide, which was due at about half past five.

We were made fast by a hawser to the English corvette. I must not let slip the opportunity of praising the courteous conduct of her captain, who lent himself in the most obliging manner to giving us all the help we needed in getting under way. Our commander, for his part, had used every means of being of service to him when he had come to anchor in this roadstead some days after us.

An anchor belonging to the English sloop served us to cast the ship's head, and after spreading our sails we stood away from the coast with a light breath of wind, which lasted too short a time for the Espérance to profit by it, although she had got under sail a few minutes after us. Carried along by the flood tide, which made itself felt at once, she was obliged to drop a small anchor and warp herself up to it, so as to get away from the coast and clear herself of the vessels among which she lay.

It was half past nine when she rejoined us. The course was then set south by west.

At noon we were in latitude 28° 5' 40" north, and 18° 36' 40" west longitude.

It was from this position that we took the bearing of the Peak of Tenerife, west 28° north, and of the eastern part of the island of Grand Canary, east 24° south.

At about one o'clock in the afternoon the course was directed south-west by south, so as to pass between the Cape Verde Islands and the mainland. We then had a fairly fresh easterly wind.

At about six o'clock in the evening the island of Gomera bore north 38° west.

1791-10-26.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 36]
On the 26th the Espérance, after asking us for our longitude, made hers known to us. The great difference found between the longitude given by dead reckoning and that given by observation left us in some uncertainty, which led us to bear away two points to starboard of the south-west by south course we had been holding until then; but later observations made us resume our first heading. The sky was very fine; we had nothing to fear in approaching the coast of Africa: besides, the lead would have warned us of our distance from it several myriametres out to sea.

1791-10-27.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 36-37]
The next morning we saw no land, which left us no further doubt as to the error in the longitude given by the Espérance's timekeepers.

We crossed the tropic of Cancer at about one o'clock in the afternoon, in 20° of west longitude. The barometer then stood at 28p 2l 8/10, and the thermometer at 19° 5/10.

1791-10-28.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 37]
The first fish to bite at the hook of one of our fishermen was a very fine dolphin (*coryphaena hyppurus*). Nothing more was needed to set the whole crew astir; but the fisherman, having hauled it in too hastily, had the mortification of finding only part of its jaw at the end of his hook.

Since our departure from Tenerife the winds had kept close to the north-east.

1791-10-29.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 37-38]
A chimney swallow (*hirundo rustica*, Linn.), no doubt newly arrived from Europe, followed us for some time without choosing to alight on our ship: it soon directed its flight towards the coast of Africa, where it was sure to find the insects on which it feeds. We were then in about 20° of north latitude, and 22° 30' of west longitude.

As there was little wind, the medusa known by the name of *medusa caravella*, Linn., could be seen floating in great numbers on the surface of the water. This species must not be touched without precaution, for, like several sea nettles, it raises blisters after a painful pricking.

The fish known as the remora (*echeneis remora*, Linn.) usually follows the shark, to which it attaches itself, because it finds the means of subsistence in the excrements of that voracious animal. It does not, however, keep company with it so exclusively as not also to follow, very often, other large fish and even ships, to which it fastens itself when it is tired of swimming. We saw several of them alongside, which from time to time went and fixed themselves to the hull.

During the night we fell in with a very numerous shoal of dolphins, which followed our ship: as they went much faster than we did, they swam round the vessel several times at great speed. It was easy to follow them with the eye although the night was very dark; for they left a luminous track behind them: this phosphoric light produced by the agitated sea-water was the more brilliant the greater the darkness and the swifter the fish; it was then that its course could be perfectly made out, even several metres below the surface of the water.

1791-10-30.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 38-39]
We were in the waters frequented by voracious fish, such as bonitos, tunnies and others of the same kind, because they find abundant food in hunting various species of fish, and in particular the flying fish (*exocœtus volitans*, Linn.). The bonitos that followed us let themselves be taken by the bait our fishermen offered them; it was, however, merely a few feathers so arranged as to present to the eyes of the fish the appearance of a flying fish, and to hide the hook from it.

We had had a little calm for some time, but the trade winds soon regained their strength.

1791-11-03.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 39]
They were interrupted again on the 3rd of November by a storm which lasted all night; and from the following day they blew as on the preceding days.

1791-11-06.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 39-40]
It was on the 6th that they left us, in 9° 6' of north latitude, and 21° of west longitude.

We felt a stifling heat, although the thermometer (it was still Réaumur's) showed only 23° above o.

Buffon's black gull (*larus marinus*, Linn.), which had come to rest on one of our yards, escaped one of the crew just as he was on the point of seizing it.

A prodigious number of bonitos stayed with us night and day; it was very surprising that this fish could follow us so long without resting.

The fishing was very lucky on board the Espérance, while the fish seemed to shun our lines.

Buffon's wheatear (*motacilla œnanthe*, Linn.), which, as is well known, is a bird of passage, came on board, wearied with crossing the seas, and let itself be caught. We met with seventeen days of calms in a belt of 5° of latitude; we escaped from it only by means of storms followed by winds that blew in squalls from east-north-east round to south-south-west, passing through south.

The storm bird (*procellaria pelagica*, Linn.) does not herald a storm so surely that its appearance is not sometimes followed by calms lasting several days. We took pleasure in watching these little birds come within a short distance of our ship's stern to seek their food on the surface of the sea.

We saw with regret that the vegetables and fruit bought at Tenerife were not keeping; the heat and damp one meets with in this belt of calms hastened their decay very quickly: one would have supposed that, gathered under a fairly warm and very dry sky, they would have kept better than those of Europe.

1791-11-07.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 40-42]
A small shark (*squalus carcharias*, Linn.), no more than a metre long, fell victim to its voracity. Anything will do for this animal when it is pressed by hunger. As soon as it had been hauled on deck it was quickly cut up, and everyone carried off his piece. The shark is, however, not a good dish; besides the repugnance naturally inspired by its taste for human flesh, it is rather hard to digest: but at sea one does not choose one's food, and fresh provisions are always preferred to salt meat.

I found, fixed in fairly large numbers to the inner walls and to the upper opening of its stomach, worms of the genus *doris* of Linné, two centimetres in length: although the shark was dead, they did not easily let go their hold; now and then one could see the two tentacles put forth which form one of the distinguishing characters of this genus.

The shark's mouth, placed beneath an elongated snout, obliges it to turn almost on its back to seize the objects it sees above it: its whitish belly, which then becomes visible even at a great depth, owing to the clearness of the sea water, tells the fisherman the moment when he must jerk the hook to strike this voracious animal.

Nature has taken good care that it should not let its prey escape; for, besides several rows of teeth shaped in the manner best suited to cutting the hardest bodies, the inside of the mouth is lined with rough points which prevent the escape of whatever it has just seized.

Ships engaged in the India trade would not have missed the opportunity of collecting the fins of this animal, which are sought after by the Chinese, because they regard them as a powerful aphrodisiac. The heat was overpowering when there was no breeze; the thermometer, however, showed only 23° above 0, although we were only 9° north of the equator, in 20° 50' of west longitude. It would seem that in these waters the thermometer is a very unfaithful measure of the heat actually felt, for although it stood some degrees below what it often marks in Europe in fine weather, we nonetheless experienced an excessive perspiration which brought out very troublesome heat rashes.

The mercury in the barometer, as is well known, varies little between the tropics: the greatest variation did not exceed 1ˡ ½. It kept close to the height of 28ᵖ 2ˡ, although we had had very great storms, which, formed over the lands of Africa, from which we were at most sixty myriametres distant, were brought to us by north-east and east-north-east winds.

1791-11-12.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 42-43]
We caught the fish known to ichthyologists by the name of *balistes verrucosus*.

We were surrounded by grampuses, followed in their slow progress by sharks drawn by the lure of their excrements.

A heavy swell from the south-east indicated winds from that same quarter blowing far off towards the equator, although north-east winds are more generally observed there in this season, when the sun has been for nearly two months in the tropic of Capricorn.

1791-11-14.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 43-45]
A shark, preceded by a few of the fish known as pilots (*gasterosteus ductor*, Linn.), came and was caught: several remoras, believing themselves safe because they had fastened on to the body of this animal, remained fixed to it for some time after it had been hoisted on board.

As it was very hot and the sea very calm, the wish to bathe prevailing over every other consideration, Piron and Saint-Agnan threw themselves into the water a few hours later, at the risk of becoming the prey of some other shark.

It had been calm almost all day. Towards eight in the evening the sky, laden with thick clouds in the south-east, threatened us with a violent storm. The night was very dark; suddenly a luminous column of great extent issued from beneath these clouds and came to light up the surface of the water: the sparkling sea still left many dark gaps, when all at once it appeared like a sheet of fire unfolding towards us; it was driven by a very strong wind that furrowed the waves; we saw ourselves surrounded by a sea of flame, and we then enjoyed the spectacle of one of the most brilliant phenomena of nature. It did not last long; but for the rest of the night the sea was much more luminous than usual wherever it was agitated, particularly in the ship's wake and towards the crests of the waves.

The force of the squall had obliged us to lower the topsails and even to bear away, for fear of being taken aback.

The heat had been overpowering all day. We were abreast of the mouth of the immense gulf formed by the recess of the coast of Upper Guinea, which runs nearly three hundred myriametres to the east.

The sea is much more phosphorescent near coasts within the tropics than anywhere else, because nature has there scattered more profusely the animalcules on which its phosphorescence depends, as I have had occasion to observe in waters very far apart from one another: I shall shortly give some details of this phenomenon.

As we were to leeward of this gulf, the currents had brought us from it the luminous bodies which abound there; but a particular circumstance was needed to produce so bright a light. The clouds from which the wind that had just stirred the waves had issued had spread through the atmosphere a superabundance of electricity, which helped to give the sea the brilliance with which we had seen it shine. It was by the wide divergence of the two little balls of my electrometer, exposed to the air, that I was able to judge how electrical our atmosphere had become.

1791-11-15.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 45-47]
A light south-east wind gave us hope of getting clear of these calms, which are met with here over a far greater extent than in any other part of the seas: it is above all on the passage to India that these vexations are greatest; they appear to depend on the neighbourhood of the coast, which one approaches much more closely when going to the Cape of Good Hope than on the route from the Cape to Europe; and so the passages from the Cape to Europe are generally shorter than those from Europe to the Cape.

Several skilful seamen are of the opinion that, when bound for the Cape of Good Hope, there is an advantage in crossing the equator much farther to the west than is usually done.

The calms met with north of the equator are due to the configuration of the coast of Africa, which in the north, a few degrees from the line, juts out nearly three hundred myriametres towards the west, whereas the great distance at which one finds oneself from those lands when south of the equator prevents the prevailing winds of those waters from being in any way modified by them.

I had kept some bottles of sea water, taken the day before while it was phosphorescent, in order to examine the small luminous bodies that cause this phenomenon. This water, poured into a glass, was set in motion in the dark. I at once saw luminous globules which differed in no respect from those usually noticed when the sea is agitated. It seemed to me quite natural to try to separate these bodies, in order to see whether the water would still keep its phosphoric property. I filtered it through grey paper: small, very gelatinous, transparent molluscs of globular form, at most one third of a millimetre in size, remained on the filter, and from that moment this sea water lost all its phosphorescence; I restored it at will by putting the little molluscs back into it. These little animals must not be left long exposed to the air, for they very soon lost all their phosphoric properties.

I have repeated the same experiment many times in waters very far apart from one another, and I have constantly found the same animalcules, which I regard as the most usual cause of the phosphorescence of sea water. Yet they are not alone in having the property of making the sea luminous; several species of crabs, some very large molluscs, etc., sometimes leave the bottom to come and light up the surface: I have often seen phosphoric molluscs of this kind a double decimetre in size; but I have always found at the same time the small luminous bodies of which I have spoken.

We learnt that day that on board the Espérance four of the sheep embarked at Tenerife had been thrown overboard, because some of the symptoms of the disease said to have been brought to us from America were thought to have been observed in these animals. This gave rise to many coarse jokes about the monks of the island, which I believe to be without foundation: I think, on the contrary, that if a more rigorous examination had been made, the crew would not have been deprived of this supply of fresh provisions.

1791-11-21.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 47]
South-south-east winds, which began to blow on the 21st of November in 4° 31' of north latitude and 18° 36' of west longitude, at last brought us out of the calms which in this season are usually felt a few degrees farther south, before one reaches the prevailing winds.

1791-11-24.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 47-49]
The bird known by the name of frigate bird (*pelecanus aquilus*, Linn.) was that day the object of our admiration. We could see two of them which, hovering at a prodigious height, were watching for their prey and waiting for it to appear on the surface of the sea.

These birds no doubt keep at this great height in order to take in an immense space at a glance; but it is very surprising that they can see from so far the small fish on which they most commonly feed; so piercing a sight depends perhaps even more on the arrangement of the humours of the eye than on the great sensitivity of the retina: this is a question well worthy of the attention of natural philosophers. The frigate bird, as is well known, is very greedy for flying fish. As soon as it spies them, it comes down from the heights of the atmosphere and flies at about a hectometre above the surface of the sea; there it keeps within reach of seizing them the moment they dart out of the water. All the frigate bird's movements are directed with admirable skill: it does not plunge head first, like the birds that seek their food under water; with its feet and neck held horizontally in the same plane, it strikes the upper column of air with its wings; then, raising them and holding them fixed against each other above its back, so that they no longer offer resistance to the air, it swoops on its prey and seizes it a short distance from the water.

Each of us, while admiring the astonishing skill of this bird, was wishing well to the flying fish; but it seldom escapes. As the fish does not rise far above the sea, the frigate bird would be in danger of plunging into it, did it not know how to check its fall by lowering its wings, so as to rise again at once and pursue other prey.

Despite the faculty nature has given flying fish of living in the water and leaving it at will, they find it hard to avoid their many enemies: if they escape the voracity of the bonitos, tunnies and dolphins by rising above the water, the frigate bird awaits them in the air; during this confusion some of them came and threw themselves on board the ship.

1791-11-25.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 49]
In the stomachs of several bonitos I found a great number of worms which must be placed among those of the genus *fasciola* of Linné, although their lower extremity, which is almost cylindrical, has a very marked swelling. They measure two centimetres; they end in a tube half their length.

1791-11-28.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 49-50]
The south-east and south winds blew so stubbornly that we were not able to cross the equator until the 28th, towards eleven at night, in 26° of west longitude, whereas it had been intended to cross it 8° to 10° farther east.

It is not usual at this time of year to meet in these parts with winds holding so much from the south and south-east; for, the sun being already far advanced into the tropic of Capricorn, the prevailing winds usually draw nearer to the east. The six to eight minutes by which we had been set to the north each day while we were held up by the calms, and the swell coming from the south and south-east, showed us the unexpected constancy of these winds.

The thermometer, observed at noon, had for eight days shown no more than 22°, and often 21°, although we were very near the equator: one is surprised to see that, at so short a distance from the line, this instrument did not indicate a greater heat; but, besides the general causes, such as the permeability of sea water to the rays of the sun, the low density of water and its evaporation, which prevent the atmosphere from taking up as much heat as it does on land in the same latitude, we had had for some days a light wind which had done not a little to cool the air.

Seamen are in the habit of baptizing after their own fashion those who cross the line for the first time: this baptism is given by drenching them with several buckets of sea water; it is sometimes carried out in a way that amuses those who are sure of not being drenched. One of the sailors, who is called Old Father Line, comes down from the maintop with a beard of oakum and presides over this sport of seafaring men.

The commander, fearing that we might not all take equally kindly to this farce, forbade anyone to be baptized.

1791-11-29.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 50-51]
On the 29th of November, when we were half a degree of latitude to the south, the sea water gave me 3° ⅘ on Beaumé's areometer for salts.

The currents were setting us towards the west. Winds, as is well known, are in a vast sea the principal cause of the differing directions of the waters.

We had every reason to fear a long passage; the Espérance, moreover, sailed much less close to the wind than we did. We feared that want of water might oblige us to put in on the coast of Brazil: this circumstance would have been all the more unfortunate since it would have entirely upset the plan of our campaign, for we had to follow the seasons in order to survey part of the lands we were to visit.

1791-12-17.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 51]
It was on the 17th of December that we passed under the tropic of Capricorn, in 28° of west longitude.

On board the Espérance they often took more than a hundred bonitos a day, whereas our most skilful fishermen together never took more than ten in a day, and even that very seldom happened. Yet it was no matter of indifference to the health of the crews whether they lived on fresh provisions or on salt meat.

1791-12-18.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 51-52]
When we were, on the 18th of December, in 25° 20' of south latitude and 28° 42' of west longitude, the thermometer observed at noon showed only 19° above 0, and 17° ½ before sunrise, although the sun was not far from our zenith. The cold had been great enough during the night to oblige the crew to put on their woollen clothes.

We had counted on westerly winds as we approached the coast of Brazil; on the contrary, they had come from the east; but, the wind having freed, we had been able to keep a fairly full course for fifteen days, as far as 28° of south latitude and 24° of west longitude.

It was to be presumed that in this latitude we should find variable winds that would favour our course towards the Cape of Good Hope; but they varied only to thwart us the more.

1791-12-26.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 52]
We still had south-east winds on the 26th of December, although we had passed 29° ½ of south latitude. The sun, which for several months had been bringing its greatest heat to this hemisphere, had pushed back the edge of the prevailing winds.

The length of our passage made us reduce the allowance to one bottle of water a day.

1791-12-27.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 52-57]
As soon as the winds had shifted to the north-east and north, the currents that had previously been setting to the west became scarcely perceptible.

Although still very far from the Cape of Good Hope, we were already sighting the albatross *(diomedea exulans)*, which is found there in great numbers.

A fact worth noting is that the variation of the compass is much greater south of the equator than north of it; for from the 14° of north latitude to the equator, in the space lying between 23° and 26° of west longitude, the difference was only 3°, or from 14° to 11°, whereas in the same space of latitude towards the south, and 4° of west longitude, from 26° to 30°, the variation of the magnetic needle went from 11° to 3° towards the west, which makes 8° of variation south of the equator; whereas in the north the magnetic needle had varied by only 3° over an almost equally large space.

Might not the proximity of the coasts of Brazil be one of the principal causes of this difference?

The least variation observed was 1° 50', in 25° of south latitude and 29° of west longitude. There is no doubt that in these waters the change of longitude has far more influence on the variation of the magnetic needle than differences of latitude. The variation increased noticeably as we advanced towards the east.

One of the officers, while taking distances of the moon from the sun in a somewhat awkward position with a brass sextant by Dollon, whose radius was two double decimetres, noticed a source of error which one would hardly have suspected. The arms of this instrument, though already very heavy, were still too weak not to bend, and thus to disturb the parallelism of the mirrors, when it was pressed with some force against the chest. The same effect did not occur with wooden sextants, because their much stronger arms do not yield to the force that acts upon those of brass. This source of error is one more reason for giving an exclusive preference to the reflecting circle of Citizen Borda. The ease with which, by means of crossed observations, one can eliminate any error that might arise from the graduation gives it a very marked superiority over all the others, when one wishes to obtain the longitude by observing the distances of the moon from the sun or from some other heavenly body.

I am sorry that this valuable instrument, though extremely easy to use, is still so little known. Each of our officers had one, which in the course of the campaign became a reliable instrument in the hands of all.

An observer of some practice can obtain the longitude to within two or three myriametres. We have reason to hope that, as the lunar tables are brought to greater perfection, the calculation of longitudes from these observations will become still far more exact.

The plants I had collected at Tenerife, though very dry at the time of my departure, had become covered, while we were within the tropics, with a very thick mould attached to the underside of the leaves, where, as is well known, the absorbent pores are found in very great numbers, and my collections had been badly damaged.

The water held in solution by the air through the direct heat of the sun is, on the open sea within the tropics, so far in excess of what the air can take up without such heat, that everything not exposed to the sun becomes covered with great dampness; that is why it is very difficult there to protect iron instruments, and even the best-polished steel, from rust.

During the whole time we had spent within the tropics, the mercury in the barometer had not risen above 28ᵖ 4ˡ, and had not fallen below 28ᵖ 1ˡ 1/10.

We knew well that our supply of water would not keep its purity in the stifling heat we were experiencing; but it would have been hard to suppose that, having on board very easy means of purifying the water before issuing to each man his daily allowance, these means would not have been fully employed.

Water kept on board undergoes on long passages the same decomposition as stagnant water, and this decomposition is singularly hastened by the heat of the climate. So great a quantity of inflammable air is then given off that one runs the risk of being asphyxiated on going down into the hold where it is stowed. This accident is, however, very rare, because the opening leading to it lets part of these noxious miasmas escape. It is none the less true that they often give rise to nervous fevers, whose malignity is in proportion to the degree of heat that decomposes the water.

As this gas, whose specific gravity Priestley was the first to make known, is much lighter than atmospheric air, and as it moreover adheres but little to water, it is easy to separate it and to restore to this drink its original purity; to do so it is enough to agitate it for a quarter of an hour.

We had on board a machine that served this purpose perfectly; it was a large tub of a double hectolitre: when it was three quarters full of water, four large iron paddles, arranged crosswise, were made to turn near its middle by means of a crank and a crown wheel; the water then received a strong agitation which, while releasing the inflammable gas with which it was impregnated, at the same time restored to it the pure air of which it had been partly deprived, and, foul as it had been before, in a very short time it differed in no way from the best water.

This very simple process completely settles the long series of questions that some natural philosophers have put to navigators on the means of making fresh water drinkable when it happens to go bad on board ships.

It will hardly be believed that, with so simple a means of purifying the water, we were often served water whose stench differed little from what it had on coming out of the hold; but the surprise will cease when it is known that the officer of the watch charged with supervising this operation usually left it to the care of a sailor, who, very soon weary of turning the crank, almost always found the water sufficiently agitated before it was drinkable: it would have been more fitting to entrust this supervision to the surgeon-in-chief, as several of us pointed out; for it was no matter of indifference to the health of all whether this operation was carried out well or badly. Nevertheless, the officer of the watch continued to be charged with this inspection.

1791-12-29.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 57-58]
On the 29th of December, under a very clear sky, the thermometer stood at 17° 8/10, and the barometer at 28ᵖ 3ˡ 9/10, when towards noon a north by east wind suddenly brought us a very thick haze, which hid the sun from us for a quarter of an hour. It is very remarkable that, instead of causing the mercury in the barometer to fall, this haze made it rise by 1ˡ ½ for the whole time it enveloped us. I dare not hazard any conjecture in an attempt to explain this phenomenon: it will astonish natural philosophers all the more since it would seem that this circumstance ought to have diminished the elasticity of the air instead of increasing it; nothing, moreover, suggested that this haze was caused by the eruption of a volcano.

1792-01-03.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 58]
On the 3rd of January we witnessed a rainbow produced by the rays of the moon: towards 10 o'clock in the evening the moon was surrounded by two concentric circles; they displayed all the colours of the rainbow, each in the opposite order to the other. The larger of these circles took up no more than five degrees of the sky. As this phenomenon, produced by the decomposition of the moon's light, appeared between it and us, the colours of the rainbow must indeed have appeared in the reverse order to those given by the sun, since in the latter case the spectator stands between the rainbow and the luminary; and so the smaller circle, which showed red at its inner edge, was bounded on the outside by violet, whereas violet formed the inner edge of the larger circle, and red its outer edge.

We were then in 32° 42' of south latitude, and 7° of west longitude.

1792-01-07.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 58]
It was on the afternoon of the 7th of January that we passed the meridian of Paris, in 33° of south latitude.

1792-01-08.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 58-59]
Having plunged Beaumé's areometer for salts into the sea water in order to ascertain its specific gravity, I obtained 3° 4/5, which gave the same result as I had already obtained near the equator. It would therefore appear that the saltness of sea water does not differ appreciably, even at great distances, in waters so unequally heated by the rays of the sun.

1792-01-09.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 59]
On the 9th of January the crews of each ship began to be exercised in firing ball: a prize of little value was the reward of those who hit the mark fixed at the end of one of the fore booms. It was noticed with pleasure that most of them aimed fairly well, although they were not at all used to firearms. On such an expedition, in which we might sometimes be obliged to defend ourselves against the savages, it was no matter of indifference that all should know how to use the arms we had on board.

1792-01-10.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 59-61]
The captain of the Espérance had half of a very fine tunny, which he was sending to the general, made fast to a buoy; our manoeuvre did not bring us near enough to reach it: a sailor threw himself into the sea to go and fetch it, although it was known that a shark had been caught that morning on board the Espérance, and the little wind then blowing ought to have increased the fear of meeting another, which might perhaps have carried off one of our best seamen.

Although we had already risen as far as 33° of south latitude, after reaching 5° of east longitude, the bonitos still followed us in very numerous shoals, though it is seldom that so many are met with in so high a latitude. The north winds were probably one of the principal causes that drew these fish away from their usual haunts. I shall remark that if our fishermen were less skilful than those of the Espérance, they were also less favoured. It was from the boatswain that the fishing lines were obtained. Ours showed such parsimony in giving them out, throughout the campaign, that in the end he drove all wish to fish from the sailors' minds. It was for the officer in charge of stores to make him feel the harmful effects of this ill-judged arrangement; but he did nothing of the kind.

The medusa known by the name of *medusa velella* took advantage of the calm to come and float in great numbers on the surface of the sea. This species differed in no respect from the one I had so often met with in the Mediterranean, where it is a dish much sought after by seamen.

It was of the utmost importance that we should have vessels that did not leak; yet we had scarcely left the roadstead of Brest when we had to resort to the pump. As we were making two centimetres of water an hour, we were obliged to pump twice a day. This precaution was all the more indispensable since the water would otherwise have reached our supply of salt, an article of the greatest importance on the voyage we were undertaking. Fortunately, the quantity of water entering the hold did not increase.

The between-decks was so encumbered that several months passed before the source of this leak could be discovered. At last it was found to come from behind a knee. When the ship had been lightened, it was found that a treenail had been forgotten and that the hole in which it should have been placed had been covered only with tar. The water had soon forced its way through this coating; the peg was replaced at once, and the ship leaked no more.

1792-01-16.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 61-63]
The albatrosses of the Cape of Good Hope, which were to be seen in fairly large numbers, told us that we were nearing that southern extremity of Africa. We did in fact sight its land on the 16th of January at about eight in the morning. Table Bay then lay four myriametres from us.

The currents which, during the prevailing winds, had made us lose a good deal of ground, having happily taken an opposite direction when we met with the variable winds, the ground lost to the west was found to be roughly made up towards the east. Our landfall at the Cape of Good Hope confirmed this observation. It is easily understood that, allowing for some irregularities on the part of the variable winds, the tendency of the waters to find their level must cause those lying in the region of these winds to flow back towards the east, in proportion as the prevailing winds carry westward the waters whose course they direct.

The nearness of land had also been announced to us by a change in the colour of the sea water, which it owes to the raised bottom on which it rests.

Seals of the species Buffon named the little seal (phoca *pusilla*, Linn.) came within a short distance of our ship to seek their food among the great masses of the seaweed called *fucus pyriformis*, Linn., which could be seen floating on the surface of the sea: these animals often fled by leaping above the water; it was then that their two hind feet, joined together in the form of fins, served them to take a purchase on the water, whose surface was to them what a vast plain is to a nimble quadruped.

We fell a little to leeward of the entrance of Table Bay, which gave us little hope of reaching the anchorage that day.

One could have wished for a finer day on which to make the land; for much rain fell, and the land was often hidden from us by a thick haze.

At about seven in the evening we were a myriametre and a half from the mountain of Hout Bay, which bore west 3° 45' north.

The point of the Cape was seen to the north by west.

Lion's Head west 3° north.

Near this point of bearing the lead gave a coral bottom at a depth of two thirds of a double hectometre. The sea was extraordinarily phosphorescent throughout the night, which we spent a short distance from the coast.
