A great quantity of luminous points were to be seen wherever the water was agitated: this phosphorescence differs from that ordinarily observed at sea only in its greater intensity, owing to a greater number of phosphoric globules. These little bodies are, as I have already said, far more numerous near coasts than in the open sea in the same latitude. I examined them again after filtering the water that contained them; they differed in no respect from those I had already observed: they were still the same small, globular, transparent molluscs, about one third of a millimetre in size.

1792-01-17.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 63-75]
A light south-west wind allowed us, the next day in the afternoon, to shape our course for the entrance of Table Bay. As soon as it had freshened a little, we steered under all sail south-east by east for the pointe des Pendus, which we ranged very close, the lead giving us fairly regularly a decametre, give or take a few double decimetres.

It was half past five when we dropped anchor in a depth of eight metres, on a bottom of grey muddy sand, at a distance of one kilometre from the shore.

The steeple of the town bore west 38° south. The flagstaff on the Lion's Rump west 3° north.

The flag of the northernmost fort west 43° north.

Robben Island north 1° west.

We had no one sick on board, although the length of our passage had reduced us to a very small quantity of water a day; but efforts had been made to make up for this privation by a liberal use of various kinds of antiscorbutics. A kind of punch, very wholesome and most agreeable, made of brandy, vinegar, sugar and water, had been issued every day to the crews towards the end of this passage. Fumigations had been carried out twice a day. The greatest care had been taken to make the sailors change their clothes whenever they were wet; and it was gratifying to see that so many precautions had not been taken in vain.

## CHAPTER III.

*Stay at the Cape of Good Hope. Depositions of two French captains, from which it appears that, while at Batavia, they had learnt from Commodore Hunter that he had seen natives dressed in the uniforms of the French navy at the Admiralty Islands. Captain Bligh, dispatched from England to fetch the bread-fruit tree from the Society Islands. Violence of the south-east winds. Local cause that increases their fury. Slave ship. Various excursions into the mountains near the town. Impudence of the fiscal. Journey to Franschhoek.*

Two health officers from the town of the Cape came on board to make sure that we were not bringing any contagious diseases: it is above all the smallpox that is dreaded there; for this disease, which is not endemic there, causes the greatest ravages there, as throughout India, when it is brought in from outside.

The captain of a merchant ship who had arrived from Bordeaux a few days before us came at once to tell us that the commander of the naval forces at the Isle of France [Mauritius], having received information on the fate of la Pérouse, had dispatched a frigate to the Cape to bring the news to the commander of the expedition sent in search of that unfortunate navigator. The frigate had left some days before to return to the Isle of France.

General Dentrecasteaux at once sent an officer to the governor of the Cape to settle the salute. This officer received from the French chargé d'affaires the dispatches that Citizen Saint-Felix, commander of our naval forces in the Indian seas, had sent to General Dentrecasteaux by the frigate the Attalante, Captain Bolle, which had sailed almost immediately to return to the Isle of France.

Here is the letter addressed to the general, with the depositions of two captains of merchant ships who had been at Batavia during the stay made there by Commodore Hunter, on his return from Botany Bay in a Dutch vessel, after being shipwrecked on Norfolk Island. *Letter from Citizen Saint-Felix, commanding the station of the Indian seas, to General Dentrecasteaux.*

I learn from private letters that you do not intend to call at the Isle of France until your return from the important expedition you are about to undertake. Deprived of the hope with which I had flattered myself of having the honour of seeing you, I hasten to send you at the Cape of Good Hope two reports relating to the object of your mission, which have just been made to me by the captains of two French vessels arriving from Batavia. You will see from them by what circumstance a Dutch vessel, having on board Commodore Hunter, commander of the English frigate the *Syrius*, together with his crew, saw near the Admiralty Islands in the South Sea men clothed in European cloth, and in particular in coats which he judged to be French uniforms. You will see also that the commodore had no doubt that these were the remains of the wreck of M. de la Pérouse, whom he had seen a great deal of at Botany Bay.

I judged that you would be interested to know of these reports, and I found them important enough to decide me to send them to you directly by a frigate which I am sending to the Cape solely for this purpose. The major de vaisseau, Bolle, who commands her, will, if he does not find you there, leave my dispatch with the chargé d'affaires of the nation, so that it may be handed to you on your arrival. Although no official knowledge of your expedition authorizes me to employ a frigate in this way, I am sure of the approval of H. M. for the course I have taken in this matter, as much from consideration of the public interest as from the wish of my heart. It was reserved for you to acquire a claim to the gratitude of the whole nation by accepting the command of an expedition that does equal honour to the sovereign who orders it and to the chief who carries it out. Whatever route you take, you will be followed on it by my wishes for your success and by the inviolable and perfect attachment with which I am, etc.

*Signed* Saint-Felix.

Isle of France, 9 November 1791.

*Report made to the chef de division of the naval forces, Saint-Felix, commanding the station of the Indian seas, by Captain Préaudet, commanding the ship the Jason, arriving from Batavia.*

The English frigate the *Syrius*, commanded by Commodore Hunter, dispatched to New Holland, was lost on Norfolk Island in the South Sea towards the end of 1790. The crew went over to the sloop that accompanied her on her mission, and proceeded to Botany Bay, where Commodore Phillip chartered a small Dutch ship to carry the shipwrecked crew, with their commander, Commodore Hunter, to England.

Having left Botany Bay in this vessel, and wishing to touch at Batavia, Commodore Hunter was thwarted by the winds and currents and carried eastward as far as 167° of longitude, meridian of Greenwich. Intending to pass through St George's Strait, he sighted the Admiralty Islands, lying in 147° of longitude from the meridian of Greenwich, and 3° 25' of south latitude. Near the easternmost of them he saw several boats filled with men clothed in European stuffs and pieces of European cloth; the uniform of the marine troops of France could even be made out among them. These people were making signs with white flags for him to approach. Commodore Hunter greatly wished to do so; but it was impossible for him to carry it out, because of the contrary currents and winds and the danger of the numerous reefs.

Commodore Hunter had seen a great deal of la Pérouse at Botany Bay, and had become particularly intimate with him. He had learnt from him that his plan, on leaving Botany Bay, was to pass through St George's Strait to go north. He has no doubt that it was on these islands that the Astrolabe and the Boussole were lost, through the calms and violent currents that prevail in that region. He told me that he himself had been carried six hundred miles to the east in ten days by their effect: which is proved by repeated observations of longitude, by the timekeepers and by the sight of land. In a word, Commodore Hunter, who was at Batavia, and whom I saw there on the voyage I have just made, appeared to me to be firmly convinced that the European clothing he saw in the boats that came from the Admiralty Islands is the remains of the wreck of the vessels under the command of la Pérouse.

Commodore Hunter is now on his way to England, from where France will probably receive from him more detailed particulars on this subject.

From what this English commander experienced in approaching the Admiralty Islands, he believes that a vessel wishing to go there ought to take the precaution of getting into the latitude very early, so as to avoid being carried off by the currents, which set to the east with prodigious speed.

Done at the Isle of France, 6 November 1791.

*Signed* Préaudet, captain of the ship the Jason. *Report by Pierre Magon Lépinay, captain of the ship the Marie-Hélène, arriving from Batavia, to the chef de division of the naval forces, Saint Felix, commanding the station of the Indian seas.*

The commander and officers of the English frigate the *Syrius*, after the wreck of that frigate on Norfolk Island, were carried to Botany Bay, from where they sailed in a small Dutch vessel which brought them to Batavia at the end of September of this year, after a passage of about six months.

One or two days after rounding St George's Channel, they sighted very early in the morning the two Admiralty Islands, to which they found themselves very close; they at once sounded without finding bottom.

They saw two canoes put off from these islands, carrying about twelve men, who would not come alongside the vessel, but who came very close to it. The weather was then very light. The vessel had against her a fairly strong current, which was carrying her away from the island; besides, the Dutch captain did not care to approach it. It was noticed that two of the men in these canoes had sword belts like those worn by officers in Europe; they made signs as if they wished to be shaved: several of them had on their clothes pieces of red and blue cloth, which proved that they had had dealings with Europeans. As Captain Hunter, commander of the *Syrius*, had learnt from la Pérouse himself before leaving Botany Bay that his plan was to pass through St George's Channel, the officers of that frigate are all convinced that he must have come unexpectedly upon these islands and been lost on them.

I, the undersigned, certify this account to be in accordance with what I gathered from various conversations with the officers of the frigate the Syrius, who arrived at Batavia after the wreck of that frigate in a small Dutch vessel with which I was there in the month of October.

*Signed* Magon Lépinay.

Isle of France, 31 October 1791.

As Commodore Hunter, returning from Batavia with his officers on his way to England, was at the Cape of Good Hope at the moment we arrived there, we might have expected to obtain there every possible particular concerning what he had seen at the Admiralty Islands. We were rather surprised that the commodore had sailed from the roadstead of the Cape two hours after we had let go our anchor there. He very probably knew the object of our mission, for we were expected at the Cape, and the general's flag left no doubt that these were the ships destined for the search for la Pérouse. It seemed very strange to us that he had not sought to give us himself the information which Captains Préaudet and Magon Lépinay had gathered from him and his officers at Batavia. We had reason to be much more surprised that Commodore Hunter not only had let no news transpire at the Cape that might lead one to believe he had met with savages dressed in the uniforms of the French navy, but had told several members of the government, and even his friend Mr Gordon, that he knew nothing of the facts announced on the arrival of the Attalante. Nothing indicated that the particulars left at the Cape by the major de vaisseau Bolle came from Commodore Hunter himself.

Captain Bligh, commanding the English sloop the Providence, bound to fetch the bread-fruit tree from the Society Islands, had come to anchor in Table Bay a short time after the departure of the Attalante. It appears that Bligh learnt nothing from Hunter relating to the depositions of the two French captains; but, on the strength of information passed on by persons who had seen the commander of the Attalante, he assured Colonel Gordon that on his return from the Society Islands he would make a search in the waters where la Pérouse was said to have been lost, in order to try to save some remnants of his ill-fated expedition.

It was the second time that Bligh was going to fetch the bread-fruit tree from the Society Islands; for on the first voyage he had made to procure this precious tree for the English colonies of the West Indies, this captain was put out of his ship following a mutiny that had broken out on board, as he made known in the account he published on his return to England.

We learnt that the Pandora, an English frigate commanded by Captain Edward, had since been to the Society Islands, where she had seized fourteen of the mutineers. She had lost four of them on running aground on the reefs of Norfolk Island. Christian, master of the ship taken from Bligh and the author of the mutiny, had gone to take refuge with nine sailors on another island, whither he had taken several natives with him. An officer of the Pandora who had arrived at the Cape asserted that Bligh had been very much in the wrong towards Christian, and that an abuse of authority on the part of this captain had been the cause of his misfortunes. Christian, despite his rank of master, had been ill-treated by Bligh's orders like the lowest of the sailors. If this is true, Bligh was not sincere in asserting that he had always shown him the greatest consideration.

There were in the roadstead of the Cape eighteen ships, of which twelve were Dutch, two French, two American and two English.

1792-01-18.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 75]
As soon as the sun was up we saluted the fortress with thirteen guns; it returned our salute with the same number.

The commander of the expedition went ashore at about nine o'clock; on this occasion the fortress fired fifteen guns, which we returned gun for gun. The governor had sent several carriages, with a great number of musicians, to await General Dentrecasteaux at the landing-place. It was to the sound of loud music that he proceeded to the governor's residence, accompanied by a few officers. He was received there by the assembled council, which returned his visit almost immediately at the house of the French chargé d'affaires, where he had taken up his lodging.

Most of the officers took lodgings ashore. It is well known that the Dutch at the Cape of Good Hope take pleasure in lodging strangers in their homes. The most usual price is one piastre a day. I went, with some of my fellow travellers, to stay with M. de Lettre.

1792-01-19.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 75-77]
Table Mountain was laden with thick clouds which covered its summit; at this season that is a sure presage of violent south-east winds, which commonly blow for two or three days. The breeze was indeed so strong until the evening of the next day that during all that time no longboat could communicate with the shore.

Although the clouds seemed fixed upon the top of the mountain, even when the wind was blowing with the greatest force, they were ceaselessly renewed; but the impulse they received on leaving the summit made them more easily dissolved, and they vanished into the air. Large portions of these clouds were often seen to break away and disappear at once.

The south-east wind soon came rushing down from the top of this mountain towards the town of the Cape, with such violence that the streets lying in that direction could be passed along only with difficulty; it was almost impossible to walk against the wind, for it drove before it, at the height of a man, small pebbles a centimetre and more in thickness, with so much force that one was obliged to seek shelter in the houses.

This furious wind, of which many travellers have spoken, seems to me to depend on the position of the land which, rising high along the shore from the town of the Cape to the western point of the entrance of False Bay, sets a barrier against the south-east winds. When these winds come to pour into False Bay, they cannot keep on in the same direction except by passing over this obstacle placed at the southern extremity of Africa. The lower air, in rising to the summit of these mountains, is compressed by the column above, which opposes its expansion: it must therefore, as soon as it has passed over these heights, react in proportion to the freedom it has to spread out. It is then that its violence is such that it sometimes makes the ships anchored in the roadstead drag their anchors and forces them to make for the open sea.

It is where these high mountains fall away that this wind has all its force; thus the wind felt at a short distance inland is much less violent, as I had occasion to observe in some excursions I made at different distances from the town.

The clouds which then cover the summit of the mountains are naturally produced by this great mass of air, which, having taken up much water over the wide sea it has just stirred up, rises to pass over the summit, where the difference of temperature makes the water *that it can* no longer hold in solution appear in the form of clouds.

The Espérance's biscayenne, which the force of the wind had torn loose from the stern of that ship during the night, was lost. To replace it, a whaleboat, a kind of light craft intended for whale-fishing, was bought from an American ship.

1792-01-20.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 77-79]
Although the south-east wind continued to blow with violence, I went out into the country around the town, where I found in great abundance the species of *chironia* designated by the names *trinervia* and *linoides*. The *gorteria ciliaris* also grew at the foot of these mountains. The pretty shrub known by the name of *brunia paleacea* covers the first hills by which one begins the ascent.

It will readily be believed that with such a wind the insects had entirely disappeared.

I visited the Company's garden, of which several travellers have spoken with enthusiasm. It is, however, no more than a large enclosure, where one notices walks of rather fine oaks. Some plots are bordered with myrtles, in the middle of which vegetables are grown, and very few foreign flowers. European fruit trees have also been planted there. The banana tree is to be seen there, its leaves unable to withstand the violence of the wind, which had cut them all into strips.

The bird called the secretary, *falco serpentarius*, Linn., was kept quite tame in a house belonging to the governor.

The menagerie, situated at the end of this garden, now held only a small number of rare animals: the ostrich, the zebra, the porcupine, the jackal, and a few birds, among which one noticed Buffon's bare-headed curlew, *tantalus calvus*, Linn.

The wind, which lost much of its force in the evening, told us that fine weather was returning.

There was in the roadstead a slave ship, lately arrived from Mozambique; four hundred Blacks who made up her cargo were at that time ashore. It was a very sad sight to see these wretches, most of them scorbutic after a very short passage, crowded into three small rooms, from which they were shortly to be taken back on board, to go and support with their sweat the luxury of some rich American. This trade had been carried on in a place where dogs are much sought after. The people who traffic in the lives of these men are not afraid to admit that it very often happens that they obtain two or three Blacks for a fine dog.

1792-01-22.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 79]
I spent the day of the 22nd visiting Lion Mountain. This mountain, which takes its name from the shape it presents at a distance of a few myriametres out at sea, offers a soil very little favourable to vegetation. Almost everywhere upon it, even down to the seashore, one finds a hard, greyish steatite, so barren that this excursion yielded me only a very small number of plants.

1792-01-23.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 79-82]
The next day I visited Devil's Mountain. The furious south-east winds, whose force is much greater at the foot of this mountain than anywhere else, have earned it this name. The charming valley which separates it from Lion Mountain is adorned with the fine species of *protea* with silvery leaves, *protea argentea*, Linn., whose bushy crowns withstand the winds that at times rush down with violence from the tops of these mountains: the leaves of these trees are covered with a down that is the thicker the more they are exposed to the motion of the air. The same thing is to be observed in almost all plants beaten by the winds, which leads one to suppose that this down serves to protect them from the damage the winds might cause them.

Here was no longer the barrenness of Lion Mountain; the vegetable productions presented themselves in crowds. The Cape tulip, *haemanthus coccineus*, Linn., carpeted the less steep slopes: a great number of species of heath sprang from the clefts of the precipitous rocks, and the pretty composite known by the name of *stæbe gnaphaloides* grew with several other plants towards their base.

Being obliged to spend a good deal of time preparing the plants I had gathered the day before, I was not able to undertake a long walk: I confined myself to going over the country around the town.

The false aloe, known by the name of *agave vivipara*, was then in full flower. I admired for some time the lightness with which the coal titmouse, *parus ater*, Linn., came to gather the sugary liquor distilled by the glands situated at the bottom of the corollas. I killed a few of these charming birds, with regret, in order to preserve their skins.

Three of us from the same expedition were following a little path a short distance from the country house of the fiscal, named Déness. This man, accustomed to command like a despot, tried to prevent us from crossing some uncultivated fields, which he took great care to tell us were his property: we were strangely surprised at such a prohibition. The fiscal could not persuade himself that we would have the temerity to go on. However, after pointing out to him that we could do no damage in fields that were uncultivated and covered with stones, we continued on our way. This petty vizier, seeing how little regard we paid to his orders, and being unable to answer our remarks, flew into a great rage and told us in his bad jargon that he had warned us and that no other explanation was needed.

Two Blacks from the town were with us: these unfortunate men trembled at the voice of the fiscal, and followed us only with great difficulty; they told us, shuddering, that it was M. Déness who had the beatings with the stick administered which are dealt out in the town of the Cape by order of the police.

It is worth noting that this officer in charge of the revenue has the right of inspection over all the Company's employees: his functions, moreover, are independent; it is a monstrous thing to see such a title granted to the head of the police, who can with impunity give himself up to the extortions for which his post affords him every facility; for he fixes the fines and receives the proceeds of them, and accordingly the pecuniary penalty is the only one he inflicts on those who can pay; the stick is for the others.

I spent this day visiting Table Mountain, so named on account of the horizontal plane its summit presents when seen from afar.

1792-01-25.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 82-85]
I crossed several times a stream which comes down from this mountain. The large worn stones met with along its banks prove that its waters pour down in torrents in the rainy season.

I had already reached about the middle of the mountain when I found the *thesium strictum*. As soon as I had climbed a little higher, I came upon the magnificent umbelliferous species known to botanists by the name of *hermas depauperata*; next came the pretty fern called *acrostichum pectinatum*; the *bubon galbanum*, the *restio simplex*, etc.

I had just climbed up slopes composed of a very hard sandstone, above which are found blocks of quartz of a fine white; these masses serve as a base for a micaceous schist laid down in very close layers.

After climbing to more than two-thirds of a kilometre of perpendicular height, I at last reached a cleft which, seen from the town, had not seemed likely to offer a passage to the summit of this mountain; but the distance had misled me, for there is a path there whose access is not difficult for persons accustomed to travelling over mountains; it is, moreover, the route most frequented for reaching this summit, which can be reached only with difficulty by any other way. Although we were at nearly a kilometre of perpendicular elevation, the heat of the atmosphere nonetheless made the thermometer placed in the shade rise to 20°.

Firewood is very scarce at the Cape of Good Hope: if the mildness of the climate spares the inhabitants from having recourse to artificial heat to protect themselves against the inclemency of the weather, they at least need fire to prepare their food: slaves are employed to go and fetch, even far beyond Table Mountain, the little wood they require. We met several Negroes carrying to the town loads of branches of various shrubs, among which I noticed the *cunonia capensis* and several fine species of *protea*. I felt great pleasure at seeing these pretty plants; but it was soon disturbed when I considered that they had been gathered only to be burnt: I took a few specimens of them, and these Blacks, whose burden I had not much lightened, went on down towards the town of the Cape. We were distressed to see these unfortunate men walking on without stopping, although the steep slope of the mountain seemed as if it must oblige them to do so.

The mountains near the town serve as a retreat for fugitive slaves whom barbarous treatment has forced to take refuge there: it is under cover of night that, driven by hunger, they approach the dwellings to seek there by stealth, at the peril of their lives, some scanty means of subsistence. One may judge of all the horror inspired in them by the treatment they are made to undergo in the town from the miserable existence they prefer to it. It would not be without danger to venture alone and unarmed towards the hollows in the rocks where these wretches, driven by despair, hide from the light of day in order to escape slavery.

A few drops of water which ooze out on these heights from between the layers of a micaceous schist offer the traveller the means of quenching his thirst.

The high sides of the cleft by which we were climbing were carpeted with several fine liliaceous plants, among which the *antholiza œthiopica* stood out for the brilliance of its fine scarlet flowers.

Having reached the top of Table Mountain, we had already begun to break into our provisions when we saw some persons from the Espérance coming towards us, who had ventured up these heights without providing themselves with food; we took pleasure in sharing our frugal meal with them.

The clouds which had hung over the summit of Table Mountain on the preceding days had yielded enough rain to form small pools in hollows of the rock, among which I found a great number of pretty plants. Almost the whole extent of False Bay could be seen from the top of this mountain, all of whose outlines I carefully explored. I came down again with an abundant harvest of plants by the same path we had followed on the way up. It was already night when we reached the town.

1792-01-26.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 85]
As soon as I had made all the preparations necessary for preserving the objects gathered the day before, I set off towards the east.

Beyond the head of the bay lies a vast plain of sand, in the midst of which one is astonished to see a prodigious quantity of plants; those most frequently met with there are various species of *diosma*, *polygala* and *borbonia*; they could not withstand so great a dryness if their roots did not strike deep into the earth to seek the moisture so necessary to sustain their life.

I sometimes had to cross small streams whose waters, supplied by the neighbouring mountains, are partly lost in the sands before reaching the sea. It is in these damp places that the pretty liliaceous plant known by the name of *gethyllis spiralis* grows.

Holes dug in the sand serve as lairs for the snakes, which are often found asleep at their edges, and which take refuge in them as soon as one approaches.

1792-01-27.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 85-86]
I went back to visit Table Mountain for the second time. I strayed a little from the route usually followed, and enriched my collection with many plants I had not yet found. It would take a long time to exhaust all the vegetable riches of a land that produces so great a variety of them.

A thick mist almost immediately covered the summit where I was and obliged me to come down. Wrapped in so dense a fog, I should have found it impossible to keep my way had I not been very close to the path that led to the foot of the mountain. Although the wind was not strong on Table Mountain, the clouds nonetheless rushed down as soon as they had passed over it, and dissolved just as they do with the furious south-east winds.

1792-01-28.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 86]
I went over the country around the town, and further increased my collection of plants.

Until then I had found only a small number of insects, for they do not thrive in places so often beaten by the winds.

1792-01-29.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 86-88]
On the 29th I made an excursion behind Table Mountain, following the path that separates it from Lion Mountain.

The *cyanella capensis* grew quite close to the seashore.

As soon as we had reached the heights, I had the pleasure of seeing the slope of the rocks carpeted with various species of heath, among which the *erica halicacaba* stood out for the oval form and the beauty of its flowers. The *disa grandiflora*, one of the most beautiful plants of the orchis family, grew on the banks of the little streams that run over these high places.

This walk was all the more agreeable to me since I was with Mr. Masson, whose travels have added much to the knowledge of botanists.

The following days were spent in making fresh searches in the places I had already been over; the vegetation there is so varied that I always found new riches.

An English frigate, coming from Tellicherry, lay at anchor for five days in the roadstead of the Cape; she was on her way to England to give an account of an engagement that had taken place between the French frigate the Résolue, carrying twelve-pounders, Captain Calaman, and the English frigate the Phœnix, carrying eighteen-pounders. The captain of the English frigate had tried to search some French vessels under the protection of our frigate.

The English, according to their custom, made a point of letting unfavourable rumours spread concerning Captain Calaman, who, according to the particulars we had from the Isle of France [Mauritius], had conducted himself in this affair with as much firmness as greatness of soul. The commander of the frigate Phœnix ought to have put an end to these rumours by making the facts known; but it seems he had an interest in disguising them; for it is unheard of that, under the flag of a government frigate, the English should have taken the liberty of searching vessels under her escort.

The English ship the Crown, which arrived a day after the frigate, behaved in the same manner.

I shall observe that, our commander having sent an officer on board these two vessels to pay the customary civilities, the two captains had the rudeness to take no notice whatever of this visit.

I had already gathered most of the vegetable productions that the country around the Cape offered in this season. I could no longer hope for abundant harvests except by going farther afield. Some mountains called by the Dutch Fransche-Hoek, lying towards the east at a much greater distance from the town than their appearance seems to indicate, had for some days inspired in me the desire to visit them: their aspect led me to hope for very varied productions there.

1792-02-09.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 88-91]
The gardener of our expedition was of the party.

A Hottentot led by the bridle a horse laden with our baggage. We had as interpreter a young Black who knew barely a few words of French.

A passport with which we had been obliged to provide ourselves was handed to me by Mr. Berg, one of the most amiable and best-informed men in the colony.

Mr. Gordon, colonel of the troops at the Cape, had given me letters of recommendation to several colonists.

Colonel Gordon is that distinguished traveller who gave Buffon the first accurate notions of the giraffe, an animal little known until then. This officer, spurred on by the desire of making discoveries in natural history, advanced in his travels into the interior of Africa as far as 21° of south latitude. He told me several times that at that distance, more than 12° north of the Cape, he made barometrical observations which proved to him that the ground stood at more than two kilometres of perpendicular elevation above the level of the sea, without his having perceived on his way any sensible rise of the land; he believed himself, on the contrary, to be on a plain of very little elevation. These observations, which he repeated at distances of several days' journey, seem to indicate that the ground rises by an imperceptible slope to a height found elsewhere only on great mountains.

I leave it to natural philosophers to decide whether in this case the fall of the mercury in the barometer might not be due to some cause other than the one that produces a similar effect when it is carried to high places.

We met many wagons drawn by three or four pairs of oxen; they were going back empty, each driven by a Hottentot who, standing towards the middle of the vehicle with a long whip in his hand, guided his team with marvellous skill. Although the leading oxen were very far from him, he nonetheless struck the ox he wished to urge on at the very spot he aimed at.

Our Hottentot jogged along smoking his pipe, and from time to time filled his stomach with the Hottentot fig, *mesembrianthemum edule*, which grows by the roadside in the midst of the sand, without giving a thought to the load of our horse, which he had following behind him; accordingly our belongings fell off several times, and they would have been left in the middle of the road if we had not warned the smoker, who kept steadily on his way; we had to frighten him with threats to rouse him from his apathy and make him more attentive.

Various species of *geranium*, *poligala*, *lobelia*, etc., covered the sandy plain we were crossing.

Having reached somewhat higher ground, we began to see a few gazelles, but they started off at too great a distance for us to be able to shoot them.

It had been night for two hours when we arrived at Bottelary, at the house of Mr. Bosman. The letter of recommendation Mr. Gordon had given me for this worthy farmer procured us a most friendly reception. It was supper-time; he was at table in the midst of his numerous family. He at once invited us to take our places beside him, and had a very pleasant wine of the Bottelary growth served to us, which some merchants in the town sell very dear as Constantia wine, to which it is nevertheless much inferior; indeed Mr. Bosman pointed out to us that it could be obtained at a price twelve times lower than the former.

Mr. Bosman, isolated in the midst of the sands on a little corner of land fit for cultivation, must have been very eager for news; but the way in which we made ourselves understood was truly laborious, for our black interpreter was even less skilful than we had thought until then. After spending a long time in saying very little, we went to take the rest of which we stood in the greatest need. There was not one of us who did not envy the peaceful life led by this respectable colonist in the midst of a family that combines with great simplicity of manners the greatest amiability.

1792-02-10.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 91-93]
As soon as day began to break we went over the country around this charming dwelling. Mr. Bosman's garden offered to our view most of the vegetables and fruits of Europe; fine plantations of almond trees rose in front of the house, and it was surrounded by vineyards, which are the chief wealth of this farmer.

As soon as the sun appeared above the horizon, Mr. Bosman's young daughters, seeing us busy collecting insects, wished to help enrich our collection. They ran over the garden with incredible lightness, and in a short time made us a very good selection among the species whose colours are the most brilliant.

As we were soon to set sail from the roadstead of the Cape, we had barely time left to go and visit the mountains of Franche-Hoek. It was with keen regret that we left these amiable hosts so quickly to continue on our way.

We arrived early at Stellenbosch, where we put up at the house of Mr. Hoffman.

The manner in which we were received at Stellenbosch formed a striking contrast with the frank and cordial welcome we had been given at Bottelary. We were here in a very pretty village, but one could not count too much on that open amenity which so well characterises the farmers of the Cape. I had thought that a letter of recommendation from Mr. Gordon, addressed to Mr. Hoffman, would have been enough to make us known; yet it was only after a very long examination of our passport that Mr. Hoffman offered to let us stay at his house. There are no more inns at Stellenbosch than at the town of the Cape; but the Dutch there likewise undertake to supply the needs of travellers for a price which keeps them from being a burden to their host. We were at Mr. Hoffman's on much the same footing as at the Cape.

The next day I went to visit the hills around Stellenbosch.

1792-02-11.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 93]
The fine tree known by the name of *brabeium stellulifolium*, remarkable for its fruits, whose shape approaches that of the almond, grew on the banks of a little river which runs through the village.

A few *orchis*, and the species of *protea mellifera*, *pallens* and *speciosa*, came with many other plants to swell my collection.

1792-02-12.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 93-95]
We set out on the 12th intending to reach Franche-Hoek towards evening.

This place, whose name indicates the abode of some Frenchmen, serves as a retreat for Protestant families who, persecuted in Europe on account of their religious opinions, crossed the seas in 1675 to settle in this part of Africa, where the governor Simon Van der Stel welcomed them and gave them every means of devoting themselves to agriculture.

The south-east breeze was blowing strongly enough to hinder our progress. It was nevertheless very far from having the same violence as the one felt at the same time in the town of the Cape, where we learnt on our return that the wind had been very furious. The great difference in the strength of these breezes is no doubt due to a local cause, as I have tried to explain above.

It was on the same day that the Espérance's boat, commanded by Citizen le Grand, being unable to reach the ship on account of the violence of the wind, was obliged to go and seek shelter behind Robben Island.

We had had to walk for nearly two hours in the dark before arriving at Franche-Hoek, at the house of Gabriel Deprat, for whom I had a letter of recommendation. As he was away, one of his neighbours, Jacob de Villiers, came to invite us to stay with him: we were very well received there.

The names of these colonists made us hope that we were going to find someone with whom to speak our own language; but these men of French origin, obliged to speak Dutch, have kept nothing of their mother tongue but the names of their fathers. The only person who still knew French was a woman eighty years of age.

The reader will not be sorry to know the French families who still live in the midst of these mountains. Here are their names:

Lombart, Faure, Rotif, Blignant, Duplessis, Marée, Ponté, Naudé, Cronier, Hugo, de Villiers, Marais, du Buisson, le Roux, Deprat, Rousseaux, Villiers, Terrons, Hubert.

We were in a beautiful valley, where the rays of the sun, concentrated by the surrounding mountains, rapidly ripen the grapes which are the chief wealth of the inhabitants: wheat is also grown there.

The two following days were spent climbing the neighbouring heights: the *protea florida* and *serraria* were among the plants I gathered there in great quantity.

1792-02-13.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 95]
These mountains are composed in great part of granite and of a very hard sandstone.

1792-02-14.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 95-101]
The vegetable mould which covers them goes to enrich the valleys where the colonists have settled; from there they must cross the sands that surround them in order to carry the produce of their farming to the town: this situation is common to all the settlements distant from the Cape. Some farmers have been obliged to go more than a hundred myriametres into the interior of Africa in search of a few tablelands of cultivable soil, scattered like so many islets in the midst of a sea of sand, where each has adopted the kind of cultivation that seemed to him best suited to the corner of land he came to clear. Black slaves, although charged with the hardest labour, are generally treated there with mildness. It is worth noting that, very unlike the Spaniards, who have always tried to make proselytes, the Dutch here leave their slaves in the most complete ignorance of their religion.

We several times saw, in the trees, snakes which the people of the country greatly dread; they lay in wait there for the birds that often become their prey.

The zebra is very common on these heights; it flees with prodigious speed as soon as it catches sight of man. The ape called magot by Buffon, *simia inuus*, Linn., sometimes came near the dwelling where we were staying. I witnessed a very singular fact, which gave me a proof of the authority of these animals over their young. A large ape, followed by a very young one, thinking itself seen by no one, took the little one in one of its fore paws and, holding it up above the ground, beat it for a long time with its other paw. If apes know how to proportion the punishment to the offence, the case must have been a grave one; for this little magot was severely whipped.

The olive thrush of the Cape of Good Hope, the widow-bird, the Cape starling, some creepers, etc., were the birds I found most often on this little journey.

The very near approach of our departure obliged us to leave Franche-Hoek much sooner than we should have wished. We were in such haste to get back to the town that we took leave of our worthy Jacob de Villiers on the 14th at about ten in the evening, and set off at once. We walked all night, and did not reach the town until the next day at the same hour, having followed the road by Paarl-Berg and Paarde-Berg. This journey was tiring enough for people who for several days had been taking scarcely a few hours of rest; indeed one of the servants from the Espérance (Emard Serpoy), who had come with us because he was fond of shooting, was so overcome with sleep towards the middle of the night that he had to sleep on the road for half an hour before he could go on following us. Although this man was very robust, the need of sleep had so completely absorbed all his faculties that it would have been impossible for him to go any farther without this moment of rest.

I learnt with sorrow on my return from Fransche-Hoek that we were about to lose three fellow travellers: they had just asked the general to be put ashore, being unable for reasons of health to follow the expedition any farther: they were the astronomer Bertrand, the naturalist Blavier and the painter Ely. Bertrand had gone a few days before to make barometrical observations on Table Mountain; he had had a fall there from which he was much indisposed. I learnt on my return to France that he did not enjoy the happiness of seeing his country again; he died at the Cape a short time after we had left it.

The town of the Cape, built in such a way that all the roofs are terraced, presents a rather fine view. Its defences on the side of the sea have been strengthened in recent years.

The commander of our ships, in view of the crowded state of our vessels, persuaded me to deposit with the agent of the French government, named Gui, the collections of objects of natural history I had made during our stay at the Cape. The latter promised me to send them on to France by the first opportunity. They never reached their destination, and I learnt at the Isle of France [Mauritius], on my return from the South Seas, that the naturalists Macé and Aubert Petit Thouars had seen them relegated to a loft in this agent's house long after our departure from the Cape; yet many opportunities had offered of which he could have taken advantage, had he been willing to keep his engagements.

The Cape of Good Hope is one of the points of the globe that most deserve to engage the attention of a trading nation. By its position it forms an almost necessary port of call for ships making the voyage to the East Indies. The provisions it supplies are abundant; but the prohibitive system increases from day to day the number of ships which try to reach their destination without putting in at this roadstead: others go to St Helena, where they take in supplies more cheaply.

The mercantile spirit of the Dutch Company has often led it at the Cape to resort to the trick of feigning a great scarcity in order to raise the price of provisions. The farmers are not permitted to deal directly with foreigners for the produce of their farms; they are obliged to deliver it to the Company, which gives them for it a price often four times lower than that at which it has reserved to itself the right to sell it. The oppressions practised by the higher officials upon their subordinates turn further to the disadvantage of travellers, who cannot escape the greed of so many people united against their interests. The aversion to the Cape as a port of call which this cupidity must naturally produce is leading the country to its ruin. A ruinous luxury, introduced some years ago among the women, has greatly changed the manners of the inhabitants: European fashions are eagerly sought after there.

It is unfortunate that there should have been governments so ill-informed of their own interests as to leave so long at the disposal of a company of merchants one of the most important points for the navigation of India. Besides, in such an association political views are very much subordinated to the spirit of gain which dominates it and which is often opposed to the national interest.

Commissioners from Europe were expected to put affairs on a better footing; but, although several had already been sent, things went no better.

At the Cape of Good Hope we replaced the provisions we had consumed before arriving there. It would have been desirable for this replacement to have extended also to the articles of poor quality with which we had been supplied before our departure from Europe. The contractors had deceived us there as to the quality of the wine: they had been paid double the ordinary price so that we should have better wine and that it should keep a long time; yet part of it was already spoilt on our arrival at the Cape: it would have been all the more important to change it since it was impossible for us to procure any afterwards. We had the choice between the wine of the country and Bordeaux wine, with which a ship lying in the roadstead was laden. I cannot conceive why this course was not taken: our bad wine went from bad to worse, and in the course of the voyage it was necessary to substitute brandy for it. This negligence deprived us of one of the most powerful means of preserving the health of the crews on a voyage in which we were besides exposed to every kind of privation.

The observations made on board the Recherche gave as the position of her anchorage in the roadstead of the Cape 33° 54' 24" south latitude and 16° 4' 25" east longitude.

The variation of the magnetic needle there was 24° 30' west.

The astronomer Bertrand had found for the site of his observatory, situated in the town, 33° 55' 22",8 south latitude and 16° 3' 45" east longitude.

He had observed 24° 31' 52" of westerly variation of the magnetic needle.

A flat dipping needle had given him 47° 25'. The greatest height of the thermometer during the whole time we lay at anchor did not go beyond 25° above o.

1792-02-16.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 102]
## CHAPTER IV.

*Departure from the Cape of Good Hope. Death of the master carpenter of the Recherche. Various occurrences. Extraordinary flight of the albatross. Sight of the island of St Paul. Its forests on fire. Prodigious quantity of insects come out of our biscuit. Violent effect of the waves. The general dangerously injured. Luminous points at the tips of our lightning conductors. Large phosphorescent molluscs. A false bearing given by Willaumez made us enter Storm Bay, taking it for Adventure Bay. General observations on the variation of the magnetic needle. Decrease in the phosphorescence of the sea water as we had moved away from land. Direction of the currents. It became necessary to warm the place where the marine clocks were kept. Anchorage in port Dentrécasteaux.*

[t. I, p. 102-103]
We were now waiting only for a favourable wind to leave the roadstead of the Cape, when a south-east breeze sprang up at about ten in the morning and decided us to weigh anchor. Hardly were we under sail when a squall came rushing down from the tops of the mountains with such violence that for some time it prevented us from steering, so that we ran the risk of falling foul of several ships lying at anchor. We were very soon past them, and it was not long before we reached the open sea.

1792-02-18.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 103-104]
At about eight in the morning we lost our master carpenter (Louis Gargan): he died a victim of the excesses to which he had given himself up while we lay at anchor at the Cape. A fever, slight at the outset, had afterwards taken on a malignant character, to which he had just succumbed. This loss was all the more keenly felt because a skilful carpenter is one of the most useful of men, above all on a voyage whose object is to make discoveries, in seas strewn with reefs, where, being ceaselessly exposed to shipwreck, one may lose along with one's ships all hope of ever seeing one's country again, if one has not the means of building a vessel to carry one there.

Two men who had hidden themselves on board at the moment of our departure from the Cape did not appear on deck until it was no longer possible to send them back ashore. We had no choice but to let them follow the expedition. One was a soldier, a deserter from the garrison of the Cape; the other a German, a very skilful maker of mathematical instruments, who had practised his trade for nine years in England. The English, he told us, were taking him to Botany Bay, with a great number of other transported persons under the name of *convicts*. He assured us that he had been among them for debt. Having seized the opportunity of escaping from the ship in which he was held, he had taken refuge in the mountains near the town of the Cape. There he spent the day in a cave, and in the evening came down into the town to buy something to live on, while waiting for the departure of the other convicts. The talents of this craftsman could not be employed on board; he could be made only an armourer, and afterwards a blacksmith. The ship's armourer had been put ashore at the Cape on account of illness.

1792-02-20.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 104]
On the 20th of February, with winds from the south-west and west, we rounded Cape Agulhas at a distance of about two kilometres.

1792-02-22.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 104]
On the 22nd we were in latitude 35° south and longitude 20° east, when the lead showed, at a depth of one hundred and twenty-four metres, a bottom of greyish calcareous sand.

1792-02-25.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 104-105]
Until then the currents had carried us to the north-west; but on the 25th they made us drift towards the south-west, because we were abreast of the Mozambique Channel, whose waters at this season set towards the south-west along the coast of Natal, which remained in sight.

1792-02-26.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 105]
The sea ran so high on the 26th that a windmill, although firmly lashed on the poop, was thrown overboard. As our ship was much too heavily laden, we found ourselves compensated for this loss by the advantage of being relieved of a weight of sixty-four myriagrams. I do not know why we had burdened ourselves with this almost useless machine, since at the ports of call where we might have found wheat we should also have found flour. Besides, a hand-mill, six times lighter, would have been less cumbersome and would have done more work.

The rolling was so heavy that our marine clocks struck against the sides of their boxes, which ought to have been made a little wider.

Many flying fish were still to be seen, although we had passed the 35<sup>th</sup> degree of south latitude.

The quarter galleries of our two ships were too low, especially for vessels that rose with difficulty to the sea. It was to be feared that they might be carried away by the waves if we remained long in so rough a sea: those on the larboard side of the Espérance had already been badly damaged.

1792-02-29.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 105-106]
It is rare at this season to pass abreast of the Mozambique Channel at a short distance from the land without meeting with violent storms. The wind was blowing from the north-east out of this wide opening when a gradual fall of 8<sup>l</sup> of the mercury in the barometer announced one to us which was of the greatest violence. The electric matter brought by the clouds was so abundant that, in spite of the outlet afforded it by our lightning conductors, the lightning struck several times within a few metres of the ship. The west wind which brought back fine weather was preceded by a rise of 2<sup>l</sup> of the mercury in the barometer.

1792-03-01.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 106]
By the 1<sup>st</sup> of March this wind had raised so heavy a sea that our consort was often hidden by the height of the waves. This ship, seen at a distance of a few hectometres, offered us a fine spectacle; she could be seen disappearing beneath the waves, emerging for an instant, then rising to the crest of the sea, laying bare a great part of her keel.

1792-03-05.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 106-107]
We could well tell by the lessening of the waves that we had passed the mouth of the Mozambique Channel; for, although the wind continued to blow with much the same force as on the preceding days, we were sailing on a sea scarcely ruffled, because we were sheltered by the land of Madagascar. Prodigious masses of the largest of all the seaweeds, the *fucus pyriferus*, were seen floating by; it had no doubt been torn from the rocks that border that great island. This fucus, several decametres long, has as the petiole of its upper leaves a swelling filled with air, which serves to keep it towards the surface of the water; it is the means nature employs to make it tend to rise from the bottom of the sea as it grows.

At about five in the evening we were surrounded by a great number of whales, which came within less than a hectometre of us. The Anglo-Americans sometimes come to these waters to hunt these enormous cetaceans; the oil they obtain from them is enough to repay them with interest for the cost of fitting out.

1792-03-06.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 107-109]
The depositions of Captains Magon Lépinay and Préaudet had decided the general to make his way as quickly as possible to the Admiralty Islands, where he thought he could arrive before the return of the eastern monsoon, after passing to the north of New Holland; but we had made very little way, since by the 6th of March we had not yet reached the 44<sup>th</sup> degree of east longitude. The fear of being detained in the Moluccas throughout the eastern monsoon, which was due to begin in the month of Germinal, led to the decision to round cap de Diemen in order to enter the South Seas.

At about half past six in the morning a boat was sent on board the Espérance to inform her captain of this decision. The wind died away all at once as soon as our ships were very close to each other. A heavy swell increased the danger of this situation. The Espérance's bowsprit was on the point of being shattered against our poop, when some boats that had just been hoisted out towed us apart.

The currents were found to be setting to the north. The ring by which the biscayenne employed for this observation was hung broke at the moment she was being hoisted on board; she fell into the sea, and the compass that had just been used was lost.

More than two hundred myriametres distant from the Cape of Good Hope, we sighted several albatrosses, *diomedea exulans*, some of which, resting on the surface of the sea, let us approach within a short distance. They could be seen from time to time plunging their heads deep under the water to seek their food.

The manner of flight of these birds is most astonishing. The beating of their wings is seen only at the moment they take flight, and very often they use their feet at the same time, which, being webbed, serve them to strike the water repeatedly in order to rise; once this impulse is given, they have no further need to beat their wings; they hold them fully spread and seek their prey by swaying alternately from right to left and skimming the surface of the sea in rapid flight. The swaying no doubt serves to quicken their progress; but it does not seem sufficient to hold them up in the air. Perhaps an imperceptible quivering of their feathers is the principal cause of this extraordinary flight: on this supposition they would have to possess special muscles; that is why I think the anatomy of these birds deserves the greatest attention.

Buffon's shearwaters, *procellaria puffinus*, Linn., were very numerous in these seas. The flight of this bird is performed by a mechanism analogous to that of the albatross, for it often flies a long time without any beating of the wings being perceptible; it is only when it tilts from one side to the other that it is seen to strike the air with the lower wing, so as to turn about instantly.

The course was set south-east by east, in order to pass between the islands of St Paul and Amsterdam; but the wind having veered to the south-east, we had to stand on the south-south-west tack.

1792-03-07.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 109]
Towards nine in the evening the wind brought us a strong smell of the sea; our latitude was then 34° 45' south, and our longitude 44° 5' east. In less familiar waters we might have feared the neighbourhood of some land. This smell probably came from a mass of fucus torn from the south coast of Madagascar and carried to this great distance by the currents.

1792-03-19.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 109-110]
One of our sailors, being drunk, threw himself into the water; fortunately it was calm, and he was brought back on board: this immersion only increased his drunkenness, and in his delirium he would have thrown himself into the sea again had he not been held back.

For twelve days, with light winds varying from south-south-west to north-north-west by way of the east, we had kept on the tack that brought us nearest to the direct course for passing between the islands of Amsterdam and St Paul. If this course was the shortest with respect to the distance to be covered, it was also the slowest because of the light weather we met with; whereas, had we stood more directly to the south, we should soon have found very fresh westerly winds, which would have driven us rapidly towards the cap de Diemen.

1792-03-28.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 110-113]
It was not until the 28th of March, when we had reached 37° ½ of south latitude, that the wind began to blow hard from the north-north-west. A great number of various species of gulls and boobies announced to us the nearness of land, for these birds never stray far from it. We did indeed sight it to the south-east at about half past one in the afternoon; it was St Paul Island, from which we were four myriametres distant: this island, discovered by Captain Valming in 1696, was named Amsterdam Island, and the one lying further south received the name of St Paul Island. Cook, who examined them on his last voyage, used exactly the opposite names, calling the more southerly one Amsterdam Island, and the more northerly one St Paul Island; it is this nomenclature that I have followed.

In the distance St Paul Island appeared covered with thick clouds, above which rose the summits of the mountains. By four o'clock we were near enough to make out perfectly that these clouds were formed over the island, from which rose a thick smoke that covered it almost entirely, especially towards the north; flames could be seen at various points, and it was soon recognised that the forests were on fire; the traces of the fire and the smoke, which appeared successively in several places, showed the progress of the blaze. The course was directed so as to pass to windward of the island and as close to it as possible: the same species of birds that we had seen some hours before sighting it were flying in great numbers about the rocks that serve them as a retreat. Many seals were swimming amid great masses of fucus torn from the coast, which we ranged along on its southern side at a distance of half a kilometre. This steep coast is very safe; the swell ran along it, and would have warned us of the danger of approaching it had it been fringed with shoals. Rocks which I took to be formed of beds of sandstone dipping about 50° from north to south made up the mountains of the south-west, which present great cliffs right down to the edge of the sea; further to the south, horizontal beds of the same kind of stone could be seen; a little stream issued from them, its waters falling into the sea in a cascade. Faces of rock displayed on a large scale those bizarre forms known by the name of *ludus*. We saw a light smoke coming out in puffs from a small underground opening a short distance from the shore: we did not know whether these forests had been set ablaze by subterranean fires or by the hand of man. I learned at the Isle of France [Mauritius], on my return from the South Seas, that an American ship had taken to the islands of Amsterdam and St Paul some men whose business was to extract oil from the seals, which are very numerous there. Although we watched attentively to discover whether our help might be called for, we saw no signal to let us know that this island was inhabited. It would, besides, have been impossible to put in there, for we could only have sought shelter under the lee of this land, where the thick smoke would have put us in danger of suffocation. The smell of this smoke indicated only burning vegetation.

The mountains slope down towards the south-east, so that in favourable weather it would be easy to land there. We saw little streams there winding their way to mingle their waters with those of the sea.

We were only a short distance from the island when night came on. The land then appeared to be all on fire, and the smoke, lit up by it, gave the sky a coppery tint, as at the approach of a hurricane.

St Paul Island, which is about two myriametres in circumference, lies in latitude 37° 56' south, and longitude 75° 2' east.

The variation of the magnetic needle there was 17° ½ west.

1792-04-01.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 113-114]
The wind, which continued to blow from north-west to south-west, made the mercury in the barometer fall gradually by 8<sup>l</sup>; it had settled at 27<sup>p</sup> 7<sup>l</sup> on the 1st of April, when very strong gusts drove us along at as much as ten knots before the wind, under the foresail and the main topsail lowered on account of the force of the wind; it was the only day of the whole voyage on which we made so great a speed. We had already reached 40° ½ of south latitude, in 85° of east longitude.

Until then we had believed that at least we had not been deceived at Brest as to the quality of the biscuit; but it was discovered too late that part of it had already been on a voyage; and so, after five months at sea, it was full of a prodigious number of larvae which turned into small dermestes of the species known by the name of *dermestes paniceus*. These insects, with which we were infested, had become very troublesome; in the evening they came to burn themselves at the light, in such numbers that they very often put it out. The larvae left the biscuit and spread into all our food; they leapt by doubling themselves up, like those that commonly live in cheese. It was a long time before the disgust they caused us began to wear off.

1792-04-02.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 114]
Violent and frequently repeated squalls called for frequent manoeuvres; Cretin, who had the watch, forgot to bring the main topsail to shiver before clewing it up; it was torn at once.

1792-04-04.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 114]
On the 4th of April, being in latitude 41° south and longitude 92° east, we saw a very great number of birds, among which were gulls and boobies, which do not stray far from land. It is very probable that we were not far from some island or some rock.

1792-04-05.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 114]
Although we were making good speed, we still saw the same species of birds on the following day. The lands that serve them as a refuge will one day be discovered, when these waters are more frequented by navigators.

1792-04-14.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 114-116]
The mercury in the barometer, having fallen from 28<sup>p</sup> 3<sup>l</sup> to 27<sup>p</sup> 7<sup>l</sup>, warned us of violent winds; they blew from the west *and* the south-west, raising a frightful sea which often broke on board: at about five in the afternoon one wave, getting partly under the mizzen channels, struck the stern of the ship with such violence that several of our seamen thought we had touched on a rock; the shock was terrible, and some of the storerooms sprang a leak at the same moment.

When a heavy sea takes a vessel on the beam, the channels are bound to suffer, the water getting under the broad planks which hold them out from the ship's side. Would it not be advisable to substitute for these planks iron bars, on which the chains of the channels would rest; or, if the planks are kept, could not a sheathing be fitted to prevent the sea from acting upon them?

The violence of the rolling had thrown the general against one of the corners of a bird-organ intended for some chief of the savages. The surgeon believed that the first of the false ribs had been fractured: the pain was so sharp that on sneezing he lost consciousness; but he soon recovered.

During the night there was a superabundance of electricity in the atmosphere, part of which was carried off by way of our lightning conductors; at their upper end a luminous point was observed which settled there several times; the sea was more phosphorescent than usual.

During the night a very heavy sea filled the between-decks, having come in through the opening in the quarter-deck where the boats were kept. I was awakened with a start by the water that flooded my cabin, and for a moment I believed the ship was going down. It took a long time to clear away this mass of water. Three or four seas like the one we had just shipped would infallibly have swamped us. We should not have run this danger if the means had been provided of closing so large an opening with a grating.

1792-04-17.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 116]
The variation of the magnetic needle was nil on the 17th of April, when we were in latitude 43° south and longitude 129° east.

1792-04-19.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 116]
The Espérance was informed that the rendezvous, in case of separation, would be at the cap de Diemen, in Adventure Bay, instead of Oyster Bay.

1792-04-20.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 116]
During the night of the 20th we lay to under the foresail, because the nearness to the coast at which our reckoning placed us did not allow us to make sail. The lead, cast at about nine in the evening to a depth of one and a half hectometres, found no bottom: on hauling it in, a great number of phosphorescent molluscs were brought up, ranging in size from one to two decimetres. Now that the compressibility of water has been clearly demonstrated, we know the chief cause that keeps these various bodies at a greater or lesser depth, according to their specific gravity.

1792-04-21.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 116-121]
As soon as day broke, sail was made to steer east-north-east.

At about half past nine we perceived a very sharp-pointed rock, known by the name of the *Mewstone;* some other rocks and land of moderate height could be seen in the east. The coast showed occasional slight indentations; mountains of moderate height could be seen a short distance from the shore, and we could make out the tall trees that crowned their summits.

We soon arrived at the entrance of a bay open to the south-east. An island was to be seen in the east; nearer to us, breakers were visible to the east by north.

The general intended to anchor in Adventure Bay. His injury did not yet allow him to leave his cabin; he could direct the course only from the bearings brought to him as they were taken. A false bearing passed on by Citizen Willaumez [^117-1] led him to give orders to manoeuvre so as to enter the bay that lay on our larboard side. It was in vain that we looked for Penguin Island, believing ourselves to be in Adventure Bay, whereas we were in Storm Bay, so named by Tasman because, having entered it in the month of November 1642, he met with a gale from the south-east which, driving him on shore, put him in the greatest danger when he tried to gain the open sea.

Being already far into this bay, we were perfectly sheltered from the west wind. The lead showed a bottom of broken shells, at a depth of 30 to 50 metres. The general was on the point of leaving it to spend the night in the offing; however, he decided to send two boats, one to the north and the other to the north-west, to try to discover some shelter. The boat that had gone towards the north found a cove that our ships could enter: the bottom there was good holding ground. Water and wood could easily be obtained there: remains of huts had been seen, and close by them had been found heaps of shells roasted by the natives.

It was too late to reach this anchorage before nightfall. As the weather was fine, it was decided, at about five o'clock, to let go the anchor in Storm Bay in a depth of two decametres, on a bottom of grey sand. It was sixty-four days since we had left the Cape. Most of the navigators who preceded us took only fifty to fifty-five days to make the same passage. It is worth noting that they stood to the south as quickly as possible, in order to reach the westerly winds. The route is a little longer; but at sea it is not commonly by following the shortest way that one arrives soonest. One should make a point of knowing well the most usual direction of the winds, so as to go in search of those that are favourable. The night continued very fine, although the air was laden with great humidity. We were sheltered from the prevailing wind from the north-west and west-north-west, of which, however, we felt some light gusts.

Many fish of very varied species were taken with the line, the most numerous of all being a species of *gadus*.

The variation of the magnetic needle, when we crossed the meridian of the Isle of France [Mauritius] at more than a hundred and fifty myriametres' distance to the south, had been 12° greater than that observed on approaching that island: this is a very great variation considering the difference of latitude.

The greatest westerly variation observed was on the 3rd of March, at 30° ½, our latitude being then 34° 30' south, and our longitude 37° 45' east; from that point it had done nothing but decrease, and had become nil in latitude 43° south and longitude 129° east, then passing to the east, where it had increased as we advanced eastward.

The westerly variation of the magnetic needle observed up to the point where it was greatest had depended more on the change of longitude than on that of latitude; whereas afterwards, as far as the meridian of the Isle of France, it seemed to depend much more on the degrees of latitude; for from the point where it had been greatest to the meridian of that island, after we had made 17° in longitude and 2° ½ in latitude, the difference in variation had been only 4°, whereas in a latitude 17° further south the declination had been found 12° greater than that of the Isle of France.

The phosphorescence of the sea water had diminished during this passage in proportion to our distance from land, so that long before sighting St Paul Island a few phosphorescent bodies could scarcely be seen when the water was stirred.

During this passage the thermometer did not fall lower than 8° above 0, and did not rise above 20°.

The mercury in the barometer had risen as high as 28<sup>p</sup> 7<sup>l</sup>, and had not fallen lower than 27<sup>p</sup> 7<sup>l</sup>.

When, on this passage, we had reached the variable winds, the currents had set us from 10' to 20' to the north; but once abreast of the south-west coast of New Holland, we had been set to the east: these different directions depend on the position of the lands.

Our tables for correcting the irregular rate of the marine clocks caused by differences of temperature extended only as far as the 15th degree of Réaumur's thermometer, and the arc of the balance for the weight-driven clock had been determined only from the 105th to the 115th degree. It had constantly been more than 115°, and the temperature of the atmosphere had very often been below the 15th degree of the thermometer. It was necessary to have at least that degree of heat in the place where our clocks were kept. A simple lamp could serve this purpose; an Argand lamp was preferred, so as to have no smoke.

[^117-1]: On our making land at the cap de Diemen, Willaumez was charged with taking the bearings. The commander of the expedition asked to be given the bearing of the *Eddystone*. Willaumez sent word that this rock then bore south 19° west, whereas it bore south 19° east of us. The general had the ship stand into the bay that lay on our larboard side, having every reason to believe that we were opposite Adventure Bay. As soon as the error had been pointed out, its cause was sought. The testimony of several officers who had heard the false bearing given led to the belief that it was not a simple mistake on the part of Willaumez. From that time this officer lost the general's confidence.

1792-04-22.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 121-123]
The same boats went back the next day to sound at the entrance of the cove where we planned to anchor, for there had not been time the day before to complete this work. At about half past nine we received the welcome news that it was a very well enclosed harbour, with a bottom of muddy sand where the anchorage was safe; it had no less than seven metres of depth at its mouth towards half-tide. The lead had shown from five to eight metres over a great extent of the harbour, which runs nearly half a myriametre inland; it was in every respect preferable to Adventure Bay; water and wood could be obtained there with the greatest ease. A contrary but light wind did not prevent us from advancing by warping; but hardly had we made a kilometre of way when the wind freshened and obliged us to let go an anchor; the Espérance nonetheless continued her manoeuvre, and before nightfall she was very near the entrance of the harbour.

The boat sent out fishing had brought back, at a single haul of the net, enough fish for everyone to be well pleased with the distribution that was at once made of it.

We were rather surprised to see, among various fish taken with the line during the night, some sharks about two metres long; they were all of the species designated by the name of *squalus cinereus.* This shark does not leave the bottom of the sea; we never saw it show itself at the surface of the waves during the whole time of our stay at the cap de Diemen. It does not appear to be dangerous to man: our sailors bathed many times, and no accident befell them; this fish finds on these coasts such abundant means of satisfying its voracity that it does not attack men; otherwise the natives of this land, who dive to great depths in search of the crustaceans and shellfish on which they live, would be constantly exposed to being devoured by these animals.

Mountains, whose perpendicular height seemed to be at least a kilometre, could be seen three myriametres off to the north. Their summits were covered with tall trees, whose verdure added still more to the beauty of the majestic spectacle they presented to us.

An officer of our ship, having gone to sound towards the head of the harbour in the morning and having gone ashore, had found some huts, and near them the remains of roasted shellfish which had evidently served for a meal of the natives of the country.

1792-04-23.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 123-131]
As it was almost calm, the anchor was weighed some hours before daybreak, in order to heave ahead on a warp. The calm still continued; it was quicker to have ourselves towed: the boats soon brought us into the harbour. A rock lying in the middle of the passage was left on the larboard side and passed very close. The lead had shown us a depth there of five and a half to seven metres; it had been found to be from nine to eleven metres in the other parts of the same passage.

We let go the anchor at about eight o'clock in six metres of water, after running some three quarters of a kilometre into the harbour, which was given the name of port Dentrecasteaux. The nearest shore lay to the east of us, half a kilometre off.

It is difficult to express the feeling that this solitary haven produced in us, situated at the extremities of the globe, where at last we found a safe shelter after having been so long buffeted by violent winds.

The same boats went to tow the Espérance: she anchored at about one in the afternoon to the south of the Recherche, about three hectometres away.

An attempt was made to move closer to the shore without having had soundings taken exactly; but we soon ran into the mud, and it was necessary to heave promptly at the capstan to get clear.

## CHAPTER V.
