*Stay in port Dentrecasteaux. Signs that its shores are frequented by the savages. Various excursions into the interior. Trees of prodigious height. Goodness of the soil. Black swans. Large trunks of trees hollowed out by fire serve the natives as a retreat. Kangaroo. Various observations in comparative anatomy. Windbreaks put up by the natives. Framework of their huts. A violent gust breaks our chain. We run aground on the mud. Encounter with a young savage. News of a strait by which one can pass from Storm Bay into Adventure Bay. Huts of the savages. Seal called* phoca monachus. *The heart of this amphibious animal has no Botal's foramen. Various other points of comparative anatomy. Signs of wild beasts at the cap de Diemen. Huts which appeared to us to have been lately inhabited. Trees suitable for shipbuilding. Viviparous fly whose larvae rapidly brought down putrefying flesh. Roasted human bones* *found by Citizen Riche. The sailmaker of the Recherche lost in the woods. The two ships ran aground on the mud. Some utensils of the savages. Position of the observatory. Variation of the magnetic needle. Establishment of the port. Departure from port Dentrecasteaux to pass through the strait of the same name. Various fires. Natives seen on the beach. One of them carried fire to various places. Anchorage in a vast bay at the entrance of the détroit Dentrecasteaux [D'Entrecasteaux Channel]. Excursion over the neighbouring lands. Natives surprised beside small fires where they were preparing their meal. The strait explored by our longboats was called the détroit Dentrecasteaux. Various anchorages in this channel. Excursions over the lands lying along its shores. Some natives crossed it on a catamaran. Various encounters with savages. Departure from the détroit de Dentrecasteaux.*

Port Dentrecasteaux, situated at the head of Storm Bay, is a basin of roughly oval shape, which runs about half a myriametre towards the north-north-east, and whose greatest breadth is about a kilometre and a half. The great forests that surrounded us on every side, and the mountains not far off that sheltered more than half the circuit of this haven, added still further to the safety of our anchorage. The heaviest weather did not prevent our longboats from sailing there without fear. A muddy bottom of about seven metres leaves no risk to be run should one happen to ground. More than a hundred ships of the line could anchor there in safety and would find all the water and wood they might need.

Towards the north-north-east, at the head of this haven, a small river flows in, which one of our boats could not ascend very far, because its course was obstructed by large trees lying across it; some wild ducks were seen there.

Flimsy shelters of tree bark set up along its banks showed that they were frequented by the natives. A portion of the seaweed known by the name of *fucus palmatus* was found there, cut roughly into the shape of a purse for counters. It was a water vessel. It was still full when it was discovered.

It is chiefly on the western shore of the harbour that water can be obtained most easily. We took in ours to the west-south-west. Our wood was taken from the opposite shore.

A fire lit towards the south, a myriametre away, told us that savages lived near us, although none had yet been seen.

In the afternoon I went ashore with the gardener and two men of the crew, to make my way towards the north-east. We were struck with admiration at the sight of these ancient forests which the axe had not yet despoiled. The eye was astonished at the prodigious height of these trees; some of the myrtle family were more than half a hectometre (more than a hundred and fifty feet) high; their bushy tops are crowned with an evergreen foliage: many, falling from old age, find support on their neighbours, and are returned to the earth only as they decay. The most vigorous vegetation forms an admirable contrast with this state of decline, and one sees in all its grandeur the imposing picture of nature which, left to herself, destroys only to create anew.

The trees of this forest, however, did not stand close enough to bar our way in. We walked for a long time over ground where the waters, sometimes hindered in their course, have formed marshes: we examined their edges. Further on we found some little streams of very good water. Almost everywhere could be seen an excellent vegetable mould, often more than four decimetres deep; it rests on a reddish and sometimes grey sandstone. Here and there one came upon a clayey soil which, soaking up water with the greatest ease, forms bogs: elsewhere this clay, carried away by the waters that filter through the ground, has left small cavities and sometimes large pools whose surface, covered with plants, hides the danger: a moment's inattention may make you fall into them; this is what happened, a few days later, to the surgeon-major of the Espérance. Being out shooting, he thought he was setting foot on solid ground, and sank into a very deep pool. He disappeared at once; fortunately he could swim.

In the woods we found some huts begun. Young branches of trees were arranged to receive the bark with which the natives cover their huts.

This excursion procured us various species of *eucalyptus*, among which was the one that White designated by the name of *eucalyptus resinifera*. It is a very large tree, whose spongy bark comes away easily and is often nearly a decimetre thick. It yields a reddish gum-resin, astringent, which may be used in medicine. We also gathered several *philadelphus*, a new species of *epacris*, and the *banksia integrifolia*, etc.

On the shore we met Citizen Riche's servant, very pleased at having killed some birds, which he was carrying to his master. This servant, recovering from an illness, was still under the authority of the surgeon-major of the Espérance, who believed he had a right to his patient's game; but neither threats of being purged, nor even threats of being put on a strict diet, could wring a single bird from him: and so the surgeon kept his word; he made him go on a diet and swallow a purge. This servant learned by sad experience the danger of resisting a surgeon-major. From that time, whenever he went shooting, he ran off as fast as his legs would carry him as soon as he caught sight of him in the distance.

We had been making our way for some time towards the north-east, and before nightfall we reached the shore near our ships, where we expected to go on board at once, for we had been promised a boat as soon as we asked for one. We could have been put on board in five minutes; but we had to wait patiently on the shore for two hours. It would have been advisable to have a boat set aside solely for the service of the naturalists.

On a lake a bird was killed that was very surprising for the singularity of its plumage; it was a new species of swan, a little larger than ours: it has all their fine shape; its glossy black colour is as remarkable as the white colour of our swan; it has only six large white feathers on each wing: a character that I constantly observed in several others that were killed afterwards. The upper mandible of the bill is red, with a whitish transverse band towards the tip. At the base of the male's bill there is a swelling forming two protuberances, which are barely noticeable in that of the female. The lower mandible is red at the edges, and whitish underneath. The feet are dark grey. *(See pl. 9)*.

1792-04-24.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 131-135]
I was not able to finish describing and preparing the specimens gathered the day before until ten in the morning. I then went to explore the land lying to the east of our anchorage.

After having several times made my way into the woods to a kilometre at most from the shore, I was obliged to return towards the beach, so difficult was it to penetrate these forests; not only did the shrubs bar the way in, but the passages were often blocked by great trees fallen to the ground. The direction from south-west to north-east which they have generally taken in their fall proves that the violent south-west winds have brought them down. These trees, whose roots are almost horizontal, have little hold on the soil; sometimes in their fall they carry away a great extent of earth, which from a distance has every appearance of a wall raised by the hand of man.

The finest trees of this country are species of *eucalyptus*; their most usual girth is six metres; I measured several that were as much as eight and a half metres in circumference. The spongy bark of the *eucalyptus resinifera*, made slippery by the dampness that constantly prevails in the midst of these dense forests, added still further to the difficulty of making our way through them. This bark comes off with the greatest ease in extremely supple pieces, which the natives use to cover their huts; these are strips, often four decimetres wide, which come away of themselves from the lower part of the trunk; pieces eight to ten metres long can easily be torn off.

Most of the large trees near the sea have been hollowed out by fire at their foot. These openings, nearly all facing the north-east, are sheltered from the south-west wind, which appears to be the prevailing and most violent wind. There can be no doubt that they are the work of men; for if the fire had been started by accident, as by the burning of the shrubs growing in the shade of these forests, the tree would be attacked all round. These hollows in the trees serve as a retreat for the natives, who come there to take their meals; we found in them remains of the crustaceans and shellfish on which they had fed: in several we also saw the ashes of the small fires they had lit to cook their food. The savages are not very safe beneath these great trees partly undermined by fire; a strong wind may bring them down; nor do they lie there very softly, for the ground is often very uneven, and we noticed no arrangement suited to lessen its hardness. Anderson speaks of hearths of clay made in these trees by the natives. The clay I found in them never appeared to me to have been arranged by the hand of man; it is sometimes found there naturally lodged between the roots at a greater or lesser height. Besides, as we shall see later, the savages build no hearths; their fire is made on level ground, and it is on the embers that they prepare their food.

Some of the largest trees, hollowed out by fire along their whole length, formed a kind of chimney, and yet continued to grow none the less.

Several large trees that we felled during our stay were found, despite the finest appearances, to be rotten inside.

After following the beach, which runs towards the south-east in various windings, we tried to make our way through some marshes, passing over the places made firm by the roots of plants; but a new species of *sclerya*, two to three metres high, whose leaves cut our hands and faces, prevented us from going further.

On this excursion I killed some birds of the genus *motacilla*, and various parrots, among which was noticed that of New Caledonia described by Latham.

We made our way towards the entrance of the harbour, where the tents of the observatory had just been pitched; we were sure of finding a longboat there to take us on board.

At about a quarter past eight the observers were awaiting the first satellite of Jupiter; but, for all their activity, they were not ready in time, and the observation could not take place. Bonvouloir, one of the ship's officers, who had long beforehand made the preliminary calculations, was so affected by this mishap that he could not hold back his tears.

One of our hunters found a young kangaroo on the seashore. This animal, after running a hundred metres or so over the sand, threw itself into the water and was killed. It is worth noting that in running it had made very good use of its four feet, supporting itself on its fore feet, which, like the hind ones, are bare of hair underneath; although, from the way it has been represented, it would seem to use only its hind feet in flight. As it runs much more by night than by day, nature has provided it with a membrane known to zoologists by the name of *membrana nictitans*, situated at the inner corner of the eye and extending at will over the whole eyeball. Its stomach, full of grass, was divided by three large and very distinct partitions; this character would appear to bring it close to the ruminant quadrupeds. Its testicles were external. These animals probably find some food on the seashore, for the prints of their feet were frequently seen on the sand.

1792-04-25.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 135-137]
After handing over some plants to the painter to be drawn, I went towards the south-east, following the windings of the beach; large, very slippery stones heaped up along its edge made the going very difficult.

We soon found, at the edge of the wood, a windbreak made by the natives to shelter themselves from the sea winds; it was composed of strips of bark of the *eucalyptus resinifera*, interwoven among stakes driven upright into the ground and so arranged as to form an arc of a third of the circumference of a circle, three metres in extent and one metre high; its convex side was turned towards the sea: a small circular space covered with charcoal, and close by some remains of shellfish, marked the place where the natives had prepared their meal. This windbreak is very useful to keep their fires from going out when the sea winds blow hard.

After crossing a tongue of land, we walked with difficulty through the shifting sands of a vast beach, over whose edges the waters of the sea came spreading. At the edge of the wood we found another windbreak of the same shape as the first and of the same height; but it was twice as long: there were remains of water vessels to be seen there. These were pieces of the *fucus palmatus* which had been torn and could no longer be of any use to the inhabitants.

We were on the shores of a lake whose waters communicate with the sea at the flood tide. This lake is no more than a kilometre and a half long, by half a kilometre in its greatest breadth.

On our way back by a more direct route through the woods, we found some huts begun. Branches stuck into the ground at both ends leaned one upon another to form hemispherical huts a metre and a half high: the leaves of a grass served as ties and strengthened this framework, which was almost far enough advanced to receive the covering of bark that makes these huts proof against the rain.

It appears that the human species is here very rare or very shy. Although a great number of people from the two ships went far afield, they met with no inhabitant.

At the cap de Diemen, owing to its high latitude, violent winds prevail, which come down in gusts from the tops of the mountains. For fear of exposing our cables to rotting on the muddy bottom where we lay at anchor, it had been decided to take them back on board and to ride by our chain. A violent gust from the north-west shifted our position, and we went aground on the eastern shore, sinking into the mud. On hauling in the small length of cable fastened to the chain, it was found to everyone's astonishment that one of the links had broken. No flaw was noticed in the iron. It appears that a brittle iron had been used in making this chain. It was fortunate for us to have put it to the test in a harbour where we ran no risk but that of sticking in the mud; elsewhere this chain, on which we should have staked our safety, would have caused our loss.

1792-04-26.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 137]
I had to stay on board the whole day to prepare and describe the numerous natural history specimens I had collected up to that time.

1792-04-27.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 137-140]
The next day, at daybreak, we set out with the intention of going as far as we could. We were put ashore to the south-east. After following the windings of the shore, a path frequented by the natives made it easier for us to cross the forest to the south. We then came out on a fine sandy beach which stretches about two kilometres in the same direction.

A charming species of *érigeron*, whose woody stem was covered with very small fleshy leaves, grew in these arid places. Although the wind was fairly light, the surf broke heavily and spread over a great extent of the beach: of every three successive waves, one could quite regularly be observed which, after rising much higher than the others, broke further up and forced us to move further back from the water's edge.

A small knoll jutting out towards the sea furnished me with the pretty species of *banksia* that Gaertner designated by the name of *banksia gibbosa*.

We were making our way through the forest fairly near the sea when one of our companions saw a young native running away, frightened by a musket fired at a bird. Informed at once of this encounter, each of us hurried up in the hope of enjoying an interview with the inhabitants of this land; but our search was in vain; the young savage had disappeared, plunging headlong into the thickest places at the risk of tearing his skin, for he wore no clothing. At the spot from which he had fled we found a windbreak set against the sea breezes.

Fairly near a spring from which flowed very pure water, I found some vertebrae whose body was seven centimetres thick, and a rather large frontal bone which I took to belong to some amphibious animal.

The hope of meeting savages made us decide to continue on into the woods and to spend the night there. We walked for an hour towards the south-east, forcing a difficult way, before reaching a great plain which extends to the shore of the sea. There grew there a fine species of *mimosa* with long, simple, oval leaves, whose veins are prominent and longitudinal: this tree bears semicircular pods, and its height is commonly eight to ten metres.

Night obliged us to seek shelter. We could not make use of those offered by the great tree trunks hollowed out by the natives: we were too far from them; we had to have recourse to a battle-axe which one of us had taken the precaution of bringing. Branches cut on the spot served to put up a hut on ground whose hardness was softened by a bed of fern of a species differing very little from *polypodium dichotomum*.

Placed on the shore, our view extended far, and we saw nothing to indicate the presence of the natives. We lit a fire, for the cold was very sharp.

Our provisions did not give us much confidence in our means of subsistence: for before leaving the ship we had taken only one day's victuals; but the men of the crew who accompanied us, being used never to travel without biscuit, still had some. With such provisions we stood in the greatest need of water; it was fetched from two kilometres away. One needed a good appetite to be content with such a supper.

We were seven, and had not much to fear from the natives. Nevertheless we arranged to keep watch each in turn, so as to be warned of their movements should any of them come to visit us.

The cold obliged us to leave our hut and go to sleep beside the fire.

1792-04-28.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 140-143]
As soon as day broke we went shooting in search of our breakfast; two of us soon brought back a crow and an oystercatcher. These birds were roasted on the spot and eaten as if they had been a delicious dish.

The evening before, we had had to limit ourselves to a very meagre portion, so as to be able to live the next day; but we perceived too late that our provisions had been entrusted to unreliable hands: for we found only four biscuit cakes left of the six we had given into safe keeping; a greater breach of trust would have forced us to return on board at once, and we should have had the grief of seeing ourselves deprived of the advantage of carrying our researches further.

We soon came to the shores of a large lake which communicates with the sea by an opening about forty metres wide. Our attempts to ford it were in vain; it was too deep towards the middle.

Among a great number of plants growing in the neighbouring woods could be seen the *schefflera repens*, and several species of a new genus belonging to the family of the pediculares and very close to the *polygala*. Among the shrubs that adorned these lands jutting out towards the sea was noticed a fine species of sensitive plant with simple leaves, whose pod was twisted into the shape of an S.

We watched with envy a numerous flock of black swans swimming away from us. Some islets covered with shrubs were to be seen to the south-east, towards the opposite shore of the lake. Various species of snipe were killed as we made our way to the south-west to reach the end furthest from the sea; the bottom of the lake is so level that barely half a metre of water is found over a space of more than a hectometre. It is covered with a prodigious quantity of shells, partly worn away by time.

Samphire was to be found along its shores. A short distance away I found a new species of parsley which I named *apium prostratum*, on account of the habit of its stem, which always lies along the ground. Its likeness to the known species of the same genus led me to regard it as a good food, and my hope was not disappointed. We carried an ample supply of it on board, where it was joyfully received by seamen who felt the need of counteracting, by the use of vegetables, the ill effects of the salt meat on which we had lived during the passage from the Cape of Good Hope to the cap de Diemen. A stream to the west of the lake brought into it its clear waters, in which we softened the little biscuit we had left.

After so long a walk it was difficult to get back to our ships by passing through forests we had not yet explored. It would have been dangerous to lose our way, having only a small quantity of victuals. The sun, already far advanced in its course, served to guide us. A fine plain at first made our going easy: several shrubs of the heath family and of the persimmon family grew there. Very dense copses then slowed our steps. The unevenness of the ground at times obstructed the flow of the waters: we often had to cross marshes; but the numerous plants with which they were covered made us forget the difficulty of these crossings. Among those I gathered there were two new species of sundew, one of which, which I call *drosera bifurca*, is remarkable for the singular shape of its leaves; these are two long points situated at the end of each leaf-stalk springing from the root of the plant.

After two days of rambling it was a great deal to reach the harbour where our ships lay at anchor. We came to its northern end, from which our ships could be seen a great way off. The difficulty of the path took away all hope of getting there within the day, when we fortunately found a longboat which carried us on board.

Crétin, one of the officers of our ship, had been sent by the general with the geographical engineer to explore Storm Bay in the large boat. On their return, after advancing several myriametres into a channel left on the starboard side when we entered the bay, they announced that everything tended to show that it was a strait. The various points sounded had everywhere offered good anchorage.

1792-04-29.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 143-144]
For the next two days I went but little distance from the ship. The mornings were taken up with describing and preparing the abundant harvest I had gathered on my last excursion.

The surrounding country, which I visited in the afternoons, furnished me with various plants of the family of the *orchis*. I handed some of them to the painter to be drawn.

Fairly regularly every evening a party went out fishing with the net, and brought back a great deal of fish. The meals served on board made a very striking contrast with those we had been obliged to make on our excursions.

It is worth noting that the naturalists, having claimed the fresh provisions to which they were entitled, to take with them on their excursions, could not obtain the smallest portion of them; biscuit, cheese, brandy, and at times salt pork, none the less made up our whole store of provisions. The reasons we put forward did indeed secure recognition of our rights, but we continued none the less to be provisioned in the same manner throughout the whole campaign. I would refrain from relating this fact, were it not likely to be of some use to naturalists who may undertake similar voyages.

1792-04-30.journal_labillardiere: (Labillardière's account for this day is given under 1792-04-29.)

1792-05-01.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 144-148]
On the 1st of May I went to the other side of the harbour, towards the west. The shallowness of the water kept the boat at a fair distance from the shore; we had to go into the water to reach land.

I followed the coast northward, making my way at times into the woods. As it was low tide, the edge of the shore was easy to walk along. Hollows dug in the sand in the shape of a funnel each harboured a small globular crab which had made the hole; as soon as one was drawn out of it, it lost no time in regaining its usual dwelling; it seemed to me that these holes, of which those of our ant-lions give a just idea, also served it as a trap for catching its prey.

I was agreeably surprised by the singular form of a new genus of fungus which was growing up from among the mosses with which the ground was covered. The arrangement of its rays led me to name it *aseroe*.

Its roots are small filaments attached to a fungous tuber, upon which rests a globular *volva*, whitish, gelatinous, marked with seven striae within and without.

From the middle of this *volva* rises a reddish stalk (*stipes*), nearly cylindrical, hollow throughout its length and open at its upper end, which is flared, of a fine red colour, and divided into seven forked rays, yellowish at their tips.

This fungus is smooth in all its parts.

This new genus should be placed next to the genus *phallus* of Linnaeus.

*Explanation of the figures. Pl.* 12.

*Fig.* 1. The fungus, shown at natural size.

*Fig.* 2. The *volva* split in two, so that the inside may be seen.

*Fig.* 3. The stalk (*stipes*) opened along its whole length.

Mountains lying towards the west, softening their slope, formed a fine valley where the waters, after uniting in a great number of small streams, ran off to lose themselves in the roadstead. The debris of the great trees with which the land is covered had given these waters a slight brown tinge.

The woods grew less dense, and we soon perceived a vast clearing; it stretched more than two kilometres towards the west. The shrubs, growing very close together, and the low grounds taken up by marshes, made it difficult of access: not only did we run the risk of sinking into the mud, but we often found ourselves stopped by a new species of *scleria*, which I call *scleria grandis*, because it sometimes rises as high as four metres; its leaves are as sharp as a piece of glass: its oval, reddish seeds contain a small oily kernel, of which the parrots are very fond, in spite of the great hardness of its shell.

The shrub most widespread in these low grounds was a new species of *embothrium*, remarkable for the hardness of its foliage. Each leaf is oval in shape and is one decimetre long by three centimetres wide.

We were following a difficult route with the intention of making our way to the place where water was being taken in. Night overtook us halfway, and to crown our misfortune, a very violent west wind brought on rain so heavy that we were obliged to seek shelter, after the manner of the savages of New Holland, in trunks of trees which they had hollowed out. There was reason to fear that such bad weather would render useless the signals we were making to have a boat sent for us. We were preparing to spend a very bad night in the midst of these forests, when we heard the voices of some sailors who were coming to look for us and take us on board.

After a great many attempts, they had at last succeeded in recovering the anchor to which the chain that had broken on the 25th of April was attached. The drag had been used in vain, for the chain was sunk too deep in the mud. The hold, moreover, was so strong that the two longboats together had constantly filled with water while hauling on the buoy-rope. The anchor lay so deep in the mud that the divers had never been able to find its bill: it had been necessary to use the great capstan. The need was then felt to double the buoy-rope in future, and to weigh the anchors from time to time, to prevent them from sinking in too deep.

Two boats had been sent out for the second time to examine the north-east part of Storm Bay as far as cap Tasman; they returned at the end of four days; it appeared to follow from their discoveries that cap Tasman and Adventure Bay formed part of an island separate from Van Diemen's Land. After having gone up the channel as far as latitude 43° 17' south, lack of provisions had prevented them from going farther. The work I had to do on board did not allow me to go far from the ship.

1792-05-02.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 148-149]
The next day we crossed a clearing lying to the north-east, which led us towards the great lake. We had indeed seen its southern part on an earlier excursion, but it remained to visit its northern shore, whose varied situations had led us to hope for an abundant harvest, and our hope was not disappointed. Its banks, often steep, were difficult of access; in many places the water came right up to the foot of these embankments. Various species of *mimosa* with simple leaves grew in the shade of the tall trees.

It appeared to us that the natives came from time to time to settle on the shores of the lake, whose shellfish assure them an abundant supply of food. We soon saw a hut which they had built a few paces from the shore; it had roughly the shape of a half-oval, fifteen decimetres high by sixteen wide at its base. Pieces of wood stuck into the ground by both ends and bent into a semicircle supported one another so as to form a fairly solid framework, which was covered with bark.

Among the many objects collected, I was struck by the beauty of the flowers of a new species of *aletris*; they were remarkable for their brilliant red colour.

The season, already far advanced, was against the multiplication of insects, and so they were very rare.

We still had a few hours of daylight: we advanced towards the south so as to get nearer the anchorage; but it was already night when we reached a sandy beach which served us as a landmark. We were a long way from the ships, and it was not until about half past nine in the evening that we arrived at the tents of the observatory, where we found every facility for getting on board.

1792-05-03.journal_labillardiere: (Labillardière's account for this day is given under 1792-05-02.)

1792-05-04.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 149-151]
For the next two days I went but little distance from the ship, because I had to prepare the skins of a great many birds and describe the objects I had collected.

The too limited space of the ship obliged me to dry in the oven the paper I used for preparing the plants.

My cabin being already full, I had no other place than the great cabin in which to put part of the plant specimens before they were entirely dried. Dauribeau, acting as first lieutenant, judged that objects of natural history ought not to encumber that space, and had my two presses put outside, with the plants they contained. I was obliged to appeal to the commander-in-chief, who condemned this act of authority and gave orders for the displaced objects to be brought back in.

At low tide a great variety of nerites and whelks was to be found along the edge of the shore. In this harbour we had the advantage of procuring very good oysters.

The eastern shore offered pyrites of very varied crystallisation. In the same place were to be seen pieces of flint whose close-set layers had the appearance of petrified wood.

One of our carpenters had killed a seal of the species known under the name of *phoca monachus*. It was twenty-four decimetres long; its hind extremities are entirely without claws; they are formed of two appendages, each edge of which is of about the same length.

Physiologists have explained in a very ingenious manner, by means of the foramen of Botal, how amphibious animals are able to remain so long under water; but having examined the heart of this seal with the greatest attention, I found no foramen of Botal in it. The same is probably true of many other amphibious animals. These inquiries will perhaps one day lead to the discovery of the true cause on which depends the astonishing faculty these animals possess of living equally under water and in the air.

Each lung is as it were divided in two by a transverse fissure.

The stomach, whose shape approaches that of the hog, was filled with a great quantity of calcareous sand, in which could be seen the beaks of cuttlefish and a few shells still quite whole. The first stage of digestion seems to be to break up the shells of these shellfish, producing a sand which does not appear to follow the course of the intestinal canal. These amphibious animals probably vomit it up, just as several reptiles cast up the bones of the animals on which they live. This sand is perhaps a ballast which makes it easier for them to keep to the bottom of the sea at very great depths.

The food on which they live being very easy to seize, nature has given them a mouth that opens very little.

The water in which they most usually live requires a great refrangibility on the part of the humours of the eye, and accordingly the vitreous humour was very dense.

These animals can let into the eye, at will, a greater or smaller quantity of light by means of a membrane called the *membrana nictitans*.

The various tasks with which I was charged prevented me from carrying inquiries of this kind any further.

The dried excrement yielded a very fine powder of a handsome, somewhat deep sulphur colour. The painter of the expedition considered it very suitable for use in the arts.

1792-05-05.journal_labillardiere: (Labillardière's account for this day is given under 1792-05-04.)

1792-05-06.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 151-154]
I had not yet been able to procure the flowers of a new species of *eucalyptus*, remarkable for its fruit, which rather resembles a coat button. This tree, one of the tallest in nature, since there are some half a hectometre high, bears flowers only towards its top. The stem is exactly like that of the *eucalyptus resinifera* stripped of its spongy bark, and moreover these two trees are of roughly the same dimensions. The trunk, very straight for at least half its length, is fit for shipbuilding and might serve for masts, although it is neither so light nor so elastic as the pine. It might perhaps be advantageous to make masts of it in several pieces, and even to hollow out these great tree-trunks along their whole length to make them lighter, strengthening them with iron hoops placed at intervals. It seems that by this means one would obtain all the strength that could be desired, since, as mechanicians acknowledge, a cylinder retains great strength even when it is hollowed out in the middle.

We had to fell one of these trees to obtain its flowers: as it leant a good deal, it fell fairly quickly. The sun was then very bright: the sap was rising abundantly, and at the moment of its fall it poured out in great quantity from the middle of the lower part of the trunk.

This fine tree, of the family of the myrtles, is covered with a rather smooth bark: the branches twist a little as they rise; towards their ends they bear alternate, slightly arched leaves, about two decimetres long by half a decimetre wide.

The flowers are solitary, and spring from the axils of the leaves.

The calyx, in the shape of an inverted urn, is of a single piece, as in the other species of the same genus, and it likewise falls when the stamens develop. Like the whole fruit, it is somewhat tuberculate.

There is no corolla.

The numerous stamens are attached to the edges of the receptacle.

The style is simple and divided at its base into four parts. There is only one stigma.

The capsule, open at its upper part, is usually four-celled, the cells containing several angular seeds; on its underside it has four angles, two of which project more than the others. Its coat-button shape led me to give this tree the name of *eucalyptus globulus*.

*Explanation of the figures. Pl.* 13.

*Fig.* 1. Branch of the *eucalyptus globulus*.
*Fig.* 2. Flower.
*Fig.* 3. Fruit.
*Fig.* 4. Calyx.

The bark, the leaves and the fruit are aromatics which might be put to domestic use, in place of those which the Moluccas have long supplied to us exclusively.

1792-05-07.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 154]
I had to spend almost the whole of the 7th preparing my collections, which were growing prodigiously from day to day. I could extend my researches only a short distance from our anchorage.

1792-05-08.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 154]
But the next day I set out in the afternoon with the intention of spending three or four days in the woods without returning to sleep on board. I was obliged to proceed in this way in order to collect the productions growing at a great distance from our ships.

We had on board a great variety of European seeds, which it was useful to propagate at this extremity of New Holland. The degree of temperature met with there gave us hope that they would succeed. The gardener busied himself in preparing a small patch of ground to which he was to entrust this deposit. A garden was dug quite close to the eastern shore of the harbour, to the east-north-east of our anchorage.

1792-05-09.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 154-157]
We went to sleep on the banks of a stream lying at the western end of the great lake, whose southern shore we followed the next day. There we saw a few pelicans, which we could not get near enough to shoot.

Piron, the painter of the expedition, was of the party: he took various views of these places. Rounded hillocks covered with very tall trees, which could be seen in the distance, added singularly to the beauty of the landscape.

We had to retrace our steps in order to make for the other shore. Piron went back on board.

I soon found an evergreen tree whose kernel, like the cashew nut, is seated on a fleshy receptacle much larger than itself. For this reason I have given this new genus the name of *exocarpos*.

On the same plant are to be seen hermaphrodite flowers together with separate male and female flowers.

The male flowers have a calyx of five rounded leaves; they have no corolla: the stamens, five in number, are small and attached to the calyx between its divisions; the germ is abortive.

The female flowers have a similar calyx; they have neither corolla nor stamens: the globular ovary has a short style; the stigma is in the form of a circular shield.

The hermaphrodite flowers have the calyx, the stamens and the ovary as I have just described them.

The fruit is an almost round, somewhat blackish nut, set upon a fleshy red receptacle, hollow in the middle, about three times the length of the nut.

The kernel is oily and has the same shape as its covering.

The principal characters of this new genus lead me to place it among the terebinthaceae, next to the *anacardium*. I have named this species *exocarpos cupressiformis*.

*Explanation of the figures. Pl.* 14.

*Fig.* 1. A branch of the *exocarpos cupressiformis*.

*Fig.* 2. Portion of a branch laden with flowers, at natural size.

*Fig.* 3. Germ with its style and stigma.

*Fig.* 4. Fruit at natural size.

*Fig.* 5. Fruit cut vertically. A cavity may be seen in the middle of the fleshy peduncle.

*Fig.* 6. Kernel.

*Fig.* 7. Portion of the woody body enclosing the kernel.

Night was coming on when we arrived on the banks of a stream, where we fixed our resting place. I noticed at this southern extremity of New Holland several species of *ancistrum*, whose counterparts grow at the southern extremity of America.

We were surrounded by charming groves formed for the most part by a pretty narrow-leaved species of *thesium*.

The cold had obliged us to light a large fire; some of us were scarcely beginning to fall asleep when we heard, a few paces away, the cry of a wild beast: this cry seemed to us rather like that of the leopard. It is probable that our fire had served us far more than we had supposed, by preventing this animal from coming any closer.

On the preceding days I had found the upper jaw of a fairly large quadruped of the class of carnivores.

1792-05-10.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 157-160]
As soon as day broke we followed the shores of the lake, close to which were to be seen five islets covered with trees, which made a pleasing contrast with the smooth surface of this great expanse of water.

We saw quails for the first time in this land; they flew off to a great distance.

After a few hours' walk to the north-east, we found on a small rise, in the shade of very tall trees, two huts of the same form as those we had already seen elsewhere; these were perfectly well kept, and it appeared to us that they had been inhabited recently.

I collected a handsome plant which forms a new genus, quite distinct from all those described hitherto. It is an iris with two stamens. On account of this singularity I have given it the name of *diplarrena*; its affinity with the genus *moræa* led me to designate it by the name of *diplarrena moræa*.

The two-valved spathe encloses several flowers which come out one after another when they are ready to open. They wither even more quickly than those of the *iris* and the *moræa*, and I should have lost all hope of having them drawn if fresh flowers had not succeeded those which vanished almost as soon as I had gathered the plant.

Like the other irises, they have no calyx.

The corolla has six deep divisions, of which the three inner ones are much smaller than the outer; of these inner divisions, the upper one is a little shorter than the other two and more swollen towards its base.

Having examined a great number of flowers, I have invariably found only two stamens, whose pointed filaments bear white anthers marked with two furrows. In place of a third stamen I have always seen the beginning of a filament, no more than two millimetres long; it bears no anther, and it is situated below the upper inner division.

The ovary is inferior: it has three angles and is borne on a long peduncle.

The style, a little longer than the stamens, is cylindrical and ends in a stigma shaped like a shepherd's crook.

The capsule is three-celled and contains several globular seeds, attached to a receptacle which rises from the middle of the cells up to their top. This genus, which naturally takes its place after the *iris* and the *morœa*, has all the habit of those plants: the leaves are likewise lanceolate, forming a sheath at the side towards their base.

I was crossing a very thick little wood when a large kangaroo left its lair at the very moment I was close upon it: at first it followed, for a distance of more than thirty paces, one of the little galleries which these quadrupeds clear for themselves through the brushwood; it could not help using all four legs in these narrow passages. As soon as it had reached the end, it set off in bounds, clearing the shrubs with such lightness that we soon lost sight of it.

A sheet of water into which a charming stream flowed was covered with a prodigious number of wild ducks, which rose quite close to us; we were so little expecting this good fortune that we could not kill a single one.

A strong breeze sprang up as night came on and seemed to threaten us with rain. We were far from any shelter; we had to sleep in the open air: a hedge which we built of branches served us as a windbreak, and under this shelter we were easily able to light a large fire.

1792-05-11.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 160-161]
Making our way westward, we crossed a vast plain in which there were here and there marshes covered with plants that hid from us the danger of going forward: the water wells up from the lowest parts and goes on to form pretty streams.

A very large kangaroo came out from the middle of a thicket four paces from me; the priming of my gun flashed without the shot going off; the animal moved away very slowly, taking one of the paths made through the groves; these are so many covered ways which cross in every direction and lie very close to one another. The numerous prints of the feet of these quadrupeds show that they must be very plentiful: as they keep to the thickest places, dogs would be needed to start them. These little paths usually lead to streams.

Our provisions were exhausted, and we had to get back on board before nightfall. We were wandering in the woods, trying to get nearer to the anchorage, when we came to the north-east end of the harbour, from which we could see our ships in the distance. It was not without trouble that we reached them; we had had to pass through places difficult of access.

1792-05-12.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 161-162]
The whole of the 12th was scarcely enough for preparing and describing what I had collected on the preceding days.

During my absence I had had a servant who stayed on board look after the preservation of the objects that required daily care, and I had the satisfaction of finding them in good condition.

Citizen Riche discovered human bones among the ashes of a fire lit by the savages. From the width of the pelvic bones he recognised them as those of a young girl; they were partly covered with pieces of broiled flesh. I will not do these peoples the injury of ranking them among the cannibals; I presume that they are in the habit of burning their dead; and these are the only human bones that were seen during this port of call.

1792-05-13.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 162-163]
On the 13th I went to the place where our water was being taken in. It was supplied by a small stream which came down to the seashore after flowing through the debris of the great trees with which this land is covered. Their decay had given the water a darkish tinge. The casks had to be rolled about a hectometre, for the shallowness of the water obliged the longboat to be kept at that distance from the shore.

There we saw the carpenters busy raising the sides of our longboat, because it had recently capsized in the harbour while under sail. Those who were in it had been obliged to swim while waiting for help to be sent to them. The officer in charge of such matters had had it fitted with masts that were too tall and a square sail far too large. It was easy to correct these bad proportions.

The wood being used was of the new species of *eucalyptus* which I have named *eucalyptus globulus*. Our carpenters judged it very fit for shipbuilding.

A constant dampness prevailed in the midst of the dense forests into which I made my way towards the south-west. There, many mosses and ferns grew with the greatest vigour. I killed there the handsome species of *merops* described by White under the name of *Wattled bee eater*, of which he has given a good figure. This bird is remarkable for two large appendages on each side of the head.

I had to prepare promptly the skins of the birds I wished to preserve, for flesh exposed to the air was very quickly covered with small living larvae deposited there by tawny-coloured flies; they are viviparous, like our own fly known by the name of *musca carnaria*. These larvae singularly hastened the putrefaction of the flesh.

1792-05-14.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 163-166]
We were to set sail the next day; I tried to make the most of these last moments and had myself put ashore on the eastern side, on the stretch of coast nearest the ship.

I arrived with the gardener at the plot where he had sown various European seeds. This spot, very well dug over an area of nine metres by seven, had been laid out in four beds; its soil was too much dominated by clay to give confidence in the success of the seeds that had just been entrusted to it.

After we had made our way into the woods, a quadruped the size of a large dog came out of a bush quite close to one of our travelling companions. This animal, white in colour and spotted with black, had the appearance of a wild beast. There is no doubt that these regions will in time add several species to the catalogue of zoologists. A vertebra whose body was more than eleven centimetres thick, found in the interior, gives hope that very large quadrupeds will be met with there.

Heavy rain came upon us towards the middle of the day and forced us to halt. The great hollowed tree-trunk which served us as shelter was more than eight metres in circumference. We thought we might light a fire in it, after the manner of the New Hollanders; but the smoke soon drove us out of this retreat.

We were trying to penetrate into places we had not yet visited. A clearing seemed likely to lead us into the plain to the north-east. We had at most three hours of daylight left. A steep slope slowed our progress: great trees piled one upon another blocked the way, and shrubs, to which the dampness of these forests gave the greatest vigour, added to the difficulties of our march. Among these shrubs grew a handsome species of tree polypody [^164-1] whose trunk was more than four metres high.

As night came on we found that we were on the shore of the small lake, at its end farthest inland. The woods prevented us from following its edges dry-shod. The water we had to cross was fortunately not deep. The darkness of the night did not prevent me from collecting there a new species of *restio*, which I was meeting with for the first time.

This lake, although it communicates with the sea at high tides, has no fish in it: a party from the Espérance had come there to fish with the seine and had caught nothing.

When we reached the seashore we still had a long way to go. It was night, and thick clouds deepened the darkness; we often had to climb over large blocks of sandstone against which the waves were breaking. We walked groping our way, at the risk of plunging into the sea, and we had great difficulty keeping our footing on the stones washed by the water and covered with fucus and other marine productions, which made them extremely slippery.

A great number of phosphorescent worms of various sizes, brought in by the waters of the sea, were the only light guiding our steps.

At last we arrived at the place that had been chosen for making the astronomical observations. No one was there any longer; the observers had just packed up.

Our sailmaker, having gone out shooting alone the day before, had lost his way in the woods, where he had been obliged to spend the night. Several guns had been fired to let him know where the anchorage lay; at length he had got on board in the afternoon, worn out with hunger and fatigue. Having set out without provisions, he had gone a day and a half without eating. He related that in the darkness of the night various quadrupeds had come and sniffed at him from a few centimetres away. Many people took him at his word: as for us, who had spent a good many nights in the midst of the woods without meeting such familiar animals, we were not so easily persuaded; far from believing that he meant to deceive, we saw in this tale the effect of the imagination of a man deprived of food and lost alone in the midst of immense forests.

[^164-1]: The reader may well expect that I shall not weary him with a long nomenclature of the productions I met with on this voyage; that will be the subject of a separate work.

1792-05-15.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 166-170]
The day before, the large anchor by which we were riding had been weighed, and a small one let go in its place, so as to get under way more easily: the Espérance had done the same. Very strong squalls from the north-west during the night made both ships drag; they went ashore and sank into the mud, where they suffered no damage: they were easily got afloat again. It was surprising that anyone should have thought himself safe on a small anchor newly let go in a muddy bottom: this kind of bottom holds well only when the anchor has reached a certain depth. It should have been foreseen that the small anchor, newly dropped, had not had time to sink in far enough to hold against such strong squalls. We were now waiting only for a favourable wind to set sail. The wind that blew thwarted us all day: it was violent the following night, and although the ship had just gone aground, Dauribeau wanted to ride by a hawser only; but the need was felt to let go a large anchor.

During our stay at cap de Diemen we had seen the natives only at some distance: those who had caught sight of us had always made off in haste; some had abandoned their household utensils, which gave us a very poor idea of their skill; these were baskets roughly made of the kind of rush known by the name of *juncus acutus*: they had also very often left behind their water vessel, which they make from a large piece of *fucus palmatus*, cut round and folded like a purse for counters. No weapons were ever found in the places they had just left; no doubt they carried them off or hid them carefully, for fear that we might use them against them.

A few scattered huts indicated a very small population; shells heaped in little mounds a short distance from the shore left no doubt that the seashore furnished the chief part of the food of these savages.

As human bones were found only once, and those partly broiled, it appears that they do not leave their dead exposed in the open air. It is difficult to know whether they are in the constant habit of burning them; perhaps they also bury them or throw them into the sea.

The great number of paths on which the tracks of various quadrupeds could be recognised proves that these are numerous there; no doubt during the day they keep to the impenetrable thickets of these dense forests.

Very numerous small streams brought their waters into the harbour. The ground was so wet within that as soon as it was dug to a small depth, water soon filled the hole.

Fishing with line and seine was generally plentiful; it was far more so still when east and south-east winds drove the fish into the bay.

Tasman discovered Van Diemen's Land in the month of November of the year 1642. When Captain Cook anchored there four years after Furneaux, in 1777, he believed himself to be the third of the European navigators to touch at this land. Cook did not know at that time that Captain Marion, after staying there for some time, had left it on the 10th of March of the year 1772. The natives behaved very differently towards these two navigators. Perhaps the gentleness of character they showed towards Cook was the effect of the notion they had formed of our firearms when Marion was obliged to use them against them.

The site of the observatory, on the starboard side towards the entrance of the harbour, was in latitude 43° 32' 24" south, and longitude 144° 46' east.

The variation of the magnetic needle was 7° 39' 32" east.

A flat needle gave a dip of 70° 30'.

The tides were felt only once a day. The establishment of the port was from nine to eleven o'clock, the water rising vertically about two metres. The winds had a great influence on the tides, often advancing or retarding them by a few hours.

On account of the calm it enjoys, this harbour is one of the most convenient that could be wished for repairing ships. Moreover the vast forests surrounding it yield a timber which our carpenters considered very fit for building; they used some of it, which wore very well.

During nearly a month's stay the sky was very little favourable to astronomical observations. The survey of these coasts would not be easy in this season; besides, the violence of the winds would put great obstacles in its way.

During our stay at cap de Diemen, the winds from north-west to south-west blew strongly; those from the north-west almost always brought storms and rain.

1792-05-16.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 170-171]
As soon as the sun had risen the frigates were towed to the mouth of the harbour; the sails were then spread, and with a north wind we steered for the new strait which it was proposed to enter.

After following, until ten in the morning, the line of the reefs, which we left to larboard in Storm Bay, we had the entrance of the strait bearing north-north-west, a myriametre and a half distant; we then trimmed our sails close-hauled.

The summits of the highest mountains were already whitened with snow. These mountains form part of a chain which runs from south-east to north-west and ends towards the head of the harbour.

We took great pleasure in recognising from the ship the places we had trodden on our various excursions.

For a moment a thick smoke was seen rising in the distance to the north of the great lake, and soon we made out five natives who had just left a fire lit on the seashore and were walking along the beach; one of them, carrying a burning brand, set fire in different places, which caught quickly and went out again almost at once.

We stood off and on as we approached the coast, where there is no danger to be feared.

A light north wind and a contrary tide prevented us from entering the strait; it was night when we let go the anchor at its entrance in fifty-eight metres, grey sand bottom. The site of our observatory then lay two myriametres to the west of us.

The mercury in the barometer, after falling for twenty-four hours, settled at 27<sup>p</sup> ½, although the sky kept a very fine appearance. We were not without anxiety, for so great a variation had never failed, during our stay at anchor, to be followed by violent winds. It is probable that they blew at a distance, but we felt no effects from them.

A fire lit by the natives was seen in the west during the night.

1792-05-17.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 171-172]
The current having become favourable towards nine in the morning, we got under way with a north wind and made short boards.

The nearness of the coast allowed me to notice at the entrance of this channel a sandstone which had every appearance of the one met with at port Dentrecasteaux.

The snow had increased prodigiously during the past night on the summits of the high mountains.

The mercury in the barometer had fallen as low as 27<sup>p</sup> 4<sup>l</sup> 4/10, and the north wind continued fairly light.

It was night when we entered the strait which was given the name of General Dentrecasteaux. We let go the anchor there towards seven in the evening in forty-five metres, bottom of black mud mixed with fragments of shells. We were in latitude 43° 20' south, and longitude 145° 10' east.

The Espérance, informed of our anchoring by a light shown near the mainmast, soon let go her anchor two kilometres from us, north 14° west.

Throughout the night the sea was very phosphorescent at the slightest disturbance.

Strong squalls accompanied by rain obliged us to veer out cable and to send down the topgallant masts.

1792-05-18.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 172-173]
A dark sky made us await with the keenest impatience the moment when we might enjoy the fine view of the immense bay that forms the entrance of the détroit Dentrecasteaux [D'Entrecasteaux Channel]. At length the horizon cleared. Wherever the eye turned, spacious inlets were to be seen, where the navigator beaten by the storm may come in full confidence to seek shelter. The eye ranged with astonishment over the vastness of these harbours, which could easily hold all the fleets of the maritime powers.

The starboard point of the entrance of the strait was seen bearing south 43° west.

As the wind blew with less violence towards eleven in the morning, we took advantage of this moment of respite to man the large cutter. The engineer-geographer set off with the intention of ascertaining whether an inlet seen bearing north 30° east might afford a passage for our ships.

The ebb tide set at from half a knot to one knot an hour towards north-west by north from eight in the evening until two after midnight.

1792-05-19.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 173-175]
The force of the wind having prevented small boats from being sent ashore, we were obliged to remain on board. But the next day we had ourselves put ashore to the south-west, half a myriametre away, on the island that borders this channel along its whole length. A boat from the Espérance had spent the night at the same spot and had taken a great quantity of fish there.

It was with the keenest pleasure that I went over this land, where I gathered many new plants, the most numerous species of which fell among the genera *melaleuca*, *aster*, *epacris*, etc.

The shores of the channel offered us an easy path through the shrubs, which grow sparsely there. We then climbed some steep places that rise perpendicularly half a hectometre above the waters of the sea. At this height sea salt could be seen, carried by the waves into the hollows of a very hard sandstone that forms the base of this land.

We had gone scarcely two kilometres when the remains of a hut and heaps of shells showed us that this island was inhabited.

It was then that we saw partridges for the first time at the cap de Diemen. A very large covey rose and went to settle at a great distance from us. It was late when we met Citizen Riche. He had spent the night with the fishermen. His offer to share the fruits of his fishing with us was joyfully accepted; he showed us a small spring where we had the pleasure of quenching our thirst with very good water, while eating excellent fish and shellfish, which we broiled on the embers in the manner of the New Hollanders. This meal very quickly made us forsake the ship's provisions.

We soon learnt that the officers composing the staff of the Recherche had debated the question whether the naturalists should retain any right to the fresh provisions distributed on board while they were ashore collecting the objects that were the purpose of their mission. Care had been taken not to call them to such discussions: no one took up their interests, and the question was very quickly decided to their disadvantage, against every notion of justice. I must add that, despite the changes that took place among the persons in charge of our table, all of them were faithful observers of so unjust a law.

It was night when our boat came to fetch us. Riche was obliged to take advantage of it so as not to remain ashore; but he had to sleep on board the Recherche, although he had the greatest need to go to the Espérance; for it is no matter of indifference to a naturalist to be taken back to the place where the means of preserving the objects he has just collected are kept.

1792-05-20.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 175-178]
A small island bearing south 42° west, half a myriametre away, had been named île aux Perdrix [Partridge Island] by some of our seamen who had explored it. Citizen Riche and I went to spend the day there, and instead of partridges we found a great number of quails. Could this have been a mistake on the part of those who had visited it first, or had the partridges left the island?

This small island lies in 43° 23' 30" south latitude and is about two kilometres long. The new species of parsley that I have named *apium prostratum* grew abundantly along its shores, almost at the level of high water. We gathered a large supply of it and carried it on board.

Several species of club-wood, *casuarina*, covered this land, particularly in the north; those of these trees that grow along the seashore seem to accommodate themselves perfectly to the moisture the sea brings them. It could be seen that their branches, by a natural inclination, had stretched out on that side. Among the plants I met with for the first time was a singular species of *limodorum*, which I had drawn: I also gathered several ferns and a fine species of *glycine*, remarkable for its flowers of a brilliant red.

This islet furnished us with no fresh water, although several abandoned huts bore witness that it had been inhabited by savages.

Two officers of our ship (Crétin and Dauribeau) had set off towards six in the morning to explore the coast that lay to the east of us; there they saw several bays, the greatest extent of which ran from north-west to south-east. Various coves could be seen in them, forming so many harbours. A strong breeze thwarted them and prevented them from going very far in. Several fires perceived at a short distance from the shore decided them to land there, and they had scarcely entered the woods when they came upon four natives busy tending three small fires, beside which they were seated. These savages fled on the spot, despite all the signs of friendship that were made to them, abandoning the lobsters and shellfish they were broiling on the embers. Close by could be seen as many huts as there were fires.

This place appeared to be fairly frequented, for there were fourteen small spots marked with traces of the fires that had been lit there.

One of these savages, very tall and powerfully muscled, had left behind a small basket full of pieces of flint; he was not afraid to come back for it, and advanced quite close to Crétin with the air of assurance that his strength seemed to give him: some of them were entirely naked and the others had a kangaroo skin over their shoulders. These savages are of a black colour that is not very dark; they let their beards grow and have woolly hair.

The household utensils they abandoned consisted of about thirty rush baskets, of the shape that may be seen at the bottom of plate 5; some were filled with shellfish and crabs. Most of these baskets are a third of a metre high. Some very small ones of the same shape were found, no more than a decimetre long; they were filled with various pieces of flint wrapped in a tree bark as soft as good tinder. Two pieces of flint struck one against the other are no doubt the means these savages employ to obtain fire: in this they differ greatly from the other inhabitants of the South Seas, and even from the other savages of the eastern part of New Holland; which would seem to assign them a different origin.

They also abandoned several kangaroo skins and water vessels.

The two officers prevented any of the sailors from seizing the belongings of these natives; they took only, for the General, one large and one small basket, a kangaroo skin and a vessel of seaweed that held five bottles of water. The shape of the water vessel may be seen at the bottom of plate 5, beside the basket. The savages had no cause to regret the loss of these various objects, for in the same place had been left a few knives, several handkerchiefs, some biscuit, some cheese, and an earthen pot, too fragile, it is true, to be a proper substitute for the water vessel that nature furnishes them.

These savages, though little burdened with belongings, scattered some of them from time to time along their way. Was this to hasten their flight, or to stop the Europeans following them by thus exciting their curiosity? I do not know.

A boat from the Espérance had gone to visit a cove nearly a myriametre away to the west. There a native had been met with who, despite all the signs of friendship, would never allow himself to be approached nearer than two hectometres. A charming brook flowed into the head of this cove. The position of this shelter, opposite an island that protects it from the swell, makes it very well suited for ships to carry out any repairs they might need.

Other inlets visited by the same boat generally offered excellent anchorages.

One bay ran so far into the north-west that its end could not be discovered. Some of these inlets are perhaps channels communicating with the sea.

1792-05-21.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 178-180]
The care I had to give to the objects collected so far kept me busy the whole day of the 21st.

The gardener set off in the biscayenne, loaded with ten persons, to go to the island where I had been the day before. After struggling in vain, in so frail a craft, against very strong and directly contrary winds, they had decided to let themselves be carried before them and seek shelter towards the north-east, a myriametre and a half away, behind a small round island lying at the mouth of the passage that had been explored. This crossing nearly proved fatal to them: the sail fell into the sea and the boat lost her way; far too heavily loaded, she was filling with water from the force of the waves. At last they arrived, worn out with fatigue, in the lee of the island, where they enjoyed a calm all the sweeter for the great dangers they had just run. Deeply anxious about their fate, the commander sent a boat in search of them towards one in the afternoon, knowing well, moreover, that the biscayenne could not have regained the ship against such contrary winds. We had the satisfaction of seeing them again as night came on. They told us that after following the coast to the south-east and south for an hour of fairly easy walking, some fires had warned them of the presence of the savages, and they had soon come upon them; they were the same ones who had been seen the previous day: they would not let themselves be approached any closer. At the fires they hurriedly abandoned, shellfish were found still broiling on the embers; and more than thirty kangaroo skins a short distance away showed the taste of these inhabitants for hunting.

It seems that they had made use of the bread and water left for them the day before; but the smell of the cheese had probably kept them from tasting it, for it was found in the same state in which it had been left. In the same place were found one of the knives and the handkerchiefs that had been put among their belongings the previous day.

Some shots fired at birds no doubt struck terror among these savages, for a boat from our ship went to the same place two days later and met none of them.

1792-05-22.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 180-182]
A party was sent to take in water at the head of a cove recently discovered towards the west. I took the opportunity to go and visit this place, which lies nearly a myriametre from the anchorage. It forms a harbour three hectometres wide and a kilometre deep, and there is enough depth of water in it for large ships to anchor. A brook brought very good water down to its head, but it was not easily taken in, because, to have it in all its purity, the casks had to be rolled, partly through the mud, more than three hectometres from the longboat. The crew might have been spared this labour, so harmful to their health, by using long hoses of canvas coated with a resinous dressing, or hoses of leather, by means of which it would have been easy to bring the water right into the longboat. The full importance of this precaution will be felt, above all when the impossibility of ascending various rivers with the boats forces navigators to take brackish water, whereas by means of a tube carried a few hectometres higher up, it could be obtained without any admixture of sea water, which makes it very unwholesome.

Along the banks of this brook grew various species of *casuarina*, one of which was remarkable for its club-shaped fruit. There was also a rather tall shrub that establishes a new genus in the family of the crucifers.

Numerous paths beaten by the kangaroos led towards the brook, where these animals frequently come to drink.

The winds that had been against us on our way to this watering place ought to have favoured us on our return; but a calm came on, and we took several hours to get back on board.

The large cutter, which had come back after four days' navigation, had explored the strait throughout its whole extent, which is about four and a half myriametres long from south-west to north-east. Nowhere had less than thirteen metres of depth been found, on a muddy bottom, sometimes of fine sand. Adventure Bay is separated from it only by a neck of land that is at most four hectometres wide.

1792-05-23.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 182]
We were now waiting only for a fair wind to follow the strait, in order to lay down an exact plan of it. The winds from the north-west and north were against us; they were moreover so light that we had to remain at anchor all day.

During the night several fires were seen that the natives had lit on the south-east coast.

1792-05-24.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 182-183]
We weighed the next morning towards half past seven, and made several tacks, standing in to within a kilometre of the land. We never found less than thirteen metres of water, on an excellent bottom.

Although in the coolest mornings the thermometer had not fallen lower than 7° above freezing point, the snow had greatly increased on the high mountains that could be seen to the west and north-west.

The favourable currents made us gain ground on each board; they turned against us towards six in the evening; we then let go the anchor in sixteen metres, grey sand bottom, fairly close to the coast and to the north of the anchorage we had left in the morning.

The natives lit more than twenty fires on the shore towards the south. Several families had no doubt been drawn to the coast by the news of our stay in this bay.

1792-05-25.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 183]
The currents favoured us towards seven in the morning, and we made a few tacks to enter a narrowing of the strait, keeping fairly close to its western shore as we advanced north-east by north.

After running half a myriametre along this channel, we entered a second bay, more than a myriametre in extent, bordered to the west by land of moderate height; the land to the east was low and separated this strait from Adventure Bay.

The anchor was let go towards half past one in the afternoon, a kilometre from the coast; then Fluted Cape was set bearing south 33° east.

We went ashore to the north-west, on a coast where the very dense woods retained the greatest moisture, although no rain had fallen for some days. A new species of *ptelea* grew very abundantly among the shrubs that covered this land.

1792-05-26.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 183-184]
We had weighed anchor towards seven in the morning, and at noon we found ourselves in a third bay, whose various inlets left us for some time uncertain of the passage we must take to get out of it; it lay towards the north-west, in the farthest inlet. The sea in this bay was no less than twenty-two metres deep towards the middle, and two hectometres from the shore the lead showed no less than thirteen metres. This bay, moreover, was as extensive as the one we had just left.

After running nearly two myriametres to the north north-east, we anchored towards half past three in twenty-nine metres, mud bottom. As we believed that a fair wind would carry us some way further before night, none of us went ashore.

1792-05-27.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 184-189]
We got under way on the 27th towards eight in the morning. The currents soon set against us and forced us to let go the anchor in twenty-five metres, bottom of sand mixed with mud. We were then in 43° 4' south latitude and 145° 17' east longitude.

Half a myriametre away to the north-east could be seen the end of the strait by which we were to leave.

A fire lit a short distance from the shore announced the presence of the natives. One of them was soon seen walking along the seashore.

Two longboats were about to carry several persons to both sides of the strait when some savages were seen paddling on a catamaran and landing on the eastern shore. As timid as those met with until then, they had hurriedly made for land, to flee through the woods, abandoning a few roughly worked spears. I went ashore on the beach from which they had just disappeared, and there I found a great number of rolled pebbles of a very fine and very hard granite.

On the beach could be seen four catamarans made of tree bark, of the shape that may be seen in pl. 44, fig. 2. Rafts of this kind can serve only on a sea scarcely ruffled; otherwise the waves would very quickly break them to pieces. Since these savages know how to hollow out tree trunks by means of fire to shelter in them, they ought to use the same means to make canoes; but they are as little advanced in navigation as in the other arts.

I had reached the mouth of the strait, where I noticed some very fine crystals of feldspar scattered here and there in several rocks of a very hard sandstone.

On the top of these hills I met with the plant that Phillip, in his voyage to Botany Bay, has designated by the name of *yellow gum tree;* it was only in seed, as Phillip had found it, so that I too was deprived of the characters indispensable for determining this genus, which has the habit of a *dracaena*. The seeds, set on a long spike, were full of a great number of larvae, which turned into small moths of the section of the tineae.

The gum-resin that exudes from this plant is strongly astringent: there is no doubt that it would be useful in medicine; the gummy principle in which it abounds must make it mix easily with our humours and cause it to be preferred to many other astringents.

Among the fine plants I then collected was a very remarkable composite, hitherto unknown to any naturalist; it forms a new genus which I call *richea*, after Citizen Riche, one of the naturalists of the expedition. This man of learning perished a victim of his love for the sciences, after having made, in a state of consumption already far advanced, a long and fatiguing voyage in which he had consulted his zeal more than his strength.

This new genus falls naturally into the third section of the *cynarocephales (Juss. gen. plant.)*

The common calyx is composed of several obtuse leaflets, scarious at the tip, of equal length, and arranged in a single row; it encloses several distinct calyces, each borne on a very short peduncle: each small calyx, composed of five to six leaflets, contains five to six florets, all hermaphrodite, each furnished with a scale almost as long as themselves.

The florets, swollen in their upper part, have five equal divisions.

Five distinct filaments, attached to the tube of the floret, bear as many anthers united in a cylinder.

The style is filiform and rises to the height of the stamens. The stigma is divided in two.

The seeds are oval, covered with a light down, and crowned with twelve to fifteen pappus bristles laden with hairs.

The glaucous colour of the leaves of this composite has led me to give it the name of *richea glauca*. Its flowers are a sulphur yellow.

An officer of the Recherche had just followed a path beaten through the woods by the savages. He soon met six of them who, entirely naked, were walking slowly towards the south, armed with spears five to six metres long. The surprise of so unexpected an encounter was painted on their faces; but, soon reassured by their numbers, they came up at the invitation of this European, and at once put on their heads a cravat and a handkerchief that he gave them. They appeared, however, frightened at the sight of a knife whose use the officer was showing them, above all when he taught them how to sharpen it, and their fear was calmed only when he had made them a present of it.
