In vain did he urge them to come towards the place where we lay at anchor; his entreaties were useless; the savages continued along the same path, moving away from our ships.

A boat had landed on the other shore near a fire from which a very thick smoke was rising. There eight natives were found, each with his shoulders covered by a kangaroo skin, warming themselves in the shelter of four windbreaks. These savages took flight as soon as they perceived the men of the crew.

An old woman laden with provisions, which she would not abandon, was very quickly overtaken by some of our sailors: she had just received a neckerchief with an air of satisfaction; but the sight of a knife that they wished to give her frightened her so much that she threw herself down a very steep slope more than fifteen metres high, and fled among the rocks, where she disappeared almost at once.

I do not know whether the persons who told the story in another way meant to make merry at the expense of those who had had this encounter: if they are to be believed, the great age of this woman had not protected her from the advances of these seamen; she nevertheless still had strength enough to escape, leaving behind two baskets in which were found a lobster, some shellfish and some fern roots about two centimetres thick: I recognized that they belonged to a new species of *pteris*, of which I had gathered an ample supply. It seems that these savages extract from them by chewing the starchy part, which is always more or less abundant in the plants of this family.

Like the other savages, this woman had a kangaroo skin over her shoulders; but she had in addition another which, tied on in the form of an apron, covered her private parts. I believe she had put on this garment rather because of the severity of the season than from any feeling of modesty; for among the natives whom Captain Cook saw at Adventure Bay, a few kilometres from this place, the women were entirely naked: now it is probable that at such short distances there cannot be much difference in manners.

1792-05-28.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 189-190]
A north wind blew during the night in squalls so violent that the Espérance dragged her anchor, although she was moored on a very large one.

We had spent more time than we had reckoned on the survey of the détroit Dentrecasteaux [D'Entrecasteaux Channel]. We had still to run half a myriametre to get out of it. The wind was against us, but the tide was in our favour, and we got under way towards half past nine in the morning. Our tacks often brought us within three hectometres of the coast, where the lead showed twenty-five to thirty metres of depth near the high land, and twelve to thirteen near the low land.

At length we reached the end of the channel. The two points of land that close it are at most half a myriametre apart, in a direction from south-east to north-west. We kept very close to the starboard one, where we found only seven to eight metres of depth. So great a shoaling of the water at the mouth of the channel gave good reason to presume that there was a very hard rock there, resisting the daily current of the flood and ebb, and the lead showed that this conjecture was well founded. This was the only bad bottom observed along the whole length of the strait, out of which we came towards noon. We then discovered, from east-south-east to south, an opening about three myriametres wide that gives passage into the open sea.

Towards the north could be seen a vast bay, or rather a gulf, broken up by islets and closed by the mainland, which could be seen in the distance; various inlets seemed to offer excellent anchorages in it.

1792-05-30.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 191-193]
## CHAPTER VI.

*Importance of the détroit Dentrecasteaux [D'Entrecasteaux Channel]. Passage from cap de Diemen to New Caledonia. Survey of the south-west coast of New Caledonia. Dangerous position of the Recherche close to the reefs that border this land. Sight of the natives on the shore. Small archipelago at the northern extremity of New Caledonia. Prodigious extent of reefs. Sight of the Land of the Arsacides and of the Treasury Islands. Survey of the western part of Bougainville Island and of Buka Island. Dangerous position of the Recherche on the shoals of Bougainville Island. Meeting with the savages of Buka Island. Fondness of these savages for music. Their bad faith. Canoes of these natives. Determination of various points of Bougainville Island and Buka Island. Anchorage at Carteret Harbour. Various excursions on the surrounding lands. Continual rains during our stay at Carteret Harbour. Various observations.*

We had just completed one of the geographical discoveries most important to navigation. It was of the greatest use to know exactly, at this extremity of New Holland where violent winds prevail, the shelters it can offer to ships beaten by the storm. A roadstead some four and a half myriametres in extent at the point of this great land might offer very great advantages to a commercial nation. One may let go the anchor anywhere in it, with the certainty of finding good ground at a depth of twelve to fifty metres. There is no danger to be met with in it. Midway between its two ends the bottom, of rather coarse sand, is less good; there is also less water, since the lead gave only twelve metres there. It would seem that the tide, entering by both ends at once, had carried these sands to the place where the opposing currents meet. One may approach the land without danger to within two hectometres. The windings of this channel offer a most varied prospect and truly picturesque scenes.

The season was advanced, and the thermometer, although we were near the 44<sup>th</sup> degree of south latitude, had not been lower than 7° above 0. Violent winds were felt out at sea, while in the strait we enjoyed the greatest tranquillity. We had not hoped to find so much safety so near Storm Bay.

Fish, which love still waters, abound in this channel, where the fishing was generally very successful.

We had hardly gone three kilometres past the outlet of the strait before its entrance could no longer be made out. The depth increased as we advanced into the open sea.

At noon our reckoning placed us in latitude 43° 1' south, and longitude 145° 19' east.

We soon doubled Cape Pillar, and then shaped our course to the north-east to go and survey the south-west coast of New Caledonia.

The mercury in the barometer had fallen as low as 27<sup>p</sup> 8<sup>l</sup>, and the north-west wind was blowing with violence. The rolling of the ship made me feel as much discomfort as at our departure from Brest. The stay we had just made at cap de Diemen had already made me lose the habit of the sea.

[t. I, p. 193-194]
We had made good way by the 30th of May, since at noon we were in latitude 40° 55' south, and longitude 150° 4' east. In the course of the morning the mercury in the barometer had fallen as low as 27<sup>p</sup> 4<sup>l</sup>, and had not deceived us in announcing violent winds. We could run only under the foresail, and even that had to be lowered; but fortunately we had the wind right astern.

Although the thermometer was not lower than 9° 2/10 above 0, the cold was nevertheless very sharp. The violent agitation of the air seemed to me to be the principal cause of the sensation we felt.

1792-06-01.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 194]
Having reached, on the 1st of June, latitude 37° 17' south and longitude 154° 5' east, we saw a great number of spotted petrels (*procellaria capensis*), and many albatrosses remarkable for the very dark tawny colour of their wing-tips.

1792-06-02.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 194]
The next day a great many flying fish, of the same species as those we had met with so often in other seas, told us, as they flung themselves on board, that we had reached the waters frequented by the bonitos.

The motion of the ship since our departure had cast me into such great prostration that I had been unable to give the care needed for the preservation of the objects collected on my last excursions.

1792-06-03.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 194-195]
On the 3rd of June the sea, having become less rough, allowed me to attend to them: they were not damaged; I merely found them covered with a little mould.

1792-06-05.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 195]
Since our departure from New Holland we had been reduced to a small allowance of water, and the heat, which was beginning to make itself strongly felt, made this privation still harder to bear. We had only a bottle a day; yet our needs increased as we advanced towards the torrid zone. We could not make up for this drink with wine, which grew worse from day to day; besides, the brandy which several already preferred to wine made a greater quantity of water necessary to them: the salt meat on which we lived further increased a thirst we had no means of quenching, and the great quantity of sea salt introduced into our humours had given them an extreme acrimony; and indeed the want of water is one of the principal causes of the diseases of seafaring men.

1792-06-06.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 195]
Cape pigeons and many other birds which we saw on the 6th of June, in latitude 34° 47' south and longitude 159° 28' east, led us to suppose that we were in the neighbourhood of some island, no doubt too far off to be seen.

1792-06-11.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 195]
Towards the middle of the day land was thought to be sighted in the east. After we had steered towards that point for an hour, the phantom vanished, and we at once resumed our course.

1792-06-15.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 195-196]
A frigate bird, having come to hover above our ship, was killed with a musket shot. This bird still had in its beak the kind of cuttlefish called *sepia loligo*. The frigate bird had probably seized this mollusc at the moment when it had leapt above the sea. I had already seen in the Mediterranean this kind of cuttlefish rise several metres above the surface of the water, by means of membranous expansions situated laterally towards its lower end; some had even at that time come and dropped on our deck.

1792-06-16.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 196-197]
Towards half past five in the morning we entered the torrid zone in 165° of east longitude.

Towards eight in the morning we sighted the Isle of Pines, which lies at no great distance from the southern point of New Caledonia; it appeared as a peak of moderate height; we soon made out the low lands by which it is surrounded on every side. Tall trees could be distinguished towards the south-east part of the island. Its position, which we determined to be in 22° 42' south latitude and 165° 14' east longitude, differed by only 4' from that assigned to it by Captain Cook, who gives it 4' less in latitude and 4' more in longitude.

Towards five in the evening we perceived the land of New Caledonia in the north-west, at a distance of about four and a half myriametres, and we stood towards it; but towards sunset we were obliged to heave to and wait for the Espérance, whose sailing was always much inferior to ours. The coast was then set from north 32° west to west 32° north. We were still too far off to see the reefs that lie between this island and the Isle of Pines. The Espérance rejoined us towards eight in the evening. We were to stand off and on throughout the night; but the calm prevented us from steering our ship.

The south-west winds had brought us all the way to New Caledonia, although we had expected to meet with the trade winds several days before making this land.

The small change in the variation of the magnetic needle during the passage we had just made is well worth noting. It may be regarded as nil from the 36<sup>th</sup> ° 1/2 of south latitude and the 154<sup>th</sup> ° of east longitude, where the declination was 11° 1/2 towards the east, to the 23<sup>rd</sup> ° of south latitude, in 164° 30' east longitude, where it was found to be 11° 4' towards the east; for over this space of 13° 1/2 in latitude and 10° 1/2 in longitude the compass did not vary by one degree, and it is known that at sea the variation can be ascertained at best only to within one degree.

1792-06-17.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 197-198]
During the night a fire lit by the savages on the Isle of Pines was perceived.

At daybreak we saw a great extent of reefs running from the coast of New Caledonia towards the south and then towards the west. The calm held us all morning between these perilous rocks and the Isle of Pines; happily a light south-west wind that sprang up in the afternoon carried us away from the breakers.

When at noon we had been in south latitude 22° 49' and east longitude 164° 40', the southern point of New Caledonia had borne north-north-west, at a distance of four myriametres. This extremity lies in 22° 30' south latitude and 164° 30' east longitude.

1792-06-18.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 198]
We had lost sight of the chain of reefs; but towards eleven o'clock their southern extremity was seen two myriametres off, bearing north-west by west. Their short distance from our ship when the latitude was taken at noon showed us that they extended a few minutes farther to the south than Captain Cook had supposed, since we saw them reach as far as the 23<sup>rd</sup> ° of south latitude, in 164° 31' east longitude.

These reefs, which we approached to within less than two kilometres, lie nearly four myriametres from the coast, and in that space enclose a very calm sea: we had to make several tacks to get out.

1792-06-19.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 198-199]
We made little way during the morning of the 19th, since at noon, being in 23° 3' 48" south latitude and 164° 8' 20" east longitude, we could still see the westernmost point of the reefs bearing north-west by north, two myriametres off. The ship's head was put to north-west by west, in order to weather them and draw nearer to the coast.

We stood off and on close-hauled under the topsails throughout the night, trying to keep at a short distance from our consort. It was necessary that we should be within reach of signalling to each other the dangers into which we might fall on this coast, bordered with reefs hitherto unknown to navigators.

1792-06-20.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 199-201]
During the night the currents had carried us back towards the reefs that we believed we had weathered. We were standing in towards the land when daylight happily came to show us the whole danger of our position. Surrounded by reefs, we had only a very small space left in which to beat about. The south-south-west wind freshened and raised the swell that was carrying us towards the breakers. We were already deeply embayed among them when the Espérance signalled them to us: Rossel then had the watch. The sails were at once trimmed close-hauled on the starboard tack, with the intention of going about to get out of this dangerous position: the Espérance had just carried out this manoeuvre and we could already see her drawing away, standing to the west.

The bell at once rang on board our ship to bring the whole crew on deck, the better to ensure the success of the manoeuvre. Rossel tried four times in vain to go about, and each attempt only brought us closer to the danger. We saw ourselves drifting onto the reefs, where the sea, ready to swallow us up, rose to a prodigious height. There was no means of letting go the anchor, for the lead showed no bottom at a hundred metres, although we were quite close to the reefs. Already each of us was casting his eyes on the objects he might seize to escape an almost inevitable death; at last, we were on the very brink of destruction when, by an unexpected stroke of fortune, a fifth attempt succeeded, and it was with inexpressible joy that we saw our ship draw away from this dangerous coast.

A few islets showed themselves between the land and the chain of reefs, which lies more than a myriametre from the shore.

The land of New Caledonia, low towards its southern extremity, was already beginning to show mountains of moderate height which, running at first from south-east to north-west, then curved round a little towards the north.

When the ship was put about as night came on, the topmen had forgotten to shift the boom of the mainyard and that of the mizen topsail yard: both were broken at the moment when preparations were made to stand on another tack: the one from the mainmast fell into the water; but that of the mizen topsail, in its fall, injured three persons, among whom was the commander of the expedition.

1792-06-21.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 201-202]
We stood out to sea to spend the night there, and the next day we drew near the land again. A south-east wind allowed us to coast along to the north-west, at a kilometre and a half, the reefs that guard its approach and lie only half a myriametre from it. We hoped to discover some break in them that might allow us to go and anchor under the shelter of this barrier, against which the waves broke in a frightful manner.

A great deal of smoke rising towards the foot of a hill not far from the seashore indicated the presence of the natives.

Since noon, when we had found ourselves in 22° 6' 58" south latitude and 163° 34' 36" east longitude, we had run nearly two myriametres to the north-west when we perceived among the reefs a wide opening that seemed to promise us a passage to go and anchor near the coast; unfortunately it was getting late, and the sea was too rough to allow us to send a boat to sound this entrance. We much regretted not being able to go and enjoy the calm that reigned behind this rampart, against which the sea spent its efforts in vain.

Hills almost entirely bare of plants rose in an amphitheatre up to the main chain, which appears to be at least eighteen hundred metres in perpendicular height, and whose direction is still towards the north-west. Three ranges of mountains of different heights could be made out, and along the whole height of the most barren peaks could be seen ravines that seemed to have been formed by the fall of the rains.

Behind these high mountains one could be seen, four or five myriametres inland, which, rising far above all the others, appeared to be at least two thousand four hundred metres in perpendicular height.

From the midst of the ravines issued a torrent that we could distinguish perfectly by the whiteness of its foaming waters, although we were very far from it.

The cold experienced on these heights no doubt obliges the natives to warm themselves. We perceived several large fires that they lit while we were beating about in the offing during the night.

1792-06-22.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 202-203]
Owing to the weakness of the south-east wind, we could not close with the reefs before noon: we were then in 21° 51' south latitude and 163° 8' east longitude; we coasted along these reefs until evening without finding the slightest break in them.

New Caledonia presented a more cheerful prospect than the day before: a few trees could be seen rising from the bottom of the ravines with which the hills are furrowed. A fire lit on the coast showed us that these arid places were not entirely without inhabitants. We soon perceived some of them.

The wind having shifted from north-east to north and to north-west, we hove to towards ten in the evening; this was perhaps not the best manoeuvre, for in the neighbourhood of reefs one must always be ready to avoid danger: it would no doubt have been preferable to stand off and on, so as to be able to manoeuvre properly in the event of some untoward encounter.

1792-06-23.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 203-204]
We were thwarted by the winds all night, and at noon we were only in 21° 37' south latitude and 162° 47' east longitude.

We had in sight some mountains covered with trees up to their summits.

Six fires perceived near the coast announced a great gathering of savages; they were probably drawn by the sight of our ships, which contrary winds held almost in the same place.

Towards three o'clock we were six and a half myriametres from land when we perceived near the shore a group of twelve Caledonians, whose eyes were turned towards us, and who seemed to be looking with astonishment at our ships so short a distance from their island.

Three natives formed another group and kept very close to two fires they had just lit.

A good spyglass showed us that they were entirely naked. They did not appear tempted to put any canoe into the sea to approach us; besides, the reefs presented a barrier that they could not have crossed to come out to our ships.

1792-06-24.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 204]
A strong south-west breeze had obliged us to stand off and on, and we found ourselves almost in the same place as the day before. The land was covered with a haze that had always accompanied the south-west winds.

The ship's position had just been determined as 21° 46' south latitude and 162° 46' east longitude when we thought we perceived among the reefs an opening that might perhaps have offered us a passage; but how were we to make sure of it with strong winds driving us onto the coast?

1792-06-25.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 204-205]
As soon as the winds had veered to the south the haze cleared away entirely: these winds, which bring cold to these parts, made the air give up at sunset the superabundance of water it had held in solution during the day; and so we then received a few large and very cold drops of water, falling very far apart from one another.

In two days we had scarcely advanced the survey of the coast by a few kilometres; on it we had seen several fires, lit perhaps by the same natives as on the previous days.

1792-06-26.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 205]
We were again thwarted during the two following days. But on the 28th a fairly fresh south-east wind favoured us on the course we intended to follow along the coast. The high mountains we had seen until then fell away considerably; their chain seemed to end there, but farther on they rose again to about the same height, and the island could be seen to be formed, towards its northern extremity, of great mountains whose appearance at that distance differed in no way from those we had observed on the previous days.

At noon we had been in 20° 28' south latitude and 161° 29' east longitude, and we soon made out that, a little before the extremity of the island, the chain of reefs was interrupted and offered a wide break, which gave us hope of an anchorage; but the wind was much too strong for a longboat to be put into the sea to sound this opening. We stood off and on throughout the night, in the hope that the weather would be more favourable the next day.

In the direction of the land of New Caledonia several islands could be seen, surrounded by reefs and linked to one another by sandbanks and other reefs.

1792-06-29.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 205-208]
The winds had made us drift so far during the night that we had lost sight of the northern extremity of New Caledonia, which was found to lie in 19° 58' south latitude and 161° 10' east longitude. This island presents a chain of mountains extending from south-east to north-west for nearly forty-eight myriametres; its mean breadth is no more than three to four myriametres. Captain Cook, who discovered it in 1772, saw only its north-east part. It was important for navigation to survey its south-west coast: the reefs that border it lie generally five to six kilometres from it, and towards its extremities, where it is narrower, they are at a greater distance: this coast, extremely dangerous at all times, is much more so with the south-west winds, which had singularly thwarted us in the survey we had just made of it.

The small number of fires we perceived on this land, and its apparent barrenness, lead me to think that it is thinly inhabited. We did not see a single canoe, although it is very easy to navigate there in the shelter of the reefs, where the sea is very calm.

Towards seven in the morning we saw, from north-north-east to east-north-east, several mountainous islands and detached rocks, which make this extremity of New Caledonia even more dangerous than its southern part. Some of these small islands are several kilometres in extent. A great number of black rocks raise their points above the water; beaten by a scarcely ruffled sea, these rocks seem to move, and at first sight one would take them for canoes rocked by the waves. We soon made out that the islets were numerous, for from the mastheads they could be seen as far as the eye could reach: they are surrounded by reefs, within which the sea takes on the tint of the reddish sand that covers the bottom. We examined them close to, and towards eleven o'clock we were three kilometres to the south of one of these small islands when we perceived reefs running from its western point and stretching out of sight to the west-north-west.

From the point of our latitude, which at noon was 20° 6' 4" south, in 161° 10' 36" east longitude, we set a small island two kilometres from us bearing east 22° north.

Another island, a myriametre and a half away, was seen bearing north 8° west: these two islands were linked to each other by reefs.

Other land could be seen bearing north 28° east.

A fire lit on the islet nearest to us, close beside a brook that came down from the mountain, showed us that these small islands are frequented by the natives.

In the evening the east wind blew in strong squalls, which would have hampered us prodigiously in any other position; but we were sheltered by the land and the reefs, and it was easy to beat about during the night.

1792-06-30.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 208-209]
A few islets towards the east appeared to close this small Archipelago. Their height diminished gradually in proportion to their distance from New Caledonia: they seem to be a prolongation of the mountains of that great island, whose bases, covered by the sea, rise here and there to form so many islets. The gradual diminution in the height of these mountains must lead one to presume that in these seas, to a great distance, there are shoals which add to the danger of navigating these parts. It will be seen that this conjecture was not without foundation.

With the ship's head to the north-west, we coasted very close along the reefs that guard the approach to these islets.

The commander sent word to the captain of the Espérance that, in the event of the two ships being separated, the rendezvous would be at Port Praslin or at Carteret Harbour.

At noon we had just had for latitude 19° 28' 10", in 160° 36' 12" east longitude, the northernmost islet in sight then bearing east of us, a myriametre and a half away.

As far as the eye could reach, the chain of reefs could be seen stretching towards north-west by north and sometimes forming windings as it turned towards the west. With an east-south-east wind it was easy for us to follow all the contours of these reefs. We had run nearly four myriametres along them since midday when we thought we perceived their end. We were already congratulating ourselves on having finished this dangerous and toilsome navigation and on entering an open sea, when the lookouts announced shoals and a line of reefs running towards the north-north-west: it was too late to venture among them; we kept our wind throughout the night.

A booby of the species called *pelecanus varius* let itself be caught on board at sunset; it differed from the ordinary species in its much less dark colour. This bird had come without mistrust to rest in the maintop beside one of our sailors: the little fear these birds have of man is a rather remarkable thing; often they even perch on the arm held out to them. Their sense of smell must be far from keen; the only openings of the nostrils to be seen are two slight slits on the upper mandible of the bill. This mandible is movable, like that of parrots.

1792-07-01.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 209-211]
We believed we had at last finished the survey of this frightful chain of reefs, which bars the sea over a space of nearly sixty myriametres from south-east to north-west, and we were already two and a half myriametres to the north of it towards midday, when we had for latitude 18° 50' south, being in 160° 32' east longitude.

We then steered north-north-east in order to make sure whether these reefs did not extend to the north-east.

One of the crew, named Moulin, perceived towards two in the afternoon, in the north, two myriametres away, a small low island covered with very thick trees and bordered on its western side by reefs that stretched to the west-north-west. This island is no more than half a myriametre in circumference; it lies in 18° 31' 10" south latitude and 160° 32' 14" east longitude.

To fulfil the promise the General had just made, this island was named île de Moulin, after the man who had first perceived it.

Towards four o'clock we sighted two other small islands bearing north-west by north, a myriametre and a half away. It was impossible for us to get past these islets before night; for this reason, towards five o'clock, we steered south-south-east, and soon afterwards lay to until the next day.

Throughout the night we were surrounded by a great number of birds that inhabit these low islands: frigate birds came, despite the darkness, and hovered a short distance above our ship, and several boobies settled on our yards. The commander had intended to go and anchor in the shelter of the île de Moulin; but we had been carried more than a myriametre to leeward, and it would have been very difficult to regain that distance against contrary currents and winds.

1792-07-02.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 211-213]
We steered north-north-east; before long we saw to the north some breakers lying not far from the two islets we had sighted the day before; we ran along them at a distance of two kilometres, following their direction towards the north-west.

From the position which gave us at noon a south latitude of 18° 7' 46", in 160° 32' east longitude, we could see the nearest reefs two kilometres to the east. We went on coasting along them, steering north-west by north.

At about a quarter past one we discovered, a myriametre and a half to the east, a low and thickly wooded island, which appeared to us to be at least a myriametre and a half in circumference; it was surrounded by rocks almost awash. Thwarted by the winds, we steered close-hauled; breakers stretched to the north-east for about a myriametre and a half, and from the midst of these reefs rose points of black rock, like those which had been seen before.

This new island lies in latitude 18° 3' south, and 160° 31' east longitude.

We stood to the north, and towards four in the afternoon we had the last of these rocks to the east, a myriametre and a half away; there the reefs, which seemed to trend towards the east and then towards the south, appeared to us to come to an end; their northern extremity lies in latitude 17° 54' south, and 160° 30' east longitude, and about six myriametres to the north of île de Moulin.

We could easily tell, from the strength of the swell, that we were clear of the reefs.

A great number of tropic birds, boobies and frigate birds had left the various islets which serve them as a refuge, and came to fly about us for almost the whole day. Several trunks of coconut palms had been seen floating, uprooted by the waves and carried wherever the current took them.

When we lay to at about six in the evening, the lead showed a bottom of fine sand at a depth of one hundred and sixteen metres, our position being latitude 17° 51' south, and 160° 18' east longitude. We remained for an hour over this bank, where the lead, cast several times, gave us depths of from one hundred to one hundred and thirty-two metres.

We had thus at last completed the survey of a fearful chain of reefs, all the more dangerous in the north because they lie out of sight of any land; although they appeared to us to be broken off to the north of New Caledonia, it is probable that they join up again too far to the east for us to have perceived it.

These reefs are, as is well known, the work of polyps; the danger they present is all the more to be feared because they form steep rocks covered by the water, which can be seen only at a short distance: if a calm sets in and the ship is carried onto them by the currents, her loss is almost inevitable; it would be vain to try to save her by letting go the anchor, for it would not reach the bottom, even quite close to these walls of coral rising perpendicularly from the depths. These coral growths, whose continual increase fills up the basin of the seas more and more, are well suited to alarm navigators; and many shoals which still afford a passage today will before long form extremely dangerous reefs.

The magnetic needle showed little change in its variation during the whole time we were coasting along this immense chain of rocks, since from their southern extremity, where it was observed to be 11° east, it had decreased by only two degrees when we reached its northern extremity.

1792-07-03.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 213]
The next day, steering north-north-west, we saw no more breakers.

1792-07-07.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 213-214]
In the evening at about half past nine, the moon being some 15° above the horizon in the east, we had in the west the spectacle of a lunar rainbow; it differed from the solar rainbow only in the lesser intensity of its colours. This phenomenon is much less frequent than it would seem that it ought to be. We were now served only a very small quantity of water, which distressed us exceedingly in waters so near the Line, and there was no means of procuring more, although we had the machine for distilling sea water invented by the physician Poissonnier; this discovery could be of no use to us, for working it requires a great deal of fuel, and when a ship is short of water, wood is not plentiful on board either.

Towards ten in the morning we sighted the Arsacides, which we made in the neighbourhood of Cape Nepean. These lands, discovered in 1767 by Surville, a French captain of the former India Company, were afterwards seen by Shortland, who, believing he had made a new discovery, gave them the name of New Georgia.

At noon we were in latitude 8° 52' south, and 154° 38' east longitude. The nearest coast then bore east by north-east of us, at a distance of three myriametres.

1792-07-09.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 214-215]
At about half past four we perceived, a myriametre and a half to the north-west, the rock called the Eddystone. From afar we took it, as Shortland had done, for a ship under sail. The illusion was all the greater because it has much the colour of a ship's sails; a few shrubs crowned its summit.

The lands of the Arsacides opposite this rock are steep and covered with tall trees right up to their summits. Several fires lit on the mountains warned us of the presence of the savages.

Our observations gave us for the position of Cape Nepean 8° 49' 10" south latitude, and 154° 56' 24" east longitude.

The Eddystone rock lies in latitude 8° south, and 154° 5' east longitude, and consequently further to the east of Cape Nepean than Shortland shows it.

We lay to from two in the morning until daylight.

1792-07-10.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 215-216]
Early in the day we sighted the Treasury Islands, four myriametres to the north-west by north; they lie twelve myriametres to the north-west of the Eddystone.

Towards noon we were half a myriametre from the western point of the island which extends furthest to the west and is the largest of this small group; its south latitude is 7° 25' 36", and its east longitude 152° 56' 34".

These islands are five or six in number, and so close to one another that from a distance one would take them for a single island; this is what General Bougainville believed, who sighted them to the west while passing through the channel to which he gave his name. The Espérance made out only three; as for us, we distinctly saw five, and perhaps from closer in a greater number might have been seen. The mountains which form these islands are of moderate height and covered with tall trees almost everywhere. This small group occupies a space of about six myriametres in circumference, and its eastern and western points run out to sea in shoals.

After going round them, we steered north-north-east to examine the western part of Bougainville Island. Towards five in the evening we were a short distance from its southern extremity, where we saw a group of ten islets, extending furthest from east to west. Covered with tall, leafy trees through which the tops of a few palms could be seen rising, these islets presented an enchanting appearance. Between them, and quite close to them towards the south, some breakers could be seen, which make their approach perilous.

Two canoes, in which we could make out a good many natives, were under sail and seemed to be heading towards us; but they passed behind the islet nearest our ship, and their rapid progress soon carried them out of our sight. On the shore of this islet we perceived a group of ten natives, and close beside them a canoe on the sand; they made no preparations to launch it in order to come and visit us. As night was coming on, we had to go about and stand out to sea.

1792-07-11.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 216-217]
After a violent rain which drenched us during the night, a thick haze hid the land from us and did not allow us to approach it until some hours after sunrise.

Reefs awash, scattered over a space of a few hectometres, were sighted towards eleven o'clock two and a half myriametres from the coast, and showed us the danger of approaching it. We could see the summits of the high mountains of Bougainville Island piercing the clouds.

The land was again shrouded in haze, and we were obliged to wait until the 13th to continue the survey of this coast.

1792-07-13.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 217-219]
We had the fine spectacle of high mountains whose slopes grew gentler as they came down to form great valleys and then spread out into vast plains, in which, however, we saw no sign of cultivation; everything was covered with trees up to the highest summits, which appeared to be at least two thousand four hundred metres in perpendicular height, and seemed to lie more than four myriametres inland.

Fires on the hills warned us of the presence of the natives.

A myriametre and a half from the coast, towards half past eleven, we were feeling perfectly secure when we found ourselves carried over a shoal which the look-out had not perceived; the water was so shallow that the fish could easily be made out upon the rock, and some points rising higher than the rest made us fear at every moment that our ship would be dashed to pieces on them.

The lead then showed us a depth of nine metres, and the boat, which was soon sent to sound this shoal at various points, found only six and a half metres at one of its ends, always on a coral bottom.

We were then caught in the most imminent danger, surrounded on every side by shoals on which we ran the risk of being wrecked.

Boats were dispatched from each ship to ascertain the depth of the sea over these rocks, where the least water found was six metres; a slightly rougher sea might have made us strike upon them and wrecked our ships.

These rocks, like the reefs of New Caledonia, are the work of polyps; like those reefs, they are built up perpendicularly, and close beside them no bottom was found at two hundred metres. These reefs rise like so many columns from the bottom of the sea; their progressive growth increases day by day the danger of navigating these waters.

Being at noon in latitude 6° 13' 11" south, and 152° 7' 51" east longitude, we lay to and remained so until two o'clock. Several tree trunks were floating alongside. On one of those which the boats brought back was found a very old notch, which showed that the inhabitants of the neighbouring island have instruments with a good cutting edge; perhaps they still have some of the axes that General Bougainville brought them.

We were drifting imperceptibly onto a shoal; but it was perceived in time for us to avoid it.

The look-outs had orders to redouble their vigilance, and yet towards half past three we found ourselves over another shoal, which we had to cross like the first, at the risk of seeing our ship broken on the rocks; the same depth was found there. The swell had been very heavy at the edges of this coral bank.

Our position was all the more dangerous because night was coming on, and these shoals lying at a distance from the coast made us fear meeting others further out to sea. How were we to avoid them in the darkness of the night? The safety of our ship had to be left to chance. We lay to until daylight, with our head to the south-west, and sounded very often without finding bottom.

1792-07-14.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 219-230]
Towards three in the morning the Espérance made signals which caused a sharp alarm on board our ship. It was thought that they indicated some danger; but it was only to let us know that she had just found bottom at a depth of eighty-three metres. We stood a little away from the coast, and at daybreak we ran close along it. The chain of mountains was then beginning to grow lower.

Some islets lying off Bougainville Island were joined to one another by reefs on which we could see the sea breaking; these were not the only perilous spots on this coast; rocks hidden under the water formed shoals running in the same direction. These coral banks were no doubt teeming with fish, for we saw many sea birds seeking their food there.

A canoe manned by six natives was behind the islets nearest our ship. As we were sailing with a good wind, we soon left it behind.

The part of Bougainville Island that we could see seemed far more inhabited than what we had seen of it until then; fine plantations of coconut palms lining the shore left us in no doubt of its large population.

Being at noon in latitude 5° 43' 12" south, and 152° 3' 26" east longitude, we saw Bougainville Island forming, together with the islets that surround it, a bay nearly three myriametres across. The General intended to anchor there; but some shoals perceived at various points of its entrance, and a sandbank towards its head, turned him from his purpose. Very low lands form the end of Bougainville Island, and before long we perceived the very narrow channel which separates it from Buka.

After standing out to sea, we lay to all night.

The heat of the day had piled up the thunder-laden matter above the high mountains; frequent flashes of lightning showed us their summits, and the thunder rolled with a terrible crash.

During the night the currents had carried us more than twenty minutes to the north. At ten in the morning we were a myriametre to the north of Buka Island; the vast plantations of coconut palms lining its shore announced a numerous population.

A canoe manned by nine savages put off from the coast and made towards us. We at once lay to to wait for them; but they stopped when they were six hundred metres from our ship; they pointed to their island and invited us by signs to go ashore. There were only seven paddlers in this canoe; two other natives seemed to be charged solely with bailing out the water the waves threw in, and with watching our movements.

A savage who had set out alone from the coast on a catamaran paddled with the greatest speed and came to join the canoe, which kept all the while to windward of us; he was a very old man, yet still very robust. After watching us for a few minutes, he went back towards the island as swiftly as he had come; one would have taken him for a messenger sent by the inhabitants, going to give them an account of what he had just seen.

The canoe left us to go to the Espérance; another, a very large one, was already alongside her.

In the distance we saw a small one manned by five natives, who came up astern of our ship and kept at a distance of about a hundred metres from it, in spite of all the invitations we made them to come on board.

A plank weighted with knives and nails was put into the water, and a piece of scarlet cloth, in the shape of a flag, had been tied to the end of a small stick fixed near its middle, in the hope of drawing these savages nearer; they did not, however, take hold of these objects until the line holding them had been cut, for it kept them closer to our frigate than they were willing to come. The sight of the piece of cloth spread the liveliest joy among them; they showed it to us as soon as they had seized it, and begged us earnestly for more.

We at last succeeded in drawing them close to the ship by throwing them handkerchiefs, some pieces of red cloth and empty bottles; one of these bottles having partly filled with sea water, the savage who received it, thinking perhaps that we were sending him some liquor good to drink, was very unpleasantly deceived when he found out the contrary; we regretted that we had not been able to warn him of the mistake in time.

These natives were acquainted with the practice of barter; they took good care to show us the price they set on their goods.

A very fine bow was sold to us for some handkerchiefs which had been passed to them at the end of a line; arrows were also received. As they saw that we had no weapons of this kind, they tried to make us feel their value by showing us the use they made of them.

One of the gunners, having gone to fetch his violin, played several airs; we were pleased to see that they were not insensible to music; they offered a great many things in exchange for the instrument; they asked for it by imitating the movements of our fiddler, using a paddle for a violin. It will readily be believed that their entreaties were in vain; it was the only violin used to make the crew dance, and the voyage was too little advanced for us to deprive ourselves of an instrument that provided an exercise so beneficial to the health of seamen.

These savages were loaded with so many presents that they soon began to make the greatest difficulties about giving their goods in exchange for ours, and they often combined skill with bad faith in order to obtain them. The commander wishing to have a bow, some handkerchiefs striped with red, the savages' favourite colour, were the agreed price; they were given to them in advance, in too great reliance on their good faith; as soon as they had received the handkerchiefs, they would no longer give the bow, but only some arrows, which were refused.

These natives have a strong inclination to merriment. They often took pleasure in repeating the words they heard us speak; the softness of their own language made it very easy for them to succeed at it.

Passionately fond of music, they were most strongly affected by lively and noisy airs. One of the officers, a fairly good violinist, played in double stopping an air in rapid time; they at first listened very attentively, astonishment painted on all their features; soon they could no longer contain their joy; various movements of the arms, keeping perfect time, and a great agitation of the whole body, were unmistakable signs of their sensibility.

The commander's expressed wish to have a bow was not lost sight of; a native promised one in exchange for a hat; but as soon as he had the hat, he would no longer give the bow.

Most of the objects passed to them were tied to the end of a line which they did not trouble to untie, for they had in their girdle a shell sharp enough to cut it on the spot.

As we had good grounds for no longer trusting their promises, one of the crew was going down from the stern of the ship by a rope ladder in order to receive a bow for a piece of red cloth, when it was noticed that, carried to the north-west by the currents, we were already much too near the coast. We could no longer steer our ship, because of the calm, and a boat had at once to be lowered to bring her head round to port. The savages, no doubt believing that our design was to bear down on them in order to punish them for their bad faith, fled with the greatest speed towards their island. Perhaps out of gratitude for the patience with which we had allowed ourselves to be robbed, they committed no act of treachery, as they had done towards the ship commanded by General Bougainville in his voyage round the world.

Four canoes were in communication with the Espérance during all this time; one of these canoes carried forty natives, of whom sixteen, employed in propelling it, had each a paddle; the others were warriors.

The Espérance told us that this war canoe had long kept its distance, and had made up its mind to approach only after the small canoes had shown it various objects they had received. The order which prevailed in the placing of the savages aboard this large canoe indicates that they have a naval tactics. Between two paddlers placed at the sides stood a warrior, holding a bow and arrows in his hand; intermediate rows were made up of two other warriors, and sometimes three, who had their heads turned towards the stern of the canoe, so as to watch every movement on that side, and were ready also to fight while retreating; these warriors had shown no hostile intentions; they had seemed to take pleasure in drinking the brandy and wine that had been given them; they ate salt pork only with a certain repugnance.

The savages who came to us had excellent teeth; for when the hardest biscuit was offered to them, none was found that could resist them.

Had these islanders had dealings with the English and the Spaniards? One of them, showing an arrow which he had just tied to the end of one of our lines to pass it to us, pronounced very distinctly the English word *arrow*, which means flèche; another, making signs to us to go ashore and pointing to it, pronounced the word *tierra*.

The Espérance told us that several had pronounced the word *bouka*, the name General Bougainville gave to their island. This word, which in the Malay language expresses negation, and which, when the first syllable is pronounced long, means *to open*, is no doubt a term of their own language, which seems to bear some analogy with Malay; it differs from it, however, enough for one of the crew, who spoke the Malay language fluently, to be unable to understand them.

The value they seemed to set on the nails and the various articles of hardware given to them taught us that they knew the use of iron.

The colour of their skin is a not very deep black. These savages are of middling stature; they were without clothing, and their strongly marked muscles announced the greatest strength; their faces are anything but pleasing, but they are full of expression. They have very large heads, broad foreheads, and a broad face as well, which is very flat, particularly below the nose; a thick and prominent chin, somewhat prominent cheeks, a flattened nose, a very wide mouth and rather thin lips.

The betel, which stains their large mouths a bloody colour, adds still further to the ugliness of their faces.

Their pierced ears were adorned with very heavy rings made of shells, whose weight had helped to give them their great size. Some had white and red stripes traced on the body; one was noticed whose hair and nose were powdered with a reddish earth which appeared to me to be ochre; some wore bracelets woven from the fibres of the coconut husk.

Their frizzled and very thick hair forms a great mass, like that of several Papuans whom we met afterwards.

They are in the habit of plucking the hair from every part of the body; only one had been seen, on board the Espérance, who let his beard grow.

All had the lower belly bound tight with a cord, which went round it several times and seemed intended only to form a point of support to increase the muscular strength of that part. One of these natives, probably with the same purpose, had his left arm bound at three different points on the body of the biceps muscle; a few flattened pieces of wood lay on the outer side of the same arm, to take the strain of the cord.

It appears that these savages can shoot with the bow with great skill. One of them had brought on board the Espérance a booby which he had just killed with an arrow; in the belly of this bird the hole of the arrow that had pierced it was noticed.

These islanders have turned their ingenuity particularly to the making of their weapons; they are worked with great care. We admired the skill with which they had coated the string of their bows with a resin, so that at first glance it might have been taken for a gut string; towards the middle it was wrapped with rattan bark, so that it should wear less in loosing their arrows. The lower half of these arrows is very light, being made of the stem of *saccharum spontaneum*; the other half is of a very hard wood, well sharpened; the point of junction is skilfully bound with about thirty turns of filaments of rattan bark, as is the lower end of the arrow, close to the part that rests on the string, to increase its strength.

Their canoes, made of several planks ingeniously joined together, are of an elegant form, well suited to give them a rapid course. *See pl. 43, fig. 2.*

As night came on, a current setting to the north-north-west produced a tide-rip which imitated the appearance of a shoal closely enough to deceive the most practised eye; a boat was sent to sound it, and no bottom was found at fifty metres.

Violent claps of thunder burst during the night from thick clouds hanging over the high mountains, while we steered south-south-west to try to hold our own against the currents.

We had just completed the survey of the western coast of two islands whose eastern part General Bougainville had examined when he discovered them. The most easterly and most southerly point of Bougainville Island lies in latitude 7° 4' 50" south, and 153° 18' 34" east longitude.

Its northern point, called Point Laverdi, lies in latitude 5° 34' south, and 152° 31' east longitude.

The coral banks we found off Bougainville Island lie in latitude 6° 11' south, and 152° 2' east longitude.

The north-east point of Buka Island lies in latitude 5° 5' 36" south, and 152° 9' east longitude.

The easterly variation of the magnetic needle, after decreasing gradually, was now no more than 7° 1/2.

The currents along these coasts carried us constantly to the north-west, by 8' to 10' a day.

The thermometer did not rise above 22°, although we were only a short distance from the equator.

1792-07-16.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 230-231]
At sunrise we saw, from north 15° east to north 22° 30' east, at a distance of about three myriametres, a flat island to which Carteret gave the name of *Sir Charles Hardy*. It lies five myriametres north-north-west of Buka Island.

Towards one in the afternoon we sighted Cape St George, at the south-east end of New Ireland. It bore west-north-west of us, about four myriametres off; its position was determined as 4° 54′ 30″ south latitude, and 150° 39′ east longitude.

We kept to windward, making short boards during the night.

1792-07-17.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 231-234]
As soon as day broke we made for Carteret Harbour, where we were soon to come to anchor. After leaving île aux Marteaux half a myriametre on the starboard hand, we steered so as to pass very close to the Booby rocks, leaving Leigh Island to port, and we came in between Cocoanut Island and New Ireland, where we anchored towards half past one in the afternoon, in sixty-three metres, on a bottom of very soft black mud mixed with calcareous sand. We were four hundred metres from Cocoanut Island.

We had the north-west point of New Ireland half a myriametre off, bearing west 12° north, and the south-east point of the same land at the same distance, bearing south 31° east.

The middle of the north-west passage of Carteret Harbour bore west 10° north of us.

Had we been only a hundred metres nearer Cocoanut Island, we should have been as in the most landlocked of harbours. One can anchor at a very small distance from the land, since twenty metres from the shore there are ten metres of water, and as soon as one moves away from it the depth increases very rapidly. We landed on Cocoanut Island to spend the rest of the day there. This small island, whose highest points are no more than one hundred and fifty metres in perpendicular height above sea level, is formed of calcareous stones of great whiteness. It has risen from beneath the waters of the sea, and time has little altered the form of the madrepores that enter into its composition; they can be recognised even on the rocks most exposed to the weather; it ends to the south-east and to the north-west in a shoal of the same kind of stone. Between it and Leigh Island there is enough depth towards the middle to give passage to ships.

As a great deal of rain had fallen during the night, so much moisture rose from the midst of the woods that clouds could be seen forming there at every moment; these clouds, which came chiefly from the lowest places, looked at first glance like the smoke of fires lit in the forest, and as soon as they had risen high enough to feel the effect of the current of air, they soon disappeared.

Tall evergreen trees covered Cocoanut Island; their roots, thrust down between the calcareous stones, found very little vegetable mould, and yet these trees grew no less vigorously, because of the great coolness of the place. It was a charming sight to see the beautiful tree known by the name of *barringtonia speciosa*, drawn by the moisture, stretching its branches horizontally far out over the waters of the sea. Various species of fig trees grew on this island. We had expected to find a great quantity of coconut palms there; this was indeed one of the reasons that had made us prefer this anchorage to several others not far off; yet we had difficulty in procuring there so much as a dozen coconuts.

We were grieved to see that among the crew who had gone ashore to cut wood, some had taken it upon themselves to fell coconut palms to get the fruit; they eagerly sought out the young leaves at the top of the tree, which are very tender; these were a most agreeable dish for men who had long been living on salt meat. Had we let them go on, not a single coconut palm would have been left on the island, and this anchorage would have been deprived, perhaps for ever, of resources so welcome to navigators.

Night overtook us in the midst of the woods, and we had the charming spectacle of a prodigious number of glow-worms, which as they flew shed a sparkling light that dazzled us more than it lit our way.

It was the hour at which the species of crab called *cancer ruricola* came out of the holes it had dug for itself. We trod on several of these crabs as we made our way back to the place where the longboat was waiting for us, and before we knew what animal we had trampled underfoot, several of the party feared it might be some venomous creature.

1792-07-18.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 234-239]
The next day I visited the south-eastern part of Cocoanut Island; various lianas prevented me from making my way very far into these forests.

Various species of *epidendrum* adorned the largest tree trunks, and grew among a great number of ferns, likewise parasitic.

Floating along the coast could be seen the fruits of various species of *pandanus*, of *barringtonia speciosa* and of *heritiera*, trees which thrust their branches, and even their trunks, out over the waters of the sea in a very remarkable manner.

Two of the crew who had followed me saw an alligator close to the shore at the south-eastern extremity of Cocoanut Island. I do not believe that this kind of animal is very widespread there; for during the whole time we lay at anchor no accident befell the great number of people who very often bathed.

Towards the eastern part of this small island I noticed several species of nautilus scattered in the midst of the prodigious quantity of lithophytes that enter into its composition.

We were astonished at the abundance and persistence of the rains; it was a torrent of lukewarm water that poured down unceasingly, and yet did not prevent us from visiting the surroundings of the anchorage.

I went back several days running to Cocoanut Island and to Leigh Island.

It was very surprising to meet there with so great a number of insects of different shapes and colours, whose activity the rains did not seem to diminish. They were for the most part beetles, which were difficult to catch. The most varied species belonged to the genus *cicindela fabr.*

We had the fine spectacle of various species of fig trees, from whose tops hung a great number of rootlets, which went down to fix themselves in the ground and give rise to as many separate trunks.

The palm *cycas circinalis* is very plentiful in the low grounds, in the shade of the tall trees. Close by we saw a freshly built shelter of branches, where some savages had come to rest. The remains could still be seen of the meal they had made of cycas fruits, whose kernels, eaten without preparation, are a powerful emetic, as several of the crew found by experience; but the savages had roasted them, and we noticed the marks of the fire on a great many of their husks.

The kernel contained in the fruit of *cycas circinalis* is very bitter; the inhabitants of the Moluccas know how to put it to better use than those of New Ireland, as I had occasion to observe towards the end of this voyage. Experience has taught them that steeping removes its harmful qualities; this process may also succeed with many other fruits, and with a great number of roots, which may in this way be made to serve as food for animals, and even for man.

On the ground could be seen many *cycas* fruits which the savages had not touched; their succulent outer covering, which gives off a very pleasant smell of apples, contains enough fermentable matter to yield, when they are put in water, a good spirituous liquor; these fruits are abundant there and may be of use to navigators.

Among the tall trees growing on Cocoanut Island, I saw with surprise a new species of areca, whose trunk, which rose to more than thirty-six metres, was only two thirds of a decimetre thick. It was difficult to conceive how a tree so frail in appearance could hold itself up at so great a height; but our astonishment ceased when we tried to fell one; its wood was so extremely hard that it withstood for some time the repeated blows of the axe. A large quantity of starchy substance, in the form of pith, occupied its centre, as is characteristic of many other trees of the same family; this pith, removed from the trunk, left a cylinder whose wood was no more than a centimetre thick; this wood is of a fine black. The fruits of this new species of areca are red in colour; they are scarcely larger than an ordinary olive, and they have much the same shape.

The *caryota urens* was one of the tall trees of these forests. Among the shrubs could be seen several species of *dracæna*. Among the tall trees I admired a *solanum*, no doubt the loftiest of the species of this genus, those hitherto known to botanists being only herbs or slender shrubs; the leaves of this one are oval, hard and very smooth.

Teak, *tectona grandis*, that fine tree so valuable for shipbuilding, grows at Carteret Harbour. I also saw there various species of *guettarda* and a new species of *hernandia*.

Mosses and ferns were very plentiful and grew with the greatest vigour in these damp places.

The western coast of Cocoanut Island is steep, and rises very high above the open sea. The calcareous stones of which it is composed are much exposed there to the weather, and so they readily fall away. I found there the nutmeg tree that Rumphius described under the name of *myristica mas* (*Rumph. Amb.*, vol. 2, tab. 5). The fruit was still not far advanced. It is more elongated than in the cultivated species. Some savage had no doubt perished among these rocks, for I found there an almost complete human skeleton.

Close by was a spot where could be seen the traces of a fire lit by the natives who put in at this coast.

The continual rains of Carteret Harbour have made some species of spiders there very ingenious; some are to be seen which have built themselves excellent shelters in the middle of their webs; it is a very close tissue in the shape of a paper cone, two centimetres high and half a centimetre wide at the bottom, with its point raised and inclined a little towards the south-east, so that the prevailing winds may have less hold on this little dwelling. The rain slides down this kind of cone without being able to get in, and cannot make it collapse, because it is held taut on every side by threads fastened to the neighbouring branches. The spider, perfectly sheltered in this house, leaves it only to seize the insects that fly into its net.

Another spider, less given to spinning than the first, protects itself from the rain by getting under a piece of leaf folded into a roughly conical shape, which it has placed in the middle of its web; everything is contrived to give solidity to this dwelling; the point, inclined a little, is turned against the south-east winds, so as to suffer less from their force.

Nature has done everything for other species of spiders, which are covered with a very hard skin, as glossy as if they were coated with the finest varnish. These suffer nothing from the heavy rains to which they are constantly exposed, and they wait patiently in the middle of their webs for some insect to come and be caught there.

Among some of these spiders, whose bodies ended in points, I recognised *aranea aculeata* and *aranea spinosa*.

Leigh Island, much smaller than Cocoanut Island, offers few different productions; its land, much lower, is of the same nature.

The steep mountains of New Ireland which border Carteret Harbour are at least three times higher than those of Cocoanut Island. Here too, right up to their summits, can be seen the marine productions of which they are partly composed.

1792-07-23.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 239-241]
On the 23rd I went onto the land of New Ireland to the north-north-west of the anchorage, near the place where our water had been taken in. The stream that supplied it appeared only very close to the sea. Further inland could be seen the traces of a torrent, and from time to time along these traces hollows filled with water, which, filtering through the sand, went to swell the little brook of the watering place. After walking for an hour along its banks, we saw it form a pretty cascade and fall from the top of a limestone rock in which could be seen vast caves that served as a retreat for large bats of the species called *vespertilio vampyrus*.

A few wild breadfruit trees grew in these parts.

I was astonished that at a time when Carteret Harbour was deluged with continual rain, we should see only the traces of the torrent and no water in its bed; but it seemed to me that the rains did not extend far enough inland to fill it; one could easily be convinced of this by the clearness of the sky towards the south-west, while the rain fell without respite at the anchorage. Carteret Harbour forms a kind of basin, in which the clouds laden with water, after passing over the high mountains of New Ireland, meet with a calm which prevents the air from holding them up; hence come heavy rains, which must take away from navigators all wish to anchor there.

Among the small plants growing in the shade of the forests, several species of *procris* were to be noticed.

Besides the nutmeg tree of which I have already spoken, nature has also given the inhabitants of New Ireland the species of pepper plant known to botanists by the name of *piper cubebe*. I saw it, over a very extensive space, clothing the feet of all the tall trees.

Our boat was sent fishing about a myriametre to the south-east, on the coast of New Ireland. There were seen some huts newly built with great skill by the savages; these had not been content, for their meals, with the roasted fruits of *cycas circinalis*. Close by these dwellings could still be seen the remains of the shellfish they had eaten.

1792-07-24.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 241-245]
The commander had come to Carteret Harbour intending to stay there at least a fortnight; but the abundance of the rains determined him to leave this anchorage much sooner.

The greatest activity had been shown in laying in the wood and water we needed, and on the morning of the 24th we made all preparations for getting under sail.

The water taken in at Carteret Harbour was very good, and had been obtained with great ease. It was easily conveyed to the longboat by means of wooden troughs; the only trouble was that of drawing it a metre lower down than the channel.

The wood was taken on Cocoanut Island, and carrying it off was all the easier because the boat could come right up to the edge of the shore. It is worth noting that the wood we cut at Carteret Harbour filled our ship with a prodigious quantity of scorpions, and with a great number of scolopendras of the species called *scolopendra morsitans*. These insects did not fail to be very troublesome to us.

The tents of the observatory had been set up on Cocoanut Island to no purpose; the continual rains had not allowed a single observation to be made; it is difficult to form an idea of the abundance of these rains; it was a torrent pouring down almost without interruption.

The thermometer, observed at noon during the whole time we lay at anchor, varied from 19° to 21°, and the barometer varied only from 28p 1l 7/10 to 28p 1l 2/10.

The position of our anchorage was determined as 4° 48' 10" south latitude, and 150° 25' 40" east longitude.

This harbour furnished us with no fresh provisions; the fishing there was not successful.

The tides were felt there only once a day and rose only about two metres.

## CHAPTER VII.

*Departure from Carteret Harbour. The Espérance loses an anchor on leaving this anchorage. Passage through St George's Channel. Sight of the Portland Islands. Various interviews with the savages of the Admiralty Islands. Their outlandish dress. Despotism of the chiefs. Canoes. Astonishing speed of their sailing. Sight of the Hermit Islands. Their inhabitants. Sight of the Echiquier. New island. Waterspout. Sight of New Guinea. Passage through Pitt Strait. Singular effects of the tides. Ravages of scurvy. Anchorage at Amboyna.*

WE weighed from Carteret Harbour on the 24th towards eleven in the morning, and took advantage of a light south-east breeze to go out by the north-west opening between Cocoanut Island and New Ireland.

The currents were carrying us to the west-north-west, and at noon we were already a myriametre to the west-south-west of our anchorage.

The Espérance did not weigh her anchor quickly enough to take advantage of the breeze; the calm came on almost as soon as she had spread her sails, and the currents made her drift towards the breakers which are seen on the starboard hand on leaving the harbour; she had to let go an anchor while waiting for the wind that was to get her out of this dangerous position.

We lay to in the hope that she would soon rejoin us; but it was half past four before that frigate had caught up with our ship. Her captain then told us that they had very nearly been lost at the mouth of the harbour we were leaving. Forced by the currents to anchor on a coral bottom, their cable had been cut by the rock at the very moment when the light south-east breeze sprang up that carried them away from the reefs. They had come too close to them to let go a second anchor to any purpose; nevertheless that frigate got off with the loss of an anchor and seventeen metres of cable.

Our position enabled us to see that St George's Channel is no more than six or seven myriametres wide at its southern end. It appears that the darkness of the sky had misled Carteret when he thought it nearly twice that breadth.

We lay to during the night, and the currents carried us into St George's Channel quickly enough to make us run more than half a myriametre an hour.

1792-07-25.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 245]
Towards one o'clock in the morning Man Island bore west-south-west of us, at a distance of half a myriametre.

A very thick haze hid from us, all day long, the high mountains of New Ireland; only a few summits showed themselves now and then, and towards the centre of the island we could see mountains of at least two thousand metres in perpendicular height. Tall trees could be made out even on the loftiest peaks.

1792-07-26.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 245-247]
We lay to from four o'clock in the afternoon, in order to reconnoitre Sandwich Island the next day; but during the night the currents carried us along so rapidly, that at daybreak, just as the sails were being set, we were much astonished to find ourselves about four hundred metres from that island. The look-out had probably fallen asleep, for he gave us no warning that the currents were setting us towards this coast, which, happily, at so short a distance, offered us no danger.

Sandwich Island is of little elevation; it is covered with trees like New Ireland; a few old trunks, having lost part of their branches, stood scattered here and there on the hillocks. Loaded with lianas and parasitic plants, they resembled so many columns hung with garlands, and added much to the picturesque appearance of this charming island.

New Ireland, opposite Sandwich Island, likewise presents low-lying ground. From the midst of a vast plain rise a few hillocks four to five hundred metres in perpendicular height.

Sandwich Island ends towards the north-west in several points, which form so many projections jutting out into the sea: five principal ones were made out; one of them has near its base a peak-shaped mountain, and this is the highest point of the whole island, although it is not more than four to five hundred metres in perpendicular height; it is consequently much lower than Carteret states. The clearness of the sky and the short distance at which we were from this small mountain enabled us to judge of its height.

A few huts in the shade of the coconut groves gave us hopes of an interview with the inhabitants of Sandwich Island; but it was no doubt too early in the morning for these savages to come and visit us, for we did not see a single one.

The westernmost point of this island is in latitude 2° 59' 26" south, and longitude 148° 29' 15" east. Its greatest length, from east-south-east to west-north-west, is three myriametres.

At its western point we noticed an islet which Carteret had not observed.

Ten days had gone by without our being able to observe the sun's passage across the meridian; but on the 26th of July the latitude we obtained at noon, 2° 50' 29" south, in longitude 148° 16' 50" east, enabled us to fix the position of the northern and westernmost point of New Ireland in latitude 2° 44' 30" south, and longitude 148° 11' 30" east. The overcast sky had misled Carteret, who had placed it more than two myriametres farther to the north.

Towards four o'clock in the afternoon we were about three kilometres from a great number of islets lying at the entrance of the channel which separates New Ireland from New Hanover, and we saw that the passage between these two islands was closed by reefs.

New Ireland ends in low land.

New Hanover presents flat ground towards the north-west, while its centre is occupied by very high mountains whose chain extends towards the south-east.

1792-07-27.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 247-248]
On the morning of the 27th we sighted the Portland Islands, which we ranged along very closely. They form a group of seven islets which, in the direction from east to west, occupy a space of a myriametre and a half. They are very flat and covered with tall trees, and they could be seen to be joined to one another by reefs and sandbanks.

These islets lie in latitude 2° 39' 44" south, and longitude 147° 15' east.

1792-07-28.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 248-249]
We continued to steer our course towards the Admiralty Islands, where Commodore Hunter, on the report of two French captains, had believed he saw some wreckage of La Pérouse's ill-fated expedition, and we made for the southernmost island of this little archipelago. Like most of the islands of the South Seas, this one is fringed with reefs lying at no great distance from the shore.

A line one hundred metres long found no bottom, although we were only two kilometres from the land.

Towards the south-west we could see a few canoes coasting along the shore within the reefs, and none of them seemed inclined to cross them and come out to us. We could also make out a few groups of savages standing on the most prominent points of land, the better to enjoy the spectacle our ships afforded them.

A large tree cast up on the breakers was at first taken by some of us for the wreckage of a ship; but the branches and roots, which were distinctly seen, left no doubt that it was a tree washed away from the coast.

The commander sent an officer on board the Espérance to concert with her captain the searches we were to make in the Admiralty Islands, in accordance with the information that had been handed to us at the Cape of Good Hope.

Night came on; we spent it beating about to hold our own against the currents.

1792-07-29.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 249-256]
Captain Huon came over to the general the next morning. It was decided that we should go and visit the island which could be seen to the east-north-east of the one we had just coasted. Indeed, according to one of the depositions that had been handed to the commander of the expedition, it was on the easternmost island that savages had been seen dressed in the uniform coats of the French navy. Towards the middle of the day we were half a myriametre from this island, when we saw natives coming down to the water's edge. A few huts showed through the coconut trees. Other islanders soon appeared on the south-east point; their number grew as we drew nearer to them. A few canoes lay high and dry on the sand, and we hoped to see some of them launched to come out to us; but the natives made no preparations to approach. As the general wished to have an interview with them, we went and placed ourselves to leeward of the island, where we found only very slight shelter, for it is of small extent. The savages appeared in crowds; some ran along the shore, others, with their eyes fixed on our ships, invited us by signs to come ashore: their cries were expressions of joy. Some of them launched a canoe; for some time they hesitated to come near our ship; but as the Espérance was farther to windward, they made towards her. This little canoe had an outrigger, and carried seven natives, who went back ashore almost immediately.

At half past one we hove to, and a boat was sent from each ship with various articles to be distributed among the inhabitants of this little island. While these boats approached it as closely as possible, the frigates kept within reach to protect them in case of an attack by the savages; for the treachery of the inhabitants of the south of the Admiralty Islands towards Carteret left us uneasy as to the intentions of these people.
