The savages, says that navigator, had twice assailed him with arrows, in spite of all the tokens of friendship he had lavished on them, when in September 1767 he reconnoitred the southern part of this archipelago.

We could see that this island was cultivated up to its summit. Various fenced plots of ground led us to think that the right of property in land is known to its inhabitants. The island as a whole has the shape of a small, fairly rounded mountain, the foot of which is lined with fine plantations of coconut trees, while the higher ground appears to be given over to the cultivation of various roots which likewise serve as food for the inhabitants.

The boats, having come within one hundred metres of the shore, found no bottom with a line of sixty-six metres: the reefs that fringe it prevented them from going any closer.

A great number of natives came forward on that side; more than one hundred and fifty could already be seen, using every sort of means to induce us to land on their island; but the reefs were an obstacle we could not get past. These islanders having thrown us a few coconuts, their liveliest joy gave way to astonishment when they saw how easily these were opened with an axe.

A savage distinguished from the rest by a double row of small shells adorning his forehead appeared to enjoy a great deal of authority. He ordered one of the natives to throw himself into the water and bring us some coconuts. Fear of approaching, swimming and defenceless, people whose intentions he did not know made this islander hesitate for a moment; but the chief, doubtless little used to meeting with resistance to his will, did not allow him time to reflect; blows of a stick, which he dealt him himself across the belly, followed hard upon his orders, and he had to obey at once. We had not expected to see man treated in this way among a tribe which had seemed to us so near the state of nature. To console this savage he was given a few pieces of red cloth, some nails and a knife, which he received with the greatest joy. As soon as he was back on the island, curiosity gathered all the others round him; every one wanted a share of our presents; canoes were at once launched: many other natives came out swimming, and in a short time there was a great throng around our boats. We were astonished that the force of the surf, and that of the waves on the breakers, had not kept them on the island.

Another chief, who was distinguished by the same ornaments as the one I have already mentioned, also made himself conspicuous by the blows of his stick which he dealt out to several of those to whom he gave orders.

These islanders, who showed the greatest joy at the sight of our nails and above all of our axes, had some difficulty in appreciating the full value of our knives. At first they insisted that the knives be closed before they would accept them; but all their fears were very quickly dispelled, and they took them as readily open as closed. We obtained from these inhabitants some spears tipped with a piece of volcanic glass worked to a point and very sharp along the edges. They also gave us combs with three teeth set very wide apart, very heavy bracelets cut from a large shell, and other bracelets made of small whelks strung on a cord whose strength equalled that of the best hemp.

These savages often repeated the word *capelle* when asking for our articles of barter. It seemed to us that by this name they meant iron, which they preferred to anything else we could offer them.

Like the natives of Buka, they repeated with great accuracy the French words they heard spoken.

One of their canoes was driven by the waves against one of our boats. It suffered some damage; but one of our oarsmen at once held it off to save it from a second blow, and one of the chiefs, mistaking our intentions, warned the paddlers, most of whom hastily abandoned the canoe and threw themselves into the water to swim back to the island; but they recovered almost immediately from their mistake, and confidence was restored.

The women kept apart at a short distance, under the coconut trees; their only clothing was a piece of matting round the waist.

The men were eager to come up to our boats: some swam out showing the coconuts they were bringing, others seemed drawn by mere curiosity; but it was very soon noticed that curiosity was not their only passion; they put all their skill into making off with our belongings. Impunity increased their boldness; and when they missed their stroke they did not lose heart, but soon threw themselves upon some other object.

One of these thieves had just seized a knife; but he was caught in the act and prevented from carrying it off: his want of success was not enough to make him give up his enterprise; he lost nothing by waiting. A flag in which red was the dominant colour had caught his eye: he found means to get hold of it, and he was not noticed until he was already far from the boat and about to land on his island.

A mirror having been given to one of these savages, he looked at himself in it with surprise and soon broke it, hoping no doubt to find again in the glass the shape of the objects he had just seen.

These islanders have skin of a not very deep black: their features are pleasant and differ little from those of Europeans. Born under a fair sky on a fertile island, they seem happy, to judge by the look of contentment painted on all their faces: they have frizzled hair, and are in the habit of leaving no hair on any part of the body. It appears that the volcanic glass with which they tip their spears also serves them for shaving; for, seeing one of our gunners who wore moustaches, they made signs to him to cut them off with this kind of glass.

The boats were ordered back towards four o'clock. Their departure seemed to affect the natives keenly, and they redoubled their entreaties to get us to land on their island. All the women then came forward to the very shore and joined their invitations to those of the men: they were no doubt much astonished at not having had greater success; but the order had been given, and our boats could not put off their departure.

It was with regret that we left these savages just as they were launching several canoes laden with coconuts, which they were bringing out to us. The delicious water of these fruits would have been of the greatest use in checking the progress of the scurvy, which was already beginning to make ravages on board both our ships: had our boats been able to wait a few minutes, a great many could have been procured.

The pleasure with which these islanders received nails and other articles of iron, and the eagerness they showed to obtain them, proved to us that they were acquainted with this metal.

These people at first showed every appearance of good faith; but they soon revealed their inclination to theft, as soon as they felt almost sure of impunity. It was observed on this occasion that the oldest were the boldest thieves.

This little island, which in its roughly circular shape measures about half a myriametre in length, lies in latitude 2° 18' south, and longitude 145° 46' east. It is extremely populous, since nearly three hundred inhabitants were seen on it.

The whitish colour of several parts of the island, in places where landslips had laid the ground bare, led me to think that its base is of a calcareous nature, like most of the islands of the South Seas.

As soon as the boats had been hoisted in we steered east by north.

1792-07-30.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 256]
The next day we stood towards the north of the Admiralty Islands. There we could see a mountainous and fairly extensive island occupying the centre of this group, whose outer edges are formed by a great number of flat islets which seem to have risen only lately from the bosom of the sea. Almost all of them are joined to one another by reefs and sandbanks.

Towards sunset we were a myriametre and a half north-east of the islets nearest to the main island.

1792-07-31.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 256-268]
As soon as day broke we steered west-south-west, drawing nearer to the land. Canoes, to which a very lofty sail gave a great deal of show, appeared in the distance.

We were to leeward of these islands, in a very extensive bight formed by their outline, and we kept about three kilometres from the coast. Several soundings were taken with a line of one hundred and thirty-six metres without finding bottom.

We could see many coconut trees on most of the islets. A great concourse of natives had come down to the shore, and some went out as far as the neighbouring reefs. The islets on which no coconut trees were to be seen did not appear to be inhabited; for no savages were visible on them.

Several canoes were launched; many were still on the sand, and six which had just made sail steered towards us. We at once hove to to wait for them: some were manned by seven men, and others by nine. Having come within about six hundred metres of our ship, these savages furled their sail and took to their paddles to come nearer still. Each canoe was under the orders of a chief who, standing in the middle of a platform, directed its handling. When these canoes had paddled about three hundred metres they stopped, and it was from that distance that one of the chiefs raised his voice and addressed us: his eloquence was entirely wasted; but the signs he made left us in no doubt that he was urging us to come ashore. The paddlers were probably not allowed to speak, but they joined their signs of invitation to those of the chief.

We for our part tried to persuade them to come closer to our ships. They could not resist the sight of large pieces of red cloth, and, after appearing to hold a council, they came on a little. Some officers, imagining that the sound of the bell would please them, had all the bells set ringing at once; but, as several people had foreseen, this noise, instead of drawing these savages to us, put them to flight: however, various flags that were waved and a few tunes played by our fiddler persuaded them to come back towards us.

Presents might win us their confidence. An empty bottle had just been sent to them, and we fully expected them to seize it as soon as it came near them; but they no doubt regarded it as a fatal gift, for they only looked at it to move away from it.

Some nails and knives fastened to a plank that was sent to them gave rise to cries of joy when the savage who untied them showed them to the others: these natives, then, were also acquainted with the use of iron.

None had yet dared to touch the bottle; but the presents they had just received won us their confidence, and one of them went and took it, after cutting with a piece of volcanic glass the cord that held it.

These natives now made no difficulty about coming right up to our ship, without, however, consenting to come on board. Little by little the number of canoes increased, and the bartering was carried on with the best faith in the world: we even saw several of these savages who, having been pushed away from our ship by the great throng of canoes before they could hand over the price of the article they had received, made every effort to bring back its value. They sought out with care the man to whom they were in debt, and some were seen to come back, at the end of half an hour, to hand over the price of the goods they had received.

A most remarkable singularity is the use to which they put the shell known by the name of *bulla ovum*; see pl. 3. Each of them had one hanging from the end of the penis: for this purpose they had made an opening below the most swollen part of the shell, so as to lodge the glans in it: this comical attire greatly amused our sailors. These natives were very reluctant to part with this ornament, on which they seemed to set a high value: its dazzling whiteness did, it is true, make a rather striking contrast with the blackness of their skin. I cannot, however, be sure that notions of modesty have no part in this odd adornment; for when they took off this shell to sell it to us, they never failed to turn away and to cover their private parts by lowering their girdle; but those who wore no girdle, having nothing to hide themselves with, took off their shell without any precautions. These people, quite unlike many other inhabitants of the South Seas, leave the foreskin all the length that nature has given it. We could easily see that the pressure exerted on the upper part of the foreskin by the shell I have just mentioned often causes a very conspicuous swelling there: this swelling is sometimes white in colour, the reticular tissue of the skin having been destroyed following an inflammation, no doubt caused by the pressure of the shell. It would seem that one must have reached a certain age to wear it, for the only child we saw was the only one who did not wear one.

The great number of canoes that surrounded us prevented several of them from coming near our ship; but some of the paddlers threw themselves into the water to bring us their articles of barter. These islanders preferred to anything we could offer them pieces of iron, in whatever form they might be: they distinguished this metal so well from any other substance that even rust did not prevent them from recognising it.

I had supposed that habit would have made these savages excellent swimmers; but their movements are too hurried, and it is only in this respect that they differ from those of our good European swimmers. They ought not, however, to have needed great efforts to keep themselves up in the water, for they kept part of their head under, so far that they had to keep their mouths shut: several kept themselves afloat by the movement of their feet alone, while they tied their articles of barter to the ends of our ropes.

If one may judge of the character of these inhabitants by their conduct towards us, they are of great gentleness: an air of kindness was painted on their features. Quite unlike the savages of the little island we had visited two days before, they gave us proofs of great honesty. One is astonished to meet with so much difference in the manners of savages living so short a distance from one another and possessing the same arts. Their conduct towards us was perhaps due only to the fact that the inhabitants of the little island had had to deal only with boats, while these were trading with ships, which overawed them.

The chiefs of each canoe usually had the articles we gave the paddlers handed over to them. We were sorry to see that they sometimes used violence to wrest them from them. One of the paddlers had just received a small piece of red serge, and he was so attached to it that he would not give it up to one of the chiefs until the latter had forced him to by dealing him a great many blows with a stick.

At the same moment, in another canoe, one of these islanders was being treated just as harshly by a chief because, taken up with the spectacle our ships offered him, the poor wretch had forgotten to bail out the water that was filling the canoe.

The savages who threw themselves into the water to come and exchange their goods for ours formed a competition which soon aroused the jealousy of those whose canoes were close to the ship: these took the greatest care to keep their place; they tried to push the swimmers away, and would not let them rest on their canoes: the latter, obliged to keep swimming continually as they brought us their articles of barter, gave great activity to this singular market-place.

These natives, like those we had seen two days before, set a much higher value on our nails than on our knives.

Several held in their hands gourds of various shapes filled with lime reduced to a very fine powder: others kept their lime in pieces of bamboo; one of them, who had a spoon shaped like a spatula, filled it with lime, and, showing it to us, no doubt with the intention of praising its qualities, made great movements of his mouth, puffing out his cheeks enormously, and seemed to wish to persuade us that this lime produced a very pleasant sensation.

Another chief had a small packet of leaves of the pepper plant called *piper siriboa*, Linn. They probably chew them without areca nut; for we saw in their mouths none of the traces that go with the chewing of betel. Moreover, we noticed these objects of indulgence only in the hands of the chiefs, to whom they seemed to be reserved.

Some of these savages wore bracelets cut from large shells, among which could be recognised sea-ears worn away in the middle and at the edges.

Most of them had their ears pierced and hung various shells from them; it is the lower lobe of the ear that they are accustomed, after piercing it, to stretch so enormously that it hangs down lower than the shoulder, as may be seen in *plate* 3. It appears that it is by means of elastic hoops inserted in these holes that they produce so great a stretching. The child I have already mentioned had two of these hoops in his ears.

Their hair is frizzled and black in colour: they often redden it with ochre mixed with oil; sometimes they tie it up with a band of tree bark. Their skin, of a not very deep black, is sometimes smeared with red on various parts of the body, and especially on the face.

We saw in their hands neither bows nor clubs, but only spears from a metre and a half to two metres long. *See pl.* 38, *fig.* 25. The volcanic glass with which they were tipped had a cutting edge on each side, and was no more than three quarters of a decimetre in length: this glass was fixed to one end of the spear, where it was held by a cord coated with a kind of mastic.

This weapon must be dangerous among a people who wear no clothing. Their skin, always bare, must find it hard, especially in places where it is somewhat stretched, to withstand so sharp a glass.

Perhaps volcanic glass is not very common in the Admiralty Islands, for these savages also had other spears tipped with a sharpened piece of wood instead of glass.

Several had the partition of the nose pierced with a hole, through which they had passed a cord, from the ends of which hung canine teeth twice as long as those of man. One of the savages who wore this ornament wished to part with it: a chief, in cutting with a piece of volcanic glass the too short cord that held it, in order to detach it, clumsily wounded the native who wore this kind of adornment.

An order the general had just given had slowed down the bartering enormously, and yet these inhabitants still had many things they wished to dispose of. One of the chiefs amused us exceedingly with his gourd full of lime, all of whose properties he seemed to point out to us with ostentation, no doubt counting on getting a better price for it. It would have been hard to imitate better than he did the gestures of our most adroit vendors of orvietan.

We saw in the hands of these islanders no articles that had belonged to Europeans. As hardly anything more was being bought, they left us to go to the Espérance with the rest of their handiwork.

Their canoes, made of a hollowed tree trunk with planks fitted along its sides, are no more than two thirds of a metre in their greatest breadth, by a length of ten metres: planks set crosswise inside support the sides and form as it were so many partitions, at the bottom of which the paddlers sit towards the two ends of the canoe.

These canoes have an outrigger about four metres long, which projects sideways to roughly the same distance. On the opposite side is a counter-outrigger which does not dip into the water, and which is two and a half metres long: it serves to rest the sail on; the chief sometimes sits on it; but he more usually stands on a platform made of latticework which covers the whole extent of the outrigger above.

The sail is woven of matting, and has the regular shape of a square whose sides are four metres long: two cylindrical poles of the same length, with which it is edged on two opposite sides, serve it as yards. When this sail is trimmed, one of its diagonals always stands vertical, and one of its corners rises more than a metre above the top of the mast, which is six metres high. The wind has great purchase on so lofty a sail, and gives these canoes an impetus that makes them cut through the water with astonishing speed.

Sometimes these savages, wishing to go slowly, make no use of the mast; they raise one side of their sail, in a horizontal position, about a metre and a half, while the rest lies on the canoe; but in this way they can only sail before the wind.

Their paddles are very broad at the bottom, and have a handle about two metres long. They use them as our sailors use their oars: it is a double lever whose fulcrum is on one of the gunwales of the canoe. One of the savages, placed in the stern, steered with his paddle.

Having remained hove to until half past ten in the morning, we went on following the coast which, as it runs towards the west, is still fringed with islets joined to one another by reefs. Beyond these reefs we noticed several fisheries made of stakes driven into the water at some distance from the shore; they resembled those we afterwards saw in the Moluccas.

As soon as we got under way, the canoes made sail to accompany us. We admired the lightness with which this flotilla cut through the water. Although the wind was fairly fresh and we were carrying a good spread of sail, the speed of these little craft was far superior to that of our ships.

Close by a fishery much larger than those we had just seen were seventeen canoes, which at once paddled out towards us. We hove to to wait for them; but as, in spite of our invitations, they kept a kilometre away from our ship, we made sail again, steering west by south.

At the close of the day two canoes put off from the coast and came out towards us. It was already night when they came within hail. One of the chiefs at once addressed us in a very loud voice. It is worth noting that the voice of all these natives is very thin. As it was almost calm, we tried to draw them close to our ship; but they did not dare come near enough to receive our presents.

It was imagined that a rocket would give them a great deal of pleasure: on the contrary, the spectacle only frightened them, and they made off in haste.

In spite of the darkness of the night, these two canoes came back towards us, guided by the light of our lantern. We sent them some articles of hardware fastened to a plank topped with a lighted candle. This light, from which we were drifting perceptibly away, held all their attention; but they did not dare come nearer to it than three or four hundred metres, and they moved away from our ship. We were much amused to hear the two chiefs addressing this candle at length. They spoke with great warmth, no doubt supposing that one of us was coming towards them with this light. Wearied, probably, by a silence that contrasted so oddly with their chatter, they went back to their island at the end of two hours. All this time a few fires had been seen burning on the shore, perhaps to show these canoes the place to which they were to return.

We lay hove to all night.

1792-08-01.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 268-269]
The next day we saw the western end of this little archipelago, which extends about nine myriametres from east to west. The westernmost islet lies in latitude 2° 11' 36" south, and longitude 143° 47' 38" east.

Reefs and sandbanks stretched out beyond it for as much as a myriametre and a half towards the south-west.

We soon saw other reefs, which extended a myriametre from east to west: they lie in latitude 2° 13' south, and longitude 143° 40' east.

During the night we made way under easy sail to the west-north-west.

1792-08-02.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 269-272]
At daybreak we sighted the Hermit Islands, discovered in 1781 by the Spanish frigate the *Princessa*, which saw them from a distance of about five myriametres. From afar their high land seemed to leave between the islands gaps wide enough to give passage to our ships; but we soon made out their low shores running out into the sea, and the reefs that joined them to one another could be distinguished.

This little archipelago is made up of thirteen islets, in the midst of which there is, as in the Admiralty Islands, a main island whose extent from south-west to north-east is about three myriametres. The islets that surround it on every side except the south are very small and very low.

We were two kilometres north of this land, and to leeward of the northern point of the large island, when we saw some canoes under sail; they were behind the reefs, in which we could see no break that would allow them to reach the open sea, and we thought they would not cross this barrier; but on coming right up to it the savages began by furling their sail, and, getting into the water, carried their canoe over the rocks to reach the open sea.

The canoe that crossed first at once made towards us; the others, five in number, followed close behind. We hove to to wait for them; but as the manoeuvre was carried out slowly, the Espérance, which was astern of us, found herself nearer to them, and they made towards her; these savages at first kept about two hundred metres from her, after handling their craft very intelligently so as to bring their sail to shiver in the wind. All the means that were used to draw them alongside were to no purpose: they came near enough, however, to throw on deck a few Otaheite apples (*spondias cytherea*) and several other fruits of different species of *eugenia*, all very good to eat. The bottles and pieces of cloth that were given them spread the liveliest joy among them; but it was noticed with surprise that they set little store by iron.

Like all the other savages we had met with until then, these showed a keen desire to see us land on their island.

One of these canoes came out towards us, while the others drew back towards the coast. In spite of our invitations, these natives kept three hundred metres from our ship. They did not dare touch the various articles we sent them with the intention of winning their confidence. Some of them, however, seemed to wish their canoe to come nearer so that they might seize them; but in the greater number fear prevailed. It was noon when we trimmed our sails to continue on our course. All the canoes then chose to follow us for some time before going back to their island: the one that had come nearer to our ship than the others followed us with greater perseverance; it was a very large canoe manned by thirty savages, who all seemed to us more robust than the inhabitants of the Admiralty Islands; they were of the same colour, and even more naked than they, for we saw only a single one who was decked with the shell that the inhabitants of those islands wear at the end of the foreskin.

These natives had come out to us with very peaceable intentions, for they had no weapons, and from on board the Espérance, which they had approached much more closely than they had us, none had been seen, even in the bottom of their canoes: perhaps they had thought that this means might persuade us to land on their shores.

These canoes, though similar in appearance to those of the Admiralty Islands, are much poorer sailers: the one that came near us had at first only one sail; but it set another astern in order to follow us: this second sail was much smaller than the forward one, and both had the shape of a rectangle one of whose sides was nearly twice as long as the other: they trimmed them in the manner of the square sails of our longboats.

Their mainsail, as lofty as that of the canoes of the Admiralty Islands, came down much lower, presenting a larger surface.

The group of the Hermit Islands, including the reefs, is about seven myriametres in circuit. The middle of these islands lies in latitude 1° 35' 38" south, and longitude 142° 41' east.

In the evening we found ourselves close to the easternmost island of the little archipelago to which General Bougainville gave the name of Echiquier [Ninigo Islands]. It is very low, and lies only five myriametres west-south-west of the Hermit Islands; reefs which bar access to it on the north-west form a wide basin where it seemed to us there would be enough water to anchor.

A great number of other islands could be seen from the north round to the west.

We carried little sail during the night, making short boards to keep to windward of this land.

1792-08-03.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 272-273]
At daybreak the easternmost island of the Echiquier bore south of us, at a distance of half a myriametre: it lies in latitude 1° 29' south, and longitude 142° 26' east.

We stood towards the west, and by eight o'clock in the morning we had already counted thirty small islands from east-north-east to west-south-west. We steered for the one that seemed to us the westernmost, and approached it to within half a myriametre: it lies in latitude 1° 34' south, and longitude 142° 10' east.

All these islands are joined to one another by reefs which seem to leave no passage. Their land is very low and covered with very tall trees.

Fresh islands came into view as we advanced, and at last we made out the south-westernmost island of this little archipelago: it lies in latitude 1° 39' south, and longitude 141° 58' east. This one is not joined to the others by reefs.

We spent the night lying to.

1792-08-04.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 273]
Towards noon the next day we sighted a low, thickly wooded island, about a myriametre and a half in extent. This new island lies in latitude 1° 31' south, and longitude 140° 47' east.

We then discovered another, smaller one to the south-west of the first, from which it is three myriametres distant: this one is likewise low and covered with tall trees.

One cannot see without astonishment, on the low lands near the equator, the rapid and vigorous growth of these trees, to which the atmosphere supplies at once an excessive moisture and an excessive heat.

1792-08-07.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 273-274]
Although for some days we had been very close to the Line, and the heat was stifling, the thermometer had so far risen no higher than 24° ½.

We saw large trees floating by, torn by the waves from the low lands. One of these trees, which had caught on the bow of our ship, slowed our progress for some time.

1792-08-08.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 274-275]
Towards five o'clock in the evening we were on the equator in longitude 135° 40' east, when we saw a very considerable waterspout forming in the south-west, at a distance of a third of a myriametre. Although the air was fairly calm around us, the waves were agitated and whitened at the spot where the waterspout had its origin. A very small cloud hung fixed a few decimetres above the place from which it rose. This waterspout had the shape of two very elongated cones joined at their apex: the base of one of these cones rested on the sea, that of the other was lost in a very thick cloud.

The clouds seemed to me to be stirred by a whirlwind which, gathering a great quantity of water, poured it down in torrents: perhaps all waterspouts are formed in this way. If, as several natural philosophers maintain, a waterspout drew up the water of the sea in a great mass, that water ought to be as salt when it falls as at the moment it was raised; which hardly agrees with experience; a trustworthy person who saw two of them fall on board a ship assured me that they had invariably yielded fresh water. On the contrary supposition, the phenomenon is easy to explain.

1792-08-09.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 275]
The clearness of the sea water was spoilt throughout the whole of the 9th by a *fucus* in very fine and very short filaments, which I met with again on the 6th of September, when I shall speak of it at greater length.

Sharks are very numerous in these waters. Several were caught of the species most widespread in the seas (*squalus carcharias*). There was one of middling size which astonished us by its voracity. Although it was pricked by four different hooks in less than half an hour, it followed us until it let itself be caught.

Being abreast of New Guinea, eight minutes from the equinoctial line, the thermometer showed no more than 25°, although we were experiencing a stifling heat, far greater than that of Europe at the same height of the thermometer. In recalling that this instrument is an unreliable measure of the heat we feel, I must point out that I am always speaking of a mercury thermometer graduated on Réaumur's scale.

1792-08-11.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 275-276]
It was for the sixth time since our departure from Europe that the Espérance nearly ran foul of us. She broke the footrope of her spritsail yard against the bow of our ship: happily the two frigates were got clear of each other by means of a spar which was at once braced between them. As it was calm, two boats were hoisted out to tow the ships and put them still farther apart: these boats then ascertained the direction of the currents, which were setting us to the north-north-east at half a knot an hour.

1792-08-12.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 276]
At daybreak we sighted the largest of the Schouten Islands, which we saw bearing south by west.

The surface of the sea was violently agitated over a wide area through which the Espérance was about to pass on the course she was holding: she feared it might be breakers, and went about; but the illusion soon vanished. This commotion was produced by a very large shoal of fish which were rising to the surface of the sea; they were followed by a great number of birds.

Although we were in the eastern monsoon, the winds had nevertheless been blowing for four days from between south-west and north-west;

1792-08-14.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 276-277]
but they went back to the south-east on the 14th of August.

That same day we sighted a small island lying very close to New Guinea, two and a half myriametres east of Providence Island; it lies in latitude 0° 18' 48" south, and longitude 133° 8' 47" east.

The continued great heat of these waters hastened the decomposition of our water: it was all the worse because the water to which we were then reduced was somewhat brackish; for the first casks filled at Carteret Harbour were taken much too near the sea, and this water had been kept in spite of its poor quality. Besides, so as not to lighten the ship of her ballast, it is customary to fill each cask with sea water as soon as the fresh water it held has been used up: this makes it necessary to clean it thoroughly when it is to be filled with fresh water; but the boatswain's mate in charge of the hold seldom took so much care; it was easy, with the machine I have already mentioned, to rid the water of its inflammable air, but it always kept a brackish taste.

1792-08-18.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 277]
The thunder had rumbled for part of the night over the lands of New Guinea, and had brought us a great deal of rain. The sky seemed to threaten a storm; but thunderstorms near the equator have a more menacing aspect than they are in fact formidable, and we were soon enjoying a very fine sky.

We could see a handsome chain of mountains running from east to west, the highest of which seemed to be at least fifteen hundred metres in perpendicular height: the tall trees with which they were covered added singularly to the beauty of the landscape.

1792-08-19.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 277-278]
Being in latitude 0° 18' south and longitude 130° 52' east, two kilometres from New Guinea, we sounded with a line of two hundred metres without finding bottom. The first signs we had of the inhabitants of this land were two fires, whose smoke we saw rising from the foot of some tall trees standing near the coast.

We were then not far from the Cape of Good Hope of New Guinea, which we doubled at a distance of two kilometres. It lies in latitude 0° 20' south and longitude 130° 34' east. We were surprised that Forest, a navigator otherwise fairly accurate, should have been so greatly mistaken as to its true latitude; the one he gave for it differed from ours by more than a third of a degree to the northward.

The easterly variation of the compass, after diminishing gradually, was now no more than a degree and a half east.

Held back by calms, we waited for the sea breeze in order to run along the coast of New Guinea, and it did not make itself felt until about three in the afternoon. The shore was for the most part sheer; there were, however, a few places whose gentle slope offered a small sandy beach where it would have been easy to land.

1792-08-21.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 278]
In the morning of the 21st we passed very close to the two small islands of Miss Palu. The smaller lies in latitude 0° 20' south and longitude 130° 7' east; and the larger in latitude 0° 19' 57" south and longitude 130° 4' 30" east.

1792-08-23.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 278-280]
We ran very close along the lands of New Guinea, intending to enter the Moluccas by Watson's Strait. It would have pleased us to explore this strait, much less frequented than those lying farther to the west. We should moreover have had the advantage of keeping more to windward than by passing through Pitt's Strait, which the persistence of the southerly winds induced us to take.

Being, at about eleven in the morning, to the north-west of it and quite close to its entrance, we found ourselves upon a shoal which stretches out from the coast of Batanta more than a myriametre to seaward. We were already well engaged upon it when the lead gave sixteen metres of depth on a rocky bottom: it was a coral bank, which the clearness of the water allowed us to see in all its whiteness. We were obliged to tack in order to get clear of this dangerous position.

We entered the strait at about half past two in the afternoon. A canoe which we sighted at its entrance, near the coast of Batanta, seemed for a moment to be making towards the Espérance; but it soon returned to the shore.

Having lain to for some time to wait for the Espérance, we noticed that the currents were carrying us through the strait at a fairly rapid rate. As the tides have much influence on these currents, they slackened very considerably towards midnight and early the next morning. Five canoes were coasting along the eastern shore, a good distance apart from one another. We noticed one which had hoisted a flag that we took for a Portuguese flag. The wind was setting us towards the coast of Salwaty and prevented us from steering towards them; none of them, moreover, seemed inclined to come to us. These savages did not know our intentions; perhaps they feared that we might be of the number of those Europeans whose greed leads them to use every means of enticing them in order to make slaves of them.

High lands, everywhere covered with tall trees, border Pitt's Strait.

We lay to all night, and at nine in the evening we heard, towards the western shore, the voices of some natives who seemed to be calling to us. A fire appeared at the same time on the western point of the entrance, near the place from which a canoe had put off at the time of our arrival in the strait.

1792-08-24.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 280-281]
At daybreak we were quite close to Passage Island, and we saw on the coast of Batanta a small village, from which came out a few inhabitants who appeared to look at us with a good deal of indifference.

Pitt's Strait, whose length is about five myriametres from west-south-west to east-north-east, has a mean breadth of one myriametre. The lead was cast from our ship to a depth of one hundred and fifty metres without finding bottom; but the boat, which sounded two hundred metres from the coast, found there, at a depth of thirty to thirty-six metres, a bottom of calcareous rock.

We tacked to avoid some shoals which lie at the exit of the strait very close to the coast of Batanta. Several persons, however, believed that there was enough water for our ships to have passed over them.

The mouth of the strait on this side is nearly three myriametres wide: two islets are to be seen there very near the coast of Batanta.

The western point of Salwaty was determined to be in latitude 1° 2' 10" south and longitude 128° 32' east.

The steadiness of the south-south-east winds took from us all hope of weathering the island of Mixoal to the east. We had to resolve to make the land to the north of Ceram, so as to reach Amboyna by passing to the west of that island.

At about six in the evening we were three myriametres from Popo Island, which bore from us south 6° west.

1792-08-25.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 281-282]
We ran along it the next day, leaving it to starboard at a distance of a myriametre and a half: it presents a flat piece of ground from the middle of which rise three hillocks close to one another. A few islets appeared quite near to the south-west: these lands extend for nearly three myriametres from north-east to south-west. Popo Island lies in latitude 1° 9' 14" south and longitude 127° 40' east.

We could see Canary Island, the island of Mixoal, and some of the islets that surround them.

In the course of the morning we lost a young seaman named Pichot, who died in a state of wasting following a dysentery from which he had been suffering for six months.

1792-08-26.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 282]
The position of Canary Island was determined the next day to be in latitude 1° 51' 36" south and longitude 127° 35' east.

1792-08-27.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 282]
In the course of the 27th our ship was surrounded by whales six to seven metres in length: they were in numbers great enough to offer fishermen, through the oil that can be extracted from them, ample compensation for their costs.

1792-08-29.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 282]
Early in the morning of the 29th we sighted the lofty mountains of Ceram, which, stretching from south-east to south-south-west, presented us with a very fine prospect.

Mountains so high must secure the independence of their inhabitants; accordingly there is only a very small number of natives, settled on a few of the lowest points of the island close by the sea, who submit to the rule of the Dutch.

1792-09-01.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 282-283]
The clouds having entirely cleared from the lands of Ceram, we enjoyed the magnificent view of several chains of mountains running parallel from east to west. The fine valleys that separate them display a very vigorous vegetation and every appearance of the greatest fertility.

Several fires were burning on the island of Ceram: we saw one on one of the highest mountains, which proved to us that their summits are frequented by the natives. This mountain appeared to us to be at least two thousand four hundred metres in perpendicular height.

We took advantage of the calm to send a boat to determine the direction of the currents, which were then setting north-east by east, three quarters of a knot an hour. As the currents among these islands depend a great deal on the tides, it may well be imagined that their direction and strength vary remarkably.

As night came on we were about two kilometres from the coast of Ceram, whose lower lands seemed to promise us shallow water: the lead, however, found no bottom at a depth of seventy-five metres.

We soon saw, rather close to the shore, various fires which seemed to us to have been lit above the water by fishermen in order to attract the fish.

1792-09-02.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 283-284]
Towards noon we could see the island of Bonoa, extending from west 20° south to south 48° west, at a distance of nearly four myriametres. This island lies in latitude 2° 58' south and longitude 125° 56' east.

Care was taken to sound very frequently while we were near the land, and no bottom was found with a line of one hundred and thirty metres in length.

A strong land breeze carried us, at the beginning of the night, into the channel formed by the island of Ceram and that of Bonoa. By the light of a fine moon we made out three islets there. It fell calm, and the currents carried us almost to the other end of the channel.

Towards midnight, the air being scarcely stirring, a wave that suddenly broke white quite close to our ship made us fear that we were near some breakers; but this wave very quickly reached us: it was a rapid current produced by the tide, which followed the direction of the channel and ran against our course.

1792-09-03.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 284-285]
We were a short distance from Kilang. The general intended to pass between that island and Ceram; but the channel, which is besides very narrow, appeared to us to be barred by reefs and a sandbank; we therefore passed to the west of Kilang, keeping very close to it. The landscape offered us fine plantations of coconut palms and banana trees, in the midst of which stood a charming village.

Our course was then directed between Kilang and Manipa.

At about eleven in the morning a tide-race raised waves which followed one another rapidly, each driven back upon the next. We afterwards witnessed several times this phenomenon, which General Bougainville and Dampierre compare to the very rapid current of a great river.

By about four in the afternoon we had doubled the island of Manipa, which is no more than half a myriametre in extent from north to south: although very mountainous, it appeared to us to be well inhabited: many canoes were coasting along its shore. This island lies in latitude 3° 21' south and longitude 125° 47' east.

That of Kilang lies in latitude 3° 17' south and longitude 125° 31' east.

1792-09-04.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 285]
A sea breeze which sprang up at ten in the morning favoured our progress towards the south, and we soon saw part of the western coast of Amboyna to the south-south-east.

Afterwards, thwarted by the southerly wind, we were obliged to beat to windward.

1792-09-05.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 285-286]
A fairly fresh breeze from the south-east took from us all hope of reaching the anchorage that day. Our scurvy patients, whose number was increasing rapidly and whose condition was growing daily more alarming, made us long for favourable winds: the continual rains of Carteret Harbour had had the greatest influence on their disease; almost all of them felt very sharp pains in the loins.

One of the first symptoms was the appearance of whitish tubercles, often the size of a hen's egg, on different parts of the body, and particularly on the arms: these swellings commonly preceded those of the lower extremities.

It is remarkable that these patients did not have their skin covered with the spots known as scorbutic spots; the scurvy of hot countries rapidly infiltrating the cellular tissue with a lymphatic humour which scarcely changes the colour of the skin.

I shall also observe that, although salted meats are one of the principal causes of scurvy among seafaring men, we nevertheless had on board two men of the crew who were violently attacked by it without having eaten any: one of them worked in the hold, and the foul air breathed there is also, together with the great dampness that prevails in it, a powerful cause of this disease.

We made tacks which brought us near enough to the western extremity of Amboyna to allow us to enter its roadstead during the night. We ran along its eastern coast at a distance of one kilometre. We had as our guide the plan of it published by Valentyn.

As soon as we had passed Portuguese Bay, we lay to to wait for daylight, which was to enable us to make out the place where we intended to anchor.

1792-09-06.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 286-291]
The Espérance had not been able to work up as quickly as we had: she was still a myriametre to the south-west of us at about seven in the morning, when we were already not far from the principal settlement of the island.

I saw again the fucus which I had previously met with quite close to New Guinea; it resembles very fine tow cut into little pieces about three centimetres long: these are filaments as fine as hairs. They were often to be seen gathered in bundles, and so numerous that they dulled the water of the roadstead.

General Dentrecasteaux sent his second lieutenant to the governor of Amboyna to ask leave to put in at the island. The governor at once assembled his council and granted us permission to anchor; but as the document which the second lieutenant of our ship presented to them in the commander's name had not yet been sent to them by the regency of Batavia, they wished to attach to our stay conditions to which we could not subscribe. It was not difficult, however, to make them understand that we had arrived several months ahead of the news from Europe, which usually reaches them only eighteen months after date. It seemed to us that they took so many precautions only to shelter themselves from any reproach on the part of the regency of Batavia, on which the government of Amboyna depends; for as soon as they had put themselves in order in this respect, they rendered us every service in their power.

We found in this small island the means of supplying ourselves, far better than we should have dared to hope, with everything we needed to continue our voyage.

A captain of the Dutch company was sent to us by the governor to show us where we were to anchor; and after making a few tacks, we let go the anchor at about half past one in the afternoon in twenty-seven fathoms, on a bottom of muddy sand. The tower of Fort Victoria bore from us east 9° north, the nearest redoubt west 35° south, the western point of the entrance of the roadstead west 26° ½ south. We were about two thirds of a kilometre from the landing place, which is a wooden jetty close to which large ships can anchor. There was at that time a ship of the company there taking in its cargo of cloves.

Eighteen vessels could be seen in the roadstead, all flying Dutch colours. Of all these ships only one was three-masted; most of the others were brigs and sloops.

The Espérance anchored half an hour after us to the north-east ½ north of our position.

## CHAPTER VIII.

*Stay at Amboyna. One of the ship's boys of the Recherche is drowned in the roadstead. Visit to the governor. Various excursions into the interior of the island. One of the naturalists falls dangerously ill. Description of his illness. Pleasant liquor of the* sagouer *palm. Sugar obtained from it. Uses of various parts of this precious tree. Means employed by the flying dragon to sustain itself in the air.* Maté *which protects the harvest from plunder. A Dutch seaman fleeing into the woods for fear of being sent to Batavia. Very skilful way of catching the* cancer carcinus. *Huts of the natives of Amboyna. Their clothing, etc. Their manner of obtaining fire; their fishing by night. Cultivation of the nutmeg and the clove tree. Long bamboo cut so as to give out very pleasing sounds in a fresh wind. Fisheries of the inhabitants. Sago palm. Extraction of its starch. Skin diseases common at Amboyna. Various reflections on the island and its inhabitants.*

At half past three we saluted the fortress with nine guns, which were at once returned gun for gun. The commander had asked all his officers to accompany him at about five in the evening to pay a visit to the governor. As I knew nothing of this plan, I went ashore with a few persons from our ship to walk about the town: it is surrounded by gardens in which the chief cultivation is that of trees, because they favour the indolence natural to man under a burning sky, by giving him in profusion fruits which require scarcely any other care than that of gathering them.

Besides the wild species of breadfruit tree found there, we were assured that there was another which bears a fruit in which all the seeds are abortive; but this fruit is of middling size, and the tree does not produce a great number of them.

Various varieties of banana and many species of orange tree grew in these charming gardens: the guava, the papaw, and various species of *anona* yielded their delicious fruits there. We noticed a few plants of henna (*Lawsonia inermis*), which rose to a height of three to four metres.

Various fragrant plants were scattered there in profusion. We met with *chalcas paniculata*, *michelia champaca* and *tsiampaca*, and several species of *uvaria*; the Arabian jasmine, *nyctanthes sambac*, rising among these charming trees, mingled its sweet scent with so many delicious perfumes. On our return to the town, one of the ministers of the Protestant religion invited us into his house. He had several kinds of spirituous liquors served to us; but perfectly clear water freshly drawn from its spring was the most agreeable drink for persons who had long been reduced to brackish water and had lived on nothing but salted meat. This worthy minister seemed quite astonished to have regaled us at so little expense. He told us that earthquakes were frequent at Amboyna, and that within the last few years one in particular had been felt with great violence: it had been accompanied by a hurricane which had lasted nearly three days; and during all that time the sea had overflowed its bounds and flooded the ground on which the town stands.

It is at the changes of the monsoons that this scourge is most to be feared, and particularly at the beginning of the western monsoon, which occurs in these parts in the month of Brumaire.

1792-09-07.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 291-292]
One of the ship's boys (Gabriel Abalen), assigned to wait at the petty officers' table, disappeared in the evening of the 7th: he had been seen on board all day; but after nightfall he was called several times in vain. This young man, of a very gentle disposition and in other respects very temperate, had nevertheless drunk enough strong liquor during the day to leave serious fears about his fate. He might have fallen into the sea, and it was well known that he could not swim.

We were all in the greatest need of staying on shore to recover our strength. The governor consented to our taking lodgings in the town.

1792-09-08.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 292-294]
It was very important for the naturalists to make the acquaintance of the governor of Amboyna, in order to have every facility for carrying out the researches that were the object of their mission; it was no doubt a pure oversight on the part of the commander of our expedition to have left us unaware of the hour of the first visit he had paid him. I asked him to be so good as to present us, and we set out for the purpose at about half past ten: M. Bourguellés and M. Van Smiehl readily offered to serve as our interpreters.

M. Van Smiehl was a German baron, newly arrived in the island. He was as yet only an aspirant to becoming, as he put it, one of the servants of the company. We afterwards congratulated ourselves that he did not yet have much influence over the mind of the governor; for he had tried to persuade him that the regency of Batavia would not approve of our ships being allowed to stay at Amboyna. Yet the baron knew very well that a year earlier two small English vessels, dispatched from Bombay to the Pelew Islands, had been received there without the slightest difficulty. They had first put in at Bouro, where, having found no provisions, they had gone to obtain them at Amboyna, and these vessels were very far from having the same claims as we had: perhaps the appearance of foreign ships in this roadstead two years running required the governor to take every sort of precaution in order to cover his responsibility: he received us in the best possible manner. We were truly sorry that he had put on his full dress for us; he was stifling with heat under a very heavy coat of black velvet: such a garment is most uncomfortable near the Line; but the Dutch governors wear it because it is a prerogative of their office.

Some refreshments were served. I wanted nothing but water, and I poured out some of that which appeared to me the clearest; but its saline taste made me think that the servants had made a mistake and had offered me some medicinal water. It was Seltzer water, which the Dutch here are in the habit of drinking as something very pleasant: it costs them as much as the best Rhenish wine. Our distaste for this drink was certainly not foreseen; yet they might well have considered that under a burning sky, after a long privation of fresh provisions, we could hardly care to drink salt water.

The general offered to introduce us also to the members of the council, and we accepted: they all gave us a very warm welcome.

1792-09-10.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 294-297]
As we were to stay at Amboyna for a month at the least, I was obliged to have carried to the place where we were to lodge a great many things needed for preparing the various productions I proposed to collect in the island. The other naturalists and I had agreed to live together in the same house. We had had it made ready and our effects had already arrived there, when to our great astonishment we found it occupied by some officers of the two ships, who nevertheless knew very well that we had rented it: the man who had the key had believed he was handing it to us when he gave it to them. This shabby trick, of which we should not have thought them capable, amused them greatly; but it was easy for us to find other lodgings.

Our fears concerning the ship's boy who had disappeared three days before were only too well founded; he had remained all that time at the bottom of the water, and it was only at about half past two in the afternoon that he was first seen floating near the ship. This small distance from the place where he had fallen into the sea seems to show, contrary to the opinion of most of the Europeans settled at Amboyna, that the currents in the roadstead are not rapid at the bottom of the water, but only at its surface; this seems to me, moreover, very probable. Indeed, the currents being produced by the tides, the waters flow into and out of the roadstead only to restore their equilibrium, which, in these circumstances, is disturbed only to a small distance below their surface.

This young man was deeply regretted by the whole crew. Several exclaimed against the carelessness of those who, having had charge of his early years, had neglected to have him taught to swim. Indeed, a few swimming lessons would have been enough to save the life of this child: it is to be wished that this example might serve others; for I have seen with astonishment that many seamen could not swim.

Our observatory was set up that same day towards the western part of the town. As this spot could not be seen from the ship, we had the inconvenience of being obliged to go all the way down to the shore to compare the rate of the timekeepers with that of the clocks.

This western part of the town, where we also lived, forms the Chinese quarter; there were few natives of the island in it, and only one Dutchman. All the other Dutch lived some in the centre of the town and others towards its eastern part.

We were so weakened that for the first few days we had to confine ourselves to a few walks at a short distance from the town.

We visited the company's garden, which has nothing remarkable about it but a very convenient bath, to which the governor regularly went every three or four days: very pure water coming down from the neighbouring hill supplies this bath. Near it there is another, intended for the women.

The Dutch at Amboyna are in the habit of going to bathe every three or four days. On those days they carefully avoid exposing themselves to the great heat, which lasts from eleven in the morning until three in the afternoon. It is indeed very rare for them to go out during that time on the other days. As for us, we had not the leisure to take so many precautions: and so two of the naturalists were attacked by very violent illnesses.

We tried several times to make our way into the midst of the large plantations of sago palms; but the water that bathed the foot of these palms often forced us to turn back: this tree, so useful for the nourishment of man, forms part of the wealth of the island.

The beach at low tide was covered in many places with a great number of crabs of the species called *cancer vocans*. They had just left the holes which they dig for themselves in rather firm ground. This singular kind of animal, one of whose claws is sometimes larger than its body, often becomes the prey of birds. I believe that the ease with which it loses its claws is the reason why one is almost always seen much larger than the other.

A short excursion to the south of the town, near the quarter inhabited by the Europeans, brought us the sight of the tomb of Rumphius. The simplicity of this monument recalled to us that of the manners of this skilful observer of nature: his tomb was surrounded by the pretty shrub known by the name of *panax fruticosum*.

We saw in the hands of the natives of the island the beautiful Philippine lory: it does not, however, come to them from so far, but from some islands lying not far to the east of Amboyna, and chiefly from the Arrou Islands. They also had another lory which is found in the forests of Amboyna, and which differs from the first in having much less vivid and less finely shaded colours: almost all these parrots could pronounce a few words of the Malay language.

Towards the middle of the day the burning sun gave us so violent a headache that it almost always forced us to seek some shade to protect ourselves from its rays.

1792-09-15.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 297-298]
On the 15th we set out very early in the morning towards the west: the heat was so overpowering towards the middle of the day that it obliged us to return to our lodging.

The naturalist who was acting as chaplain fell so dangerously ill that we could not leave him for a single moment for four days in succession. The malignant fever with which he was attacked had alarming symptoms. Extremely fetid evacuations were accompanied by frequent vomiting, twitching of the tendons, a very small pulse and a great prostration of strength. The nervous affection was carried to so high a degree that at each evacuation the patient suffered fainting fits which made him lose consciousness. A violent spasm had settled in the lower extremities and caused very sharp pains there.

Although this disease was certainly contagious, no danger could prevent us from giving our fellow traveller the care he had a right to expect from our friendship: and so we did not allow ourselves to continue our researches in natural history until he was out of danger.

1792-09-16.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 298]
The next day the symptoms became still more alarming. The pulse more and more contracted, great intermissions in its beats, hiccups which often lasted nearly half a quarter of an hour, a great prostration of strength, and a face altogether ravaged made us fear for the patient's life.

The night was equally alarming.

1792-09-17.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 298-300]
On the 17th, towards daybreak, the pulse rose perceptibly; a little suppleness in the beat of the artery gave us the promise of a profuse sweat, which came a few hours later and drew our friend back from the gates of death.

His convalescence lasted no more than eight days.

This kind of fever, caused by stagnant waters under so burning a sky, was treated with diluent drinks and antispasmodics. Ether, given very often and in small doses, had had the advantage of sustaining his strength while lessening the violence of the symptoms.

M. Hoffman, surgeon of the military hospital, came to see the patient several times a day. Our surgeon-major also attended him.

M. Bourguellés, treasurer of the company, had persuaded the commander of our expedition that all the combined knowledge of the physicians of Europe was not worth, for the treatment of such illnesses, the science of a Malay doctor. One of the most skilful had been called in: it was not by internal remedies that he meant to cure, for he gave the patient nothing to take; but after rubbing the skin a little on various parts of the body, and after massaging the lower extremities, he uttered with a mysterious air some words which he seemed to address to the Supreme Being; then he conjured, as we were told, the evil spirits which these islanders regard as the cause of diseases. M. Bourguellés was overjoyed to see that this physician was doing his utmost to achieve some success. We let him proceed as long as we saw that nothing harmful could come of it; but we were obliged to stop him when, taking a bucket of water freshly drawn from a well, he prepared to drench the patient. This was precisely a short time before the critical sweat which proved so salutary to him.

The Malay doctor was no doubt applying all his science; but he did not know that he might thereby suppress the critical perspiration of which the pulse had given us the comforting promise.

1792-09-19.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 300]
By the 19th our patient was well enough to need such constant care no longer.

We went into the country towards the west. After following for a long time the banks of a small river which empties into the roadstead a short distance from the town, we were returning laden with fine plants when, as night came on, we met some natives who had just had a successful fishing and were preparing to grill their fish. We had the pleasure of seeing them kindle a fire by means of two pieces of bamboo rubbed against each other and cut in the manner that I shall presently explain.

1792-09-20.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 300-303]
We spent half the day making our way towards the south, and we soon came to a hill where we found some young natives who had just set their snares to catch birds: these were hairs arranged in running knots and tied to a very long cord which lay on the ground and was fastened to a small piece of wood fixed in the soil.

I supposed that they used some bait to attract the game, but they told me that they used none; and they admitted, accordingly, that they caught few birds.

We could see, rising from the foot of the hills, fine palms which the natives call *sagouer*, and which Rumphius has described under the name of *saguerus...*, *vol. 1*, *fig. 13*. From the freshly cut stalks of their bunches there dripped a very pleasant liquor, which was received in pieces of bamboo fastened to their ends. Under so hot a sky this liquor ferments very quickly, and it would soon turn sour if these inhabitants did not know how to make timely use of the wood of the *soulamea*, which loses almost entirely its great bitterness through fermentation, and enables this liquor to keep for a very long time.

One of these palms can yield six to eight litres of liquor a day for more than two months of each year. Care is taken to renew the incision in the stalk every day in order to make the flow easier.

Since the heat of the sun favours the rise of the sap, one would be inclined to think that this tree ought to give a greater quantity of liquor by day than by night: the case is, however, quite otherwise, because the dampness of the night, which is absorbed by the leaves, mingles with the juice of the palm and makes it flow more easily; but the liquor obtained during the day contains far more sugary extractive matter than that which flows during the night. This extract is a kind of sugar which the Malays call *goula itan* (black sugar): it usually comes in small loaves having the shape of the hemispherical vessel in which the superfluous water was evaporated. Its colour is close to that of chocolate, but darker. When these small loaves are broken, yellowish and shining grains are to be seen, especially towards their centre; this leads one to suppose that it would not be difficult to bring them to the degree of crystallisation needed to make them a sugar of good quality: such as it is, the natives use almost no other, that of the sugar cane costing seven to eight times as much.

One would be tempted to suppose, from so exclusive a use of *goula itan*, that the sugar cane does not grow in their island; yet they cultivate this precious grass: almost all of them have a few plants of it in their gardens; but they are content to relish its juice, which they press out by chewing.

Besides the property this fine palm has of yielding a pleasant and wholesome liquor, the leaf-stalks are furnished towards their base with filaments of which the natives make very good ropes. From the shape and blackness of these filaments one would take them at first sight for horsehair, although they are nearly twice the ordinary thickness of horsehair. The young fruits preserved with sugar make an excellent conserve.

A few landslips towards the foot of the hills exposed a hard, light-grey steatite, which forms their base.

1792-09-21.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 303]
In an excursion that I made to the south-west I found several rocks of very soft schist of a pale grey colour, and close by them some very hard asbestos.

One would be inclined to think that in an island so little distant from the equator, the preparation of objects of natural history would be singularly favoured by rapid drying. The contrary, however, happened, and I needed great care not to lose the fruit of my botanical collecting. For the air, in passing over the waters of the sea, becomes charged with a great dampness which is very harmful to preparations of this sort, and the heat of the climate very quickly destroys those of these objects which retain it too long.

1792-09-22.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 303-306]
On the 2nd of Vendémiaire we set out towards the east as early as four in the morning.

We had to cross several times the pretty stream known by the name of Vaï-Tomon, whose waters ran into the sea a short distance from the eastern side of the town: its banks were covered with a great number of plants, among which were to be seen several species of *jussiæa*. I noticed on the surface of its waters the one designated by the name of *jussiæa tenella*: I admired the foresight of nature in the preservation of this plant; large oval tubercles filled with air are arranged along the stem to keep the plant afloat: these vesicles differ little from those with which most fishes are provided; only each vesicle here is made up of a great number of bubbles, because they had to be protected against a destruction which would bring about that of the plant when they happen to be bruised by the various bodies carried along by the current.

In spite of the shade of the neighbouring trees, the *elæocarpus monogynus* was covered down to its lowest branches with beautiful, elegantly fringed flowers. In these solitary forests, whose thick foliage the sun can scarcely pierce, one notices with astonishment the brightness of the colours of several species of parasitic plants of the orchid family, fixed for the most part on the largest trunks of trees. From the less thickly overgrown places there rose the tree of the family of the aralias designated by the name of *cussonia thyrsiflora*, whose broad palmate leaves were the ornament of these woods.

Among the great number of lizards busy chasing insects, I admired the lightness of the one called the flying dragon (*draco volans*, Linn.): it was during the greatest heat of the day that this pretty animal darted swiftly from branch to branch, spreading two wing-like membranes by means of which it sustained itself for some time in the air. Nature having denied it the muscles needed to beat these kinds of wings, it can only spread them so that they check the speed of its fall. With its hind legs it gives itself an impulse which, while not preventing it from descending, sometimes carries it several metres; for this purpose it climbs to a height roughly equal to the distance of the point towards which it means to leap.

On my way back I wished to take some branches of various plants cultivated in a garden belonging to a native of the island; but those who accompanied us warned me of the danger to which they believed I was about to expose myself: they showed me a small shed, and for some time repeated to me, with an air of respect mingled with fear, the word *maté*, until our interpreter came to explain to us that by this term, which means a dead man, they meant the former owner of this garden, who had been buried under the small shed we could see. These inhabitants are persuaded that the soul of the dead man wanders about these places, watching over the preservation of their produce for the present owner. They believe that anyone else who took possession of it would die within the year: this belief is so generally held that it is rare for any inhabitant in such a case to allow himself to touch another's property; and this *maté* is a scarecrow which almost always secures the harvest to its rightful owner.

The general went on board to review the crews; he gave promotion to all.

1792-09-23.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 306-312]
My collections were already so numerous and required so much care that I spent almost the whole of the 3rd preparing them; but the next day Citizen Riche and I went up the river called *Batou ganton*, which empties into the roadstead to the west of the town: it runs between banks in a fairly deep bed which it has cut for itself between hills that are often difficult to climb. We proposed to go up it as far as possible, trying to follow its banks exactly; but their steepness made us decide to cross the water, which was seldom more than half a metre deep.

We had scarcely gone a few paces when we met a Dutch seaman who had escaped from the large ship laden with cloves that was on the point of sailing for Batavia. Fear of perishing from the contagious disease so fatal to Europeans, even when they stay there only a short time, had led this unfortunate man to remain hidden in the woods until his ship had left. We pitied his lot, and we were then very far from foreseeing that the stay he so dreaded was reserved for us at the end of our voyage.

On the banks of this river there grew in abundance a new species of *begonia*, remarkable for the smallness of all its parts.

A fine-grained handsome granite formed the base of these hills: the quartz, usually fairly white, was sometimes coloured in it by green steatite, and at other times by iron, which gave it a rust colour. The mica was distributed through it fairly uniformly; black schorl occurred in it in rather small needles.

Our guides took advantage of the moments when we were busy collecting some objects of natural history to lay in a supply of the kind of crayfish called *cancer carcinus*, which is very plentiful in this little river. Their manner of catching them gave us a high opinion of their dexterity.

This crayfish usually sought its food in the best-lit places; it moved about them slowly, but as soon as anyone approached it fled with extreme rapidity. The islanders nevertheless managed to catch a great many, and it was by one of the eyes that they seized them: for this purpose, having tied to the end of a rod a horsehair in which they had just made a running knot, they made themselves masters of the animal by passing into this knot the stalk that supports the spherical part of the eye. When they missed their stroke, the crayfish was seldom long in coming back and almost always ended by letting itself be caught.

Having used up all our provisions early, we hoped to find something to buy from the natives to tide us over until the end of the day. It was already three in the afternoon when we advanced confidently towards a small hut near the banks of the river: but what was our astonishment! To everything we had asked for, we got no other answer than *trada*; and it was the mistress of this little dwelling who was thus telling us that she had nothing of all we wanted: we took good care to have her assured that we would pay punctually for everything she supplied us with. We were all the more astonished at this pretended scarcity because the constitution of these natives bespoke abundance. I learned afterwards that these peaceable inhabitants have not always reason to be pleased with the conduct of the Europeans who rule in their island. They believed they had good grounds for not trusting our promises: however, a few glasses of arrack and various articles of hardware which we distributed at the right moment won us their confidence.

We were invited to sit down under the shed formed by an extension of the roof of the hut; the crayfish from the little river were served to us in profusion. Sweet potatoes and yams were grilled for us, and we had for drink the already slightly fermented wine of the sagouer palm. This liquor, which when freshly drawn from the tree is called *sagouer mouda* and *aer saguero mouda*, is far more pleasant than coconut water. The young girl who was busy preparing our meal joined to a very agreeable face and a charming figure an air of candour which added greatly to the interest she inspired: as soon as she had brought us some fruit, she would at once go and sit down behind her mother, and it was only from there that she cast a few glances towards us to satisfy her curiosity.

This frugal meal held the greatest charms for us. Our reflections on the life of the man who undertakes long voyages added still further to the idea we formed of the happiness of these islanders, whose needs nature supplies with so liberal a hand.

The construction of their houses is suited to the beauty of the climate, and their lightness makes it unnecessary to dig down to the rock to lay their foundations.

As they never experience a harsh season, the walls are built so as to allow free passage to the air: they are palisades, often made of bamboo stems set very close to one another.

The hut of our host, standing on a plot three metres wide and four long, had, instead of bamboos, leaf-stalks of the sago palm, which, though set very close to one another, nevertheless left some gaps through which the outside air had free access to the dwelling.

These leaf-stalks, though very light, are very strong, because they are covered with a very hard rind. The inside is filled with a spongy substance which the inhabitants use in place of cork.

Everything in this dwelling had been taken from the sago palm, even the roof, whose ridge, raised about three metres, was covered with the leaflets of this precious tree; they had been folded and fastened on a long stick, and thus formed rectangles often the whole length of the hut and two decimetres wide: laid overlapping one upon another, they were impervious to the heaviest rains.

The two sides of this roof sloped at about forty-five degrees; and part of it formed, towards the entrance of the hut, a small shed intended for taking the cool air; it was there too that the food was prepared, for the want of a chimney would have made the hut uninhabitable if a fire had been lit inside it.

I was surprised to see these people, who are so fond of repose, sleep on a kind of lattice of sticks set half a decimetre apart from one another. The bed was very hard despite the mats that covered it; but one enjoyed on it the coolness of the air which circulated freely through the gaps.
