It was raised half a metre above the ground: underneath were stored part of the household utensils, which consisted of three earthen pots of their own making, intended for cooking their food, a few bottles of prismatic shape which they had bought from the Europeans, and spoons which they had cut out of large shells common at Amboyna. Among these shells could be recognised different species of nautilus, often mother-of-pearl, and also the species known by the name of *pinna rudis.*

We also noticed under this bed a pickaxe and a large knife shaped like a butcher's cleaver, called *pissau* in the Malay language; these two implements had come to them from the Europeans.

The temperature of the climate does not oblige them to clothe themselves; accordingly their wardrobe consists only of what is strictly necessary to cover what decency does not permit to be left exposed.

A pair of drawers, which often reach no lower than the middle of the thigh, or a piece of blue cloth tied round the loins, is the only garment of the men who work the land.

The dress of the women is naturally more costly; they have a kind of shift of the same cloth which comes down to mid-leg and is held by a girdle round the loins.

Our presents had excited their gratitude. The young girl, after disappearing for a moment, came back to offer us some fragrant flowers: she needed thread to tie them into nosegays; we witnessed the speed with which these natives know how to obtain it from the false aloe, called *agave vivipara.* The master of the house went at once to cut a leaf of this plant, and, resting it on his thigh in order to scrape it with his large knife and remove the pulp, he drew out a bundle of filaments as long as the leaf and as strong as those of our best hemp.

On our way back we met a slave whose decrepitude aroused our curiosity; but it was in vain that we asked him how old he was, he could never satisfy us, for he did not know. It seemed surprising to us that he should not know the number of years he had spent in servitude.

1792-09-24.journal_labillardiere: (Labillardière's account for this day is given under 1792-09-23.)

1792-09-26.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 312-319]
On the 6th I went up the roadstead in a canoe with a double outrigger. Some of the sportsmen took this opportunity of reaching the east of the town fairly quickly, and joined our party. We followed the right bank of the roadstead at a short distance from the shore: the waters, extremely clear, let us see, at a depth of six to eight metres, a white bottom made up of madrepores, over which we could perfectly distinguish a species of ray remarkable for large circular spots of a rather deep sky-blue, and various other fishes of the most brilliant colours. Among our paddlers we had a Papuan who was skilful enough to catch several of them. Standing at the forward end of the canoe and holding in his hand a bamboo lance armed with an iron point, he darted it with force the moment he caught sight of a fish: this lance, on account of its lightness, came up out of the water in roughly the same direction, so that after penetrating to a great depth it came back to our Papuan, who seldom failed to catch hold of it again, although we were all the while making way.

When we were three kilometres from the town, we admired the charming situation of a country house belonging to the governor, at the foot of the mountains whose chain ends in a gentle slope fairly close to the roadstead.

A small hut inhabited by natives, standing halfway up the hillside and surrounded by clove trees and banana trees, added singularly to the beauty of the landscape.

The depth of water had diminished prodigiously, and although our canoe drew scarcely more than two decimetres, we were nevertheless obliged to stand off from the shore to avoid touching on the rock.

Having come more than a myriametre from the town, and passed a few fisheries, we landed on the right bank near a hut whose master supplied us with all the coconuts we wished for. We had with us some seamen who, finding this liquor much too sweet, mixed enough brandy with it to suit their taste, and we were pleased to see that our host did not dislike this drink.

After breakfast each of us set off as best he could to fulfil the purpose that had brought him. The meeting place was fixed at the spot where we had just landed.

For my part, I resolved to tackle the eastern mountains.

I followed a path much frequented by the natives, and left it to plunge into the woods whenever some clearing made my way in easier.

Several landslips having laid the rock bare in many places, one could see a very hard sandstone which formed the base of these mountains. I had also noticed the same kind of stone as far as the shores of the roadstead along which we had just come.

Soon, among the various shrubs growing in this low ground, I gathered a very handsome species of composite of the genus *conysa,* remarkable for three principal veins on each leaf, as in several species of *melastoma:* it has so much the habit of the plants of that genus that one would be tempted to refer it to them, if one did not see its flower.

Buffon's phalanger (*didelphis orientalis,* Linn.) lived at the foot of these mountains: I met with several, which passed at a short distance from me, fleeing with great speed.

As soon as I had reached about three hundred metres of perpendicular height, I noticed a complete change in the nature of the soil. Beds of limestone of great purity and perfectly white crowned these heights, which then offered me a fairly level stretch of ground of great extent.

Here could be seen a garden surrounded by bamboo palisades, which was very well cultivated although very far from any dwelling. There was no possible means of watering it to be seen: the vegetation was nevertheless very vigorous, so great was the humidity of the air in these elevated places: large plots were given over to the cultivation of the species of pepper called *capsicum grossum,* of which the islanders consume a great deal.

A small shed built on the western side of the garden offered us a shelter, under which my guides, tormented by thirst, found very good water in long bamboos which I had supposed to be meant for quite another use. This water had been brought from the foot of the mountain: we made use of it as though it had belonged to us.

Although it was very hot, they took it into their heads to light a fire. I was very far from foreseeing the design of these people, who, like the most savage nations, take pleasure in having the dry grass found in the clearings devoured by the flames. Soon one of my guides was imprudent enough to go and set fire to a large bush. The air was at that time very calm; but a light wind which rose shortly afterwards drove the flames towards the garden, and I had the grief of seeing part of the palisade that surrounded it burnt, without being able to check the progress of the fire.

The way in which these natives obtain fire well deserves to be described. Their method is not so quick as a good steel; but they have the advantage of finding almost everywhere the material that produces it, for a piece of bamboo is all they need.

This is how they go about it. They split into two equal parts a length of bamboo half a metre long: in one of the pieces they make a lengthwise slit, and they shape the other so that it has a sharp edge and is only four centimetres wide. They put some scrapings of the same wood in the hollow and beneath the slit of the larger piece, which they then lay on a level surface, convex side uppermost; they then fit the other piece into the middle of the slit, where they have cut a notch to receive it, and, pressing down hard, they work it to and fro like a saw: in less than a minute the scrapings catch fire.

The tallest tree of the forests that covered these heights was the *canarium commune.* I was astonished to see that the limestone lay bare in the midst of these great woods, and that the debris of the trees had not yet been able to cover this ground with a layer of vegetable mould: it could be seen only in the cracks of the stones broken up by time. These stones looked like vast tablelands of the same nature as those I had several times come across in our Alps. The numerous cavities that had formed in them seemed to show that the rains had carried away their most soluble parts.

Driven from the spot by the smoke of the spreading fire, I went on towards the south-west, where in the middle of the woods I found many plants of the *nam-nam* of the Malays, *cynometra cauliflora,* Linn., which is grown in gardens for its fruit, whose taste comes close to that of a good, slightly tart apple.

After following the banks of a stream whose waters ran out fairly near the place where we had landed in the morning, curiosity led me to visit a hut standing near the sea. There I found an old man who, contrary to the custom of these islanders, wore a long beard: he was busy cooking, in a large earthen pot, some whelks which he had just gathered at low tide at the foot of the mangroves near his dwelling. This venerable old man, without showing any surprise at my visit, at once offered to share his meal with me. A long spine taken from the leaf-stalk of a sago palm was handed to me on the spot, and, following my host's example, I used it to draw out of the shell the flesh of the whelks he had served me on a banana leaf.

The old man's companion soon came to join him, and I should have been much surprised at the prodigious difference in age between them, had I not been told that these islanders set their happiness in marrying very young girls. Their faces light up remarkably whenever they speak of a young woman (in Malay *paranpouang mouda*); and on the other hand it is a truly comical thing to see the horrible grimace that distorts their whole face when they speak of an old woman (*paranpouang toua*).

I tried to make this good old man understand how unhealthy it was to live so near the mangroves, where the stagnant waters might bring on violent illnesses. In vain did I urge him to build another hut on higher ground; the only answer he sent me was that this seashore supplied him with his food.

The *nipa* palm grew in the midst of these swamps: its leaflets are much used for covering huts.

The sportsmen had already arrived at the meeting place. We were all extremely thirsty, and we hoped to obtain coconuts as easily as on our arrival at this same spot in the morning; but the man to whom the garden belonged was away, and there was at that time no one in the hut but his wife. It was in vain that we urged her to sell us a few coconuts, offering to send one of our guides up the neighbouring trees to pick them. She told us that she was not at liberty to sell us any; besides, not one of our guides would have dared to climb those coconut palms in the absence of the master of the hut, and had he not come back we should have gone without coconuts; for he had placed at the foot of these trees a *maté,* for which our guides showed as much respect as for the other I have spoken of before: like the first, it had the form of a small shed topped by a roof about two-thirds of a metre high, and covered with leaflets of the nipa palm; this shed was supported by four bamboo posts half a metre apart from one another.

From the middle of this roof there hung a length of bamboo about two decimetres long, tied to a cord and covered with half a coconut shell. In it, I was told, had been shut up some belongings of the dead man who was buried beneath this little shed. They gave me to understand that it must not be touched, and I yielded to their wishes, having no desire to go against the customs of these people.

The sun was about to set when we embarked to return to the town. Our Papuan gave us yet further proofs of his skill; while we were under way he harpooned various species of fish.

It was already night when we arrived.

1792-09-27.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 319-320]
Almost the whole of the 7th was spent in preparing and describing the objects gathered the day before. From this excursion I had brought back the pretty lizard called *lacerta amboinensis.* I observed that it changed colour like the chameleon; its most usual colour was green, and it often turned a dark brown. This lizard let itself be caught easily, although it runs fast; for it allowed one to come near enough to seize it by the tip of its tail, which is of extraordinary length.

In the evening I went down to the shore to examine the marine productions to be found there, and I stayed until nightfall. I saw many fishermen there, who kept in their canoes a short distance from the shore, and who took advantage of the darkness of the night to attract the fish by fires lit close to the surface of the water. Pieces of wood resting on the booms of the double outrigger of the canoes burned with a very bright flame. One of the fishermen kept the fire going and took the greatest care to keep it away from the outrigger booms, which he easily did by dropping into the water any pieces of wood that might have spread the flame: meanwhile others were busy surrounding with their nets the fish drawn from a great distance by this brilliant light; and we soon perceived that these islanders were very skilful fishermen.

1792-09-28.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 320-325]
We set out very early in the morning of the 8th to go over to the other side of the roadstead. We had about six kilometres to go by water, and the passage was dangerous in a canoe whose outriggers were not strong enough to keep it well balanced under so heavy a load. We were very eager to visit places we had not yet explored, and we embarked without knowing the full danger of our undertaking; but we soon saw one of the outriggers go under water as soon as any of us leaned over a little, and without the greatest precautions we should have capsized. Had this accident befallen us towards the middle of the roadstead, with the swiftness of the currents, it would have been difficult even for the most skilful swimmers to regain the shore. The danger lessened as we drew near the place where we were to land; but what astonished us exceedingly was the imprudence of a servant from the Espérance who, though he could not swim, and was quite certain to drown if we capsized, several times threw our canoe off its balance.

At last we arrived.

The seashore was covered with the shrub called *scævola lobelia*. It likes the shore, and I had found it there too in New Ireland.

The waters of high tide came up to wash the foot of the handsome tree whose name of *heritiera* recalls that of one of our ablest botanists, Citizen l'Héritier.

Going on towards the west, I found among the pebbles rolled up on the shore some very porous lavas, which were nevertheless much too heavy to float. As I noticed no stones in the interior of the island that had undergone the action of fire, it may be presumed that these were brought into the roadstead by waters stirred up by some volcanic explosion; for earthquakes are frequent in these parts, and the inhabitants still spoke to us with dread of one in particular which, twelve years before our arrival in their island, caused the greatest havoc there: the houses were uninhabitable for several days, and some even collapsed.

In the island of Banda, not far off and to the east of Amboyna, there is an active volcano.

At Karuku, a small island a myriametre away and also to the east of Amboyna, there are hot springs so hot that, according to the reports of various Europeans, they will harden an egg in five minutes. The scalding vapour that rises from these waters does no harm to several trees that are continually bathed in it; on the contrary, they show a very vigorous growth.

The small island of Karuku is given over chiefly to the cultivation of the clove tree.

In the gardens tilled by the natives I found some nutmeg trees, the largest of which were no more than seven metres high, their trunks being no more than two-thirds of a decimetre thick. They already bore a great deal of fruit. The nutmeg tree likes the shade of tall trees; these were sheltered by the *canarium commune*. It is the same tree, too, that serves them as shelter in the island of Banda, which the Dutch have set apart chiefly for their cultivation.

The council of the Dutch company, which sits at Batavia, finding that the produce of the nutmeg trees of Banda was sufficient for export, and wishing moreover to prevent any smuggling of this precious commodity, ordered, some years before our arrival at Amboyna, that all the nutmeg trees there should be destroyed. This order was carried out, and very few escaped; but a hurricane that struck in the same year upset all these calculations founded on greed. It did at Banda what the council had just had done at Amboyna.

Orders were afterwards given by the same council in an attempt to repair the harm that had been done at Amboyna. It was resolved to re-establish the cultivation of the nutmeg there; and so those found along the roadstead are still very young: in several gardens of the town, however, and opposite the house of the commandant of the place, some much larger ones could be seen, which had escaped the destructive orders issued by the government of Batavia.

We found the handsome laurel called *laurus culilaban*, which yields by distillation an aromatic oil much sought after: the natives know how to extract this precious oil, in which they trade.

The largest clove trees we saw on this excursion were no more than seven metres high, and their trunks no more than two decimetres thick: the natives are obliged to deliver their produce to the Dutch company for about the hundred and fiftieth part of the price at which it is sold in Europe. We saw a great many cloves which they had spread on mats in the shade of their sheds to dry them properly before handing them over to the company's agents. These natives took great care not to expose them to the rays of the sun, which would have carried off part of the essential oil of this excellent spice.

While I was on the shore I heard wind instruments, whose chords, sometimes very true, were mingled with dissonances that were not unpleasing: these well-sustained and very harmonious sounds seemed to come from so far away that for some time I believed the natives were making music on the far side of the roadstead, nearly a myriametre from where I stood. My ear was much deceived as to the distance; for I was not a hundred metres from the instrument: it was a bamboo at least twenty metres high, which had been set up vertically on the seashore. Between each joint there was a slit about three centimetres long and a centimetre and a half wide; these slits formed so many mouthpieces, which, when the wind entered them, gave out pleasant and varied sounds. As the joints of this long bamboo were very numerous, care had been taken to cut the notches facing different ways, so that from whatever quarter the wind blew, it would always meet with some of them. I can compare the sounds of this instrument to nothing better than those of the harmonica.

The trial we had made of our canoe in crossing the roadstead had put us on our guard to fit it out better for our return. The outriggers were strengthened, and we paddled towards the town without fear of drowning.

1792-09-30.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 325-326]
A few hours of the 10th were spent in visiting the governor's cabinet of natural history, where I admired a large collection of fine butterflies perfectly preserved. I noticed many very rare duplicates there: one large box was entirely filled with the beautiful species named *papilio agamemnon*. There was also in this cabinet a fine selection of shells, among which were more than twenty wentletraps, *turbo scalaris*, Linn.

The secretary of the council also had large collections of this kind. The taste for collecting objects of natural history is fairly widespread among the Dutch; it is a powerful means of advancement for them when they know how to send such things at the right moment to people who have influence in the council of Batavia or in Europe.

Captain Huon obtained many rare shells from the secretary of the council, who gave him, among others, one of the most precious and rarest of shells (the glassy nautilus), which this captain bequeathed by his will to the museum of natural history in Paris.

1792-10-01.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 326-332]
The next day we went towards the entrance of the roadstead, following the coast in the canoe we usually made use of.

At that very moment the tide, rising with great force, produced a swift current, particularly towards the middle of the roadstead. For all the skill of our paddlers, we should have gained nothing by struggling against such an obstacle: as its strength was greatly diminished near the shore, we kept as close to the coast as we could; the canoe's shallow draught made this very easy.

I fully expected to find the current much weaker along the shore; but I should not have thought the difference so considerable. The principal cause seems to me to lie in the adhesion of the water owing to its nearness to the land; whereas farther out, the sea being much deeper, the upper layers that form the current slide easily over the lower layers, and the friction is greatly diminished. When the current is very swift towards the middle of the roadstead, there is often none at all along the edges; sometimes it even runs in the opposite direction there, which must be put down to the various points of land that jut out into the sea.

In an inlet on the edge of a sandy beach we noticed some fisheries formed by an enclosure of bamboos set close enough together that the fish could not escape. The opening by which they entered was dry at low tide, so that the fish brought in by the flood could not get out once the water had drawn back a little. Besides, the fish, which most usually seek deep water, move towards the far end of this enclosure, where even at the lowest tides the sea is still a metre deep. This reservoir offered fish that were easy to take, and man was not the only one who came to fish there; several species of heron could be seen in it. Our presence had already put some of them to flight; but several others still stood with their long legs sunk deep in the water, waiting patiently for some fish to come near enough for them to seize it. These reservoirs are also much frequented by kingfishers: some were perched on the bamboos, and from time to time they could be seen swooping down on the fish, which provide them with abundant food. We soon came to a point of land projecting far enough into the roadstead to have led the Dutch to build a redoubt on it: it was at that time abandoned, as was another that we could see on the opposite shore, nearer the entrance of the roadstead. We landed a short distance from this first redoubt, and from there we went to the country house of the chief surgeon of the hospital, Mr Hoffman, with whom we were on friendly terms.

After a quick breakfast in which spices were lavished in such a way as not to let us forget that we were in the Moluccas, I went to explore the neighbourhood of this dwelling, where some marshy ground offered me, among a great many other plants, the handsome holly-leaved species of acanthus, *acanthus ilicifolius*, Linn., and its variety with entire leaves.

We then went back to the redoubt, which is semicircular in shape on the sea side and no more than a hundred and sixty metres long by a hundred wide: it is formed by walls two metres high, pierced with fourteen openings, in each of which a cannon is placed; on the landward side these walls were no more than a metre thick, while those facing the roadstead were twice as thick.

While I was ashore, Citizen Riche had our paddlers diving, and they often brought him up very precious marine productions. The roadstead of Amboyna abounds in fine shells rarely met with elsewhere; the most fragile, being sheltered from the motion of the sea in its various inlets, are often found there perfectly preserved.

Our Papuan now showed that if he was the most skilful diver of all our guides, he was also the merriest. His truly burlesque humour greatly amused his companions; he acted various pieces of comedy which, he told us, give the greatest pleasure among the Papuans: one of those he repeated most often, because he was sure of general applause, represented a woman who came on stage to give birth. He took the moment when we were at our meal to treat us to the finest part of the piece, and he played his role with scrupulous realism.

Some inhabitants of the South Seas also have comedies of this kind. Captain Cook relates in his second voyage that in the Society Islands he attended a similar performance.

I took advantage of our Papuan's good humour at that moment to learn from him how the Papuans went about severing the umbilical cord; he told me that it was burnt through a third of a decimetre from the navel, an operation that has been practised by some surgeons. The Papuans use a well-lighted firebrand for the purpose. We re-embarked to go farther, still following the same shore. Some *erythrina corallodendron* caught the eye with their beautiful bright red flowers.

On the slope of the sandstone rocks that formed the steep edges of the neighbouring shore grew some screw pines, *pandanus odoratissima*, which, leaning over the sea, gave the place a very picturesque appearance: the large spherical fruits hanging from the ends of their branches increased their natural lean towards the waves. Several fruits that had reached maturity already covered the surface of the water.

These enchanting spots gave us cause to congratulate ourselves on our outing. After spending some time there we re-embarked to go still farther towards the mouth of the roadstead.

A charming spot near a dwelling occupied by natives led us to land on the shore. The master of the hut was away; in this peaceful abode we found a young mother who, surrounded by her children, was greatly amusing them by accompanying her pleasant voice on an extremely simple stringed instrument: it was a length of bamboo a decimetre and a half long, fitted at one end with a skin like a drum: three strands of rattan bark fixed to the two ends of this cylinder, each stretched over a bridge, formed the strings of the instrument, which was laid crosswise on the knees. The two outermost strings sounded an octave, and the middle one a fifth with the farthest string. A hoop a centimetre high at each end served to hold up other strings, which were meant to make the instrument more resonant: these strings were tightened or slackened by means of a knot that tied them together two by two, and which could be slid at will along almost their whole length, as on our drums. A small blade of bamboo bark was used to set vibrating the strings raised by the bridges. The accompaniment, though very monotonous, seemed to please our guides immensely, their ears being accustomed to this kind of music.

This dwelling was surrounded by nutmeg trees that were still young, yet already bearing well, although at Amboyna people are not generally very satisfied with their cultivation; the surroundings formed a fine orchard where we never tired of admiring the brilliant flowers of the *eugenia malaccensis:* the *averrhoa carambola* was to be seen there, whose fruit pleased us greatly by its agreeable tartness.

The edge of the shore was adorned by a large plantation of the species of tree named *aeschinomene grandiflora;* its flower, the largest among the leguminous plants, is commonly a fine white and sometimes also red. The natives often eat it cooked, and sometimes even raw in a salad.

The bark of this tree yields a bitter extract which is used as a tonic in fevers.

The day was drawing to its close; the current was against us. We were obliged to hug the shore very closely, and it was night by the time we reached the town.

1792-10-02.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 332-333]
As soon as I had arranged in the most suitable manner the produce of my last excursions, I went off towards the south-east a short distance from the town. I found still more plants to add to my collections. On my way back I saw a white Negro of Papuan origin. He had fair hair: his skin was white and freckled like that of Europeans with red hair; but he did not have weak sight, as is usually the case with other albinos.

This young Papuan, the slave of a Dutchman, had not been long at Amboyna. When I came up to him he was busy playing an instrument which I was surprised to see among those of these peoples: it was a Jew's harp made of bamboo, cut from the hardest part of that wood; it was not quite so large as the iron ones we know. As the tongue could not be bent to make it vibrate with the finger, a small cord fixed to one end of the instrument served to give it the jerk needed to set the tongue in motion, which then gave out the same sounds as the iron blade of our Jew's harps. He told me that this instrument was a great favourite with the Papuans.

1792-10-03.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 333-337]
For some days we had planned to go to the country house of the commandant of the place, which stood towards the head of the roadstead; his son went with us.

Day had not yet broken. It was barely five o'clock when we were already in our canoes.

We soon arrived beneath a roof surrounded by trees which gave a wholesome shade in these burning climates, and they were no idle ornament of this delightful abode, for almost all of them bore excellent fruit. Of the various custard apples offered to us, the best were of the species known by the name of *anona muricata.*

We re-embarked shortly after our arrival, and we were already nearly a myriametre from the town when we passed a point of land beyond which the roadstead stretches a long way towards the north.

A fresh south-east wind slowed our progress and drove against our frail craft a sea that was very troublesome indeed. At that moment a large boat laden with water was coming out of this inlet, into which flows a river that supplies the ships; it was going on board the Espérance. Water is fetched from so great a distance only because it is much easier to take in there than near the town, where, however, very good water is also to be found.

The current caused by the ebb was against us, but our paddlers redoubled their efforts, and at last we landed towards the head of this vast arm of the roadstead.

For some time we walked in the shade of nutmeg trees, which were here in much greater numbers than in any part of the island we had visited until then. These too were young plants.

The son of the commandant of the place had many relations here. We were close by the house of one of his cousins, who was a native of the island: we had to dine there in the manner of the inhabitants; fish, sago bread, rice and some fruit made up our meal. As no spoons were served to us, we were obliged to follow our host's example and take the food with our fingers, and we ate none the less heartily for that.

We all got on fairly well with the sago bread. The fish was strongly seasoned with pepper; but a few glasses of *sagouer* water lessened the violence of its effects. During our meal we had the pleasure of music. A kind of spinet accompanied a man's voice, a drum played the bass, and the tam-tam the double bass.

After dinner our host took us in his canoe a kilometre towards the east.

There we saw a man at work on a sago palm. This tree, half a metre thick, had lately been felled; it had already been opened along part of its length, which in all was no more than twelve metres, and a great deal of sago had been taken from it. This palm, keeping, like the other trees of that family, much the same diameter throughout, yields about as much sago in the upper part of its stem as near its root (a very exact figure of a young sago palm may be seen in *pl. 42, fig.* a). Its trunk is formed on the outside of a very hard woody layer no more than a centimetre thick. It is a great cylinder filled with a starch through which, along the whole length of the trunk, run woody fibres about a third of a millimetre thick, often half a centimetre apart from one another.

The sago is pounded after being taken out of the tree; it is put into bags made of a kind of canvas furnished by the leaf-stalks of the coconut palm towards their base. Very clear water is poured several times over these bags, carrying the starch through, while this sort of sieve holds back part of the woody fibres.

The water charged with starch is received in troughs made from the lower part of the leaf-stalks of the sago palm. These troughs are cut a metre long. At the end of each is fixed a sieve which retains part of the starch as it settles, and the woody fibres that escaped the first washing are seen floating on the top.

This sieve, too, had cost no preparation. It was of the same nature as the other, and presented a web of crossed fibres, differing from that of our cloths in that their several layers were simply laid one upon another along their whole length; but a few short fibres passing from one layer to the next bound them together and made them into a firm web.

To remove the woody fibres found in the sago starch, after it has been washed in the bags, it is passed again through troughs, commonly four in number, set one above another, so that whatever has not settled in the first is received in the second, and so on.

The tissue of the sago palm well deserved examination, and so I cut off a section of it, in which I noticed a texture common to many other palms, as Citizen Desfontaines has so well described in a memoir on the plants with one seed-leaf.

1792-10-04.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 337]
For the next two days I could go only a very short way from the town, because unremitting care was needed to preserve my numerous collections. An intelligent assistant would have saved each naturalist much precious time, which he could have employed in a far more useful manner.

1792-10-05.journal_labillardiere: (Labillardière's account for this day is given under 1792-10-04.)

1792-10-06.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 337-341]
But on the 16th it was scarcely daylight when we were out on the roadstead. We crossed it, heading towards its mouth, and landed near a redoubt about a myriametre from the town. The roadstead was fully seven kilometres wide at this spot; and so enemy ships would have no more to fear from this bastion than from the first one I have already spoken of: it is built in exactly the same way; only this one is nearer the entrance of the roadstead.

Close by, a few huts formed a small hamlet in which there reigned an air of cleanliness that showed the comfortable circumstances of its inhabitants. The sea supplies them with abundant food, and most of the buildings were surrounded by well-cultivated gardens.

Some of these islanders raised poultry to take to the town market. We accepted the invitation of one of these worthy inhabitants, who would not be refused in treating us to fresh eggs. Most of the gardens were surrounded by shrubs, among which could be distinguished the *jatropha curcas*, whose plants, set very close together, made good hedges: its seeds have a rather pleasant taste of hazelnut. The natives warned us that, eaten even in small quantity, they caused great drowsiness; they did not know that the narcotic property of this fruit resides in the part known to botanists by the name of embryo. I had the pleasure of teaching them that by removing it the kernel could be eaten in perfect safety.

We went on into the interior, where we noticed a few annatto plants, *bixa orellana*, cultivated with little care. Having come very close to the entrance of the roadstead, we could see in the distance some large canoes beating up to reach it, and some others that were already near its mouth.

Our little canoe had come to the meeting place when the rising tide raised a sea that gave the paddler no little trouble; the water at once became very choppy. We had to wait for it to calm down before re-embarking to go to the other side of the roadstead, farther than we had yet gone.

For some time we coasted along the shore, so as to stem the tide more easily and make up for the drift that the strength of the current was about to cause us. A great number of dolphins, *delphinus delphis*, heading swiftly towards the head of the roadstead, passed so close to us that those who could not swim were in lively fear that the canoe would be overturned.

We soon landed near a small dwelling situated in one of the most beautiful spots in this island.

The fishermen on the other shore had furnished us abundantly with fish, and one of us wished to have it dressed in the manner of the inhabitants of the South Seas. Coconut water was to be the principal seasoning. He had pepper added to this dish so much praised by Captain Cook. We were pleased to see that it was greatly to the taste of our hosts, to whom it was unknown; they had eagerly supplied our guides with everything needed for complete success. The one who had given the orders for the preparation of this excellent dish acquired the reputation of a very good cook among these people, who amused us greatly by asking us over and over again whether he was not the head cook of our ship.

In the neighbourhood of this hut I admired the handsome shrub known by the name of *abroma augusta*. The *hedysarum umbellatum* made a fine show among several new species of the same genus. The nutmeg trees drew thither pigeons of the species called *columba alba*, Linn. Those we shot had their crops full of nutmegs.

The excessive perspiration caused by this burning climate often gives rise to diseases of the skin. Five of our hosts had their bodies covered with scaly tetters, whose scales, falling off, were at once replaced by others, and were all the more conspicuous because their colour contrasted strongly with the coppery tint of their skin. This disease often spreads over every part of the body. We also saw some children affected with another skin disease which did not seem to cause them any suffering: almost their whole body was covered with large warts no more than a third of a decimetre apart from one another.

I seldom visited huts at Amboyna without finding musical instruments in them. Here again I saw one I had not met with elsewhere; it was a recorder whose lower end divided into two diverging branches pierced with holes placed in the same way on both, thus forming two flutes which gave out the same notes fairly true. These natives were very fond of playing in unison; they used one hand for each branch.

I returned to the town on a dark night; the waters of the roadstead showed me masses of small bodies which lit up the surface in the form of broad patches of light. The water I took from the most phosphorescent spots left on the filter through which I passed it some small molluscs which in no way differed from those I had already examined before reaching the Cape of Good Hope, and elsewhere, at great distances from land.

We landed on the shore near the town at high water. We had to walk more than three hundred metres through the water, as our canoes could come no nearer to the bank because of the shallowness. The fishermen had just lit fires to attract the fish, which the flood tide had brought in in such quantity that we saw their nets loaded with them.

1792-10-07.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 341-343]
The next two days were spent in exploring the neighbourhood of the town. I was surprised to meet with so many different species of plants in so small an island; but no doubt the nearness of Ceram enriches it with part of the plants of that large island.

In the evening the governor gave an entertainment on the occasion of the birthday of one of his sons; this son was in Europe, finishing his education there: all the naturalists were invited, and we went to Government House an hour after sunset. The coolness of the air then permitted dancing; the ball had already begun, and several country dances had been formed in the great hall where the governor had received us on the first visit we paid him with General Dentrecasteaux.

This hall was a kind of gallery decorated with a few engravings and a small number of very mediocre pictures hung at great distances from one another. The walls were merely coated with a few layers of lime; yet it would have been very easy, and at little expense, to adorn them with fine wainscoting, since the island furnishes several woods suitable for marquetry.

Almost all the young daughters of the company's officials were at the ball. Although the heat of the climate might well dispose one to avoid any hurried movement, we were surprised to see that these young ladies had adopted a manner of dancing that did much to hinder the display of their graces; they were content to walk slowly, barely forming the figures; and this air of nonchalance contrasted strangely with the extreme lightness the male dancer put into the various steps of these country dances.

The orchestra was composed of four Black slaves who played the violin, and another who played the bass.

The ball was followed by a splendid feast, which was served in the same hall.

From the small number of guests assembled towards half past nine, I thought the supper party would not be large; but most of them, caring little for dancing, did not come until about ten in the evening.

Gaiety presided over this meal, which lasted a good part of the night, while the ball soon began again and did not stop until sunrise.

We were surprised not to find at this entertainment Mr Strampfer, one of the ministers of the Protestant religion, who had given us a very warm welcome; but we soon learned that he had lately fallen into disgrace with the governor, because, after giving very assiduous care for several years to the education of his children, the poor man had taken it into his head to claim the payment that was due to him: in vain did he represent that the honour, so much vaunted to him, of having attended to the education of the governor's children was not altogether enough for the father of a family; he could obtain nothing more.

1792-10-08.journal_labillardiere: (Labillardière's account for this day is given under 1792-10-07.)

1792-10-09.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 343-344]
I spent part of the 19th in going through several gardens where, among the plants that adorned them, one noticed the China box, *murraya exotica*, which formed very fine walks. The variegated carmantine, *justitia variegata*, and the variegated croton, *croton variegatum*, so remarkable for the beauty of their flowers and their foliage.

Henna, *lawsonia inermis*, called by the natives *boungnia laca*, is used, as in Asia, to dye certain parts of the body, and particularly the tips of the fingers: it is the Chinese who make most use of it.

Soon I found myself near a hut surrounded by a great number of coconuts hung from the edges of the roof and from the neighbouring trees. The master of this cabin told me, pointing to his large family, that he was preparing to make a great plantation of coconut palms: most of these coconuts had already sprouted, and he was not to commit them to the ground until the young plant had reached about half a metre in height. He assured me that without this precaution many would have rotted without coming up.

1792-10-11.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 344]
The time of our departure from Amboyna was drawing near; the collections I had made in this charming island were carried to the ship, whither I repaired in the evening of the 21.

1792-10-12.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 344-367]
The haste with which everyone in the expedition had been urged to go on board the frigates the evening before had led us to suppose that all was ready for departure, and that only contrary winds could prevent us from setting sail. However, we still had to replace part of the water that had been used during our stay at anchor; this work was not finished until the afternoon, and we could not leave until the next day.

The men of the crew were very well pleased with this port of call; they had enjoyed there all the leisure they could wish for, and slaves had even been employed to bring us our supply of water and wood in large longboats called *yacou*.

Our ship had just been caulked, and the rigging, having been examined with scrupulous attention, was found to be generally in good condition.

The island of Amboyna, called *Ambon* by the natives, was then the first of the Dutch governments in the Indies, after the general government of Batavia.

The latitude of the site of the observatory, towards the western end of the town, was found to be 3° 41' 40" south, and its east longitude 126° 9'.

The variation of the compass needle there was 1° 13' 20" west.

A flat needle gave 3° of dip.

Although the heat was oppressive, the thermometer nevertheless varied each day, fairly regularly, only from the 22<sup>nd</sup>° to the 25<sup>th</sup>°.

The barometer stood fairly constantly at 28<sup>p</sup> 2<sup>l</sup>; its variation being no more than 1<sup>l</sup>.

The time of high water at our anchorage at the syzygies was half past twelve, and the water rose about twenty-five decimetres. The tides are felt twice a day.

The roadstead of Amboyna forms a channel about two myriametres long, with a mean width of two-thirds of a myriametre. Its shores often afford good anchorage, though sometimes a coral bottom. Towards the middle the water is too deep to let go the anchor.

The fort called Fort Victoria is built of brick; the governor and some members of the council have their residence there. It was then falling into ruin, and whenever the cannon were fired from it, it always suffered some very visible damage.

The garrison was made up of about two hundred men, of whom the natives of the island formed the greater number; the rest were some of the company's soldiers come from Europe, and a weak detachment of the regiment of Wirtemberg.

Most of the European soldiers were tormented by the desire to see their native land again; but none could foresee the moment when he would be allowed to return there. Some who had been lured with this vain hope for many years were an example to the others that cast gloom into their souls.

The small number of soldiers who survive a stay in the Indies makes those who have spent a few years there all the more valuable; and so the Dutch company is seldom faithful to the promises it makes them to let them go back to Europe when their time has expired. First every sort of means is tried to make them sign on a second time; and those who carefully avoid anything that might tend to prolong their stay in the island do not obtain their freedom any the sooner for it. I met some of these unfortunate men who had been kept there for more than twenty years, although by the terms of their agreements they ought by then to have been free.

The island of Amboyna is divided into several districts, which in many places form so many villages called nygri. The command of each nygri is given to a native who is honoured with the title of orancaye. This man, to whom the policing of his small canton has been entrusted, is himself strictly subordinate to the Dutch government; it is to the government that he refers in serious cases. The Dutch usually choose as orancayes natives who follow the Protestant religion, preferring the old chiefs or their nearest relations, and above all those who are best off.

Each of these orancayes has about a hundred natives under his supervision. The Dutch company, in investing them with this authority, presents them with a silver-hilted sword. These chiefs are dressed in the European manner, all in black: they wear a three-cornered hat with very sharp and deeply lowered corners; shoes also go with this ceremonial dress, which they put on only when they are obliged to appear in public or to present themselves before the Dutch chiefs.

The name of orancaye is formed from two Malay words, *oran kaya*, which, literally translated, mean rich man. The dignity of orancaye is no empty title; it gives these petty chiefs the means of making their fortune, which they seldom fail to use, however oppressive they may be to those under them; for in laying the poor Amboynese under contribution on behalf of the company's agents, they take care not to forget their own interests. It sometimes happens, however, that this fortune crumbles faster than it was made, when the company's agents find ways to turn the greed of the orancayes to their own advantage.

The inhabitants of Amboyna speak the Malay language; it is very soft: its affinity with the language of the peoples of the South Seas has led me to give, towards the end of the second volume, a fairly extensive vocabulary of it, which I collected at Amboyna and in the island of Java, where I stayed a very long time at the end of this campaign.

The use of betel has been established among these peoples from time immemorial. They take a few young leaves of the pepper plant named *piper siriboa*, in Malay *siri*, and after covering them with a little very pure lime made from shells and freshly slaked, they chew them with areca nut: some interrupt this pleasure only at mealtimes and when sleeping. I was very much surprised that, in spite of the continual use of lime, these peoples should generally have very sound teeth; they do, however, take on a blackness which penetrates the enamel without lessening its polish in any way; and so they are in the habit of cleaning them frequently, and the powder they use is not very elaborate; they obtain it from a limestone of middling hardness, which they grind on sandstone. They also use a piece of sandstone to wear down the outer part of the incisors.

These peoples are not content with chewing betel; they receive from Malacca an extract of bitter plants known by the name of *gamber*, which they also use for chewing.

Mountains of moderate height cover the island of Amboyna, chiefly in its eastern part.

The coffee grown there seemed to us inferior to that of our islands, the Isle of France [Mauritius] and Réunion. The Dutch settled in the Moluccas seem moreover to care little how it is prepared for them. Their servants are all in the habit of roasting it to such a degree that it is almost reduced to charcoal; this is to make it easier to grind, and because they use only wooden mortars and pestles for the purpose.

Most of the marshy places are given over to the cultivation of the sago palm, which provides the inhabitants with very wholesome food: it is among the provisions they lay in for their long voyages, as is the kernel of the canary nut, which they dry so that it will keep. This kernel is even more pleasant to the taste when fresh.

The rice consumed at Amboyna is not a product of the island; it would, however, do very well in most of the low-lying ground, where the water springing from the foot of the mountains offers every possible facility for its cultivation; but the Dutch company has forbidden the growing of this commodity, because its sale is a means of drawing back out of the natives' hands the coin it is obliged to give them for the cloves they supply to it. In this way they prevent any increase in the money in circulation, and always keep the produce of the inhabitants' labour at a very low price. Besides, rice being in fairly general use among those who are somewhat well off, it becomes a lucrative branch of trade in the hands of the company's agents who supply them with it. They draw it chiefly from the island of Java.

It is thus that this government, consulting only its own interests, stifles all industry among these peoples, by forcing them to abandon, so to speak, every other kind of cultivation for that of clove trees and nutmeg trees.

The Dutch take care to limit the cultivation of spices, so that it shall not greatly exceed ordinary consumption. These means, destructive of all activity, suit well enough, moreover, with the indolence of these peoples. Many farinaceous roots and a great number of trees afford them abundant food almost without cultivation, as if nature had wished to make up to man for the inertia to which she seems to have condemned him under so burning a sky.

Grafting would no doubt be a means of improving the various fruits that grow in this island; but no one, even among the Europeans, has yet succeeded in making a graft take; they have always let it dry out before the circulation of the sap was established between it and the tree on which they had set it. Yet it would be easy to prevent this mishap by keeping up a suitable moisture until one was sure that the graft had succeeded.

European vegetables take poorly to the heat of the climate.

A very small banana, named *pisang radja*, is considered the best kind; after the litchi and the mangosteen, it is the best of the fruits I ate at Amboyna. They also have several species of litchi, among which must be counted the *ramb-outan* of the Malays, *nephelium lappaceum*. Three celebrated botanists, Linnaeus, Jussieu and Gærtner, have been mistaken in placing this genus, no doubt because they had not had the opportunity of seeing the parts of its fructification complete.

Linnaeus classed it in the family of the spurges, Jussieu placed it in that of the composites, and Gærtner put it in that of the amentaceous plants; but it evidently belongs to the family of the soapberries.

The same prohibitive system that we had seen followed at the Cape of Good Hope was followed likewise at Amboyna. To avoid any rise in the price of provisions, the company undertook to supply us. The natives furnished it at a paltry price with provisions which it knew how to turn to good account with us.

The Dutch have made into law a practice more pernicious still. The principal officials of the company have the right to take from the natives, without paying, the victuals needed for their daily consumption. Nothing more oppressive than this arbitrary levy can be imagined. The most industrious man, like the most idle, is almost certain that he will be left barely enough to live on; and so most are content to live by an easy cultivation, passing in idleness a time which, under any other regime, they would have employed in acquiring a certain comfort.

The fiscal completes the oppression of the inhabitants: he is in charge of the police; he has the right to impose for his own profit fines which he fixes according to his own greed and the wealth of the natives whom it often pleases him to find guilty, without their having committed the slightest offence. It was Mr Mackaye who then held this post. He was very different from most of his predecessors; the inhabitants of the island had nothing but praise for his humanity, and he deserved all the more credit for doing good, since his position enabled him to do them every possible harm with impunity. This worthy man kept telling us that he would rather live in modest circumstances than grow rich by using such means. One day, when explaining to us all the rights of his office, Mr Mackaye told us that some sailors from our ships had caused a disturbance during the night, at an unseasonable hour, at the house of a very rich Chinese who sold arrack and other spirituous liquors. He told us with great simplicity that he could, in this case, have taken advantage of the rights of his office, got a great deal of money out of this Chinese, and imposed a heavy fine on him for his own profit. Many others, he told us, would not have failed to do so; but I never repent of having done good.

The clove tree is the chief crop of Amboyna and of several islets lying to the east of that island, where it thrives as well as can be. The Dutch keep residents there to prevent the fraudulent export of this precious commodity.

It appears that the soil and lie of the land in the island of Banda are even better suited to the cultivation of the nutmeg tree than the island of Amboyna, for it is generally acknowledged that the nutmeg of the latter island is inferior.

Formerly the nutmeg tree and the clove tree were spread through the islands of Ternate, Tidore, Makian, etc., in much greater quantity than at Amboyna and Banda; but the Dutch, wishing to appropriate these precious trees exclusively to themselves, forced the sovereigns of the former islands to destroy the plantations: they keep agents with them who make rigorous inspections there, and the trees are grown only at Amboyna and on the other islands that are under the immediate dependence of the company, and where it can keep up continual surveillance. This inquisition practised by Dutch greed is singularly thwarted by the birds, which go and deposit the seeds of the spice trees in the islands neighbouring those where they are cultivated; which has further led the company to station residents there, whose chief mission is to search continually in order to destroy all those they can find: often, too, these trees are found sown in places so steep that they escape the most active surveillance.

The slaves brought into the Moluccas are for the most part taken from Macassar and Ceram. The women of Macassar generally have pleasing features and are of middling stature; their hair is not frizzy; their skin, which is of a tint even more yellowish than that of European women afflicted with the green sickness, nevertheless causes the natives of the Moluccas to call them white women, *paran-pouang pouti*.

Before the Dutch had established the slave trade, the islanders of Ceram had the barbarous custom of eating the prisoners they had taken in their fights. It is painful to learn that they have given up this atrocious custom only because they get more profit from selling their captives. If an apparent good has come of it, it has moreover given them more frequent occasion for war. Man must have sunk to the lowest degradation for the introduction of slavery to have been for him a step towards civilization. It may nevertheless be said of these peoples, who were formerly cannibals.

The Dutch who have settled in the Moluccas speak only Malay to their slaves; they take good care not to teach them their mother tongue, so as not to be understood by them when they converse among themselves.

As soon as the Dutch company had appropriated to itself the exclusive trade of the Moluccas, it tried to learn their population; then, by exaggerated calculations designed to give a high idea of the subject lands, it was made to amount to a hundred and fifty thousand souls; which, according to more recent approximate calculations, and in the most general opinion, was double the number of its inhabitants. The quantity of cloves harvested there each year amounts to about two thousand bales, each weighing twenty-four myriagrammes three kilogrammes. The harvest of two years makes the cargo of three ships, of which two are sent in one year and the other the following year. The export of this commodity, like that of nutmeg, sometimes exceeds ordinary consumption: it is known that in that case the Dutch company has the surplus burnt, so as to keep them always at the same price.

For all its efforts to appropriate the spice trade exclusively to itself, what escapes it through smuggling is reckoned at a fifth of the annual harvest. As the meagre salaries of its agents do not lead them quickly to fortune, several use means which are dangerous, it is true, but easy, to extricate themselves from this state of distress. In spite of the company's vigilance, they succeed in stealing a small part of its spices from it.

Only a short time before, the governor of Banda and the deputy governor had been dismissed and sent to Batavia for having diverted to their own profit part of the produce of that island; but abuses have been carried to such a point that this example will serve only to spur the others to behave with more cunning so as not to be found out.

This smuggling trade is carried on particularly by the canoes of Ceram, because that large island lies very near the spice islands; what goes out is sold to English ships, which give in exchange Indian cloths, opium, firearms, gunpowder, lead, hardware, and tin, which the inhabitants of Ceram value highly and of which they make bracelets, earrings, etc.; some of these articles are afterwards resold at Amboyna.

The Dutch have two trading posts on Ceram; one at its south-west end, and the other at Savaï. General Bougainville had been misinformed when he reported that they had been driven from the latter post. They have lost, it is true, very extensive possessions in other parts of that large island, but they have kept that one.

The resident who received General Bougainville during his stay at Buru had died several years before. We had the pleasure of seeing his widow at Amboyna, who still keeps a pleasant memory of the stay of the French. Her fondness for our language had led her to employ every resource she could find so far from Europe to have it taught to her children.

The Chinese are almost the only foreigners whom the Dutch admit here; but they are obliged to become naturalized; after which they can no longer return to China. They are allowed to trade by sea within the Moluccas, and it is at Macassar and at Batavia, where ships arriving from China are admitted, that they can obtain the goods those vessels bring from there. They are all given over to trade. Some have bought at a very high price the exclusive privilege of selling various articles; and so they sell them very dear. They use every sort of means to make money: their reputation often suffers greatly from it; but they have lost all feeling in that respect. A few Jews whom the Dutch company has allowed to remain in the island compete with them in trade; but they do not make their fortune there: the Chinese have many advantages over them through their numbers and their connections.

The company's customs officer is a Chinese; he is, moreover, the head of his compatriots settled in the island, and is in charge of policing them in the minor cases that the administration of Amboyna has not reserved to itself. We went to his house one day with one of the ministers of the Protestant religion, and there we drank some very good tea. The table was covered with a great variety of fruits very well preserved in sugar: one of the best was the young nut of the fruit of the *sagouer* palm. This chief, who is called the Chinese captain, pointed out to us with an air of satisfaction his coat of arms, variegated in a great number of colours; it was displayed in profusion in the room where he received us; his bed was surrounded with it on every side.

His house, like those of the other Chinese, in no way resembled the dwellings of the natives of the island. The Chinese build much more solidly; their houses are built like those of the Europeans, apart from a few differences in the arrangement of the rooms. The frame of the building is of wood; the earthen walls are faced with a very thick rendering, coated with several layers of lime.

The frequency of earthquakes and hurricanes has led to wooden houses being preferred. Hardly any but the public buildings are built of stone. It almost always happens that, at such times of turmoil, the inhabitants are obliged to leave their dwellings and take refuge in small, very lightly built huts, where they are much safer than in their houses, which the winds and earthquakes sometimes throw down.

We enjoyed fairly fine weather during our stay at Amboyna; the winds did not blow violently there; those that made themselves felt from the south-east to the north-east were very light.

The market where the various fruits of the country are sold is held in the Chinese quarter. The Malays call this place by the term *bazar*, as do the Arabs. It is particularly towards the end of the day that the merchants gather there; they stay until nine o'clock in the evening. Each merchant is lit by one and more often by two torches made of the resin called *dammer*, yielded by a species of *cycas* known by the same name; it is the *dammara alba*, *Rumph. Amb.*, vol. II, chap. XII, tab. 57. They wrap it in *sagouer* leaves, without adding any wick; it burns with little smoke; one need only take care to lower from time to time the *sagouer* leaf, which turns to charcoal, so as to keep it level with the resin as it is consumed. These natives are lit very cheaply: each torch of *dammer* two decimetres long by a third of a decimetre thick costs them about one centime of our money, and gives a fairly bright light for more than three hours. This resin also serves them as a torch in their huts.

Some other foodstuffs are sold at this *bazar* as well; and far more dried fish is to be found there than fresh. Under a burning sky and in an atmosphere prodigiously laden with moisture, fish would very quickly putrefy if the inhabitants had no means of drying it promptly. When it is cured in the smoke of a gentle fire, its flesh acquires a taste that makes them prefer it to fresh fish. The Molucca Islands, after being for a long time under the dominion of the Arabs, the Moors and the Malays, passed under that of the Europeans. The Portuguese, the Spaniards and the Dutch contended for them after establishing trading posts and forts there. The Dutch finally remained masters of them, and for many years they have enjoyed the exclusive trade in spices. These various sovereigns have brought about such a change in the manners of the natives of Amboyna that it is very difficult now to perceive any traces of their original character. The Portuguese introduced the Catholic religion among these peoples. The Dutch have made every effort to turn them towards Protestantism, regarding this as the means more capable than any other of subjugating them; and so they have a great number of schools there, in which the children of the natives are instructed in that religion and learn to read and write in Malay. The service is held in the Malay language in a church set apart for the natives, and in the Dutch language in another set apart for the Dutch. They have two ministers for each.

The Chinese, as may well be supposed, have their pagoda here.

Some natives of the island who have kept the religion introduced by the Arabs and the Moors have a mosque. It is particularly on the other side of the roadstead, to the north of the town, that the greatest number of true believers are to be found. The Dutch have succeeded much better in making proselytes to their religion in the neighbourhood of their principal settlement. The rod of iron with which they rule this wretched people brings it so close to slavery that it is not surprising to meet among them a share of the vices that belong to that state of human degradation.

Although these peoples are accustomed to giving up almost everything they possess to the Europeans, there is one matter in which they are very little disposed to resignation. Jealousy is carried among them to such a pitch that it would be very dangerous to venture any indiscreet remarks to their wives. The fear of no punishment whatever could prevent them from carrying out their revenge.

Among the Dutch, the men have kept their European clothes as ceremonial dress, but they all wear waistcoats with sleeves, so as to be able to take off their coats when the master of the house to which they are invited urges them to make themselves comfortable, setting them the example himself. Those who wear wigs do not fail to hand them to one of their servants, and then cover their heads with a large cap of very fine white linen. As for the European women, they wear a petticoat that comes down very near the ground, a gown in the form of a shift open in front, which falls no lower than the petticoat and is held in by a sash, and their hair is rolled in a spiral at the back of the head and fastened by two long crossed pins: such is their ordinary dress. The wives of the natives who are well off and live in the town wear garments of the same shape, but commonly black. Blue ones are especially sought after by the country women.

The women slaves have for a gown a kind of shift which is not open in front like that of free women.

Free men wear a curved comb on their heads. Slaves bind theirs with a handkerchief.

The Chinese, as is well known, received the spices of the Moluccas many centuries before the Europeans took possession of them. The Greeks and the Romans knew them too. They were for a long time the object of the searches of the first navigators who made their way into the eastern seas. These precious aromatics, then concentrated in a small number of islands, have since been carried into very distant countries, where they thrive perfectly. We have reason to hope that one day our colony of Guiana will rival the Moluccas and, by procuring for the whole world a greater quantity of spices at a moderate price, will make them more generally used. They are also cultivated with success in the Isle of France and Réunion. We took on board the Recherche two hinds and a stag, with the intention of enriching New Holland with this handsome species of quadruped.

We had a good supply of fowls, ducks and Guinea geese.

We took no cassowaries with us. Although they are kept here as poultry, they are not easy to obtain; for they are not native to Amboyna, but are brought there from the large islands lying towards the east. This bird would bear sea voyages badly; besides, its flesh is black, tough and not very succulent. In proportion to the space it would have taken up on board, it would have offered far less to eat than the poultry with which we had provided ourselves; for, apart from its thighs, which are strongly muscled, since nature has especially designed this bird for running, the rest of its body is of very modest bulk relative to its height.

Our roots were chiefly sweet potatoes and yams.

Fine bunches of bananas and various kinds of gourds hung about the stern of the ship.

We had bought a good number of pigs and goats.

We carefully kept our cow, although her milk had already dried up; for it would have been impossible to replace her. There is, it is true, among the domestic animals of Amboyna a species of buffalo common in India; the female gives little milk; besides, this almost untameable quadruped would be very dangerous and very troublesome on board.

Our butcher, whose charge it was to feed the livestock, had been able to procure only a very hard and very dry fodder made up in great part of *anthistiria ciliata;* but fortunately he had provided himself with large banana stems, which for a long time furnished these animals with succulent food. As they were reduced to a small ration of water, the moisture of these plants was very useful to them.

The flour obtained for us at Amboyna was of middling quality; they could supply us with only about five hundred myriagrammes. This scarcity, real or perhaps feigned, made us pay an excessive price for it.

We found very little European meat there. The second governor, however, had a good supply of Hamburg beef (it is a dish much sought after by seafarers). He was good enough to let the commander of our expedition have part of it; but when we were out at sea, a great piece of dishonesty on the part of that officer's servants came to light. The fleshiest part of these pieces of beef had been removed, and nothing had been delivered to the general but precisely the bones and the sinewy parts.

Young bamboo shoots, cut in slices and pickled in vinegar, make an excellent provision for a long voyage; we took a great many with us. These young shoots are generally very tender. Care is taken to gather them in good time: they are sold in the market like vegetables and can serve in their stead. They are often a metre long and a third of a decimetre thick.

We had laid in a supply of cloves and nutmegs preserved in sugar. In this case the husk of the nutmeg is the only edible part; unfortunately ignorant confectioners had chosen nutmegs that were too far advanced. The cloves, already as big as middling olives, still kept too aromatic a taste to make a pleasant preserve: one must have an Indian palate to relish these delicacies. I will say as much of the ginger, of which we also had preserves.

The supply of sago was far too large, for only a very small part of it could be consumed; the men of the crew could never get used to this food, wholesome as it was, and despite all the arguments of our surgeon-major, after a few months they conceived such a disgust for it that they preferred even the worst salt meat to it.

We had scarcely a few casks of drinkable wine left. The only spirituous liquor that could be obtained was arrack, of which several casks were bought. Some travellers praise this liquor far too highly; it is not worth even a middling grape brandy.

1792-10-13.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 368]
## CHAPTER IX.

*Departure from Amboyna. Singular effect of the tides. View of various islands. Ravages caused on board by the species of cockroach called* blatta germanica. *Navigation along the south-west coast of New Holland. Death of the blacksmith of the Recherche. A gale drives us towards the coast. We anchor in the baie de Legrand. The Espérance loses at anchor two iron braces of her rudder. The chain by which she rode at anchor broke. Various excursions on the neighbouring lands. New species of swan. Sea salt found at more than two hundred metres of perpendicular elevation; how it had been carried there. Citizen Riche lost for more than two days on the mainland. Departure from the baie de Legrand to continue along the coast. Want of water obliges us to leave it. Arrival at cap de Diemen. Anchorage in the baie des Roches.*

[t. I, p. 368-369]
We now waited only for a favourable wind to sail. As early as half past seven in the morning a light breeze sprang up from the south-east: the anchor was weighed at once, and towards eleven o'clock we were already at the mouth of the roadstead, the western point of which bore west 6° 15' north, and the eastern point east 6° 15' south, we being two kilometres distant from the latter.

It was ascertained from the observations made at noon that the westernmost part of Amboyna lay in latitude 3° 46' 54" south, and longitude 125° 53' 48" east.

The wind continuing all day at south-east, we kept close-hauled on the larboard tack.

1792-10-14.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 369-370]
One of the ship's boys of the large vessel of the Dutch company which had lately sailed for Batavia had hidden himself on board the Recherche, and showed himself almost at the very moment when the captain of the Espérance sent word to the general that he had just found on board six fugitives from Amboyna; namely, three soldiers of the company, a sailor, and two Negro slaves. These unhappy men were fleeing a land where they all groaned almost equally in servitude.

The general had allowed the crews to take on board, on their own account, pigs and poultry; our ships were accordingly crowded with them on every side. They had been placed almost all between decks, and they were all the more troublesome to us because the foul stench they gave off was considerably increased by the heat of the climate. The variation of the magnetic needle appeared to us to be nil on the evening of the 27th, being in latitude 7° 10' south, and longitude 123° 14' east.

1792-10-17.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 370-371]
We had already witnessed several times a phenomenon which never fails to alarm navigators, because they sometimes take it at night for breakers: we saw it again on the 29th, very early in the morning. The air being scarcely stirring, we perceived the sea whitening in the distance: waves driven with force followed one upon another and reached us in a short time; a very strong chopping sea, caused by the water having just received an impulse different from that which had been given it by the wind that had blown during the night, succeeded this movement of the waters. The cause appears to me to lie in the tides which are felt between lands where the currents acquire a velocity proportionate to the narrowing which the waters of the sea meet with there.

We sighted the island of Kisser, which we perceived towards nine in the morning, extending from south to east by south; it is very mountainous, especially in its western part. Its greatest extent is from west-south-west to east-north-east; it lies in latitude 8° 13' 2" south, and longitude 123° 32' 17" east.

A very overcast sky did not allow us to make out the north coast of Timor until towards four in the afternoon, although we were only a myriametre distant from it: very lofty mountains raised their summits above the clouds. During the night we perceived fires kindled on them at different heights. No doubt the inhabitants feel the need, at that elevation, to protect themselves against the cold of the night, and perhaps they also seek to keep wild beasts away from them. These fires served us as lighthouses to direct our course along the coast, whenever a few breaths of wind came to interrupt the calm which prevailed for a good part of the night.

1792-10-18.journal_labillardiere: (Labillardière's account for this day is given under 1792-10-17.)

1792-10-19.journal_labillardiere: (Labillardière's account for this day is given under 1792-10-17.)

1792-10-22.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 371-372]
Towards seven in the morning, on the 2nd of Brumaire, we were half a myriametre from a small settlement which the Portuguese have on the west coast of Timor; they call it Laphao. Its position is in latitude 9° 22' 45" south, and longitude 122° 23' 36" east.

The Portuguese flag which had just been hoisted there bore from us south 30° east. We were saluted with five guns. A canoe with a double outrigger came out at once to reconnoitre our ships, which it approached very closely; but it soon returned towards the shore without having spoken to us. Shortly afterwards we drew still nearer to the land: natives and a few canoes could be seen on the beach. The lead was cast several times with a line fifty-eight metres long without finding bottom.

The island of Batou was sighted towards four in the afternoon to the south-west, at about two myriametres' distance; it is separated from Timor only by a channel half a myriametre wide.

1792-10-24.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 372-374]
Calms being very frequent along the coast of Timor, we stood off from it in the afternoon of the 4th with the help of a southerly wind, and made to the westward, without however finding fresher winds there. These calms seem to be caused by the heat, which is all the greater here because at this season the sun darts its rays almost perpendicularly.

The continuance of calms makes navigation very laborious along these coasts, where one is constantly in fear of being set ashore by the strength of the currents. The making of charts of these various lands is extremely difficult because of the currents, which are very irregular; accordingly those that have been made up to this day show very great discrepancies.

A great number of whales of various species came several times and surrounded our ships; they spouted water almost up to our side. We could well see, from how little fear we inspired in them, that they had never been pursued by fishermen.
