Our ship was crowded with lories bought at Amboyna; their piercing cries did not leave us a moment's peace during the day; they did not take kindly to life on board ship, for some of them died every day. They were seized with convulsive movements which vitriolic ether did indeed have the power to calm, without however preventing them from dying.

Mortality had spread to our hens as well; most of them were attacked one after another by violent ophthalmias caused by the coolness of the nights; and those that had lost their sight soon died of hunger. It would nevertheless have been very easy to prevent this mishap by sheltering these creatures from the night wind with a cloth suitably fitted in front of the coops.

The water of Amboyna had been much praised to us for its property of keeping a very long time at sea without spoiling; but it proved otherwise with us; it was already very foul, and could no longer be drunk until it had been vigorously shaken to drive out the inflammable air, which fortunately adheres to it only feebly. This unexpected decomposition certainly arose only from the little care that had been taken in cleaning our casks. Enough of the ferment of the old water had remained in them to corrupt this new water quickly.

It is certainly very disagreeable to have for drink water as foul as that of the dirtiest marshy places; but one is entirely reassured on learning that, by shaking it for a few minutes, as I have indicated above, it recovers its original purity.

1792-10-26.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 374-375]
As early as half past four in the morning we perceived by starlight the island of Savu, which bore from west 13° south to south 27° west. We were only two kilometres from the coast. We steered west so as to pass to the north of this small island, and towards half past nine we found ourselves off the bay where Captain Cook cast anchor on his second voyage, after passing through Endeavour Strait; we could make out five canoes afloat quite close to the shore, where they were sheltered from the swell, which broke upon a small reef awash.

The island of Savu presents an enchanting prospect; it is intersected, especially towards the south-west, by very fine hills, whose gentle slopes must offer the natives a soil favourable and easy to cultivate.

Coconut palms scattered in clumps along the shore sheltered a few huts which further embellished these charming plantations. This island lies in latitude 10° 25' 48" south, and longitude 119° 45' 19" east. The Dutch have a small settlement there.

Towards the middle of the day an islet was observed bearing from south 46° 30' west to south 57° 50' west, at a myriametre and a half's distance. It did not appear to us to be more than a myriametre in length: its position is in latitude 10° 28' 50" south, and longitude 119° 56' 17" east.

1792-10-27.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 375]
From six in the morning we saw New Savu, east 31° 30' south, at the distance of a myriametre. This small island, whose land is very low, lies in latitude 10° 37' 28" south, and longitude 119° 2' 47" east.

At sunset we perceived part of the island of San del Bose, about four myriametres to the north-north-east; it is covered with mountains of moderate height; it lies in latitude 10° 27' 4" south, and longitude 118° 6' 34" east.

The position of an islet which bore from north 1° east to north 3° 30' west, at four myriametres' distance, was determined as latitude 10° 27' south, and longitude 118° 7' 5" east.

1792-10-28.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 375-376]
In the course of the 8th the currents ceased to set us to the west and carried us ten minutes to the north. The deep indentation of the land of New Holland to the south of Timor is probably the cause of this change in the direction of the currents, which set constantly from east to west through Endeavour Strait: they soon resumed their westerly direction, making us drift from twenty to twenty-four minutes a day.

It is worth noting that Captain Cook, after passing through Endeavour Strait, found in these waters, as we did, a difference to the north over twenty-four hours, but even greater than the one we met with there.

1792-10-29.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 376]
After we had lost sight of the island of San del Bose, we met with no land before arriving at the south-west coast of New Holland. The light weather we were experiencing made us fear that we should arrive there a little too late to complete its survey.

1792-11-01.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 376]
We were probably not very far from some rocks on the 12th in the afternoon, for we were surrounded by a great number of birds which never stray far from land, and we did not lose sight of them until nightfall.

1792-11-02.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 376]
We also saw many of them the next day. Navigators who sail these seas should redouble their attention to avoid running upon the rocks which serve these birds as a retreat.

1792-11-14.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 376-378]
Our stag fell overboard during the night through an opening left at the end of the gangways, much larger than was necessary for the working of the ship; besides this loss, we had also to regret that of a hind which had lately been handed over to our butcher only because she was so ill that she would soon have died. Captain Huon was informed of this accident, and was urged to take every possible means of preserving the stag he had on board; but it died before our arrival in New Holland. When we passed the Trials we were too far from them to see them; we saw, however, many seabirds, which no doubt go there for refuge during the night.

The species of cockroach called *blatta germanica* had multiplied to such a degree during the several months we had been within the tropics that it caused us extreme annoyance. These insects were not content with our biscuit; they also gnawed linen, paper, etc.; everything was good to them. Their taste for vegetable acids could not but surprise me; as soon as a lemon was slightly split open, they soon finished it off; but what astonished me still more was the speed with which they emptied my inkstand whenever I forgot to stop it. The causticity of the vitriol with which they gorged themselves seemed to have no harmful effect on them.

The Amboyna sugar obtained from the *sagouer* palm was a bait by which they let themselves be caught. We destroyed a great many by putting a small quantity of this sugar with water in a vessel into which they came and threw themselves.

These insects tormented us even more by night than by day; they continually disturbed our sleep by crawling over every part of the body that was uncovered.

The cockroach named *blatta orientalis* had appeared almost as soon as we left the port of Brest; but having quickly disappeared, it had been replaced by this one.

1792-11-15.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 378]
In the course of the 26th we were carried 38' to the north-west. The Trials, from which we were not far distant, and some shoals, were no doubt the cause of such strong currents.

1792-11-17.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 378]
We left the tropical region in the course of the 28th.

The same day the mercury in the barometer rose to 28<sup>p</sup> 5<sup>l</sup>; which seemed to me all the more surprising as it varies little within the tropics. Besides, it is the only time in our whole campaign that it rose so high in a similar latitude. Although the thermometer was not lower than 18°, we nevertheless felt a keen sensation of cold.

1792-11-19.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 378]
We began to meet with the zone of variable winds at about 26° of south latitude.

Our goats were dying day by day for want of proper food: we lost two more in the course of the day.

1792-11-26.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 378-379]
Towards five in the afternoon the Espérance, being to windward of us, was on the point of running foul of us; there was nevertheless a wind favourable for steering properly; this negligence of the officer of the watch might have caused much damage to our ships and forced us to abandon the plan of visiting the south-west coast of New Holland, which we were soon to sight. A boom was fortunately placed in time to enable us to avoid the collision.

1792-12-04.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 379]
The sight of several species of gulls and other birds which seldom stray far from the coasts told us that land was near. The west-south-west wind was blowing too violently to allow us to close with it at once. The sea, moreover, running very high, and the horizon being much obscured by clouds, determined us to steer south-east by south, in the hope that the next day circumstances would be more favourable to us.

At noon we were in latitude 34° 12' south, and longitude 112° east.

We passed the night lying to, and sounded several times with a line of two hundred and twenty-five metres without finding bottom.

1792-12-05.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 379-382]
It was scarcely half past two in the morning when we stood to the east-south-east, and as soon as day broke the Espérance signalled land to us in the north-east at a distance of about three myriametres; it was the western extremity of the south-west coast of New Holland, discovered in 1622 by Leuwin. We saw a low land extending from north-west to south-west.

At six o'clock we put our head east by south, and when we were a myriametre from the coast we followed it in its trend towards the south-east. A very fresh west-north-west wind drove us with such force that we made three myriametres an hour.

The interior was strewn with sand-covered dunes, which presented a spectacle of the greatest barrenness. These hillocks, scattered over low ground, seemed from a distance to form so many islets: the spaces between them bore a few shrubs whose foliage, of a blackish hue, betrayed a stunted condition.

Rocks rising sheer from the midst of these sandy plains revealed how the dunes had been formed; they no doubt rested upon other rocks of the same kind, whose shape had made it easier for the sand driven by the winds to gather there. It must be very rare to find fresh water on such land, where the rainwater no doubt filters down to great depths before meeting with strata that stop it.

In the morning our blacksmith was found dead in his bed. The day before he had taken part in a feast which the gunners used formerly to keep punctiliously. They had long been saving a great many provisions for this meal. This unfortunate blacksmith, worn out, like all of us, by the abstinence to which we had been condemned since our departure from Amboyna, had trusted too much to his appetite. An attack of apoplexy had carried him off. This loss would have been irreparable had chance not brought on board, at the Cape of Good Hope, a very intelligent workman who succeeded him.

Being at noon in latitude 34° 45' 36" south, and longitude 113° 38' 56' east, the nearest coast bore a myriametre from us to the north-east, and we saw land from west 15° south to east 40° ½ south.

The mountains began to form a fairly regular chain, the highest not appearing to exceed four hundred metres perpendicular. Large tracts entirely bare of vegetation could be seen on them; elsewhere there were feeble, thinly scattered shrubs, amid which one saw a very small number of trees of moderate height.

The mountains sometimes appeared in several ranges, rising by degrees one above another.

Towards four in the afternoon we perceived some breakers at a short distance from the coast, and a little beyond them to the east two rocks, a kilometre from the shore, which we passed very close. The larger was remarkable for a cleft in its middle, from which rose perpendicularly, about fifty metres above the level of the sea, a detached piece having the form of a very flattened blade; I took it for sandstone, and the rock that served it as a base was of the same kind. We admired the fine effect of the waves which, driven with violence, took on a perfectly white colour as they rose to the very top of this rock, and fell back in a sheet, revealing this singular rock, which then seemed to emerge from the bosom of the waters.

We now saw the coast extending fairly regularly towards the east-south-east, and its small windings were terminated by capes, the most prominent of which projected scarcely two kilometres into the sea.

Driven by a furious wind, we were not without fears, finding ourselves so near a land that offered us not the slightest shelter; but we stood off from it during the night, steering south-south-west. A very heavy sea from the west-north-west strained our ship prodigiously. Having sailed for so long in fair seas, we had lost the habit of bearing so much motion: the violence of the wind came in gusts and allowed us to carry very little sail.

1792-12-06.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 382-384]
On the morning of the 17th, towards half past six, we put our head north-east to close with the land, which we soon saw again in that direction, being driven by a very fresh westerly wind. We had fallen off a little to leeward. The coast now extended almost due east. The interior presented the same aspect as on the previous day. We noticed there vast yellowish tracts which we took for so many plateaus of hard stone, on which not the least trace of vegetation could be distinguished.

At noon we were already in latitude 35° 17' south, and longitude 115° 12' east. Soon the mountains grew lower and we had a view of a vast sandy plain, where hillocks could be seen scattered here and there at great distances, some of which formed, on the shore, capes projecting only a little way into the sea.

Towards four in the afternoon we passed a group of rocks lying near the coast and scantily covered with shrubs, whose dismal green bore witness to the barrenness of the soil. Towards six o'clock we were abreast of an inlet whose full depth we could not see: one would have been perfectly safe there from the furious winds which had been blowing ever since we began to coast along these shores. A cape running out from north-west to south-east nearly a myriametre towards the open sea, a few islets and several rocks lying at the entrance of this bay, afforded good shelter from winds off the sea; but the strength of the swell prevented us from sending a boat to sound this opening.

We lay to during the night.

Being half a myriametre from the coast, a line of eighty-three metres gave a bottom of broken shells and madrepores, mixed with a fairly transparent quartz sand: this indication led me to presume that good holding ground would also have been found in the bay we had just passed.

1792-12-07.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 384-385]
Throughout the night a sky free of clouds allowed us to see the land, from which we kept at no great distance, always finding the same kind of bottom.

The west wind was not blowing very strongly, and as early as half past four in the morning we spread our sails to run along the coast, which extended to the north-east; it soon curved round towards the east and the south-east.

At eight o'clock we passed off a bay which appeared to us to be about three myriametres deep, with an opening at least as wide; it is open to south-east winds, and one would be safe there from westerly winds.

Farther on we saw, out to sea, a few small rocks lying not far from the coast.

Being at noon in latitude 34° 48' south, and longitude 116° 52' east, we perceived in the interior, to the north 4° west, a mountain higher than any we had seen on the preceding days; standing alone in the midst of vast sandy plains, it produced a very picturesque effect, and appeared to be about five myriametres from the coast: its jagged summit showed many very prominent peaks, most of them perpendicular. They could be seen along the whole extent of the mountain, which measured a myriametre and a half from east to west. This configuration leaves no doubt that the stones composing it are extremely hard.

We had not yet perceived any sign of inhabitants since we began to coast along these arid shores. It was to be presumed that some spring of pure water must draw them towards the foot of this mountain. Soon the smoke of two great fires which they lit there made their presence known to us.

Having doubled, towards half past four, a cape terminating in a few rocks lying a short distance from the coast, we found ourselves off a bay as wide as, but less deep than, the one we had seen in the morning; it was bordered by land generally very low; towards its eastern part, however, a few hillocks detached from one another could be seen. It affords good shelter from west and south-west winds; but it is entirely open to south-east winds.

Red-tailed tropic birds and a few albatrosses of a darker hue than those most common at the Cape of Good Hope flew around us.

We lay to during the night, and on sounding every hour we constantly found sixty-six metres of depth on a bottom of grey sand.

1792-12-08.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 385-387]
As early as half past four in the morning we steered north by east to close with the coast, and we saw it almost at once, from north 2° east to west 25° north. A clear horizon allowed us to make out still other low lands extending towards the north-east.

We soon passed between the mainland and some reefs lying two myriametres off it. Towards eight o'clock we left others two and a half myriametres to seaward, and we soon saw that an islet which we perceived towards the east was joined to the land by a chain of reefs which, running out to sea, obliged us to stand on the southerly tack until we had weathered them.

Three fires lit one after another on the point of land from which the reefs extended told us that there were savages there. The produce of the sea is no doubt the principal resource of these peoples who live on so barren a soil.

Being at noon in latitude 34° 11' south, and longitude 118° 22' east, we had the small island I have just mentioned bearing north 38° west, at two kilometres' distance.

Other fires lit along the coast raised, like the first, great columns of smoke, the inhabitants no doubt wishing to make their presence known to us.

Towards half past four we left to seaward an islet four myriametres from the coast; it was joined to a bank of reefs which extended more than a kilometre towards the east. The lead then gave us twenty-one metres of depth, and some time afterwards a line of forty-two metres did not reach bottom.

A calm prevailed for a few moments towards the close of the day, but a light south-east wind soon allowed us to stand on the south-west tack, which we held throughout the night.

The lead, being cast every hour, showed a bottom of quartz sand mixed with fragments of shells and madrepores, in a depth of from fifty to sixty-six metres.

1792-12-09.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 387-390]
At daybreak all sail was set, with a fresh west-north-west wind, heading east.

Since six in the morning the mercury in the barometer had fallen more than 3<sup>l</sup>. Although the sky was fair, this sure sign of a great disturbance of the equilibrium of the atmosphere deserved the most careful attention. We nevertheless ran before the wind among islets lying about a myriametre from the coast, very uncertain of finding a passage between those we perceived in the distance; we were already far in among them towards ten o'clock, when we saw that they were joined to one another by reefs; the look of the sky was threatening, the horizon had just become overcast in the west-south-west, and soon the wind blew from that quarter with the utmost violence. In vain did we search for a long time among these reefs for some gap that would allow us to gain the open sea; as we had no other way out than the passage by which we had entered, we went about to make for it. The violence of the gale having forced us to take in most of our sails, the ship made so much leeway that we very quickly fell to leeward of this opening. Our running rigging giving way on every side, our manoeuvres could now be carried out only slowly; in vain did we several times stand for the passage to get out; each time we had to go back among the dangers and continue beating about in a space strewn with rocks hidden under water at various depths, upon which we were exposed at every moment to see our ship dashed to pieces; a very practised eye was needed to make them out in so heavy a sea. Citizen Raoul, a very well-informed young seaman in whom the general placed great confidence, had gone up to the masthead of the mainmast, and from there directed the course of our ship. Several times we found ourselves carried quite close to reefs hidden by the waves, and he made us avoid them all, although it was very difficult to see them, even from so short a distance.

The Espérance, which held her wind even less well than we did, was already quite close to the coast, having no other course left but to run aground there if she did not find some shelter in which to drop anchor. Towards one in the afternoon we perceived her from very far off, in a place where it did not seem to us that there could be an anchorage: she had just clewed up all her sails; we were very anxious about her situation, believing that she had just struck; but the steadiness of her masts very soon reassured us, showing us that this frigate was at anchor: her distance and the strength of the wind prevented us from making out the signals she was making to us.

We did not hesitate to go and seek the same shelter. The general at once ordered us to bear away under the foresail, north by east, and we were soon near the Espérance, which was feebly protected from the swell by an islet. We were warned from the deck of that frigate to keep very close along the land, so as to be better sheltered than they were. As we coasted along the small island we had the frightening spectacle of a furious wave which, having swept over its southern point, opened as it plunged down a chasm that laid bare part of the base of that rock. The fear of approaching too near the land made us drop anchor towards five o'clock to windward of the Espérance, but not far enough inside the anchorage to avoid falling upon her should our ship drag her anchors. The danger was all the greater as our first anchor could not hold us: the axes were already ready to cut away the masts so as to give the wind less purchase; but a second anchor held us fast. We were anchored in thirty-eight metres, on a bottom of quartz sand mixed with fragments of shells.

Violently tossed by the swell, we were exposed to almost the full violence of the wind, and we feared to see our cables part, for we should have fallen upon rocks on which the sea was breaking in a frightful manner.

As night came on we let go a third anchor to be the more certain of holding against such violent strains.

1792-12-10.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 390-393]
The mercury, which had fallen in the barometer as low as 27<sup>p</sup> 8<sup>l</sup> ½, rose noticeably as soon as day broke, and announced to us the end of the gale.

The swell having considerably abated, Captain Huon sent his boat on board the Recherche and informed us that the day before the Espérance had been driven towards the land so rapidly that she was on the point of going ashore, when Citizen Legrand, an officer of distinguished merit, had gone up, at the height of the gale, to the masthead of the mainmast, and had come down again almost at once, crying out with enthusiasm that the ship was saved from danger. He pointed out the position of the anchorage he had discovered and gave assurance that the vessel would be safe there. The safety of both ships hung upon this discovery; for the Recherche, obliged to beat about during the night among these perilous reefs, after struggling as long as she could against the force of the gale in the hope that a change of wind would allow her to gain the open sea, would infallibly have been lost.

This bay, which bears the name of Citizen Legrand, will recall the signal service which that able seaman rendered to our expedition; his advice had been to anchor nearer the land, and it was unfortunate that it had not been followed, for the chain which the Espérance had let go on the larboard side had been broken during the night by the force of the swell, and that frigate, riding now by a single anchor only, had soon been carried towards the coast, when fortunately another anchor had held her. This ship also lost the two iron braces of her rudder; she had no spare ones: these braces were broken by the violent blows which the swell gave the rudder in the combined motions of pitching and rolling; the pitching motion, all other things being equal, is much quicker at anchor than on the open sea.

From the place where we lay at anchor we counted twelve islets, as well as the rocks and breakers which sheltered us. The sea in this vast basin could send very heavy swells against us; but fortunately we were anchored on a bottom of good holding ground.

The islet under the lee of which we lay bore from south 25° west to west 3° north. In the morning a boat was sent from each ship to sound there; we intended to draw nearer to it: everywhere excellent ground was found; fifteen metres of depth were had at a short distance from the land.

Some persons, in order to reach the shore, were obliged to jump into the water, for the boat would have been dashed to pieces had anyone tried to bring it close enough to the coast to land dry-shod.

Several seals of the species called by Buffon the little seal, *phoca pusilla*, Linn., lay peacefully in the sun on the rocks and along the beach; some allowed themselves to be killed with blows of a stick. It is worth noting that the figure Buffon has given of this amphibious animal was no doubt made from a badly stuffed skin: it is represented there with a neck much slenderer than the head, as is characteristic of most quadrupeds; but this animal, being chiefly designed for swimming, approaches the fishes, and has a head smaller in bulk than the neck.

In the same figure the ears are represented as wide open, whereas they have nearly the form of a cone, with no other opening than a lengthwise slit on the outer side; it seems that nature wished to prevent water from entering the ears of this animal when it dives; for it can close this slit completely when it is in the sea, and open it, but slightly, when it has come out.

There was also found there a numerous flock of swans, several of which let themselves be taken by hand; but the others, warned of the danger, soon flew off. This new species, a little smaller than the wild swan, is of an ash grey, somewhat lighter in hue under the belly; the bill is blackish, and has at its base a swelling of a sulphur yellow; the feet are lightly tinged with red.

The main topsail had split a little the day before when we went about while struggling against the gale. Advantage was taken of the fine weather in the morning to shift it.

1792-12-11.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 393-397]
A light south-east wind had succeeded the gale. As the moment was favourable, we had ourselves warped very early in the morning towards the land, from which we were then only about three hundred metres distant.

I went ashore on the small island which bore south-west of us; it is hilly and is no more than four kilometres long by two kilometres wide.

The swell had not yet subsided enough for landing to be easy; we had to seize the moment when the wave rose to let our skiff, held by a small line, approach the land, and each time one of us sprang on to the shore. As the gunwale of the skiff, on which one had to set one's foot to jump ashore, sloped, and the coast was steep, we ran the risk of falling into the sea and being rolled over by waves that followed one another very closely and from which a good swimmer would have had great difficulty in extricating himself. This was not the only peril we had to fear; we might also become the prey of a large shark which kept a few paces behind us. We had seen it prowling round our ships since daybreak, and it had followed our boat as though it coveted one of us. The chaplain of the Recherche fell into the water and was about to be devoured by this creature, when fortunately the coxswain of our boat rescued him from the danger.

Some sailors of the Espérance, walking about on the rocks, killed with sticks a great many seals of different colours; there were white ones, grey ones more or less dark, and brown ones verging on black; they were nevertheless all of the same species, designated by Buffon under the name of little seal; their flesh was found very good.

The islet on which we were is composed of a fine granite in which quartz, feldspar and mica predominate; the last occurs in blackish plates: a few needles of black schorl are also to be seen in it, but in very small quantity; this granite was bare in many places. The vegetable mould which had lodged in the less steep places was covered with shrubs, sometimes so close together that one could make one's way through them only with great difficulty. I gathered there a magnificent species of *leptospermum*, remarkable for its silvery leaves and its brilliant red flowers.

I saw there several new species belonging to the family of the thymelaeae, which have only two stamens and of which Forster has made a new genus under the name of *banksia*. I also noticed new species of *rumex*, *lobelia* and *buplevrum*.

The western part of this islet presents, at one of its highest points, a plateau of limestone whose beds follow the gentle slope of the mountain: beds of the same stone no doubt once covered the other parts of the island, with the granite core as their base; but they have probably fallen away and left the steep places bare, for in the north-east, where the mountains descend by a fairly gentle slope, some limestone is still found at a short distance from the shore. I was never able to perceive any shells in it, despite the searches I made to discover some.

From the summit of this small island we could make out in the distance part of the reefs and rocks on which our ships had nearly been dashed to pieces before reaching the anchorage. Their number still frightened us, and we marvelled that we had been able to escape so many dangers.

Two gulls, male and female, of the species called by Buffon the *bourgmestre*, *larus fuscus*, Linn., came to rest on these heights a short distance from us. The female having been killed by a musket shot, the male, frightened by the noise of the report, at first took flight, but he soon returned to the same spot, unwilling any longer to abandon his mate, and let himself be killed at her side.

I had also fired small shot at a seal which was lying rather far from me; it felt itself wounded and, mistrusting its strength, did not dare to throw itself into the water. I was so well hidden that it could not see me. Soon I saw another, a very large one, which, drawn by the cries of the wounded animal, came and licked all the places from which its blood was flowing; the latter submitted to this as though it felt some relief from it; but at the sight of a longboat approaching them they threw themselves into the sea.

A little while afterwards I made out others coming towards the edge of the shore; before venturing to land they never failed to raise nearly half their bodies above the water, and they remained some time in that attitude, sniffing and looking on every side, trying to make out whether there was any danger for them in coming to rest on the rocks. As I had gathered the day before an abundant harvest of natural history objects of various kinds, I had to spend part of the day on board describing and preparing them.

1792-12-12.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 397-398]
Towards five in the afternoon men were sent to pitch the tents of the observatory. I wished to take this opportunity of going ashore on the islet where I had already been. The tide was only beginning to rise, so one could still land there, but it would soon have been impossible to get back to the boat, and we should have been obliged to spend the night ashore. This consideration prevented several of my companions from landing. The gap to be crossed to reach the shore was about seven metres, and at each wave the sea rose there to more than two metres of perpendicular height. One had to pass between one wave and the next, at the risk of being swept into the sea; which is what happened to the second surgeon of the Recherche. He had just told us that he was going to reach the shore almost dry-shod; but not crossing quickly enough, he was carried off by a heavy wave which swept him along the coast; fortunately he could swim, and he came back towards the boat, but in a very different manner from what he had counted on when he wished to make a show of his nimbleness before us.

Those who had gone ashore were obliged to spend the night there; they had no provisions but a little biscuit. Driven by thirst, they were forced, on a very dark night, to walk more than two kilometres across the rocks to procure water, and, to crown their misfortune, it turned out to be brackish.

Enormous sharks of the commonest species, *squalus carcharias*, frequently appeared in the basin where we lay at anchor. One was taken on board the Espérance which was about four metres long, and much stouter than it should have been in proportion to its length.

As everything led us to foresee that it would be impossible to replenish our supply of water at this anchorage, the second in command gave orders that only three quarters of a bottle a day should be served out to each person. The commander-in-chief and he had as much as they pleased. I believed, however, that water was a common store, the privation of which ought to have extended to all alike.

1792-12-13.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 398-403]
The geographical engineer of the Recherche set off at daybreak in the large cutter to reconnoitre the islets of this little archipelago and to see whether there might not be a passage to the east between the reefs; he was also to look for a convenient watering place. I ardently wished to be included in such an expedition; but as geographical operations have little connection with the researches of naturalists, we were not told of the hour of departure, for which everything was arranged so secretly that I learned of it only at the moment the boat pulled away from our frigate.

Being unable to obtain a longboat to carry me to the mainland, I decided to spend this day on the south-west island, whose outline I followed, making first towards the north-west. I soon arrived in the south-west near one of the highest summits, where I found a small stream of fresh water issuing from the cracks of a granite rock; this discovery gave us great joy, for we had for some time been reduced to a very small quantity a day.

Close by I perceived hollows filled with very clear water, which I had reason to believe as fresh as that which trickled from the rock, since it was more than two hundred metres perpendicular above the level of the sea. I was mistaken; it was very salt, and farther on other hollows filled with the same water showed on their edges crystals of sea salt in rather thin plates, which from a certain distance resembled ice. This fact having been related on board by persons who accompanied me, some, to explain the cause of this phenomenon, suggested that the waves might well rise to that height in heavy weather, although the coast was protected by fairly large rocks, lying, it is true, at no great distance from the foot of the mountains. As this stream, which was very feeble, supplied us only slowly with the water needed to quench our thirst, we were obliged to rest on its banks, and soon small drops of salt water with which we were wetted showed me that the air was carrying up to us the sea water, reduced to fine spray by its shock against the rocks. Our clothes were soon covered with it, as if they had been exposed to a light fog; this water had lost none of its saltness.

A few birds were waiting for us to withdraw so as to come and quench their thirst. I killed there the charming fawn turtle-dove, remarkable for the six to eight golden feathers which it bears towards the base of the wings. White has for this reason called it the *golden winged pigeon*, pag. 43; he has given a good figure of it. I had already found the same species at cap de Diemen.

We took there many penguins of the species called *aptenodyta minor*, which Captain Cook had also met with in New Zealand; they were likewise hidden in very deep holes in the rocks, from which it was often very difficult to pull them out.

One of the highest summits, which I visited that day for the first time, was formed of limestone arranged in almost horizontal beds, like that which I had already met with on these heights; it was of a very fine grain, rarely showing a few slight cavities. Here too I noticed no shells; I presume that it was produced by a slow deposit of calcareous matter carried in a state of solution.

This change of ground furnished me with a few plants I had not yet found.

I gathered there a new and very striking species of *eucalyptus*, of which I shall now give the description.

The tallest stems of this shrub are no more than four metres high; they are smooth and furnished, chiefly towards the end of each branch, with alternate leaves, oval, elongated, slightly curved, about a decimetre long.

The flowers, which are sessile and borne commonly to the number of eight to ten at the end of a common peduncle about three centimetres long, present all the characters of the genus *eucalyptus*. Their very numerous stamens have long fawn-coloured filaments; the style projects a little beyond the stamens.

The very elongated calyx is pushed outwards by the stamens as they develop, and falls when they have reached their full growth.

The capsule, open at its upper part, has three cells and sometimes four; it is surmounted by a small portion of the base of the style, which is divided into as many parts as there are cells. Each cell contains many angular seeds.

The form of the calyx has led me to give this shrub the name of *eucalyptus cornuta*.

Having resolved to spend the night ashore, we looked for a convenient spot and at last found a hollow in the rock where for some time we were perfectly sheltered from the wind and the rain, which came on at the close of the day. The cold was sharp enough to induce us to light a fire; besides, we had not many provisions, and after I had chosen from the birds of my day's shooting those I wished to keep for my collection, I gave the others to my companions, who prepared them by grilling them. We were expecting to make a fairly good supper and then to sleep very peacefully, when suddenly the wind shifted and rushed into our grotto, from which we were forced to get out very quickly so as not to be suffocated by the smoke. This mishap made us regret that we had not gone back on board; for the wind was strong enough to put out our fire before our penguins were fully grilled, but we nevertheless found them very good.

An ample supply of water which we had brought down from the top of the mountain pleasantly reminded us, as we ate this meal, that here at least we could drink as much as we pleased.

1792-12-14.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 403-406]
As soon as it was light I made my way towards the south-west. Among many other plants, I gathered at the foot of the mountains, in a marly soil, a leguminous plant which must be placed among those whose corolla is papilionaceous and whose stamen filaments are separate from one another.

It forms a new genus, which I call *chorizema*.

The calyx is of a single piece, and divided into four parts at its margin. The upper division is broad, notched, and longer than the others; the three lower ones are equal to one another, narrow, and ending in a point.

The upper edge of the standard is notched, and it almost entirely covers the wings and the keel.

The stamens, ten in number, are all separate from one another.

The ovary is oval-oblong, and ends in a curved style.

The legume, of an oval shape, is filled with a great number of black, almost spherical seeds.

This plant is perennial; its leaves are simple, alternate, sessile, leathery, long, toothed, and have two small spines for stipules.

The shape of the leaves led me to give this species the name of *chorizema ilicifolia*.

*Fig.* 2. Flower.

Very early in the morning the Espérance had sent a boat to the mainland to make some astronomical observations. Citizen Riche had also gone ashore there. The rendezvous had been fixed for two o'clock in the afternoon, at the landing place; but he was waited for in vain until seven in the evening. The boat was obliged to return on board, because it had no provisions, and because, besides, it lay at anchor in a spot which might have become very dangerous had the swell increased ever so little. A written note was left on the shore to let Citizen Riche know, should he come back to that place, that they would return to fetch him the next day at daybreak, if the weather allowed.

The engineer-geographer who had been sent to survey this small archipelago arrived at nightfall; he had fixed the position of more than twenty islets scattered over a space of about one degree both in longitude and in latitude. He landed at several points without finding a convenient place for taking in water; the only stream of fresh water he had met with would scarcely have supplied the daily consumption of our ships. Behind the point of the mainland which bore east-north-east of us, he had found a good anchorage, shallower than the one we occupied.

It is at this archipelago that Nuyts's discovery ends. We were astonished at the precision with which its latitude had been determined by that navigator, at a time when instruments of observation were still very imperfect. I must make the same remark with regard to almost everything that Leeuwin had discovered of this land.

For some days the winds had been blowing from the east, inclining to the north in the morning and to the south in the afternoon. It is the sands, strongly heated by the rays of the sun, that cause this daily variation. The air of the atmosphere enjoyed a great equilibrium with winds of this sort, and accordingly the mercury in the barometer commonly stood at 28<sup>p</sup> 3 to 4<sup>l</sup>.

1792-12-15.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 406-417]
The weather being favourable this day, a boat was sent in search of Citizen Riche. This naturalist, carried away with enthusiasm at the richness and novelty of all the productions of this land, which until then had been visited by no observer, had doubtless forgotten himself in contemplating them and had very quickly lost his way; he had not yet come back to the landing place.

On advancing in the direction he had been seen to take the day before, our people saw some natives at very close quarters, with whom, however, it was not possible to communicate; for they always fled as we advanced towards them.

Riche's situation was all the more alarming since he had been absent for nearly a day and a half, and we knew that he had set off without provisions into an extremely barren country.

The boat, which returned at about two o'clock in the afternoon, brought the sad news that he could not be found. Captain Huon at once came to report this to the general, who consulted with him on the measures it would be proper to take in so unfortunate a situation. The general having invited the naturalist Deschamps and myself to come to his cabin, Captain Huon informed us of all the steps he had so far taken to find our unfortunate colleague: he reminded us of the dangers to which he might have exposed himself in advancing alone into the interior, where perhaps he had fallen by the hands of the savages; besides, he told us, he could foresee nothing but the most fatal outcome, for he thought it wholly impossible that Riche could have been lost for so long.

The nature of these burning sands, entirely without water, made all the conjectures we could form about his situation still more dreadful.

As our store of water was already partly consumed, and none had been found to replenish it at this anchorage, Captain Huon, after telling us that it would be very disadvantageous to prolong our stay there any further, added that it was evident that further searches could only harm the expedition, without offering the slightest hope of finding our unfortunate colleague.

Deschamps, on whose mind these arguments had had all the influence that was desired, did not hesitate to be the first to propose departure, siding with the captain and declaring that we could not hide from ourselves that nothing remained for us but to mourn the loss of our friend.

These probabilities did not have the same effect on me; but I had to persuade seamen, and I used the means I thought most fitted to convince them, citing in support of my opinion an example drawn from the voyages of the most celebrated of navigators. I reminded them that Captain Cook had two sailors who went astray, in December 1777, on Christmas Island, one for a whole day, and the other for forty-eight hours; that Cook had had them searched for with the greatest care by several parties; that Christmas Island, however, is a very small low island, scarcely covered with shrubs, whereas New Holland, where Riche had been lost, was immense. I therefore asked that at least as much time should be spent in searching for our unfortunate friend as Captain Cook had spent in searching for one of his sailors.

This argument had all the effect I wished.

A boat at once set off from each ship for the mainland, and I had the pleasure of being among those who were to use every care and make every effort to bring our unfortunate fellow voyager back on board.

The general had a gun fired every half hour, so that, if Riche were still alive, he might direct his steps more surely towards the anchorage.

The wind favoured us, and we were soon ashore.

After advancing in various directions, we returned to the landing place at nightfall. We had gone over ground entirely covered with sand, where we had found vast stretches wholly bare of vegetation. I was surprised to see on these distant shores the grass known by the name of *spinifex squarrosus*, and I once more admired the ease with which plants growing on the sea shore spread to prodigious distances.

In these arid places grew a handsome plant which comes near to the *iris*, and which naturally takes its place beside the genera *dilatris* and *argolasia*; it forms, however, a new and very distinct genus, chiefly by its irregular corolla.

I designate it by the name of *anigozanthos*.

The flowers have no calyx.

The corolla has the form of a tube divided at its margin into six unequal parts, curved inwards; it is covered with reddish hairs.

The stamens, six in number, are attached below the divisions of the corolla, which is placed upon the ovary.

The style is simple, as is the stigma.

The capsule is roughly spherical and coloured like the flower by which it is surmounted; it has three cells filled with a great number of angular seeds.

The top of the stem is covered with reddish hairs, like the flowers.

I have called this species *anigozanthos rufa*. *Explanation of the figures. Pl.* 22.

*Fig.* 2. Flower.

*Fig.* 3. Flower slit lengthwise and laid open to show the stamens.

*Fig.* 4. Stamens, magnified.

*Fig.* 5. Capsule.

Although the heat on this land was very great during the day, we nevertheless felt a rather sharp cold at night.

As soon as dawn began to appear we divided into two parties; the one I was with advanced towards the north, and the other towards the north-west.

We were steering by the compass and had covered at least one myriametre across plains of calcareous sand, which we saw heaped up in various places, when we came to a rather narrow hollow where the green of the plants made a pleasant contrast with the dreariness of the country we had just crossed, and announced to us a very fertile vegetable soil. There we noticed some cavities which offered us a little fresh water, but it was too far from the shore to be of use to our ships.

Continuing on our way, I noticed in the midst of these sands some rocks of a calcareous nature, where I gathered some fine plants that still held out against the aridity of the soil. Among the great number of those of the protea family which I observed there, I shall mention two new species of *banksia*. I call the one *banksia repens*, and the other *banksia nivea*; the creeping *banksia* and the silvery *banksia*.

The first has a creeping stem, covered with a thick reddish down, and ending in flowers gathered together in the form of a cone.

The leaves are pinnatifid, and when they are very young they are seen covered with the same down as the stem, so much so that one might take this plant for some species of *acrostichum*; but when older they are very smooth.
