I also found there the *eucalyptus cornuta*, and many other plants of the myrtle family.

After four hours of rather brisk walking we reached the shores of a large lake which communicates with the sea.

The natives had recently set fire to several places through which we had just passed.

We saw no kangaroos, but their droppings, which we noticed on all sides in great abundance, showed us that this quadruped is very numerous on this coast: we also noticed there other droppings which bore a singular resemblance to those of a cow, but we did not see the animal to which they belonged; in the sand could be seen the prints of cloven feet more than three quarters of a decimetre broad. There is no doubt that this land supports quadrupeds much larger than the kangaroo: it offers little food for birds; and accordingly on this excursion I found only two species, a *muscicapa*, which I afterwards met with in the Moluccas, and the beautiful species of red-crested cockatoo, *psittacus moluccensis*, which was seen there in flocks of several hundreds. When I tried to approach them, they always took flight a long way off, and flew in rapid bursts, uttering piercing and very disagreeable cries.

The shores of the lake, which we followed for some time as we drew near the sea, are somewhat marshy; it stretches far inland, since the party that went to the north-west also came to its shores; some of them came to meet us to tell us that they had noticed, quite close to the lake, towards the part of it farthest from the sea, the prints of shoes which left no doubt that Riche had passed that way; but the marks of bare feet that appeared quite close to his gave cause to fear that he had been carried off by the savages into the interior. One circumstance that further increased the likelihood of this conjecture was that his pocket handkerchief was soon found on the sand, and a few paces farther on one of his pistols. At a short distance a little smoke could be seen rising from an abandoned fire, around which were found some scraps of paper on which Riche's handwriting was recognised. The sand in this spot also showed the impression of someone who had rested there.

We were all returning towards our boats, lamenting the fate of our unfortunate fellow voyager, when, as we were about to reach the landing place, and having lost all hope, we saw one of those who had stayed behind to guard the boats running to meet us to announce that Riche was still alive, and that he had just come to the landing place, exhausted with hunger and fatigue. He had been ashore for more than fifty-four hours, and had taken no other provisions with him than a few pieces of biscuit. The state of prostration to which he was reduced did not allow his friends to let him give way to his appetite, and it was only by testing the digestive powers of his stomach by degrees that we gave him some food. His face, at first entirely drawn and ghastly, revived little by little. When he had recovered from the stupor into which so long a deprivation of food had thrown him, he told us that fairly near the fire which had been found still alight, there was a small stream of fresh water where he had quenched his thirst; that by dint of searching among the plants akin to those whose fruits can serve as food for man, he found a shrub of the ebony family which supplied him with some small fruits, but in too small a quantity to meet his needs. On the very first day that he lost his way he found the spring near which some of his belongings had been discovered. He spent the night there, and the next day he searched all day long for the anchorage of our ships, without being able to find it. During the whole of this painful march he did not find a single drop of water; but chance happily brought him back in the evening to this same spring, where he spent the second night as well.

Having caught sight of some savages in the distance, he had tried to communicate with them, in order to learn their manner of feeding themselves and to ask them for some food, for he was violently tormented by hunger; but they had always taken flight as he advanced towards them. (In this climate men are under no necessity of clothing themselves; all were entirely naked.) They often set fire to the dry grass that was scattered over the sands.

A few kangaroos of the large species and a few cassowaries were the only animals Riche had seen. Although in a state of exhaustion, he had carried until the last day a large collection of very interesting productions; but his strength diminished so rapidly in the course of the last day that he had had great difficulty in dragging himself along the shore in search of our ships; he had then been obliged to abandon everything, even what he valued most. As soon as he had recovered from his exhaustion we brought him back on board. In vain did we make all the agreed signals to announce that we had had the good fortune to find him; people were so convinced beforehand of the uselessness of our search that we were not understood until the moment our boat was quite close to the frigates, and Riche could be seen among us. The horrible situation in which he would have found himself, had the opinion formed about him prevailed, must inspire the greatest dread and serve as a terrible warning to captains and naturalists who undertake a distant voyage; for had we left this anchorage the day before, he would have ended his life by the most frightful of deaths, amid all the anguish of the most terrible despair.

Although this fact proved that it was possible to be lost for more than two days in this land, most of our seamen would still not admit it; some preferred to believe, and to say, that Riche had meant to go astray; as if one could suppose that he had gone of his own free will to expose himself to all the horrors of cruel hunger.

During the whole time we stayed at this anchorage it was impossible to fish with the seine; but on board the ships some fish were caught with the line, among which were the *labrus cyprinoides* and several new species of the genus *perça*. We were at anchor in latitude 33° 55' south, and longitude 119° 32' east.

The variation of the magnetic needle was found to be 6° to the west.

In the evening all the boats were hoisted in, and we waited for the next day to weigh anchor, if the winds allowed.

1792-12-17.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 417]
They varied from east-north-east to east-south-east, and at six in the morning we were already under sail.

We passed to the north of the small island that had sheltered us, and stood out towards the open sea.

Being at noon in latitude 34° 12' 54" south, and longitude 119° 21' east, the southernmost rocks bore east 2° south of us at a distance of about two thirds of a myriametre, and the northernmost land bore north 1° east.

For some days easterly winds had prevailed, and made us fear great hindrances in surveying this coast. Analogy gave this conjecture still greater likelihood. Indeed, at the Cape of Good Hope, which extends even a few degrees farther south than this part of New Holland, the easterly winds are likewise the prevailing winds at this same season.

1792-12-22.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 417-418]
By about the middle of the day on the 3rd of Nivôse we had still got no farther than latitude 34° 24' south, and longitude 120° 22' east, and we had not yet lost sight of the islets of the small archipelago where we had anchored.

The easterly winds had been fairly fresh in the afternoon, but at nightfall they blew off the land and brought us a stifling heat. We soon found ourselves in the midst of an extraordinarily thick fog; the air had become laden with a very great humidity which penetrated everywhere: I cannot better compare it than to that which the south winds bring over the Mediterranean at a short distance from the coast of Africa in the season of great heat. The sands heated by the rays of the sun had increased the property that atmospheric air has of dissolving water, and we found ourselves as it were in the midst of a vapour bath of mild temperature.

The darkness of the night made us lose sight of the Espérance at about eleven in the evening, and she did not answer our signals until three hours later, by a gunshot which we heard from a great distance. The winds were light.

1792-12-23.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 418-419]
We made short boards close-hauled, and as soon as it was light we saw that frigate at a short distance from us; they soon began to blow hard from the south-west and for some time drove us along at a great rate towards the east.

At noon we were in latitude 34° 14' south, and longitude 121° 2' east, and two hours later we saw behind some islets a large inlet which appeared to us to offer excellent shelter. Natives made their presence known to us by fires, whose smoke we saw rising, rather far from the shore, from several points very distant from one another.

The barometer having fallen even lower than when the storm had forced us to anchor in the rade de Legrand, we stood out to sea so as not to be driven down upon this dangerous coast; we then lay to, and remained so all night with our head to the south-south-east and south.

The sea was very high: the winds blew furiously from the south-west to west-south-west; after increasing by degrees they raged with the greatest violence for almost the whole night, and raised the waves to a prodigious height. We had never yet been so violently tossed by the storm.

The south-west winds here are almost always violent, and add greatly to the dangers to which one is exposed in running from west to east along this low coast, often guarded by reefs which one may fear not to see in time to weather them.

As soon as it was light we steered towards the land.

1792-12-24.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 419-420]
The winds had settled in the west-south-west and had brought back fine weather.

About the middle of the day we were in latitude 33° 42' south, and longitude 122° 4' east, when from the mastheads a part of the coast was seen beyond several islets, from west to north-west, which still appeared very low; we soon saw it form a fairly uniformly raised bank running eastwards, behind which no land could be seen.

As night came on we stood off from it and then lay to.

1792-12-25.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 420]
The next day we continued to follow it, and towards three in the afternoon we were only two kilometres from it: it had constantly presented the same form to us over a length of more than three myriametres. The thin horizontal strata could be perfectly distinguished there, offering exactly the same forms as the limestone I had found in the rade de Legrand.

I am inclined to believe that this cutting away of the mountains over so great an extent is the work of the waters; for they must have undermined these lands at their base, and the upper part must have subsided and fallen into the sea, forming the rampart that makes this coast inaccessible. We noticed a few small landslips there, by which, however, it would have been very difficult to climb; we were so close to it that we had to go about and stand out to sea; forty metres of depth were then found, on a bottom of calcareous sand.

1792-12-26.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 420-422]
Very early in the morning we saw the coast stretching towards the north-east, and with south-west winds it was easy for us to follow its windings. We still saw the same steep rampart which, rising fairly uniformly to about ninety metres, showed from its top down to sea level the parallel strata of which it is composed.

Towards the middle of the day the coast changed its appearance, curving a little towards the south-east; it then appeared broken by small sand-covered hills which, sloping gently down, ended in a very low beach. The sea then took on a greenish tint, even far out, and indicated a change of bottom to us; but a line twenty-eight metres long could not reach it.

The breeze soon blew very fresh. Experience had taught us to fear on this coast the south-west winds, which had become almost always violent; we therefore stood off on the south-east by east tack to gain the open sea.

The want of water was keenly felt on both our ships, and if we could not very soon find some to take in we should shortly be obliged to leave the coast; whereas, had we taken it up at its easternmost part so as to run along it from east to west, we should have had the advantage of taking in a good supply of water at cap de Diemen, instead of which ours was already half consumed when we began our survey of this land at its westernmost point. This consideration and many others should lead one to follow it from east to west; besides, the violence of the westerly winds exposes ships to the greatest dangers, whereas the easterly winds, which are the most constant, never blow violently.

1792-12-27.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 422]
We were only two kilometres from the coast, and the lead showed a bottom sometimes of coarse sand and sometimes of rock, the depth varying from eighteen to twenty-eight metres.

At noon our latitude had been 32° 19' south, and longitude 124° 52' east, the nearest land being two thirds of a kilometre to the north-north-west; it bore from north 69° west to east 20° north: it soon presented the appearance of a rampart, like the coast we had previously run along; but it differed from it in that its upper part rose by a gentle slope into the interior. A few shrubs were noticed there which seemed to suffer less than those we had so far seen along this same coast.

The sea was covered with the species of fucus called sea grape, *fucus natans*.

1792-12-30.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 422-423]
Thwarted by easterly winds, by about the middle of the day on the 11th we had still got no farther than latitude 32° 8' south, and longitude 126° 42' east, when we saw a fog rise which presented to us on all sides the appearance of flat land. The illusion was so striking that those who came up from between decks believed we had just entered a vast basin. We were, however, two myriametres from the coast, but this fog did not allow us to make it out.

In the evening the sky grew dark on the side of the land, and lightning flashed from the thickest cloud; then the fog that ringed the horizon cleared away: the wind shifted to the west and became very fresh.

1793-01-02.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 423]
Towards evening Captain Huon informed the commander of the expedition of the damage the Espérance's rudder had suffered. He told us that on board his ship they had long been reduced to three quarters of a bottle of water a day, that they had been obliged to stop serving out the antiscorbutic drinks, etc., and that thirty casks of water then made up the whole supply of his frigate.

1793-01-03.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 423-425]
The next morning at about half past ten the general sent him a letter to inform him of the decision he had taken regarding the situation in which the two ships found themselves.

At noon our latitude was 31° 52' south and our longitude 129° 10' east, and we could see the land from east to north 10° west, being one myriametre from the nearest shore. As soon as the boat was hoisted in, we stood on close-hauled on the larboard tack with an east-south-east wind, and steered for cap de Diemen, leaving an extremely barren coast of which we had just run along more than one hundred and sixty myriametres, in a general direction from west by south-west to east by north-east. Fifteen months before us, Vancouver, likewise thwarted by easterly winds, had been forced to leave it after being able to survey only about seventy myriametres of it.

Before reaching this land we did not foresee that we should meet with violent winds there so frequently, especially at this season, which must be the fine season in these waters, the sun having already been for more than two months in the southern hemisphere. Might this violence of the winds be caused by the prodigious difference between the slight warmth of the atmosphere at sea and the heat of the sun concentrated by the burning sands of the mainland?

The currents we felt along this coast always followed the direction of the winds.

The Espérance was in still greater distress than we were; besides, that frigate had suffered several damages at the last anchorage; she needed an excellent shelter in order to make all the repairs she required. From four o'clock the land could no longer be seen even from the mastheads; and at the same moment a line of sixty metres showed a bottom of fine sand mixed with fragments of lithophytes and shells.

1793-01-04.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 425]
The lead continued to be cast every two hours, and each time the depth of the sea was found to have increased by four to five metres: it had always increased almost imperceptibly as we drew away from the coast, which, on the 16th at about six in the evening, lay twenty myriametres from us; a line one hundred and thirty-three metres long then showed a bottom of fairly fine sand mixed with gravel, and from that moment no bottom was found, although soundings were taken at various times. This slow increase in the depth of the sea near this coast, by showing that the land sinks beneath the waters by a scarcely perceptible slope, leads me to suppose that the land stretching into the interior of the island rises by a likewise very gentle slope, so that its high mountains are too far off to be seen from the shore.

1793-01-06.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 425-427]
The day before we had been carried 23' to the west, and in the course of the 18th of Nivôse 21' in the same direction. At noon we had *35° 30'* of south latitude; the rapidity of these currents towards the west perhaps depends on some channel separating the lands of New Holland from those of cap de Diemen, between Point Hicks and the Furneaux Islands. Captain Cook, in surveying the eastern part of New Holland, saw no land in this space, which extends about twenty myriametres, and believed himself to be at the entrance of a great gulf. Perhaps it is in this part of the coast that the mouth of a channel begins, which, after forming various windings, opens to the west in the same latitude as that in which we met with such strong currents.

We did not have westerly winds until about the 40<sup>th</sup>° of south latitude; they carried us as far as cap de Diemen, varying from south-west to north-west.

Towards ten o'clock we saw a great number of cetaceans of a new species pass at a short distance from us, which appeared to me to belong to the genus *delphinus*. They will easily be recognised by a large white patch which they bear on the back behind the dorsal fin; the upper part of the body is of a blackish brown and the belly white. The largest were more than three metres long: they were preceded by a great number of dolphins, *delphinus delphis*, and they swam in schools like them, performing with great rapidity much the same movements as those cetaceans.

We lay to during the night, intending the next day to make the land one degree below the latitude of cap de Diemen. We hoped to discover a harbour there which might henceforth have offered great advantages to navigators intending to survey the south-west coast of New Holland with the help of the easterly winds.

1793-01-18.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 427]
From half past four in the morning we sighted the land from north-east by north to east by south-east, the nearest coast bearing east-north-east at a distance of three myriametres.

The wind was south-west; for some time we stood on close-hauled on the starboard tack. Two hours later, as we were now only one and a half myriametres from the shore, a line one hundred and fifty metres long showed us a bottom of very coarse sand and broken shells.

We saw a steep coast and, at a short distance inland, a chain of mountains of moderate height, running in much the same direction: this land was almost everywhere covered with tall trees.

At noon we were in latitude 42° 51' south, and longitude 142° 49' east; the land to the north-east could only be seen through a haze which heavily obscured the horizon on all sides.

1793-01-19.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 427-429]
The variation of the magnetic needle had increased very rapidly since it had become easterly, for it was observed to be 7° east.

The coast offered us no inlet that might lead us to expect to find a good anchorage there. By noon we had already reached latitude 43° 22' south and longitude 143° 28' east; we were only one myriametre from the land, and from north 7° west to east 23° south it still showed us fairly high mountains.

At six in the evening we doubled the cap méridional at a distance of two myriametres. It is remarkable that, through the various windings of the coast we had just followed, we had constantly had the wind astern. It seems to me that the high mountains, setting a barrier against the winds, force them to run along the coast.

Above all the other mountains we could make out the one we had seen covered with snow the year before, when we had anchored in port Dentrecasteaux; but as this time we were in the season of the greatest heat, we saw snow only in the large hollows where it was sheltered from the rays of the sun for a good part of the day; this mountain is remarkable for a small cone-shaped peak which crowns its summit.

As night came on we passed fairly close to the Mewstone, and soon lay to with a very fresh westerly wind.

Soundings were taken several times with a line of one hundred and sixty-six metres without finding bottom.

As we were being driven down upon the coast by south-south-west winds, we were forced to beat to and fro.

1793-01-20.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 429]
We had just found at noon latitude 43° 44' south, and longitude 144° 16' east, when the Mewstone bore west 16° 30' south, and the Eddystone south-south-east 1° east. The nearest coast bore north-north-west of us at a distance of three kilometres.

1793-01-21.journal_labillardiere:
[t. I, p. 429-431]
Very early in the morning of the 3rd of Pluviôse we were at the entrance of Storm Bay. The wind was blowing from the east-south-east, and prevented us from running into détroit Dentrecasteaux [D'Entrecasteaux Channel], where we intended to anchor in a cove we had discovered the year before, which was extremely convenient for making all the repairs our ships needed; but we had to resolve to enter the baie des Roches, which we had been led to name thus because of reefs almost awash lying towards its middle; it is the first cove on the larboard hand on entering Storm Bay, and runs from north-east to south-west: the Espérance anchored there very early.

Having got a third of the way into this bay, we found bottom with a line five metres long; it was not prudent to go any farther without having soundings taken along the course we were to hold, and this was all the easier as we had several boats in the water. Crétin, who had come to sound in this roadstead the year before, told the general that no less than five metres of depth would be found there; which put a stop to any further search. This assertion ought not, however, to have been wholly accepted, for besides the fact that Crétin had not spent enough time on his soundings to answer for the depth of the sea to within half a metre, it was doubtful whether he had carried out this operation at low tide; which might make a difference of at least a metre and a half and cause us to touch. In spite of these considerations, they did not hesitate to steer to larboard, drawing still nearer to the low land; and so we soon ran aground, but fortunately on sand. It was half past nine. The wind rose in violent gusts from the tops of the mountains and drove us violently towards the shore, sinking us deeper and deeper into the sand.

The Espérance at once sent us her longboat and her large cutter, which, together with our own boats, tried in vain to make our ship cast to starboard by towing her. The need was then felt to carry out a kedge anchor to the west-north-west, so as to hold our ship by a strong hawser that would keep her from being driven closer to the shore; then, to lighten her, the sea water with which most of our casks were filled was run off into the hold, and at the same time all the pumps were set to work to empty it. As soon as we were relieved of this weight, we hove at the capstan on a heavy anchor which had been carried out close beside the first; but it was only towards one o'clock in the afternoon, after the greatest efforts, that we managed to get clear of this sandbank and that our ship was at last afloat.

END OF THE FIRST VOLUME.

1793-01-22.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 5-6]
# ACCOUNT OF THE VOYAGE IN SEARCH OF LA PÉROUSE.

## CHAPTER X.

*Stay in the baie des Roches. Various excursions into the interior. Goodness of the soil. Singular structure of the bark of several trees peculiar to New Holland. Difficulty of penetrating the forests. Inland the trees are not hollowed out by fire as they are on the sea shore. Coal towards the north-west of the cap méridional. Meeting with the savages. Their very peaceable conduct towards us. One of them came to watch us at night while we slept. Several accompanied us through the woods. Various other meetings with these inhabitants.* *They broil shellfish on the coals to eat them. Polygamy established among these peoples. Their fishing. The women go in search of crustaceans and shellfish, sometimes diving to great depths. One of the savages comes on board. Their knowledge of botany.*

[t. II, p. 6-8]
I WENT ashore at five in the morning, near the entrance of our anchorage. Along the beach I saw blocks of sandstone whose debris had formed the very fine quartz sand over which I walked for some time.

The Espérance had already found, in a small cove towards the north-west, a watering place whose water was very good and very easy to take in. The stream that supplied it fell into the sea from a height of more than one metre. It was very easy to lead it right into the longboat with wooden troughs.

We soon came towards the head of the bay, where we found a hut skilfully built by the savages. We admired the skill with which they had arranged the sheets of tree bark that covered it; it was impenetrable to the heaviest rains: its opening faced the sea; the wish to see the inside made us go in.

We had been told that some people from the Espérance had seen, the day before, quite close to this hut, three natives sitting round a small fire, but that these savages, frightened by the noise of a musket fired at a bird, had fled in haste. We soon had further proof of their presence at this end of the bay, and it seemed to us that they habitually came to sleep in the hut. We were soon sorry to have gone into this cabin, for the vermin that clung to our clothes bit us very disagreeably a short time afterwards.

The flood tide had just brought the sea water into the low ground inland; we saw many ducks there, which would not let us approach nearer than a very great distance. This fear they showed of man made me think that the natives hunt them.

We had found few insects in the woods, but on our return to the shore we were amply compensated. As the sky was very fine, the insects had been flying everywhere, and among the great number that had tried to cross the bay, many *thermes* and various beetles of very odd shapes had fallen into the water; the wind had driven them up onto the sand, where it was very easy for us to pick them up.

1793-01-23.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 8-9]
The next day, at daybreak, we had ourselves put ashore towards the head of the roadstead, whence we entered a large valley which stretches to the south-west between very high hillsides. From the top of one of the highest we could see the whole country as far as the foot of the great mountain which lay to the north-west of our ships. The snow still lingering on its summit made a very picturesque sight, and set off the fine green of the tall trees which seemed to grow there vigorously.

Various species of *embothrium* were to be seen on the slope of the hillsides where we were. Lower down we saw very clear water welling up in several places and running into a lake where I saw some pelicans, which unfortunately I could only shoot at from a great distance. This lake lies in the middle of a large plain whose soil, in the lowest places, is composed of a clay soaked with water and covered with the roots of various plants, which form a rather poor peat lying on shaking ground. This ground, split open in several places to a width of a few decimetres, shows within a very watery mud covered with water. I had the pleasure of gathering near these bogs a great number of plants, among which I noticed several new species of *calceolaria* and *drosera*.

We soon walked on a vegetable mould which I found to be the same to a depth of more than half a metre over the whole breadth of the valley. The temperature of the climate there would greatly favour the cultivation of most European plants; besides, a few ditches dug in suitable places would give the waters the drainage needed to do away with almost all the marshes found there and turn them into fertile land.

As night came on we were near our landing place, where we saw several heaps of oyster shells brought there by the natives, which had led our fishermen to look for oysters in the roadstead. At low tide they found quite close by a bed of oysters, of which they laid in a large supply. The flood tide also brought into this inlet several species of ray, some of which were caught by these same fishermen.

1793-01-24.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 9-10]
I spent the 6th describing and preparing everything I had collected since our arrival in the baie des Roches. I was astonished at the great variety of productions still offered me by this part of New Holland, where I had already made very thorough searches the year before for more than a month, though, it is true, in places several myriametres distant from those we had just gone over, and in a much more advanced season; and so I found there a great number of plants which had already disappeared at the time of our first stay on this land.

1793-01-25.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 10-13]
We set off the next day at dawn, intending not to return on board for two days, and resolved to carry our searches to a great distance from our anchorage. We landed to the south-west and followed, roughly in that direction, a path made by the natives, where we noticed fairly fresh prints of bare feet, among which could be seen those of very young children: some families, frightened by our stay in the baie des Roches, had doubtless gone to seek another retreat where they believed themselves safer.

After an hour's walk we stopped in a low place where the waters of the neighbouring hills drained away. Several species of *leptospermum* throve so well in this moisture that they had become very large trees, whereas elsewhere I had so far found them only of the size of small shrubs. Some here were more than thirty metres high, although the trunk of the tree was not two decimetres thick; one of these species was remarkable for its bark, about three centimetres thick and composed of a great number of layers lying one upon another, very easy to separate, and as thin as the finest China paper: this singular structure of the bark is met with only in New Holland; it is much the same in the *eucalyptus resinifera*; I had also observed it on the south-west coast of this same land in two large trees, one of which belongs to the protea family and the other to the myrtle family.

We soon found a windbreak set against the strong south-west breezes. Near it we saw the site of a fire which appeared to us to have been lit recently. The natives had left there part of the stalk of the *fucus palmatus*, which they eat after broiling it, as we had occasion to see later on.

The south-west wind, which had been preceded by a great fall of the mercury in the barometer, blew in the afternoon in violent gusts which brought us rain just as we reached the sea shore quite close to the cap méridional. A shrub of the rue family happily formed very thick clumps there, which offered us excellent shelter: this tree grew vigorously on these heights, although it was exposed to the full violence of the furious winds that prevail in these parts.

I have given this new genus the name of *mazeutoxeron*.

The calyx is bell-shaped and four-toothed.

Four petals are attached at the base of the calyx.

The stamens, eight in number, are fixed on the receptacle. The ovary is oval in shape. The style is not quite so long as the stamens. The stigma has four divisions.

The capsule has four cells, each formed of two valves; it is covered with hairs.

Each cell contains two to three almost spherical seeds.

This plant has opposite, rounded leaves, covered with a thick down, and tawny in colour beneath.

The flowers are solitary and placed in the axils of the leaves.

I designate this shrub by the name of *mazeutoxeron rufum*.

*Fig.* 2. Flower.
*Fig.* 3. Petal.
*Fig.* 4. The petals have been removed to show the stamens.

For some time we walked northwards across heaped-up sands, before going down to the beach, whose windings we followed with great ease for a long way; but we were at last stopped by a sheer mountain jutting out into the sea. In vain we tried to get round it; it was impossible for us to make our way through the thickets that surrounded it.

Night was approaching; we retraced our steps, intending to look for a convenient place to spend the night near a stream we had already crossed. A thick bush was the best shelter we found there. We further lined it with branches, expecting to be perfectly sheltered from the weather; but the south-west wind blew with such force during the night that it drove the rain in on all sides. To crown our misfortune, the cold was very sharp and forced most of us to draw near the fire, although one got even wetter there than in this sort of hut.

1793-01-26.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 13-15]
As soon as day broke we left our wretched lodging and went over the dunes that surrounded us. In a few places which appeared to have fallen in not long before, I observed that some of these heaps of sand rested upon a hard steatite of a dark grey colour, and others upon sandstone. I noticed the same a moment afterwards along the shore: a very large rock jutting out into the sea not far from the coast showed the same kind of steatite in every part; this rock, which is very high, is pierced through at one of its ends.

The waves had torn from the bottom of the sea the sponge called *spongia cancellata*, which we saw cast up in great quantities on the shore. In the midst of these dunes grew a new species of plantain, which I name *plantago tricuspidata*, from the shape of its leaves; it must be ranked among the most useful plants that this land furnishes for the food of man. The hope of finding some vegetables fit to be eaten as a salad had led the most provident among us to bring the seasoning required for such a dish: the leaves of this plantain were very tender, and the salad they furnished us was exceedingly to the taste of all the company.

Various grasses, among which I noticed several new species of *festuca*, served to bind the sands. A new geranium, with a very small herbaceous stem and deeply cut leaves, was among the plants I gathered: it was the first plant of this genus that I had seen in this land.

I had already noticed a few burrows dug in places where the sand was firm enough. Soon I saw a greater number of them; but I did not know what animal had made them, until a kangaroo of middling size started up at our approach and went to ground in one: in vain did we fire several shots into it in the hope that the smoke would drive it out; it stayed crouched there throughout.

Soon a great many kangaroo tracks beaten through a small wood roused the ardour of two sportsmen who were with us; they were not long in catching sight, in the midst of a meadow watered by a charming brook, of several of these quadrupeds, none of which, however, would let itself be approached.

At length we got back on board, all the more weary because for more than forty hours we had not slept a single moment.

1793-01-27.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 15-17]
I spent the four following days in going over the country round our anchorage; towards the south-south-east I found there a fine tree which seemed to me to belong to the family of the conifers, to judge by the arrangement of its stamens and the resinous smell of all its parts; but I was never able to obtain its fruit, although I afterwards came upon many other trees of the same kind. No doubt the season was not yet far enough advanced: the stamens I noticed on it appeared to have lasted over from the preceding year. I mention this tree not only because of the singularity of its leaves in a tree of this family, for they are broad and deeply divided at their edges, but also because of their usefulness in the making of beer: their extract, bitter and at the same time aromatic, made me think that it might serve like that of the spruce. The trial I made of it with malt showed me that I had not been mistaken.

This fine tree is often as much as one metre thick, with a height of from twenty-five to thirty metres: its wood is very hard, of a reddish colour, and takes a fine polish.

The thick forests lying to the north-north-west of our ships offered me a great number of trees of moderate height which throve very well, in spite of the shade cast over them by enormous trees of *eucalyptus globulus*.

I shall give some particulars of a new genus of the family of the St John's worts, which was the ornament of these solitary places and which I call *carpodontos*.

The calyx is of four scarious leaves joined at their upper part; they come away as the corolla unfolds.

The corolla is formed of four petals attached beneath the ovary.

The stamens are numerous (thirty to forty).

The ovary is elongated and topped by six or seven styles, each of which has a pointed stigma.

The capsule opens into six or seven woody valves, split on the inside along their whole length and marked with two teeth at their upper end.

The seeds are few and flattened.

This tree, which does not rise above eight or ten metres, is rather slender.

Its leaves are oval, opposite, leathery, glossy, and covered with a light coat of resin which exudes from their upper side; the underside is whitish, and the transverse veins are scarcely perceptible on it. I have given it the name of *carpodontos lucida*.
