1793-01-31.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 17-19]
On the 13th we had formed the plan of going to visit the highest of the mountains in this part of New Holland: its varied situations gave us hope of a great number of new productions. Each of us carried provisions for five days, in the belief that this time would be enough to accomplish our purpose. We set out very early in the morning, fairly well supplied with biscuit, cheese, salt pork and brandy, our usual provision on our distant excursions. After going half the way along the road we had already followed before in going to the cap méridional, we came upon a vast clearing which made our march westward easy as far as the foot of the hillocks we had to cross, and at length we plunged into the midst of the forests, with no other guide than the magnetic needle.

We made towards the north, and could advance only slowly, being obliged at every step to get over the obstacles presented by enormous trees piled one upon another; most of them, uprooted by the storm, had carried away in their fall a part of the ground in which they had grown; others, fallen from old age, were worm-eaten throughout, and often the lower end of their trunks could be seen still standing upright in the midst of the enormous heaps of their remains.

After an extraordinarily toilsome march we at last reached the summit of a mountain, from which we saw to the south the middle of the roadstead of the cap méridional, and to the north-west the great mountain towards which we were directing our steps.

Night soon forced us to halt. We lit a large fire, beside which a sweet sleep came upon us and relieved us of the fatigues of the day. We slept in the open air, because it would have been very difficult for us to build a shelter quickly among these great trees, their branches being placed chiefly towards their tops; besides, this part of the forest was bare of shrubs. We had looked in vain for some large trunks hollowed out by fire; but these are met with only in places frequented by the natives; we had seen a great number of them along the seashore, and there we had noticed many paths beaten by them; nothing, on the contrary, showed us that they had ever come into the midst of these thick forests.

The air was extremely calm; I woke towards midnight, and finding myself alone in the midst of these silent forests, whose majesty the faint light of the stars still allowed me to glimpse, I was filled with a feeling of admiration for the grandeur of nature beyond all expression.

1793-02-01.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 19-20]
From daybreak we held the same course as the day before: the difficulties grew greater and greater; often the trunks thrown down one upon another formed an almost impenetrable barrier, and obliged us to climb up onto the highest of them and so walk from tree to tree at the risk of falling from a great height; for many of them, being covered with a spongy bark soaked by the constant damp that prevails in these thick forests, offered us only an extremely slippery and difficult passage.

The day was already far advanced when we reached the summit of a mountain, from which we saw in its whole extent a long valley that we should still have to cross before arriving at the foot of the mountain we had intended to visit: the distance separating us from it appeared to be about three myriametres, and this space was occupied by forests as thick as those we had just made our way through. It was doubtful whether we should take no more than two days to reach the goal we had set ourselves, even supposing that our march were not slowed by great swamps or other obstacles impossible to foresee. About the same time would be needed to return: by this reckoning we should have been without provisions for three days. Besides, these forests did not offer us the least means of subsistence; we were therefore obliged to give up our plan.

The great chain of mountains appeared, over a vast extent, to run from north-east to south-west.

In the forests we had just gone through we found the same kinds of stone that we had already met with towards the cap méridional. We could see this cape to the south by east: we took that direction, and went to spend the night at the edge of the forest, near a brook that flowed at the foot of the mountains.

1793-02-02.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 20-23]
The difficulty of making our way through the woods led us to resolve thenceforth to follow the beach as far as we could, and to take advantage of the clearings that ran down to it in order to strike inland: in this way we could go over a great extent of ground in a short time; but first we had to get past the steep bluff which jutted out over the beach and had stopped us a few days before. Fresh attempts at last succeeded, and after the greatest difficulties we managed to make our way through the dense thickets that guarded the approach to it: once out of them we were able to continue our march along the seashore, where for some time we found an easy road, the mountains coming down to it by a gentle slope; but we were soon obliged to clamber over steep rocks, at the foot of which we saw the sea breaking in a frightful manner. This road, difficult as it was, was nevertheless frequented by the natives. We found one of their spears on it: this weapon was a long, very straight stick which they had not taken the trouble to polish, but which they had sharpened at both ends.

The flank of the mountains, laid bare over a very great extent, showed us a horizontal seam of coal whose greatest thickness did not exceed one decimetre. We traced it over a distance of more than three hundred metres. It rested upon sandstone and was covered by a dark brown schist. These signs lead me to suppose that at a greater depth excellent coal would be found in abundance. It is known that the richest mines of this fuel are commonly found beneath sandstone.

The rust with which I saw the water oozing from the rocks strongly coloured was the first sign that told me these mountains contained iron; but I soon found fine pieces of haematite of a bronzed red colour, and farther on an ochreous earth of a fairly bright red. Tripoli was also scattered in small separate pieces along the path we were following; it had probably come away from the upper strata, which could no longer be made out because great falls of earth had hidden them.

Several new species of *lobelia* grew out of the clefts of the rocks, which became steeper and steeper; some of them were sheer and rose more than two hundred metres perpendicularly above the level of the sea. Very recent traces of falls made us decide to take our way through the woods and to approach these rocks no more except with the greatest caution.

For some time we walked among shrubs, most of which were of the heath family and of the ebony family. Soon we were drawn by a frightful noise whose redoubled bursts seemed to us to follow the movement of the waves, and we saw with the greatest astonishment the terrible spectacle of the destructive effects of the sea, which is continually undermining these steep shores. The base of an enormous rock was already swallowed up beneath the waters, while its top was hollowed into a vast vault hanging more than two hundred metres perpendicularly above, which, by echoing the sounds, increased the noise of the repeated shocks of the violent waves breaking against their sides.

We had passed the first two capes that lie to the west of the cap méridional. We went back towards the latter, where we spent a very bad night, for unhappily we were not far from stagnant waters, and the great calm of the air had left us exposed to all the fury of the mosquitoes.

1793-02-03.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 23-24]
Low tide fell in the morning: we reckoned on taking advantage of it to get shellfish, of which the bad quality of our provisions made us feel a pressing need; but the sea breeze came and disappointed our hopes by raising the waters to about the same height they would have reached at high tide; so we had to content ourselves with our salt provisions.

The waterfall of the cap méridional, which when Furneaux touched at this land carried a great deal of water to the sea, was almost dry at the time we were there. It could nevertheless be seen plainly from the traces of the torrent that its flow must be considerable in the rainy season.

We found lying dead on the beach a seal of the species called *phoca monachus*. Two heavy bruises it had on its head led us to suppose that it had perhaps been dashed against some rock, in spite of itself, by the violence of the waves.

Making our way towards our anchorage, we found to the east-north-east of the cap méridional two large pools, and in going round their edges we saw several kangaroo burrows there. A new species of *utricularia* displayed its charming flowers on the surface of these still waters. I was surprised that these stagnant waters did not give off a fetid smell, as usually happens: it is likely that they were rapidly renewed by filtering through the ground.

It was three in the afternoon when we got on board. We learned that one of the gunners of the Espérance, named Boucher, had just died of a consumption of the lungs.

1793-02-04.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 24-25]
The time left to me after describing and preparing the objects I had collected on the preceding days I spent in visiting the low lands lying to the south-east of us. I made my way easily into these forests, whose trees stood fairly far apart from one another. Almost everywhere I found excellent vegetable mould. I cut specimens of several sorts of wood there, in order to learn the various uses to which each of them might be put. The fine tree which I believe to be of the conifer family, and of which I have already spoken, offered great resistance to the saw; no doubt it is the tree of this family that would furnish the most compact wood.

I had long wished that most of the seeds we had brought from Europe which might succeed here should be sown on this part of the coast in good vegetable mould with sufficient moisture; but on my return I saw with regret that a very sandy and very dry piece of ground, rather near the head of the bay, had just been dug and sown.

1793-02-05.journal_labillardiere: (Labillardière's account for this day is given under 1793-02-04.)

1793-02-06.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 25-27]
On the 19th the gardener and I, with two men of the crew, set out very early in the morning, intending to spend two days in succession going over the country round port Dentrecasteaux. We landed at its entrance on the western shore. It was the time of low tide, and by a lucky chance we found ourselves on an oyster bank, from which we laid in an ample supply.

It was with pleasure that we saw again a piece of country we had visited several times the year before. Most of the little brooks we had met with there, and even the one from which we had drawn our water at that time, were now dry.

We soon reached the head of the harbour, and in going up the river we found very dense and marshy thickets which often slowed our steps.

Snakes are not common at the cap de Diemen: I saw two, however, asleep in the sun on large tree trunks; but at our approach they made for the hollow trunks which served them as a retreat. They were of the species of colubrine snake that I had already found the year before, and which is in no way dangerous.

Although the course of the river was obstructed almost at every step by large trees, we were nevertheless obliged to go up it for more than two kilometres before finding one that gave us the means of crossing to the other bank without too much difficulty.

We then made towards the north-east, and crossed very conveniently a great plain where the natives had lately burned part of the vegetation. We soon reached the head of the great lake, whose shores we followed down to the sea; and after going over a great extent of ground we returned to its far end to spend the night close beside a brook we had already crossed. As the sky was very fine, we slept in the open air, sheltered only by large tree trunks lying on the ground; but the cold, which soon made itself keenly felt, forced us to light a large fire.

It is remarkable that the temperature of the air at this extremity of New Holland sometimes varied by 17° between day and night (from the 6<sup>th</sup>° to the 23<sup>rd</sup>°. The thermometer referred to is always the mercury thermometer graduated on Réaumur's scale). It is true that this narrow land, lying in so high a latitude, is little able to retain for long the heat imparted to it by the rays of the sun; this great difference in temperature did not fail to inconvenience us, inasmuch as it forced us to burden ourselves during the day with very cumbersome clothing. I should further observe that the variation of the thermometer observed on board during the same time did not go beyond 5° to 6°.

1793-02-07.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 27-40]
As soon as day broke, while the two men who had accompanied us were still asleep, the gardener and I went forward alone towards the part of the lake opposite to the one we had visited the day before.

I had the pleasure of gathering several species of *mimosa* with simple leaves, all the parts of whose fructification were developed. I already possessed some specimens of them, but they were very incomplete.

After going at least three kilometres, we thought we heard some human voices ahead of us. We redoubled our attention as we went forward a few paces, when all at once there came from the same spot a cry made up of several voices together, and through the trees we saw a great number of natives, most of whom seemed to be busy fishing along the edge of the lake. As we did not know their intentions, and were moreover unarmed, we did not hesitate to decide on rejoining our two travelling companions, each of whom had a musket. We at once cut through the woods to get out of sight of the savages, and tried to conceal our flight from them so as not to be pursued.

After telling our two men the reason for our return, I let them know my keen desire to communicate with these inhabitants; but first we had to arrange our means of defence so that we could use them in case they should attack us. We hastily made up a few cartridges and set off towards the place where we had seen them; it was still only nine o'clock. We had hardly gone a few paces when we met them. The grown men and the boys were drawn up in front, roughly in a half-circle; the women, the girls and the children stood behind, a few paces off. As their bearing did not seem to me to show any hostile intent, I did not hesitate to go up to the eldest; he accepted with a good grace a piece of biscuit which I offered him and which he had seen me eat: I then held out my hand to him as a sign of friendship, and had the pleasure of seeing that this savage understood me very well; he gave me his, bowing a little and at the same time raising his left foot, which he drew backwards as he bent his body. These movements were accompanied by a pleasant smile.

My travelling companions also went up close to the others, and at once the best understanding reigned between us and these inhabitants. They received with joy the neckerchiefs we offered them: the young people drew still closer to us; one of them had the generosity to give me some little whelks pierced near the middle and strung on a cord: this ornament, which he called *canlaride*, was the only one he possessed; he wore it round his head. A handkerchief replaced this present and fulfilled every wish of our savage, who came forward so that I might bind it round his head, and who, putting his hand to it again and again, showed the greatest joy. We had, as I have already said, a good deal of clothing because of the coolness of the nights; we parted with the greater part of it in favour of these islanders.

The women very much wished to come nearer to us, and although the men made signs to them to keep apart, curiosity was every moment on the point of prevailing over every other consideration. Confidence, however, grew more and more, and they then obtained leave to approach. It seemed very surprising to us that in so high a latitude, where at this early season of the year we already felt a fairly sharp cold at night, these people should not feel the need to clothe themselves. Most of the women, indeed, were entirely naked, like the men. Only a few had their shoulders and part of their back covered with a kangaroo skin, worn with the fur against their flesh; among these we noticed two who each had a child at the breast; another had for her only garment a strip of kangaroo skin half a decimetre wide, wound six or seven times round her belly: another wore a collar of skin; some others had their heads bound with several turns of a rather thin cord. I found later that these cords were made for the most part from the bark of a shrub of the family of the thymelaeas, very widespread in this land.

Soon a battle-axe which we used to cut some branches aroused the admiration of these inhabitants. As they saw us disposed to give them what we possessed, they were not afraid to ask us for it; and as soon as we had granted it to them they were overjoyed: they also felt the full value of our knives, and received with pleasure some tin vessels. As soon as I had shown them my watch it excited their envy. One of them in particular made known to me his desire to have it; but he very quickly gave up his request when he saw that I did not wish to part with it.

The readiness with which we gave them our belongings no doubt led them to suppose that from then on they might take everything that belonged to us without troubling to ask for anything more; for this reason we were obliged to set bounds to their desires; but we saw with satisfaction that they gave back, without the least resistance, the things we could not leave with them.

I had given them many things without asking anything of them. In my turn I wished to acquire a kangaroo skin, at a moment when, among the savages about us, there was only one young girl who had one. As soon as I had proposed that she should give it to me in exchange for a pair of trousers, she fled and ran to hide in the woods. The other natives appeared truly grieved at this refusal. These good people joined me beside the young girl and called to her several times. At length she yielded to their entreaties and came up to hand me the skin. Perhaps it was only from shyness that she had been reluctant to part with this kind of garment; she received in return a pair of trousers which, given the customs of these ladies, was of much less use to her than the skin that served to cover her shoulders. We showed her how they were used; but for that we had, of course, to put them on her ourselves. She lent herself to it with the best grace in the world, resting both hands on our shoulders to steady herself while she raised her legs one after the other to receive this new garment. Wishing to avoid any cause of misunderstanding, we preserved on this occasion all the gravity of which we were capable.

These savages were forty-two in number, of whom seven were grown men and eight women; the rest appeared to be their children, among whom we noticed several girls already of marriageable age and even less clothed than most of the mothers. We invited them all to come and rest by our fire; as soon as we had got there, one of these savages made us understand by unmistakable signs that he had come to reconnoitre us during the night: to make us understand that he had seen us sleeping there, he put his right hand against one side of his head, which he bent at the same moment, closing his eyes to express sleep; with the other hand he pointed out to us the place where we had spent the night; then by other signs no less expressive he showed us that at that time he had been standing on the other side of the brook, from where he had watched us. Indeed, one of us had been woken towards the middle of the night by a noise of branches being stirred, and had even thought he heard some of them break; but, overcome with fatigue, he had soon fallen asleep again; besides, he believed that it was surely a kangaroo that had come to pay us a visit. Our fire had served as a landmark for the native whom this tribe had charged with coming to observe us: as for us, although we had been entirely at the mercy of these savages the whole night, we had none the less slept the most peaceful sleep. One of the men who were with us then told us that the evening before, at sunset, having seen smoke on the other side of the lake, he had supposed that natives were gathered there; but it had not occurred to him, he told us, to mention it to us when we had come together again.

We wished to show these savages the effect of our firearms, after making them understand as best we could that they had nothing to fear from them; they seemed, however, somewhat frightened by the noise of the explosion.

These natives have woolly hair and let their beards grow. Plates six, seven and eight give a far more exact idea of the character of their features than anything I could convey by long descriptions. It may be observed (plate 7) that in the children the upper jaw projects well beyond the lower, but that, sinking with age, it comes to lie in the adult roughly in the same line. Their skin is not of a very deep black; but no doubt it is a beauty among these people to be very black, and to appear still much blacker than they really are they cover themselves with charcoal dust, chiefly on the upper parts of the body.

On their skin, particularly on the chest and shoulders, may be seen raised weals arranged symmetrically, sometimes forming lines a decimetre long, sometimes dots placed at various distances from one another. The corrosive by means of which they had produced these kinds of raised marks had not, however, destroyed the reticular tissue of the skin, for there it kept the same colour as the other parts of the body.

The custom of pulling out two of the upper incisor teeth, which on the report of some travellers had been believed general among these inhabitants, has certainly not been adopted by this tribe, for we saw none of them who lacked any teeth in the upper jaw; and they all had very fine teeth.

One of the sailors who were with us thought he could not treat them better than by offering them brandy; but, being accustomed to drink nothing but water, they spat it out very quickly, and it appeared to cause them a very disagreeable sensation.

These savages, being quite naked, are apt to hurt themselves, especially on the lower extremities, when they go through the woods. We noticed one who walked with difficulty and who had wrapped one of his feet in a piece of skin.

For some time I had no longer seen the young girls, and I thought they had all already withdrawn into the woods; but, looking behind me, I was surprised to see seven of them who had gone and perched on a thick branch more than three metres above the ground, and from there were watching our slightest movements with great attention: they were all crouching, and made a charming group.

We were a long way from the shore where a boat was to wait for us and take us on board. It was time to set out in order to reach it. We were leaving these peaceable inhabitants with regret when we saw the men and four young people separate from their band to accompany us. Soon one of the most robust went off into the wood, from which he came back almost at once holding two long spears in his hand; but as he came towards us he made signs to us to have no fear; he seemed, on the contrary, to wish to place us under the protection of his weapons. No doubt it was so as not to alarm us that they had left them in the forest when they came to meet us in the morning.

The other natives whom we had just left came up to our party again. As soon as we had invited the man carrying the spears to show us his skill, he seized one in his right hand at about the middle, then, raising it to the height of his head and keeping it all the while level, he drew it back towards himself three times in succession with jerks, setting up a very noticeable quivering at both its ends; then he threw it nearly a hundred paces. This weapon, borne up along its whole length by the lower column of air, travelled in a fairly horizontal direction over more than three quarters of that distance. The quivering he gave it before throwing it no doubt helped to speed its forward motion and to keep it longer in the air.

This savage was good enough to comply with our wishes by throwing the same spear several times in succession; then he aimed at a mark we pointed out to him, and each time he came near enough to it to give us a high idea of his skill. A moment later another showed us two holes in a kangaroo skin which appeared to have been made by the point of a spear, thus letting us know that they use it to kill these quadrupeds. Indeed, they throw it with enough force to pierce the animal right through. At length we set off with our new guides, whose pace was slow enough for us to follow them easily. It seems that they are not accustomed to making a long journey at a stretch; for we had hardly walked half an hour when they made us sit down, saying to us *mèdi*; we stopped at once. This halt lasted only a few minutes, after which they got up, calling to us *tangara*, which means *let us go*. We at once set off again. In the same way they made us take four more rests at roughly equal intervals.

The attentions these savages lavished on us astonished us greatly. If our way was encumbered by heaps of dry branches, some of them walked ahead of us and cleared them to the sides of the path; they even broke off those which, still attached to fallen trees, blocked the road we were following.

We could not walk on the dry grass without slipping at every moment, especially on slopes; but these good savages, to keep us from falling, held us up by taking us by the arm. It was in vain that we tried to persuade them that none of us would fall even if he were helped by nobody; they none the less continued to give us these marks of tender affection; often, indeed, two of them would place themselves, one on the right and the other on the left, to support us still better. As they obstinately persisted in their intention of rendering us these kindly services, we decided to refuse them no longer.

They certainly suspected that we had formed the plan of going to port Dentrecasteaux, for twice we took the wrong way, and each time they put us back on the one leading straight to it.

A small incident gave us reason to believe that they sometimes catch birds by hand. A parakeet of the species figured in pl. 10, which I shall shortly describe, passed quite close to us and alighted a little way off on the turf. At once two of the young savages broke away and chased it, and they were on the point of laying hands on it when the bird flew off.

It may be presumed that at the cap de Diemen no snake is to be met with whose bite is to be feared; at least, if there are any, the natives know well how to tell them from the others; they pointed out to us one which slid through the grass quite close to them, but it did not appear to inspire them with any fear.

At length they led us near to the place where we had been anchored the year before. The eldest of them was very thirsty; he at once had one of the young men bring him an oyster shell to use as a cup; but he had to dip it many times before he managed to quench his thirst.

As we were very close to the garden which had been made the year before under the direction of Citizen Lahaye, gardener to the expedition, we resolved to visit it; we took advantage of the moment when the savages were seated; we wanted to arrange for them to stay with our two sailors, for fear that they might go and damage any plants that might have succeeded; but one of them was determined to follow us; he examined the plants of this garden attentively and pointed them out to us with his finger, appearing to distinguish them perfectly from the native vegetation. We saw with regret that there remained only a small number of cabbages, a few potatoes, some radishes, cress, wild chicory and sorrel, and all in very poor condition: these plants would no doubt have done better nearer a brook which we could see towards the west. I had at least expected to find the cress planted along its banks; this can surely only have been an oversight on the gardener's part.

Our boat had not yet arrived. We very much wished these savages to see it close to; besides, we reckoned on persuading some of them to come on board with us; but they were already leaving us to rejoin their families. However, at our invitation they put off their departure, and we walked together along the beach towards the entrance of the harbour. Trees lying on the sand gave them an opportunity of giving us an idea of their agility by leaping over them. As for us, we were too tired to amuse ourselves by showing them what we could do; but I believe that, savages though they were, a fairly agile European might have got the better of them in this kind of contest.

As soon as the boat had arrived we invited some of them to embark with us. After taking a long time to make up their minds, three of them were willing to get in; but it appears that they had had no intention of leaving their band, for they got out hastily as soon as we made ready to leave the shore.

We then saw them walking quietly along the sea, looking towards us from time to time and uttering cries of joy.

1793-02-08.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 40-47]
The next day we went back in great numbers to these same savages.

We had been coasting for some time beyond port Dentrecasteaux when a fire we saw near the sea made us decide to go ashore. Soon some natives came to meet us, expressing by their cries the pleasure they felt at seeing us again. Our fiddler had brought his violin, reckoning to rouse in them by loud tunes the same enthusiasm we had observed among the islanders of Buka; but his self-esteem was truly piqued by the indifference of these people. Savages are generally little moved by the sounds of stringed instruments.

Going forward over the heights that border the sea, we soon found gathered together part of the natives who had welcomed us so well the day before. A lively joy showed in all their features when they saw us approaching; there were nineteen of them round three small fires, making their meal of mussels as fast as they cooked on the coals. Some women went from time to time to detach these shellfish from the neighbouring rocks, and came back only when they had filled their baskets. On these same fires could also be seen roasting the kind of seaweed called *fucus palmatus*, and when it had become softened to a certain degree they tore it into pieces to eat it.

We watched with much interest all the pains taken by one of the mothers to quiet her child, still at the breast, whose tears our presence had provoked; she only succeeded by putting her hand over its eyes to keep it from seeing us any longer.

None of these inhabitants appeared with weapons; but perhaps they had left them close by in the woods? for when several of us had shown a wish to go into them, one of the savages earnestly begged them not to go that way. We did not insist, for fear of giving them some cause for mistrust; some of the crew, however, wishing to elude the vigilance of this sentinel, went a little way along the shore so as to be able to enter the forest without his knowledge; but one of the women, perceiving their design, gave horrible cries to warn the other savages, who urged them to come back towards the sea.

We could not tell to what to attribute their aversion to our food; but they would not taste any of what we offered them; they would not even allow their children to eat the sugar we gave them, taking great care to take it out of their mouths as soon as they were about to eat it. Confidence, however, was established to such a degree that one of the women who was suckling a child was not afraid to entrust it to several of us.

I had thought that these inhabitants, spending most nights in the open air under a sky of very variable temperature, would have been subject to violent ophthalmias; yet they all had very sound eyesight, with the exception of a single one who had a cataract.

Some were sitting on kangaroo skins, and some others had a little pillow, which they call *roéré*, about two decimetres long and covered with skin, on which they rested one elbow.

We noticed with surprise the singular posture of the women when they are sitting on the ground. It seems to be good manners among these ladies, whose knees are then set wide apart, to hide with one of their feet what decency does not permit to be seen in that posture, although in other respects most of them are entirely naked.

These people seemed to me so close to the state of nature that their least actions appeared to me worth observing: I shall not, therefore, pass over in silence the correction which a father inflicted on one of his children for having thrown a stone at the back of another, younger still; he struck him rather lightly on the shoulder; this correction made him shed a few tears and kept him from doing it again.

The painter of the expedition let these savages know that he wished to have his skin covered, like theirs, with charcoal dust. His request was received favourably, as it was bound to be. At once one of the natives chose some of the most crumbly pieces of charcoal, which he crushed by rubbing them between his hands, then applied this powder to all the uncovered parts of the body, using nothing but the rubbing of his hand to fix it, and soon our friend Piron was as black as a New Hollander. The savage appeared as pleased as could be with his work, which he finished by blowing lightly to drive off the dust that adhered very little, taking particular care besides to remove any that might have got into the eyes.

We set out for port Dentrecasteaux; at once more than half of these peaceable inhabitants rose to accompany us: four of the young girls also joined the party; they received with indifference the clothes we gave them, and so as not to burden themselves with a quite useless load they at once laid them down in the coppices beside the path we were following, no doubt intending to pick them up on their return. What proves that they set little store by presents of this kind is that we did not see them wearing any of those we had given them the day before. Three of these young persons were already of marriageable age, and all were of an extremely merry disposition. One of them was noticeable in that her left breast had not yet undergone any development, while the right had reached its full size. This passing deformity in no way affected her gaiety. Several times, as they practised running on an extremely smooth beach, some of our party tried to catch them. We saw with pleasure that Europeans often ran better than these savages. The men followed at a grave pace, each with his hands placed one against the other and resting on the small of his back; sometimes the left hand, carried behind the back, held the right arm near the middle.

No doubt we lost a great deal by not understanding the language of these natives, for one of the young girls told us a prodigious number of things; she talked to us for a very long time with extraordinary volubility, although she must surely have noticed that we did not understand her; but no matter, talk she must.

The others tried at various times to charm us with songs whose modulation struck me singularly by their great resemblance to those of the Arabs of Asia Minor. Several times two of them sang the same air together, but always a third apart from each other, making this chord with the greatest accuracy.

In the midst of the sands grew a species of fig-marigold almost in every respect like the Hottentot fig, *mesembryanthemum edule*; it differed from it essentially, however, in the colour of its flowers, which are red, whereas those of the Hottentot fig are yellow; but like it, it bore fruits whose taste comes very close to that of extremely ripe sweet apples. These fruits were the delight of the New Hollanders, who sought them out carefully to eat them on the spot. During this long walk some of them took us by the arm from time to time, meaning to help us walk.

A young girl, having caught sight from a distance of a head which the master gunner of the Espérance had carved on the foot of a tree, at first appeared extremely surprised and stopped for a moment; then she went up to it with us, and after looking at it attentively she named its different parts to us, pointing them out at the same time with her hand.

We soon arrived at the entrance of port Dentrecasteaux.

Two of the young girls, away from the other natives, were following the various windings of the shore without mistrust in company with three of our sailors, when these men took advantage of one of the most secluded spots to behave towards them in a far too free manner; but they were received quite otherwise than they had hoped. These young persons at once fled onto the rocks that jutted farthest into the sea, appearing ready to throw themselves in and swim if they had been pursued: they soon made their way to the place where we were gathered with the other savages. It appears that they kept this adventure secret, for the most perfect understanding continued to reign between them and us.

Wishing to know whether these islanders are skilful swimmers, one of the officers threw himself into the water and dived several times, but it was in vain that he urged them to follow him; yet they dive very well, as we later had occasion to see, since it is in this way that they obtain a great part of the food on which they live. We invited them to eat with us some oysters and lobsters which we had just grilled on the coals; but all refused, except one, who was willing to taste a lobster. At first we thought that the hour of their meal was still a long way off; but we were mistaken, for they soon ate, though of food they prepared themselves; it too consisted of shellfish and crustaceans, which they grilled much longer than those we had offered them.

We saw some of these savages busy shaping into the form of a spatula, and polishing with a shell, small pieces of wood intended for prising off the rocks the ear-shells and limpets on which they feasted as fast as they cooked.

The time had come for us to return on board. None of these natives would come with us; they left us, going off into the woods.

1793-02-09.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 47-49]
The engineer-geographer of the Recherche set off in the large cutter on the morning of the 22nd to survey the extent of the vast bay which lies at the entrance of détroit Dentrecasteaux [D'Entrecasteaux Channel]. We were soon to make sail for the same channel.

In the course of this day all the establishments which had been set up on shore during our stay in baie des Roches were abandoned. The repairs to the two ships were finished. The trial made the year before of the wood of the *eucalyptus globulus* had decided our carpenters to use it in preference to the other species of the same genus.

I made my way deep into the thick forests which lay to the north-west of us. In the shade of the great trees grew various species of shrubs of the family of the terebinths; the *fagara evodia* stood out among them by its fine foliage. In these dark places the eye rested with pleasure on the *carpodontos lucida*, whose branches were entirely covered with beautiful white flowers.

Advancing towards the south-west, I crossed some clearings where I killed a charming species of parakeet, which I designate by the name of black-spotted parakeet of cap de Diemen (*see* pl. 10). I had already met with it in several other places, but always in low and open ground. It appears that, quite unlike the known species of the same genus, it does not perch, for I constantly saw it rise from among the grasses only to settle there again almost at once. The form of its feet, furnished with very long and only slightly curved claws, is a fair indication of the habits of this bird, whose plumage is green, spotted with black; some of these spots are surrounded by small yellowish bands; the underside of the wings is ash-grey, with a broad band of pale yellow across it; black and yellow predominate on the belly; the lower feathers of the tail are remarkable for their transverse bands, some blackish and others pale yellow, placed alternately: a few small reddish feathers are to be seen at the base of the bill, above the upper mandible.

1793-02-10.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 49-57]
The next day we landed near port Dentrecasteaux with a great number of people from both ships, in the hope of seeing the savages again. Some of them soon came to meet us, giving us marks of the greatest confidence; first they examined the inside of our longboats with much attention, then they took us by the arm and urged us to follow them along the shore.

We had gone scarcely two kilometres when we found ourselves in the midst of forty-eight natives; namely, ten men, fourteen women and twenty-four children, among whom there were as many girls as boys. Seven fires were burning, and round each was gathered a small family.

The youngest children, frightened at the sight of so great a number of Europeans, at once ran to take refuge in the arms of their mothers, who lavished on them marks of the greatest tenderness. These children were very soon reassured, and they showed us that they were not free from little passions, from which arose quarrels that the mothers settled almost at once with a light correction; but they soon put an end to their tears with caresses.

We already knew that these savages had little taste for the sound of the violin. It was hoped, however, that they would not be insensible to it if lively airs with a very marked measure were played. At first they left us some time in uncertainty; our musician redoubled his efforts, reckoning on winning their applause; but the bow fell from his hands when he saw this numerous assembly put their fingers in their ears so as to hear him no longer.

These people are covered with vermin. We admired the patience of a woman who was long occupied in ridding one of her children of them; but we saw with great disgust that, like most blacks, she crushed these loathsome insects between her teeth and swallowed them on the spot. It is worth noting that monkeys have the same habits.

The little children were very curious about everything that had any brightness; they made no secret of detaching the metal buttons from our clothes. The mothers, less jealous of their own adornment than of their children's, held them out to us so that we might fasten on them the ornaments we were giving to the mothers themselves.

I must not forget to mention a prank played by a young savage on one of our sailors. The latter had set down at the foot of a rock a bag full of shells. The native at once carried it off stealthily to another spot and let him look for it for some time; then he brought it back to the same place, and was greatly amused by the trick he had just played.

This numerous assembly was transported with admiration on seeing the effects of gunpowder when we threw it on glowing coals. All of them begged us to let them enjoy the same spectacle several times over.

Unable to persuade themselves that there were only men among us, they long believed, in spite of all we told them, that the youngest were women. Their curiosity on this point went a good deal further than we should have thought; in the end they were convinced only after they had been allowed to ascertain the fact for themselves.

It is hard to know whether it is from coquetry that the women have adopted a practice which will certainly never be in fashion among our fine ladies, although it removes a good part of the wrinkles produced by pregnancy. The skin of their belly was marked with three large semicircular ridges placed one above the other.

One of these savages had on his head several very recent marks of burning. Perhaps they apply the actual cautery in various diseases, a custom established among many other peoples, and especially among most of the Indians.

We saw them take their meal towards the middle of the day. Until then we had had but a faint idea of the pains the women take to procure the food necessary for the subsistence of their families; presently each of them took a basket and was followed by her daughters, who did the same; then they made for some rocks jutting out into the sea, and from there they ventured to the bottom of the water to look for crustaceans and shellfish. As they had already been there a long time, we became very anxious about their fate; for they had dived in among sea plants of great length, among which the *fucus pyriferus* was to be seen; we feared they might become entangled in them and be unable to regain the surface of the sea; at last they reappeared, and showed us that they could easily stay under water twice as long as our most skilful divers. An instant was enough for them to take breath, then they dived again several times over, until their basket was nearly full. Most of them were furnished with a small piece of wood cut in the shape of a spatula, of which I have already spoken; they used it to prise off, from rocks hidden under the water at great depths, very large sea-ears: perhaps they picked them out, for those they brought up were all very large.

At the sight of the great lobsters which filled their baskets, we feared that these crustaceans would tear the unfortunate women with their enormous claws; but we soon perceived that they had taken the precaution of killing them as soon as they had caught them. They came out of the water only to bring the fruits of their fishing to their husbands, and often they went back to dive again almost at once, until they had gathered a store large enough to feed their families: at other times they warmed themselves for a while, their faces turned towards the fire on which their catch was broiling, and they had lit other small fires behind them so as to warm themselves on all sides at once.

They seemed to begrudge remaining idle for a single moment, for even while warming themselves they were still busy broiling shellfish, which they laid on the coals with the greatest care; but they took much less trouble over the lobsters, which they threw carelessly into the midst of the flames; as soon as these were cooked, they shared out the legs among the men and the children, keeping for themselves the body, which they sometimes ate before going back to the bottom of the sea.

We were all more distressed than I can say to see these poor women condemned to such hard labour. Besides, they ran the risk of being devoured by sharks, or of becoming entangled among the fuci that rise from the bottom of these seas. Several times we urged the husbands at least to share their toil, but always in vain; they stayed all the while by the fire, feasting on the best morsels: they also ate broiled fuci and fern roots. From time to time they busied themselves in breaking branches into small pieces to feed the fire, taking care to choose the driest. Their way of breaking wood showed us that their skulls were very hard, for they used them as a fulcrum; with their hands fixed near the ends of each piece, they bent it hard until it snapped. Their heads, being always uncovered and often exposed to all the inclemencies of the weather in this high latitude, acquire the ability to withstand such efforts; moreover, their hair forms a cushion which deadens the pressure and makes it much less painful on the crown of the head than on any other part of the body. Most of the women could not have done as much, for some had their hair cut rather close and wore round the head a cord which went round it several times; the others had only a simple crown of hair (*see plates 4 and 5*). We made the same observation with regard to several children, but never with the men; these have the back, the chest, the shoulders and the arms covered with woolly hair.

Two of the most robust of the band were seated in the midst of their children, and each had two women beside him; they indicated to us by signs that the women belonged to them, and so gave us yet another proof that polygamy is established among these peoples. The other women, who had only one husband, likewise took care to let us know it. It is hard to say which are the happier. Burdened alike with the most toilsome labours of the household, the former have the advantage of sharing them, and this perhaps makes up for sharing the husband's tokens of affection.

Their meal had already lasted a long while, and we were much surprised that none of them had yet drunk; but they waited until they were fully satisfied. Then the women and girls went to fetch water in the vessels of seaweed of which I have already spoken; they drew it at the nearest spot and set it down close to the men, who drank it without distaste, although it was very stagnant and very muddy. Thus they ended their meal.

When we went back towards port Dentrecasteaux, most of these savages accompanied us, and before leaving us they gave us to understand that in two days, after following the windings of the shore, they would come very close to our ships. To show us that they would have made this journey in two days, they traced with their hand the daily course of the sun, taking care to indicate two of them by as many fingers.

When we re-embarked to go on board, these good people followed us with their eyes for some time before leaving the shore; then they went off into the woods; their path at times brought them out on the sea-shore, and at once we were made aware of it by shouts of joy with which they made the air ring. These demonstrations ceased only when a great distance had put them out of our sight.

During the whole time we spent with them nothing indicated to us that they had chiefs; on the contrary, each family seemed to us to live in perfect independence; we only noticed in the children a great subordination towards those who had given them life, and in the women towards their husbands. It seemed to us that the women took good care not to arouse their jealousy; nevertheless, on our return, a man of the crew boasted of having been very well received by one of the beauties of cap de Diemen; but it is hard to know how far the thing was well founded.

1793-02-11.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 57]
On the 24th I went to the south-east, where I found more to add to the observations I had already made on the various productions of this land.

1793-02-12.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 57-64]
The next day everything was ready for our departure, and we were waiting only for a fair wind to set sail; but as a calm held us back, we saw with pleasure that the savages who, at our last meeting, had promised to come in two days very close to our anchorage, had kept their word. Indeed, towards the middle of the day we perceived a fire a short distance from our watering-place, and there was no doubt that it had been lit by them, for all the crews were on board. At once a great number of us embarked in several longboats to be at the meeting-place these inhabitants had appointed. It was then for the first time that General Dentrecasteaux had the pleasure of seeing them. They soon left their fire and followed for some time paths cleared through the woods along the shore, so as to come still nearer to us. We were going to meet them, and when we were close to them they stopped, and seemed to us very pleased to see us land on the coast. There were five of them. One of them carried a piece of rotten wood, lit at one end, which burned slowly; he used this kind of match to keep fire, taking pleasure from time to time in setting light to clumps of brushwood in which there was very dry grass. The others, having been invited by men of the crew to dance in a ring with them, imitated all their movements rather well; they let us tie round their necks with cords a great number of the articles we had just given them; soon their bodies were for the most part covered with them, and they seemed very satisfied; but they gave us nothing, for they had brought none of their belongings with them, probably so as to walk more easily.

A native to whom a hatchet had just been given showed us great skill in striking a great number of blows in succession on the same spot, wishing to imitate one of our sailors who had just felled a tree. He was shown that he must strike in different places to make notches, which he did on the spot, and he was overjoyed when he had brought the tree down. They were astonished at the speed with which the trunk was sawn through. We made them a present of some hand-saws, which they used with great ease as soon as we had shown them how.

The way in which we had seen them fish led us, with good reason, to suppose that they had no hooks; we gave them some of ours and taught them how to use them, congratulating ourselves on having provided them with the means of lightening one of the most toilsome labours with which the women are burdened.

These savages were much surprised to see us set fire, at the focus of a lens, to the spongy bark of the *eucalyptus resinifera*. The one among them who seemed the most intelligent, seeking to learn for himself the effect of this lens, directed the concentrated rays of the sun on to his thigh; but the pain he felt took away all desire to repeat the experiment.

We showed one of these natives our two frigates through a good telescope, and he soon yielded to our invitations and embarked in a longboat to go on board the Recherche. He climbed aboard with an air of assurance and examined the inside of the ship with much attention; then he turned his eyes chiefly to the objects that can serve as food for man. Guided by the likeness between the form of the black swans of cap de Diemen and that of the Guinea geese he saw on board, he asked for one, giving us to understand that it was to eat. When he was opposite our hen-coops, he seemed struck by the beauty of a very large cock; it was offered to him, and on receiving it he let us know that he would soon broil it and eat it. He was loaded with presents. After staying in the ship for more than half an hour, he asked to go back; he was at once taken ashore. We had brought a monkey there, which greatly amused these savages. One of the men of the crew had taken a kid there, which for some time was the subject of their conversation; now and then they spoke to it, saying *mèdi* (*rest yourself*).

They have given particular names to each plant. We made sure that their knowledge of botany is invariable by asking several of them, and at different times, the names of the same plants.

At this meeting we had the means of adding a great deal to the vocabulary of their language which we had already collected, and which is to be found at the end of this volume. On comparing it with the vocabularies that several travellers have given us of the language of the inhabitants of the east coast of New Holland, it will be seen that it bears no relation to them; which proves that all these peoples are not of the same origin.

The savage who had been on board soon left us, showing us much gratitude and pointing to the cock, which he had just slung over one of his shoulders.

The others, before going away, gave us to understand that the next day their families would come to the place where we were; but they seemed to understand us when we told them that we were to set sail that very day, and they appeared truly grieved at it.

Our observatory, situated towards the south-south-east, about one kilometre from the anchorage, was in latitude 43° 34' 37" south, and longitude 144° 37' east.

A great number of observations made on board gave 7° 34' east for the variation of the needle, whereas at the observatory only 2° 55' east was found. So great a difference no doubt arose from some magnetic point; besides, we had already found signs of ferruginous matter a short distance from this spot. It is worth noting that at the observatory of the Espérance, some six hundred metres from that of the Recherche, the variation of the needle was 8° east. It was ascertained that this difference did not depend on the compasses used, for it was found to be the same when the same compasses were carried in turn to both observatories.

The dip of the needle was 72° at the observatory of the Recherche, and 71° at that of the Espérance. During our stay in baie des Roches the winds varied from north-west to south-west, and often blew in strong gusts. The sky was seldom clear, and yet little rain fell.

The tides were felt only once in twenty-four hours. As the winds had a great deal of influence on them, the time of high water in this bay could not be determined with precision. The greatest perpendicular rise of the water was only sixteen decimetres.

Our seamen had lost much of their ardour for fishing at this port of call, for this toilsome exercise, which they carried on chiefly at night, did not excuse them from the work of the ship; so that after staying up to fish, they were none the less obliged to work all day like those who had slept soundly through the night. Care ought, however, to have been taken not to damp the zeal of the fishermen, for it was in the general interest to have an abundant supply of fresh provisions; besides, it was unjust not to grant at least a few hours' rest during the day to men who had spent the night procuring for the whole crew a pleasant and very wholesome food.

We put ashore on this land a she-goat and a young he-goat, in the hope of naturalising these quadrupeds there: they will no doubt thrive perfectly on the mountains of this extremity of New Holland, and will one day be a great resource to navigators; only it is to be feared that the savages may destroy them before they have had time to multiply.

## CHAPTER XI.

*Departure from baie des Roches to pass through détroit Dentrecasteaux. The ships run aground in this channel. Various excursions on the neighbouring lands. Meeting with natives. They had left their weapons in the woods, and took them up again on their way back. Our anchorage at Adventure Bay.*

1793-02-13.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 64-65]
At daybreak, with the wind at south-west, we weighed from baie des Roches and steered east-north-east until we were clear of it, intending to anchor in détroit Dentrecasteaux [D'Entrecasteaux Channel].

Natives gave us signs of their presence by several fires which they had lit on the eastern shore.

We had already crossed the great roadstead which lies at the beginning of the channel, and were running in perfect security very close along the shore on our larboard hand, when at about half past one in the afternoon we grounded on a small shoal of sand mixed with mud. The ebb had just set up a current against us. As the sea kept falling, we had to wait until half past six for the high tide to float our ship. The Espérance had sunk into the sand even deeper than we had, for she could not get clear until about eight o'clock.

The cutter sent off five days before came back after surveying several very deep inlets which form excellent anchorages; it had not found any river. It is worth noting that all those we saw at cap de Diemen are small, which indicates a much broken land.

The cutter was laden with black swans, which had let themselves be approached very closely and had been shot. It had not been easy to secure those which had only been wounded, for as they could still swim with great speed, it had been necessary, in order to reach them, to chase them rowing with all our might.

1793-02-14.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 65-67]
All through the night we saw several fires which the natives had lit on the sea-shore towards the south-south-east, three kilometres from the spot where we lay at anchor.

We had hoped that a fair wind would allow us to set sail again in the morning; but it was against us, and the general decided that we should remain at anchor until the next day. We then went ashore towards the south-east on a low coast from which it was easy to reach Adventure Bay in a short time.

Among the various shrubs which adorned these places, I shall mention one which I refer to the genus I have described earlier under the name of *Mazeutoxeron*. It agrees with it in all its characters; only the petals, distinct from one another at the base, cohere by the middle part of their edges, but they can be separated without tearing. The style is simple and pointed.

I have given this new species the name of *Mazeutoxeron reflexum*, on account of its leaves, which are bent towards the ground; they are hairy and whitish beneath.

The greenish flowers are solitary and come out from between two small oval leaves; towards the middle of their peduncle they have two thread-like appendages a little longer than the calyx.

Citizen Beaupré, engineer-geographer, set off in the evening in the general's cutter for the great inlet we had perceived the year before to the north on leaving détroit Dentrecasteaux [D'Entrecasteaux Channel]. The chief object was to find out whether it might not offer some opening communicating with the open sea, and whether Maria Island was really separated from the mainland; for this question had not been sufficiently cleared up by Marion, nor even by Captain Cook.

1793-02-15.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 67]
The north wind which blew all day on the 28th prevented us from weighing anchor. We went ashore, while our fishermen went on towards the mouth of the channel. The flood tide brought a great many fish there; they caught several species of rays of very great size. Some were noted weighing more than twelve myriagrammes.

1793-02-16.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 67-72]
The next day, in the morning, we spread our sails, but with a wind too light to stem the current, which was against us; so we soon let go the anchor.

Towards the middle of the day some natives appeared on the eastern shore, one kilometre from our ship; others soon joined them, and we already counted ten of them when they lit a fire, round which they sat down. From time to time they answered the shouts of our sailors with cries of joy. We soon went ashore in great numbers to see them close at hand. When we were a short distance from the coast they came towards us unarmed, and their smiling looks left us no doubt that our visit gave them pleasure. They were no more clothed than those we had met in the neighbourhood of port Dentrecasteaux; but we were rather surprised to see that most of them held the end of their foreskin in their left hand, no doubt from some bad habit, for we noticed nothing of the kind in the others who came to join them a little later. Their joy showed itself in great bursts of laughter; at the same time they put their hands on their heads and stamped their feet, while their faces showed us that they were extremely pleased to see us. We invited them to sit down, speaking to them in the language of the other natives we had already met at this extremity of New Holland; they understood us very well and at once complied with our invitation; they also understood the other words of the vocabulary of the language of these peoples which we had collected, and we did not doubt that they spoke the same tongue; Anderson, however, has made known some words of the language of the inhabitants of Adventure Bay which bear no relation to those we were in a position to verify.

These savages showed us much gratitude when we gave them some pieces of cloth of different colours, glass beads, a hatchet, and a few other articles of hardware.

Several other savages came out of the woods and approached us. There was no woman among them, but only a few young men; one of these, of middle height, was remarkable for a form which we all admired and which, even in the judgement of our painter, was of the finest proportions. From his attire we took this savage for a dandy of New Holland; he was tattooed with great symmetry: his hair, covered with grease, had been thickly powdered with ochre.

One of the natives gave us to understand that he had already seen ships in Adventure Bay; perhaps he meant to speak to us of Bligh, who had come to anchor there at the beginning of 1792, as we learned a few days later from several inscriptions we found carved on the feet of trees. An officer of our ship did not think he would frighten them by showing them the effect of our firearms; but as most of them had not been warned, they were terrified by the noise of the explosion; at once they stood up and would not sit down again. Thinking that their women and children had withdrawn a short distance into the woods, we let them see that we wished them to come near us; these savages gave us to understand that we should find them after walking for some time through the woods along a path leading towards the south-south-west, which they at once took, urging us to accompany them. We followed them; but they soon showed us that they wished to see us go back to our ships, and they moved away from us, often looking behind them to watch our movements. However, at the word *quangloa* (in their language *will you come*), which I spoke, they stopped, and I had time to rejoin them with an officer of the Recherche. They went on leading us along the same path, which seemed to us much used, and we walked at a slow pace so that the men of the crew should have time to join us. We went on in this way for a quarter of an hour, holding them all by the arms, when all of a sudden they quickened their pace so that it was hard for us to follow them any longer. It seemed to us that they wished us to leave them, for some would no longer let themselves be held by the arms, and walked alone at some distance from us; a man of the crew, wishing to catch up with one of these runaways, ran after him shouting at the top of his voice, and spread alarm among all the others, who at once made off in haste and kept at a good distance from us. No doubt they wished to reach alone the place where they had left their weapons; for after quickening their pace still more, they turned a little off the path, and we soon saw each of them take up three or four spears, which they carried off, most of them heading towards Adventure Bay, while others went off towards the west. Then they invited us to follow them, but we would go no further, for we had no wish to imitate them in their running; besides, it was time for us to go back on board.

These natives seemed to us to bear the closest resemblance to those we had seen a few days before; only we noticed some of them who were missing one of the middle incisors of the upper jaw, and others who were missing both. We could not learn what this custom arises from; but it is not general, since most of them had kept all their teeth.

It appears that they, like the others, know nothing of the use of the bow. They were almost all tattooed with raised dots, placed sometimes in two lines one above the other, roughly imitating the shape of a horseshoe; often these dots were in three straight parallel lines on each side of the chest; some were also to be seen towards the lower part of the shoulder-blades, etc.

Several had the navel swollen and very prominent, but we made sure that this deformity did not come from a hernia; perhaps it was owing to the too great distance at which they cut the umbilical cord.

They let us know that they lived on fish, like the other inhabitants of cap de Diemen. I must remark that we did not see a single one of them with the slightest trace of any skin disease; which does not agree with the opinion of those who have asserted that fish-eating peoples are subject to a kind of leprosy; history even relates that those Greeks in Egypt who would not adopt the diet of Orpheus were attacked there by elephantiasis.

We reached the ship a little before sunset. The wind having become fair, we got under way, and went to anchor one myriametre further on.

1793-02-17.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 72-73]
The next day the anchor was weighed very early; but it had to be let go again almost at once, for the wind turned against us.

I landed on the eastern shore, from which I made my way into the forests along paths much frequented by the savages. I soon observed a new species of *exocarpos*, which I call *exocarpos expansa*, because its branches spread much wider apart from one another than those of the *exocarpos cupressiformis*; its fruit is larger than that of the latter species.

We were warned by two guns fired on board the Recherche that she was about to get under way; we at once went on board that ship, and at five o'clock we were under sail; but the breeze was so light that we made little way before night. From the spot where we let go the anchor we reckoned we had only about one myriametre more to reach the end of the channel; but, thwarted by winds and currents, it took us four more days before we could get out of it.

1793-02-20.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 73-74]
In the meantime the cutter which the general had sent off to make geographical researches came back after five days' absence. It had discovered several bays hitherto unknown; the furthest to the north extended as far as the 42<sup>nd</sup> ° 42' of south latitude, and the easternmost stretched as far as the longitude of Cape Pillar. The channel which separates Maria Island from the mainland had been sighted. We saw with astonishment the prodigious number of shelters which, from the cap méridional as far as the meridian of Cape Pillar, offer an unbroken succession of excellent anchorages over a space of about eight myriametres from west to east, and about ten myriametres from north to south.

It appears that at this season fresh water is also very scarce in these new bays; however, towards the head of the one which runs furthest to the north a river was found in which, for a distance of about fifty paces from its mouth, even an hour after high water, there were no less than two metres of water in perpendicular depth, and it was quite fresh, for its current was strong enough to drive back the waters of the sea and keep them from mixing with it.

1793-02-22.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 74-82]
On the 5th of Ventose, at about half past eleven in the morning, we anchored in Adventure Bay in twenty-two metres of water, on a bottom of mud mixed with a little sand.

The nearest shore lay to the south-east of us, one kilometre off, and Penguin Island bore north 51° east.

A cutter was at once sent off to see whether we could easily take in water towards the north-west, at the watering-place shown by Captain Cook in the plan he has given of this bay; the east-south-east winds caused a very troublesome surf there; so we preferred to water towards the south-east; but the water showed the effects of having been taken in a spot too low and too near the shore, for it was slightly brackish.

This bay being open to the east and south-east winds, they sometimes brought a heavy swell on to its western shore, which, flowing back on all sides, made landing rather difficult.

During the time we lay at anchor I made excursions every day on the neighbouring lands; but I found there little to add to the numerous collections I had made at cap de Diemen.

Penguin Island, which I went to visit, is no more than a hillock scarcely detached from the great island, for at low tide I crossed almost dry-shod the channel which separates it. It is composed of a dark grey sandstone, as is a good part of the shores of Adventure Bay. It was overlooked on the south by Fluted Cape, which is formed of a reddish sandstone laid in beds parallel to one another and perpendicular to the horizon. The difference in the colour of its beds gives it from afar the appearance of deep flutings, which has earned it the name it bears. It can only be through a printer's error that Anderson is reported to have found this cape formed of a white sandstone.

I gathered on Penguin Island a new species of wormwood, remarkable for its broad leaves of a light fawn colour; a *eucalyptus* of middling height, which will easily be recognised by its opposite, sessile and glaucous leaves; an *embothrium* with very deeply cut leaves; several beautiful species of *philadelphus*, whose flowers are scentless, etc.

We found a raft which the waves had cast up on the western shore of Adventure Bay. Perhaps it had served some savages to come from Maria Island into this bay. It was made of tree bark, of roughly the shape of the one figured in pl. 44, fig. 2, as broad, but shorter by more than a third. The pieces of bark of which it was made were in layers much thinner than those of the *eucalyptus resinifera*. They had been bound together by ties made of grass leaves, which formed a network of very wide meshes, most of them in the shape of a fairly regular pentagon.

Close by we saw some limestone rocks which ended a vast sandy beach. On its edge we found the remains of an establishment which had been made by Europeans for sawing timber; there were the stakes they had used to pitch a tent, and some large blocks on which it seemed to us they had set instruments for making astronomical observations.

The steep hillsides which border the sandy beach a little further to the north showed hollows which seemed to us to be rather frequented by the natives, as we judged from the black colour with which the smoke had stained them, and from the remains of shellfish and lobsters we found in them.

Several inscriptions carved on the feet of trees informed us that Captain Bligh had anchored in this bay in the month of February 1792; he was bound for the Society Islands, to take on board the bread-fruit tree and carry it to the English colonies of the West Indies lying between the tropics.

Bligh had with him on his expedition two botanists, who sowed, a short distance from the shore, some cress, a few acorns, some celery, etc. We saw three young fig trees, two pomegranates and a quince planted by them, which had done very well; but it seemed to us that among the young plants they had entrusted to this soil, one had already perished, for the following inscription, which we found on a large neighbouring trunk, announced seven:

*Near this tree capt<sup>tn</sup>. W<sup>m</sup>. Bligh planted 7 fruit trees 1792 mes<sup>rs</sup>. S. and W. botanists.*

The other inscriptions were worded in much the same terms. They showed the same marks of deference on the part of the English botanists towards the commander of their ship, in giving only the initials of their own names, and in stating that the captain had himself sown and planted these various vegetable productions which he had brought from Europe. I very much doubt whether Bligh was greatly touched by the honours these botanists wished to pay him.

Towards the south-east, a short distance from the beach, we found an apple tree whose stem was nearly two metres high and half a decimetre thick. It did not seem to us ever to have been grafted.

Our fishermen were rather fortunate at this anchorage. The fires they lit on the shore during the night drew a great quantity of fish into their nets. This means had already succeeded so completely for the fishermen of the Espérance in détroit Dentrecasteaux [D'Entrecasteaux Channel] that they had laid in a stock of fish for several months, some of which they preserved in a strong brine and the rest after drying them.

I was present several times during the day when the seine was hauled, and I always observed some new species of *diodon*. I admired the quickness with which these little fish, the moment they were touched, puffed themselves up and raised the spines with which they are covered; but they lowered them again and kept them laid flat along their whole length against the skin as soon as they thought themselves out of danger. It will be seen from this observation that the attitude given to fish of this genus by inflating them as much as possible, in which they are displayed in cabinets of natural history, is not the one they most commonly have.

We put ashore near the northern shore of this bay a she-goat that was with young and a young he-goat, with earnest wishes that the savages would let these quadrupeds breed on their island. Perhaps they will multiply there so far as to bring about a complete change in the way of life of the inhabitants, who, being then able to become pastoral peoples, will leave the sea-shore without regret and enjoy the pleasure of no longer being obliged to dive in search of their food at the risk of being devoured by sharks. The women, being condemned to these toilsome labours, will feel the value of such a gift even more keenly than the men; but it is to be feared that they may kill these quadrupeds before they have multiplied, for it seems that this is what happened to the sow and the boar which Captain Cook had left them; at least none of us saw the slightest trace of these animals.

For the latitude of the observatory, which had been set up two kilometres to the south of our anchorage, we had 43° 21' 18" south, and for its longitude 145° 12' 17" east.

The variation of the needle observed at the same place was 7° 30' east.

## CHAPTER XII.

*Departure from Adventure Bay. We pass very close to New Zealand, to the north of it. Meeting with its inhabitants. Discovery of several islands hitherto unknown. Anchorage at Tongatapu, one of the Friendly Islands. Eagerness of the natives to come on board and to procure us fresh provisions. We salt a great number of hogs. The islanders are much given to theft. One of our sentries is murdered during the night by a native who steals his musket. The murderer is handed over to General Dentrecasteaux by King Toubau, who returns to him the musket that had been stolen. Queen Tiné comes on board. Toubau gives an entertainment for the General. Queen Tiné also gives him one. The blacksmith of the Recherche falls under the blows of clubs dealt him by natives, who strip him in broad daylight within sight of our ships. Young bread-fruit plants are taken on board to enrich our colonies with this precious plant.*

1793-02-27.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 82]
We weighed from Adventure Bay at about eight in the morning; we were driven along by strong squalls from the south-west, and we soon doubled Cape Pillar, behind which we saw several fires lit by the savages. We then stood towards the north, where we ran about eight myriametres in sight of the coast, leaving Oyster Bay to the west, and then we shaped our course for the Friendly Islands.

1793-03-11.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 82-83]
At daybreak, on the 22nd of Ventose, we sighted the islets called the Three Kings.

At about eight o'clock we were in longitude 169° 56' east, when we had the middle islet of this group bearing north, half a myriametre off, and we determined its latitude to be 34° 20' south.

We saw three main rocks of moderate height, lying almost on the same parallel, not far from one another and surrounded by other much smaller rocks. In spite of the haze which had just risen, we could still make out others towards the north which formed part of the same group.
