They were extremely barren, and we did not suppose them to be inhabited. However, a thick column of smoke rose from the easternmost islet and told us of the presence of savages. No doubt they have chosen this abode because they easily find the means of fishing among these reefs.

At a quarter to eleven we perceived the land of New Zealand, which we approached, standing to the east with a light breeze from west-north-west.

The natives had lit a great fire on the highest of the hills which border the sea and run out as far as North Cape. At about half past five we were not far from this cape, when two canoes put off from the shore and made towards us.

1793-03-14.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 84-87]
They soon came up with us, and stayed for some time astern of our ship before venturing alongside; but, judging well of our disposition towards them, they came up with confidence; besides, these savages were no doubt aware that the Europeans who had visited their coasts had never been the first aggressors; they at once showed us bundles of New Zealand flax (*phormium tenax*), waving them to point out to us all its beauty, and they offered to trade with us. It was with marks of great satisfaction that they received the cloths of various colours which we gave them, and they always handed over to us, with scrupulous exactness, the price that had been agreed upon.

They gave iron a very marked preference over all the other articles we offered them. This metal is of such great value to this warlike people that they broke out into the liveliest joy when they learned that we had some; although at first we had shown it to them only from a great distance, they nevertheless recognised it perfectly by the sound given out by two pieces struck against each other.

In exchange for our goods these inhabitants gave us almost everything they had in their canoes; we regarded it as a mark of the greatest confidence that they made not the least difficulty about parting with all their weapons in our favour.

The longest spears they gave us were not more than five metres in length, with a thickness of four centimetres; the smallest were half as long. They were all made of a single piece of very hard wood, which they had polished perfectly.

They gave us lines and fish-hooks of various shapes; to the end of some of these they had fixed feathers, a bait which they use to attract voracious fish. Several of these lines were very long and had at their end a piece of hard serpentine, to make them sink to great depths in the water. We admired the fine polish they had given to this stone, which was spherical in shape and topped by a small protuberance through which they had bored a hole to pass a cord. It must be very difficult for these savages to pierce such hard stones, and no doubt they spend a great deal of time on it; but they have all the leisure they need to devote themselves to work of this kind, for their wants are few, and the sea besides furnishes them with very abundant food. They sold us a great deal of fish which they had just caught: there is such a quantity of it along the coast that, in the short time we remained hove to, we saw several very numerous shoals which, rising to the surface of the sea, set it in motion over a very wide space at different times, producing much the same effects as currents which, in calm weather, pass over shoals.

These savages even stripped off their garments to obtain our articles of trade.

Some of the young men wore ear-pendants made of a serpentine of great hardness; they were cut into an oval, and most of them were about a decimetre long.

The men wore, as a kind of trophy, a small piece of a human ulna, which hung on their breast at the end of a cord passed round the neck *(see pl. 25)*. They set a high value on this ornament.

It is known that these peoples eat human flesh greedily; accordingly anything that awakens in them the idea of such food gives them the greatest pleasure. One of the crew offered a knife to one of them; but, wishing to show him its use, he pretended to cut his finger, which he at once put to his mouth, feigning to eat it; immediately the cannibal, who was watching his every movement, showed an extreme delight, and we saw him laugh heartily for some time, rubbing his hands together. They were all very tall and powerfully muscled. They left us a little after sunset.

At the same moment a third canoe arrived from the nearest part of the coast; it was manned by twelve islanders, who at once asked us for hatchets in exchange for their goods. One of them had already obtained one, when another addressed us in a manly voice, shouting with all his might *etoki (a hatchet)*, and he did not fall silent until he had been given one.

It was already night. The Espérance was too far from our ship for us to be able to see her; we burned a few priming charges to induce her to make her position known to us; but we saw with surprise that these natives, far from showing any fear of the effects of gunpowder, carried on their trading all the same. It had already been dark for more than an hour when they paddled away towards the coast.

As we remained hove to, the lead was cast at different times. It always gave us a bottom of fine sand at a depth of sixty-six to ninety-three metres.

[t. II, p. 87-88]
The land winds, which were faintly felt during the night, were followed towards daybreak by north-west winds. We were still very close to the coast, and it would have been easy for us to go and anchor in the baie de Lauriston [Doubtless Bay]; but the sad events that befell Captain Marion, and afterwards Furneaux, decided the general to pass on.

I nevertheless thought it my duty to point out to him how important it would be to take from New Zealand the liliaceous plant known by the name of *phormium tenax (New Zealand flax)*, in order to carry it to Europe, where it would thrive perfectly. The fibres drawn from its leaves have a strength far superior to that of all the other vegetable products used for making cordage; cables that might be made from it would withstand the greatest strains. No one should have appreciated better than the commander of our expedition the full usefulness of this plant to our navy. We nevertheless continued our course towards the Friendly Islands, steering north-east.

Besides, it would have been advantageous to put in at the northern extremity of New Zealand in order to verify there our observations, which led us to place North Cape 36' further east than Wales gives it. It will be acknowledged, however, that we have good grounds for giving them a just preference over those of that astronomer, when it is known that he determined this point only from the longitude he had observed in Ship Cove, having followed the trend of the coast along Captain Cook's track; but it must be remembered that this celebrated navigator had no timekeeper on his first voyage, and it is well known that this instrument is indispensable when one wishes to fix with accuracy the trend of a coast where irregular and very rapid currents are met with.

1793-03-15.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 88-89]
Towards four in the afternoon the sailor at the masthead called out that he had just sighted a large rock to the north-north-east. Soon we were surrounded by a great number of sea-birds, among which we noticed many boobies and gulls. It was already night when we passed about six hundred metres to leeward of this rock, from which several of these birds could be heard crying; but by the light of a fine moon we made out on the most prominent points a whiteness, which we attributed to their droppings.

This rock, which lies in latitude 31° 33' 20" south and longitude 179° east, is not more than a kilometre in circumference and is seventy to eighty metres high. A few reefs were noticed off its western point.

We were entirely sheltered from the swell as we passed to leeward of this rock, so that had there been any rock awash in our track, we should have been warned of the danger only at the moment our ship struck upon it and was wrecked. These risks would not have been run had we rounded it to windward, or else to leeward but at a proper distance.

1793-03-16.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 89-90]
The next day, at first light, we sighted the Curtis Islands; they are two in number, very small, and nearly two myriametres apart. The southernmost is not more than two kilometres long from north to south; it is steep, very barren, and studded with a great number of rocks whose highest points rise about one hundred metres perpendicular above the level of the sea. Their whitish colour led me to think that they were calcareous in nature, like the greater part of the islands found in these seas.

The other island is fairly round, covered with verdure, and as high as the first; it is steep along almost the whole of its shores, yet a landing might be made on the west side. It lies in latitude 30° 18' 26" south and longitude 179° 38' east.

Towards six in the evening we saw, a long way off to the north-north-west, a new land, which decided us to pass the night hove to.

1793-03-17.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 90-91]
The next day, as soon as it was light, we saw it again towards the north, still more than five myriametres off; but by about five in the afternoon we were quite close to it, and had already seen the whole of its circuit, which is about two and a half myriametres.

We gave the name of la Recherche [Raoul Island] to this island, which lies in latitude 29° 20' 18" south and longitude 179° 55' east. Its shape is roughly triangular. Towards the centre the ground rises about five hundred metres perpendicular above the level of the sea. On its coast we saw a few small landslips by which a landing might be made.

In all the places where the cliffs were sheer we could make out perfectly the arrangement of the thin, parallel, horizontal layers of a whitish and no doubt calcareous stone of which it is formed. The interior showed us great steep slopes. Trees could be seen even on the highest summits.

A shoal lying very close to the coast on the north-west extended at least six hundred metres in that same direction.

Eight rocks, a few hundred metres apart from one another, ran out into the sea to a distance of half a myriametre towards the east-south-east.

Between the north-west point and the west point we noticed a small inlet where very good holding ground would probably be found; one would be perfectly sheltered there from easterly winds.

Between the north-west and south-east points we saw a small stream falling into the sea, and a short distance away, in a place where the cliff was sheer, could be seen a large mass of a rather dark red earth, perhaps a clay, which appeared to be embedded, as it were, in the calcareous stone.

1793-03-21.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 91]
On the 2nd of Germinal, towards nine in the evening, we entered the torrid zone in longitude 184° east: it was the fourth time that we had crossed the tropic of Capricorn.

1793-03-22.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 91-92]
The next day at one in the afternoon we sighted Eua, one of the Friendly Islands; it bore north-west of us, about seven myriametres off; but we were soon to see it from fairly close at hand: the fine verdure that covered it on every side announced the fertility of its soil. The land is of moderate height.

It was half past six when we hove to in order to wait for the Espérance. We spent the night standing off and on.

1793-03-23.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 92-98]
On the 4th, towards seven in the morning, we were no more than about three myriametres from Tongatapu, and yet we had difficulty in making it out, for the land is rather low. Soon we ran very close along its eastern coast, standing to the north and north-west so as not to miss the opening that leads to the harbour, which is reached only after passing between reefs lying very close to one another, the gap in which cannot be made out until one is a short distance from them.

As soon as we were about the middle of this passage, many outrigger canoes came out to meet us, laden with fruit, pigs and fowls, which they offered us: they were manned by two or three natives; four were rarely seen in them. As one of them was coming towards us at too great a speed, its outrigger came away, and we had the distress of seeing the three paddlers fall into the water; but, much less put out than we should have thought, they swam towards the nearest shore, taking their little craft with them, and it was very quickly set afloat again. Boats of this kind are so frail that they must often be exposed to such accidents; accordingly the canoes that passed close by this one scarcely seemed to notice it.

They all carried provisions; we noticed one, however, that had none, and we supposed it had nothing to offer us; but we were mistaken: it was handled by two men whose faces showed great merriment as they pointed out to us two women who were paddling with them; their signs left us in no doubt that they were making us very gallant offers.

In the distance we could see large canoes under sail.

Towards half past eleven, being in the narrowest part of the passage, we found bottom in the middle with a line of eleven metres. It did not seem to us to be more than four hundred metres wide.

At the moment when we had been on the point of entering it, a large canoe had come out ahead of us and invited us to follow it into a much wider passage which lay on our starboard hand; but when it saw us take another course, it came back and kept ahead of us for some time longer, wishing to show us how we should steer.

At length we reached the roadstead of Tongatapu, and after making several boards to fetch the anchorage we let go the anchor two kilometres south-west of Pangaimotu, in twenty-one metres of water, on a bottom of very fine grey sand.

We saw a western point of Tongatapu at west 3° north; the western end of Pangaimotu at north 24° east; and at north 20° west the end of the reefs on that same side.

At once we were surrounded by natives, who came aboard our ship in such numbers that the deck was very soon covered with them. Several had come in double canoes of the shape of the one shown in *plate 28*.

A native, followed by several others who appeared to hold him in great respect, announced himself as one of the chiefs of the island. He asked to see the commander of our ship, and immediately had a pig brought, which he gave him as a present. This islander showed great gratitude on receiving a hatchet from the General's hands.

In less than an hour a dozen pigs were obtained by way of barter, the smallest of which weighed at least five myriagrams. A hatchet of middling size was given as the price of each.

The General had instructed one of his officers to deal with the islanders for such provisions as they could supply us with, and, to avoid any competition that would have been harmful to the victualling of our ships, he had forbidden anyone else to trade; but it proved impossible to enforce this order entirely. Besides, it was difficult to resist the eagerness with which the natives pressed their wares on us; each displayed his as best he could. We were particularly amused to see them holding their little pigs under their arms and pulling them by the ears from time to time to let us know that they wished to sell them.

A chief of the warriors, named *Finau*, came aboard towards five in the afternoon. He was a man of about forty-five, of middling stature and very fat. Like the other inhabitants, he had all the features of a European. His body was covered with scars in several places; he pointed out two on his chest which, he told us, were the result of spear thrusts he had received in various battles against the inhabitants of Fiji.

The portrait of this warrior, *pl. 8 fig. 2*, is a very true likeness; his hair, powdered with lime, was dressed in such a way that one would have thought he was wearing a wig.

He sat down on the watch bench with four natives, and ordered all the others to squat down; he allowed some, however, to sit on the arms chest. I do not know whether these last were great personages; but we noticed among them an elderly man who was followed by a young girl, and who used all his eloquence to tempt those of us who came near her.

*Finau* gave the general as a present the largest pig we had yet seen since we had been at the anchorage; he also gave him two very handsome clubs made of *casuarina* wood, in which were inlaid plates of bone, some cut round, others in the shape of starfish, while others represented birds, though rather badly drawn. This chief seemed well pleased when the General handed him a hatchet, a large piece of red cloth and a few nails. To show his gratitude, he at once raised each of these objects to the left side of his forehead, after taking them in his left hand.

Towards sunset we asked him to send off our ship all the natives, whose crowd had become prodigious. We wished none of them to remain, so as not to have the trouble of watching them during the night; but perhaps his authority did not extend over all of them, for after driving off only the greater part, he left us and made for the western coast of Tongatapu.

One would hardly guess how he set about getting these islanders, who were hampering us to an excessive degree, off our ship. He chased them, brandishing his club with such force that they found no way of escaping the blows of this murderous weapon but by throwing themselves into the sea.

Almost all their clubs are made of *casuarina* wood, which is extremely hard; we saw some, however, made of bone, and they were a little more than a metre long. As these islanders have no quadruped that could furnish them with such bones, there can be no doubt that they come from some large cetaceans.

Besides many fowls, they also sold us pigeons of the species called *columba aenea*, breadfruit, coconuts, yams and several varieties of bananas of delicious flavour.

We had urged all the natives to go ashore before nightfall, for several had not come merely to satisfy their curiosity or to sell us their goods. We had not been slow to notice that they had stolen a great many things from us. All the canoes had already left, however, and there still remained on board six islanders who, having no other means of returning ashore than by swimming, begged us to let them spend the night on deck; there was one, though, who preferred to swim back, although we were about two kilometres from the nearest shore. We admired the ease with which he performed all his movements. He swam all the while on his belly, his neck entirely out of the water; with his left hand he made very small movements, keeping it always in front of him, while he gave a very wide sweep to his right hand, bringing it back at each stroke as far as the thigh on the same side: at the same time his body was inclined a little to the left, which added further to the speed with which he cleaved the water. I have never seen a European swim with so much assurance or so much speed.

1793-03-24.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 98-105]
*Finau* came back the next morning to spend a few hours on board; he was particularly amused in watching every least movement of a monkey belonging to one of our gunners.

The tents of the observatory were pitched on the south-west coast of Pangaimotu, and cloths of various colours and a large quantity of hardware were carried to the same spot in order to obtain fresh provisions in exchange. As the inhabitants brought us a great many hogs, the General resolved to renew our salt provisions; Citizen Renard, one of the surgeons-major of our expedition, kindly undertook to supervise this work.

An enclosure was marked out with a rope fastened to the tops of stakes driven into the ground at intervals of four to five metres. It was with such barriers that we proposed to keep back, day and night, the inhabitants, more than two thousand of whom, most of them come over from Tongatapu, were already gathered around us.

*Fatafé*, one of the sons of the late king *Poulao*, came to the same place very early. He took it upon himself to keep good order among the natives; accordingly the trading went on with the greatest tranquillity; but we saw with regret that, to make himself obeyed, he used means as barbarous towards them as they were painful to himself; for if any one of them dared to overstep by even a few decimetres the enclosure that had been marked out, he immediately, by way of warning him to withdraw, hurled at him whatever came to hand, without regard to the harm that might result. A young man who had come forward a little too far nearly lost his life for having been inattentive to the orders of *Fatafé*, who at once flung a very large log at him with force; but he was lucky enough to dodge it.

We had to cross this crowded circle to make our way into the interior of the island; it was very difficult not to knock against the feet and legs of the natives, who were seated on the ground very close to one another, all with their legs crossed; yet, far from being angry, they gave us their hands to steady us when, for fear of hurting them, we did not know where to set our feet. Very few followed us. We found many of the inhabitants busy building huts in order to settle on the island of Pangaimotu; they had been drawn there by our having chosen this small island for buying the provisions they could supply us with. Several of these huts were already finished. The islanders we met there received us with various marks of great affection.

The ground occupied by each of these dwellings was not usually more than three metres wide by five long. The roof, about two metres high in the middle, came down to the ground in a very steep slope. On one of its sides an opening had been made, which sometimes took up the whole length of the hut, but so low that one could enter only by stooping to the point of having to support oneself on one's hands: on the opposite side there was another opening, lower still and narrower, which seemed intended to promote the circulation of the air. Elsewhere a greater number of openings were to be seen, but smaller, and placed even along the width of the dwellings. We admired there the fine weave of the mats spread on the ground. The roof was thatched with the leaves of the coconut and of the palm called *corypha umbraculifera*, and sometimes also with sedges and grasses. Under such a roof one could stand upright only towards the middle, but these people usually remain squatting inside; they can therefore get quite close to its edges.

Around these peaceful dwellings one often met extremely obliging and moreover very robust men who took care to inform strangers of the facilities they might find with the fair sex in these happy islands. The wish to oblige no doubt counted for much in their offers, but it appears that their own interest also had some share in them; for they never forgot to ask for some reward in return for their information.

For some time we followed the edge of the shore, where we saw a great number of very vigorous breadfruit trees, although their roots were washed by brackish water. Soon the sea, swollen by the flood tide, obliged us to turn back into the interior of the island, where we crossed dense woods in whose shade grew *tacca pinnatifida*, *saccharum spontaneum*, *mussænda frondosa*, *abrus precatorius*, the pepper plant which the inhabitants use to make *kava*, etc. We then walked over ground used partly for growing sweet potatoes and partly for the species of yam called *dioscorea alata*; elsewhere we saw young plants of the *vacoua*, *pandanus odoratissima*, whose leaves are used for making mats. Further on we found fields of the paper mulberry, which they cultivate for its bark, from which they make cloth to clothe themselves. The *hybiscus tiliaceus* grew wild along the borders of these various plantations and quite close to the sea: its bark also furnishes them with material for cloth, but much less fine than that of the paper mulberry.

Some natives who followed close on our heels affected to have no other aim than to be of use to us; we caught some of them, however, putting their hands into our pockets from time to time to make off with our belongings; but each time we noticed it we forced them to give them back. One of them, however, having seized a knife belonging to one of the crew, ran off as fast as his legs would carry him and disappeared into the woods.

We soon came upon a group of islanders who were preparing to take *kava*. They invited us to sit down beside them; we stayed there the whole time they were preparing this drink. They give the same name to the species of pepper plant that forms its basis, whose roots, long, fleshy and very tender, are often more than a decimetre thick. First they cleaned them with the greatest care; then they chewed them to reduce them to a kind of paste, from which they formed little balls of about a decimetre in circumference. They laid these one by one in a large wooden bowl, and as soon as its bottom was covered, the balls having been set a decimetre apart from one another, they filled it with water. This liquor was at once stirred and then served out to all the company. Some drank from coconut cups, and others from cups they made on the spot out of banana leaves.

The thick roots from which the *kava* had just been made had very fine woody fibres running lengthwise, which settled at the bottom of the drink. The man who served it gathered them together in one hand and used them as a sponge to fill the cups.

We were pressed to take our share of this beverage; but one would have had to be spared the sight of its preparation to yield to the invitations of these worthy people. The chaplain of our ship, however, had the courage to swallow a whole cupful. Wishing also to know the flavour of this root, I preferred to chew a small piece of it myself, which I found acrid and stimulating. Everyone then ate yams freshly baked in the ashes, and bananas, no doubt to lessen the heat one feels in the stomach after drinking this intoxicating liquor.

The inhabitants set great store by the pepper plant from which they obtain it. Its stem, often thicker than the thumb, is fairly straight and stands up by itself. They cut several pieces of it between the joints and made us a present of them, indicating to us that they put them into the ground in this way to propagate the plant.

We were not far from the observatory tents when some other inhabitants pressed us to eat some fruit, among which we had the pleasure of seeing that of the *spondias cytherea (Otaheite apples)*. Everyone sat down; Citizen Riche had just laid a battle-axe on the ground when a native slipped stealthily behind him, snatched it away and ran off with all his might; we at once gave chase, but he was already too far off for us to be able to catch him. A chief who happened then to be close by wished to have the battle-axe restored to us and also ran after the thief, but he soon came back and seemed much distressed at not having found him.

Soon we reached the enclosure where the trading was going on. *Fatafé* was still there. We learned that he had caused a sabre and several other articles to be returned, which belonged to various members of the crew and had been stolen by the inhabitants. Riche applied to him to try to recover his battle-axe; but *Fatafé*'s searches were fruitless.

1793-03-25.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 105-109]
A great number of canoes surrounded our ships, although the General had given orders to compel them to keep away; but there they got a better price for their goods than at the market already set up on the shore, where little was bought except provisions, whose price did not vary, whereas on board they often received a great deal for fancy articles. Besides, these canoes carried on another trade, still more strictly forbidden by General Dentrecasteaux's orders; but as the sentries were lax in enforcing them, many young girls easily escaped their watch and came in at every moment through the ports.

We had ourselves put ashore very early on the nearest coast, where we had the pleasure of seeing that these islanders possess the sugar cane. They offered us some very thick canes, which we accepted. They sold us several birds, among others a charming species of lory which they assured us had been brought to them from Fiji, a handsome species of turtle-dove remarkable for a red spot on the head and known by the name of *columba purpurata*, the species of rail called *rallus philippensis*, the pigeon called *columba pacifica*, etc.: several had the lizard known by the name of *lacerta amboinensis*, which they offered us as being very good to eat. The natives who followed us hampered us greatly by their numbers and even by their eagerness to oblige us. Seeing us gather plants, several of them picked up indiscriminately all those they found, made them up on the spot into very large bundles and brought them to us, wishing then to load us with the burden. Others, seeing us collect insects, kept asking us whether they were not meant to feed the birds we had just bought; but most of them pretended to feel great affection for us while they helped themselves to our belongings. In vain did we try several times to rid ourselves of them; the means we used were no doubt far too gentle to succeed with these peoples, who are accustomed to being treated very roughly by their chiefs.

*Fatafé*, accompanied by another chief, had gone to dine with the General, who made a present of a red coat to the one and a blue coat to the other. Decked out in these new garments, which they had put on over their usual dress, they were under one of the observatory tents when *Finau* appeared at the entrance and showed great jealousy at seeing them so dressed. He withdrew with a very discontented air, saying that they were all passing themselves off as chiefs *(egui)*, and he went off to take *kava* with others. We did not know what to make of the hasty withdrawal of *Finau*; we supposed, however, that he was less powerful than *Fatafé*, and that he avoided appearing before him so as not to have to pay him the honours due to his rank.

The officer who had charge of buying provisions had a very trying task to perform; for, although he had fixed a constant value for each article, the natives, always counting on selling dearer, never parted with their goods until they had haggled over the price for a long while.

Driven by hunger, we withdrew under the tent where the provisions bought during the day were stored; we were followed there by two inhabitants whom we took for chiefs. One of them showed the greatest eagerness in choosing the best fruit for me; I had put my hat on the ground, thinking it in a safe place; but these two rogues were plying their trade: the one behind me was skilful enough to hide my hat under his garments, and he went off before I had noticed it; the other soon followed him. I was all the less wary of this trick since I should not have believed that they would dare to take so bulky an object, at the risk of being caught in the enclosure into which we had let them come; besides, a hat could be of very little use to these peoples, who usually go bareheaded. The skill they had shown in robbing me proved to us that this was not their first attempt, and led us to suppose that they often steal from one another; besides, the chiefs might well have some interest in the thefts committed against us, for we often saw them seize whatever they found in the hands of their subjects, whom they plundered quite openly.

It was always repugnant to us to deal severely with these rascals; but it was time to curb their boldness, for it only grew with impunity. To this end it was proposed to show them the effect of our firearms on a cock placed at the end of a long pole; but the improvidence was committed of using a double-barrelled gun which had been exposed during the previous night to the damp of the atmosphere; first it misfired, then it hung fire, and another gun had to be resorted to in order to bring down the cock; and so these inhabitants seemed to retain a far higher opinion of their own weapons than of ours when another cock, which had been tied to the end of the same pole, was pierced by one of these islanders with a long arrow tipped with three diverging points. To take aim at the bird he had placed himself directly beneath it and had moreover raised himself as high as he could on tiptoe, so that the end of his arrow was not four metres from it. All the others had their eyes fixed on him and kept the deepest silence; but as soon as he had hit the mark, their cries of admiration let us know that they did not usually succeed so well, even at so short a distance.

The arrow he had just shot was nearly three metres long; they also have smaller ones, which they likewise keep in bamboo quivers.

1793-03-26.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 109-114]
Two sentries kept watch day and night over the safety of the establishment we had set up on the island of Pangaimotu. They were quite enough to keep off any natives who might have tried to slip in stealthily to steal the goods we had deposited there. No doubt it had not been feared that they would force their way in openly, for no precaution had been taken to guard against a surprise attack; yet an islander took advantage of a very heavy shower which came on towards daybreak to creep up behind one of our sentries, and struck him so violently on the head with his club that the man fell under the blow, although it had been in great part warded off by his helmet. On the instant the assassin carried off his musket. The other sentry immediately gave the alarm to those of us who were sleeping in the tents. The alarm was a lively one; everyone ran to arms, and several drew still closer to the sea with the intention of making for the longboat had the islanders fallen upon them in a great crowd. The cry of alarm was heard aboard the Espérance, which since the day before had moved in within hail; she at once let off some rockets to warn the Recherche; but all fear of a general attack on the part of these natives was soon dispelled, for it was very quickly ascertained that most of them were still asleep round our establishment and that those who had just been woken were moving away from it; besides, an officer who came in from the interior of the island almost at the moment of this murderous attack reported that he had met a great number of inhabitants, and that all of them had seemed to him to be sound asleep.

The commander of our expedition went ashore towards six in the morning with a well-armed detachment. He gave orders to strike the tents at once and carry them on board, together with all the articles that had been deposited in the enclosure for trading.

Our withdrawal greatly distressed several chiefs, who came up to the General to express to him all the grief this unfortunate accident had caused them; they loudly condemned this cowardly treachery, saying that the culprit had deserved death and that he would not long survive this crime. They tried every means to have the trading continue as before.

Our detachment, having advanced a little way into the interior of the island to observe the disposition of the natives, found nearly a thousand of them who had slept in the neighbourhood of our establishment; it urged them to move further away, which they all did except a small group of armed men who, at once raising their clubs and spears, refused to fall back a single step. Perhaps this boldness, which made us regard them as the accomplices of the assassin, ought to have been checked; but a chief named *Toubau*, one of the king's kinsmen, fell upon them impetuously and, with great blows of his club, soon had them dispersed.

The General, before embarking to return on board, made some presents to the various chiefs gathered round him. He required them to hand over the assassin to him, and to return the musket he had stolen, as well as a sabre which had been taken the day before from one of our gunners, and he warned them that only on this condition would he allow the trading to begin again.

All the inhabitants withdrew as soon as our longboat left the shore; but no sooner had it reached the ship than several of them went over the ground we had just abandoned and searched very carefully to see whether any of our belongings had been left there. We noticed one who contrived to pull out the nail that had been used to hang one of our clocks on a post.

*Finau* came aboard in the afternoon and gave the General a present of breadfruit, yams, a hog and bananas: he received a hand-saw, a hatchet and several joiner's chisels; but we saw that he gave the hatchet a very marked preference over the other tools. After listening with the greatest attention to our account of the murderous attack just made by one of the inhabitants upon one of our sentries, he promised to have the musket returned to us the very next day, and told us that he would bring us the assassin, on whom he wished to do justice in our presence. He asked to see the gunner who had been wounded. The man had a very large wound on the head; but fortunately it presented no danger, for the violence of the blow had been deadened by the helmet he was wearing. *Finau* showed much feeling on seeing this wound; he made the patient a present of a piece of cloth made from the bark of the paper mulberry, to be used in dressing his wound; and indeed this cloth has qualities that make it very well suited to such a use.

*Finau* having ordered several natives of his train to make *kava*, they at once chewed some thick roots of the pepper plant of the same name, and this liquor was soon prepared. He drank first, and the rest was shared among the other inhabitants, who, like *Finau*, then ate bananas. Out of respect for him they all remained squatting on the deck, while he was seated on the watch bench.

We showed this chief several engravings from the voyages of Captain Cook. It was with the greatest respect that he pronounced several times the name of that celebrated navigator, whom he called *Touté*. It is worth noting that, although we found it very easy to pronounce the words of these inhabitants' language, it was not the same for them with ours; for example, trying to repeat the word *François*, they all pronounced *Palançois*; instead of *Beaupré*, *Beaupélé*, etc., etc. *Finau* spoke to us of Tahiti, and told us he had seen Omai at Nomuka. Perhaps this was the same *Finau* who had been on terms of particular intimacy with Cook on his last voyage; yet that captain says he was a fine tall man.

The people of his train talked to us for a long time of King *Toubau*, whose power they extolled; and to show us how far superior he was to *Finau*, they raised the right arm very high as they uttered his name, and then brought the left hand to the elbow to show the degree of *Finau*'s inferiority.

1793-03-27.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 114-119]
*Finau* admitted this pre-eminence of *Toubau*, who, he announced to us, was to come aboard the next day.

I had planned to go and spend the day on the island of Tongatapu with some of my fellow voyagers; but the general urged us to put off this excursion until the chiefs had proved to us that they had truly resolved to put a check on the brigandage of their subjects.

Many canoes surrounded our ships; none, however, was allowed to come alongside. Several islanders, weary of being unable to carry on any kind of trade, amused themselves by fishing with nets about eight metres long by nearly a metre and a half wide, whose meshes were about a quarter of a square decimetre. From the shape of these nets, several of which we had already bought, we had supposed that the inhabitants used them as we use the seine, dragging them along the beach; but we were much astonished to see them cast in the open roadstead, much as we cast the casting-net. Pieces of lithophytes fastened to their lower edge carried them rapidly to the bottom of the sea; but the fishermen at once dived to draw the two ends together by means of small cords attached to them, and so enclose the fish, which they put into their canoes. It will be understood that to catch fish in this way in open water they must be abundant. These fishermen no doubt went to so much trouble only because they were violently tormented by hunger; for, having no means of cooking their fish in their canoes, they resolved to eat it raw.

Towards nine in the morning three chiefs came aboard to announce that we were soon to receive a visit from *Toubau*, supreme chief *(egui laï)* of Tongatapu, of Vava'u, of Nomuka, etc.; that he was going to hand over to us the assassin we were demanding, and return to us the musket he had stolen. Indeed it was barely eleven o'clock when *Toubau* arrived with several chiefs. The assassin lay at his feet, face down, his hands tied behind his back. He had him brought aboard at once, and then had the musket brought, with its bayonet, which the man had taken from one of our sentries. Two pieces of paper-mulberry bark cloth, so large that each of them, spread out, would have entirely covered our ship, two hogs and several very large mats were the presents he made to the commander of our expedition. The warrior *Finau*, not disdaining to act as executioner, at once raised his club to knock the culprit on the head, and it was with some difficulty that he was prevented from doing justice on him before our eyes; at last he handed him over to the General's disposal, no doubt believing that he wished to reserve to himself the infliction of the punishment due to his crime: and indeed the wretch was already offering his neck, imagining that his last hour had come; meanwhile our sentry, whom he had felled with a blow of his club, asked that the criminal's life be spared: we then contented ourselves with having him given a few strokes of a rope's end across the shoulders; but *Finau*, finding this punishment far too mild, again raised his club to despatch him. In vain did the General shout to him with all his might *icaï maté* (that he must be allowed to live); *Finau* assured us that he would nevertheless not escape the punishment he had deserved. As we were examining several marks of blows from a club that this man had already received on the head before he was brought to us, we were told that he had been so ill-treated at the moment of his capture. The general asked our surgeon-major to dress his wounds, and then he was taken aboard the Espérance, with the intention of putting him ashore during the night in order to try to save his life.

King *Toubau* received as a present from the general's hands a red coat, which he put on at once, and a large hatchet besides; *Finau* also had a red coat, but a much smaller hatchet: a few small hatchets were also distributed to other chiefs. They were all on deck, forming a circle round *Toubau*, who sat on the watch bench with *Finau* on his right and another chief named *Omalaï* on his left.

 *Toubau* seemed to us to be at least sixty years old. This old man was of middling height and fatter still than *Finau*. His garments were of the same form as those of the other islanders, differing from them only in the fineness of their texture. He wore a very handsome mat fastened about his body by a girdle of cloth made from the bark of the paper mulberry.

When *Toubau* gave the order to make *kava*, we urged some of the chiefs to busy themselves with the preparation and to chew themselves some roots of the *kava* pepper which we offered them; but they steadily refused, appearing to disdain having anything to do with this work. It was entrusted to men of an inferior class (*moua*), who were seated towards the middle of the circle formed by the chiefs.

The rain, which came on meanwhile, increasing rapidly, we thought that each of them would have sought shelter; but they braved this setback without leaving their places, except the king, who withdrew into the General's cabin with *Finau* and *Toubau-Foa*, one of the king's kinsmen. *Kava* was brought to them in cups that had just been made from banana leaves, and then they were offered bananas. The General invited all three to dinner, but the king would not allow either of these chiefs to sit at the same table as himself; he tasted every dish, rejected most of them, and ate very little of those he seemed to like, with the exception of sugar. The general had made him a present of a bird-organ, which amused him greatly and which he played during almost the whole meal.

These islanders, who shave with the edge of a shell, spend a great deal of time on this operation. They were struck with astonishment when they saw how quickly our barber shaved several members of the crew; each of them wished to be shaved by him; he also had the honour of shaving his majesty.

The king having informed us of his departure towards half past three, it was proposed to take him ashore in our large boat, which he accepted. He was followed by a great number of canoes, and soon arrived at the island of Pangaimotu with most of the chiefs who had accompanied him on board. As soon as he had landed on the shore he had yams, a breadfruit, pork and bananas brought to him; but we were much surprised to see him eat with a very hearty appetite, for we had supposed he was not hungry, having done so little honour to the General's dinner; we ought not, however, to have presumed that our dishes had not been to his taste, since the other islanders all took to them perfectly; perhaps it is a point of etiquette that his majesty should not indulge his appetite on days when he is a guest, especially with strangers. He then delivered a speech in which there was no doubt some question of our friendly dispositions and of the resolve we had formed to punish those who should rob us, after which he went over to the island of Tongatapu.

1793-03-28.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 119-128]
Towards nightfall *Finau* brought back the sabre that had been taken from one of our gunners. He returned it to the General and made him a present of a very large fish of the genus *perca*, called the Sanguinolent. Before leaving us he announced to the canoes that surrounded us that trading would begin again the very next day.

Very early in the morning of the 9th our boat carried a great quantity of cloth and hardware to the island of Pangaimotu. The canoes surrounding our ships were invited several times, to no purpose, to go to the market which had just been re-established on that small island; it was thought, however, that a sure means had been found of keeping them away from our vessels when they were seen to flee in haste as soon as water had been thrown at them with a pump; but the success was not lasting, for, having very soon learnt that they ran no other risk than that of getting wet, they no longer stirred from the spot they occupied, however much the same pump continued to be turned upon them. Dauribeau, flag captain on board the Recherche, then gave orders that they should be capsized every time our boats went ashore, and soon our biscayenne, setting off for the nearest shore with various instruments intended for astronomical observations, pulled hard towards a canoe carrying three men and two girls; she had soon knocked off its outrigger, and we should have had the pain of seeing those two pretty creatures fall into the water, had not the men prevented the mishap by throwing themselves into the sea; two of them held their little craft steady while the third refitted the outrigger, and they were soon paddling off towards Tongatapu. The other canoes, warned of the danger, were adroit enough to avoid those of our boats which afterwards tried to overturn them.

*Finau* came on board very early in the morning with *Toubau*, the king's brother. These two chiefs invited the General to attend a feast which the king proposed to give him on the island of Tongatapu the day after next. Having asked us to show them the effects of our swivel guns and carronades, they displayed as much fright as admiration.

When we reached the shore we noticed with surprise that the market was very well supplied, although there were not a third as many islanders as on the preceding days. Everything went on there in the greatest order.

It was still the same officer (Lagrandière) who dealt with them for the provisioning of our ships. He congratulated himself exceedingly on having thought of having ends of iron hoops cut into the shape of joiners' chisels, and on turning them to good account with these people. Yet we had on board a great number of very good tools which had been bought in Europe to be given to them. We could not conceive why the satisfaction he ought to have felt in furnishing them with durable implements did not prevail over every other consideration.

While walking through the interior of the island we saw a barber busy shaving one of the chiefs after his own fashion. The chief was seated, with his back leaning against his dwelling. The barber, using as his razor the two valves of the kind of shell called the rising sun, held the one in his left hand pressed against the skin, while with his right he applied the edge of the other valve to the roots of the hairs, which he scraped at repeatedly and removed, so to speak, one by one. We were astonished at so much patience, and we left them, as may well be believed, long before the end of the operation.

The potter's art is not very far advanced among these people; we saw in their hands earthen vessels, very porous, which they had fired only rather lightly. They kept fresh water in them, which would very soon have filtered through had they not taken the precaution of coating them with a layer of resin; consequently they can be of no use to them for cooking their food. These people showed us some of a rather handsome shape which they told us had been brought to them from Fiji *(see pl. 31, fig. 8)*. We saw them drink in turn from these vessels, which they take care to enclose in a wide-meshed net so as to carry them easily. As soon as they had emptied a few, they went to refill them at small holes they had dug in the ground so that the water might collect there. This water was barely brackish, although it was drawn only about three hundred metres from the shore. As we needed to replace what we had consumed since leaving Adventure Bay, we dug a hole more than a metre deep in the ground, a good distance from the coast, into which very drinkable water at once collected. With it were filled galley casks, which some natives of the class of the *toua* were willing to carry on their shoulders down to our longboat; but the part of their bodies on which the iron hoops of the casks rested, being bare, was soon chafed, and before long they gave up this kind of work; they readily agreed, however, to drag the casks on a small cart we had brought from Europe. The *toua*, twelve in number, sang to mark the moments when they had to combine all their efforts at once. Their number soon rose to twenty, and at first they did not ask for any increase in the reward that had been agreed for each trip (twelve glass beads); but a few days later they set a higher price on their labour. They assured us that on Tongatapu water was found only in pools, or by digging in the ground as at Pangaimotu, but that very good spring water could be had at Koa, a small island near Toufoa.

I had not yet seen a single dog since we had been at anchor. In the afternoon an islander brought us one to sell, assuring us that its flesh was very good to eat; they call this animal *kouli*; in these islands it is usually fawn-coloured and small, and comes fairly close to the wolf-dog.

Citizen Riche told us that the murderer of whom I spoke above, having been carried during the night before to the western coast of Pangaimotu by a boat from the Espérance, had hesitated for some time to go ashore, and had asked the boatmen who conveyed him, with a very anxious air, which way *Finau* had gone on his return the evening before; at last he made up his mind to land on the island, and crawled on his hands for a distance of more than three hundred paces along the beach before daring to venture inland. Quite near the market to which the natives came to bring us their provisions we noticed a woman of extraordinary corpulence, at least fifty years of age, around whom the natives formed a very large circle; some of them, in our presence, showed her marks of respect by taking her right foot and placing it on their heads, after making a deep bow; others came and touched the sole of her right foot with their right hand. Several chiefs whom we knew showed her still other tokens of deference. We were told that this was Queen *Tiné*. Her hair, cut to a length of two-thirds of a decimetre, was covered, as was part of her forehead, with a reddish powder.

Having expressed the wish to go on board the Recherche to see the commander of our expedition, she urged us to accompany her, and at once embarked to go there with part of her court. She gave several very handsome mats, a hog and some yams to General Dentrecasteaux, who presented her with various pieces of cloth, on which she seemed to set a great value.

Wishing to learn what sensations the sound of the voice accompanied by the violin and the sistrum would produce on these people, we noticed with pleasure that this music was agreeable to them; but a few airs played on a bird-organ won still more marked applause.

Queen *Tiné*, not wishing to be outdone by us, ordered some young girls of her train to sing. One of the prettiest rose at once and soon received our applause. Yet she sang nothing else than

[musical stave]
apou lelley; apou lelley; apou lelley; apou lelley;

which she repeated for at least half an hour; but she displayed so much grace in the movements with which she accompanied this air that we were sorry she stopped so soon. Her arms were thrust forward one after the other, following the measure, while she raised her feet, yet always keeping to the same spot; each beat of the measure was marked with the forefinger, which struck the middle finger after being bent back by the thumb, and sometimes the thumb was brought against the middle finger and the forefinger. The charm of these movements owed a great deal to the fine shape of the hands and arms, so common among these people, of which this young person offered a very striking example. A little later two other young girls repeated the same air, singing it in parts, constantly making harmonies in fifths, and several men rose to dance to the sound of their melodious voices; they marked the measure with movements like those of the young girls, first with their feet and often by bringing one of their hands to the opposite arm.

We took the words of this air (*apou lelley*, fine evening) for a compliment on the part of these islanders, who were congratulating themselves on spending the afternoon with us.

The queen tasted the various dishes we offered her, but above all she gave the preference to bananas preserved in sugar. Our steward stood behind her, waiting for the moment to clear away; but she spared him the trouble by keeping the plate and the napkin for herself.

*Tiné* was very jealous of the honours which the chiefs dared not refuse her when they met her; and so some of them avoided finding themselves in her presence. *Finau* and the king's brother *Toubau* were on board and had just promised us to stay to dinner when she came; at once they begged us earnestly not to let her come up on deck; she was not long, however, in arriving there, and we saw these two chiefs flee in haste to their canoes, for they would have been obliged, as several of the inhabitants assured us, to come and take her right foot and very respectfully bring their heads close to it to mark their inferiority. The queen told us with an air of satisfaction that even King *Toubau* was bound to show her these marks of respect, because it was from her that he held his dignity.

After telling us that she would remain on the island of Pangaimotu for as long as we stayed in this roadstead, she urged the General to settle ashore and sleep in her dwelling. I do not believe that this old queen had any other aim than to procure him a pleasanter and healthier abode than the ship; but the General had no opportunity of judging exactly the motive of these obliging offers, for he did not accept the invitation.

One of our sailors was holding in his hand a piece of cooked bacon which *Féogò*, one of *Tiné*'s ladies of honour, seemed to wish to taste: he offered it to her and she received it with gratitude; but as she could not allow herself to eat in the queen's presence, the latter was good enough to go and sit down about twelve paces farther off, so that her attendant should be at a distance from her; but before leaving her place she had received from this young person the same tokens of respect that other natives had already shown her in our presence.

Two hours before sunset *Tiné* expressed the wish to return to the island of Pangaimotu, and shortly afterwards embarked in our large boat with part of her train.

We already knew from Bligh's narrative that, at the moment when he was preparing to leave the island of Toufoa, the sailor he had sent ashore to cast off the painter of his launch had been killed by an islander; natives of Tongatapu told us that this murder had been committed by a chief named *Moudoulalo*; but we could not learn what motives had driven him to such an excess of barbarity. Every one of us was astonished at the coolness with which these people gave us this account.

1793-03-29.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 128-132]
We had already seen several knives of English make in the hands of the natives. Early in the morning *Finau* brought us a blunted bayonet which he had had from Captain Cook, and asked us to sharpen it.

In the afternoon we went over some islets lying at short distances from one another between Tongatapu and Pangaimotu; they are joined together by a shoal which is almost entirely uncovered at low tide.

We came first to a sandbank newly risen from the bosom of the waters, which the islanders call *Iniou*, on which, however, the beginnings of vegetation could already be seen. Then, wishing to reach the small island of *Manima*, we had to cross a fairly rapid current which, a short while after low tide, was no more than two metres deep, and which carried water all the warmer for having just passed over a beach strongly heated by the rays of the sun. There we found one of the queen's ladies of honour, to whom we made some presents of glass trinkets; at once she sent for two hens to offer us. We burdened ourselves with them for fear she might have been unpleasantly affected by our refusal. She took great care to let us know that she was not giving them to us by way of exchange, making a point of repeating with an air of dignity *ikaï fokatau*, and of announcing to us by the word *adoupé* that she was making us a present. Indeed, the chiefs never proposed to exchange their goods for ours; they made us presents and received everything we offered them.

It is worth noting that the islanders brought many cocks to our market, but very rarely hens: they kept these to hatch eggs; and so they sold us very few eggs.

The two hens we had to carry away had been caught in our presence with the same kind of net that we had already seen cast in the open roadstead to catch fish.

The island of *Manima* has little cultivated ground; we saw some fields of yams there, however, and some coconut and banana trees.

After crossing a channel as shallow as the first, we came to *Onéata*. Curious to examine the interior of an artfully built dwelling, we were much surprised to see a chief who, seated very gravely towards the middle of his hut, was allowing a person from our ship the greatest liberties with one of the prettiest girls of the island. While offering us coconuts, he warned us that he could not let us drink their milk inside that dwelling. We could never have imagined that this witness of the party we had just interrupted in his own hut would have been so intolerant towards people who had come there only to quench their thirst; we made it our duty, however, not to cross him.

Meanwhile two natives arrived holding in their hands some opened and very ripe coconuts, with which we saw them prepare a dish of which they appeared very fond. With shells fitted to wooden handles they scraped out the kernels, which they crushed with a very hot stone so as to reduce them to a pulp, to which they gave the consistency of a pudding after mixing it with freshly cooked bread-fruit; then they made it into little balls, which they ate on the spot. Under a large shed we saw a double canoe twelve metres long which the natives had put there to shelter it from the weather.

We were fairly near the small island called *Nougou nougou* when some of the inhabitants pointed out to us, under the name of *Mackaha*, an islet very close to Pangaimotu. We made our way towards the latter island, and as the tide was rising we had to wade in up to our waists to reach it. We soon came to the place where the queen regularly held her court; it was a short distance from our market, in the shade of a very leafy bread-fruit tree. She was giving a vocal concert there, in which *Fatafé* sang while beating the measure, which all the musicians followed with the greatest exactness. Some sang their parts, accompanying the simple melody of the others with various modulations. We noticed at times dissonances by which the ears of these people seemed much gratified.

Meanwhile we saw a great many islanders arrive, each carrying on his shoulder a long pole from the ends of which hung yams and fish, with which they at once formed the base of a four-sided pyramid that they raised to nearly two metres. This present was intended for General Dentrecasteaux, to whom *Tiné* was giving a feast. She warned us of the danger of walking alone on the island towards the close of day, assuring us that thieves might take advantage of the darkness of night to rob us after attacking us with clubs.

1793-03-30.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 132-141]
On the 11th the General set off as early as six in the morning to accept the invitations of King *Toubau*, who proposed to give him a feast on the island of Tongatapu. We accompanied him with almost all the officers of our expedition and a well-armed detachment.

Some natives who followed us in their canoes made us coast westward for some time, to take us to a place where, they told us, we should find a great number of inhabitants gathered together with several of their chiefs. As soon as we had arrived *Finau* came forward to receive the General and escort him into the midst of a great concourse of islanders over which *Omalaï* presided; this chief invited him to sit on his left, after ordering the natives to range themselves in a circle around him. We rested for a moment on mats spread on the ground in the shade of several trees of *cerbera manghas* and *hernandia ovigera*, whose fruit serves these people as an ornament. Shortly afterwards we went to see a very lofty roof which sheltered a war canoe twenty-five metres long, the inside of which was strengthened with very solid knees placed about a metre apart. *Finau*, after making us admire the construction of this double canoe, told us that he had taken it in a battle he had fought against the people of Fiji.

Proceeding westward we went through a vast enclosure formed by palisades whose stakes, set obliquely, stood fairly close to one another, and in the midst of which grew the bread-fruit tree, the banana, the palm *corypha umbraculifera*, etc. Farther on, in a much smaller space, we found a little conical hut in which, we learnt, had been laid the remains of a chief who had died a short time before, and we were warned that it was forbidden to enter it.

We then walked for nearly a quarter of an hour along a narrow path bordered with palisades on both sides; we followed it as far as a very extensive open space where King *Toubau* was expected shortly *(see plate 26)*.

We were invited by *Omalaï* to take the cool air there under a roof which had roughly the form of a half-oval, five metres wide by twelve long, and whose ridge, about five and a half metres high, was covered with *vacoua* leaves which made it impenetrable to the heaviest rains; it was supported by ten pillars and came down to within two-thirds of a metre of the ground, on which very handsome mats had been spread. This spot was about two decimetres higher than the surrounding ground, which protected it from flooding.

At last *Toubau* arrived with two of his daughters; they had poured a great quantity of coconut oil on their hair, and each wore a necklace made of the pretty seeds of the *abrus precatorius*.

The islanders had gathered in great numbers from every side; we reckoned that there were at least four thousand of them.

The place of honour was no doubt on the king's left, for he invited the General to sit there. The General at once had the presents intended for *Toubau* brought forward, and the king showed him much gratitude for them; but nothing that was offered him excited the admiration of this numerous assembly so much as a piece of crimson damask, whose bright colour made them cry out on every side *eho, eho*, which they repeated for a long time, showing the greatest surprise. They raised the same cry when we unrolled some pieces of ribbon in which the colour red predominated. The General then gave a she-goat in kid, a he-goat and two rabbits (a male and a female); the king promised to take the greatest care of them and to let them multiply on his island.

*Omalaï*, whom *Toubau* told us was his son, also received some presents from the General, as did several other chiefs. On our right, towards the north-east, we had thirteen musicians who, seated in the shade of a bread-fruit tree laden with a prodigious number of fruits, sang together in several parts. Four of them held in their hands a bamboo from one metre to one and a half metres long, with which they struck the ground to mark the measure; the longest of these bamboos sometimes served to mark every beat. These instruments gave out sounds rather like those of a tabor, and they stood to one another in the following proportion. The two middle-sized bamboos were in unison; the longest was a tone and a half lower, and the shortest two tones and a half higher. The musician who sang the counter-tenor could be heard well above all the others, although his voice was a little hoarse; at the same time he accompanied himself by striking with two small sticks of *casuarina* on a bamboo six metres long, split along its whole length. Three musicians placed in front of the others further endeavoured to express the subject of their song by gestures which they had no doubt carefully studied, for they repeated them together and in the same manner. From time to time they turned towards the king, making movements with their arms that were not without grace; at other times they bowed their heads swiftly down to their chests and shook them repeatedly, etc., etc. Meanwhile *Toubau* offered the General some pieces of cloth made from the bark of the paper mulberry, and had them unfolded with much ostentation to make us aware of the full value of his present.

The minister seated on his right ordered the *kava* to be prepared, and soon a wooden vessel cut in an oval shape, one metre in length, was brought in full of it *(see pl. 31, fig. 9)*.

The musicians had no doubt kept their finest pieces for this moment, for at every pause they made we heard cries of *mâli, mâli* on every side, and the repeated applause of these people showed us that this music made a very lively and very agreeable impression on them.

The *kava* was then distributed to the various chiefs by the man who had given the order to prepare it. He had it carried to them in cups made on the spot out of banana leaves, and each time he offered one he pronounced in a fairly loud voice the name of the person for whom it was meant. He had *Finau* served first, saying *mayé maa Finau*; he did the same for the other chiefs, all of whom bore names that we pronounced very easily: the reader will perhaps not be sorry to know some of them, *Nufatoa*, *Fefé*, *Mafi*, *Famouna*, *Fatoumona*, etc. Several of the chiefs must no doubt judge the quality of this liquor before the king drank of it, for he was offered only the fourth cup. None was presented to his daughters. Indeed, it always appeared to us that this liquor was reserved entirely for the men.

Notwithstanding the General's presence, the king soon fell asleep and snored very loudly, sitting cross-legged with his head bent down very close to his knees. As soon as he awoke we showed him a drawing of a cow, and asked him whether the one Cook had given to King *Poulao* had multiplied. He recognised the quadruped perfectly, calling it *boakka touté*, and told us there were none left on Tongatapu, but that there were some at Apaé. Several natives, however, imitating the lowing of these animals quite well, assured us that some were to be found on Tongatapu; but many others denied it, so that we could not learn what had become of the bull and the cow that Captain Cook had left on this island. It was the same with the horse and the mare he had given to *Feenou*. Perhaps they were afraid we might ask them for some of these quadrupeds.

We left the assembly and made our way eastward, climbing a gentle slope; at first we followed paths bordered with palisades, from which we soon emerged to cross fields of yams in full bearing; farther on, freshly turned earth presented to us every appearance of fertility.

We soon reached the top of a small hill, in a charming spot where the inhabitants had formed, with palisades and some skilfully trimmed shrubs, a kind of rotunda four metres across, under which could still be seen the residue of the roots of the *kava* pepper plant which they had chewed. It was surrounded by twenty-four little huts built round the edge of a circular space fourteen to fifteen metres across; all of them were thatched with coconut leaves interwoven with one another, and they had roughly the form of half an oval, two metres wide by three long, divided at the top along its whole length by a very narrow slit, which was nevertheless its only opening, and whose edges had to be parted in order to get in. Some natives who had followed us told us that the king often came to take *kava* at this place with several chiefs of the island, and that afterwards each went to sleep in these kinds of huts.

On our way back towards the place of the feast we went round the largest circle formed by the inhabitants, among whom we noticed several wives of *egui*; that of *Fatafé* drew almost every eye by her beauty; but she took care to give warning from time to time that it was her duty to remain faithful to her husband. This is how she expressed herself: *tabou mitzi mitzi*. These words are of too great a frankness for me to allow myself to give their literal translation, as may be seen in the vocabulary of the language of the Friendly Islands to be found towards the end of this volume.

In the hands of a woman who appeared to enjoy fairly high consideration we noticed a kind of mat about two-thirds of a metre square, woven of white hairs from a horse's tail; perhaps they came from those Cook had left on this island? but she would not satisfy our curiosity on this point.

The king had ordered his subjects to bring the presents he intended for the General; already, since half past ten, we had seen a great many islanders arriving at intervals, each carrying on his shoulder a bamboo two metres long, from the ends of which hung rather small fish of the genera *scarus* and *chaetodon*, most of them cooked and wrapped in coconut leaflets; others brought bread-fruit, yams, etc., etc.; and soon, by crossing their bamboos, they raised two portions of triangular pyramids, one two metres high and the other only one metre. The raw fish already gave off a most offensive smell. *Toubau* went away at about one o'clock in the afternoon, without saying anything to anyone. We then left the assembly, and were accompanied as far as our landing place by *Finau* and *Omalaï*, who had a whole hog, freshly cooked, brought to us, along with fish, yams and bread-fruit, inviting us to sit down and take our meal; but their hog was not half cooked, according to the custom of these people, and so we preferred to go and eat on board.

At once they begged us to accept these various dishes, which they had carried into our longboat, while other natives, carrying out *Toubau*'s orders, filled it with the provisions they had just taken down from the pyramids raised for the commander of our expedition. In a short time everything was ready for our departure.

Our boats having been obliged to stand off from the shore on account of the low tide, we could reach them only after crossing a bank of coral covered with water for a distance of more than three hundred paces; but we found some very obliging natives who, not wishing to let us get wet, carried us as far as some rocks awash, against which others came with their canoes to take us out to our boats.

Our bearers appeared well pleased with the articles we gave them as a reward; but during this short passage other inhabitants made still more profit out of us, robbing us quite at their ease after slipping stealthily up behind us while the first were holding us on their backs; these rogues, however, were not all equally successful, for we pursued some of them and forced them to give back what they had just taken.

As soon as we arrived on board, the officer in command told us that during our absence he had had an islander seized just as he was carrying off a great many articles of hardware which he had stolen from between decks, and that *Fatafé*, condemning the robbery of which the natives were daily guilty towards us, had made a show of declaring loudly that this man ought to be put to death; but it had soon been perceived that this was only a ruse on the part of the chief, for as soon as the thief was struck with rope's ends he begged for his pardon, which he did not obtain; and as the number of strokes the rascal was to receive had been fixed at twenty-five, and they were given him, *Fatafé* seemed extremely affected by it.

1793-03-31.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 141-142]
Fairly early in the morning we had a visit from *Tonga*, who came with *Toubau*, his father and the king's brother. They both took a great deal of trouble to explain to us all the dignities of their family.

*Tonga* several times gave us proofs of great intelligence, and particularly when we showed him a chart of the Friendly Islands drawn up by Captain Cook. He first cast a rapid glance over the archipelago, then, stopping at Tongatapu, he pointed out to us that several reefs had been laid down which did not exist, and told us that towards the north-west we should find a passage by which it would be very easy for us to gain the open sea with our ships. This information was all the more useful to us because we had intended to leave this roadstead by the narrow pass through which we had entered, where we should no doubt have had to contend with the prevailing winds, whereas with those same winds we should have every facility for going out by this new pass. *Tonga* offered to show it to us, and was kind enough to spend the night on board so as to take Citizen Beaupré, engineer-geographer, who was to fix its position, there at daybreak the next day.

During an excursion we made over the land nearest the anchorage we noticed, in the midst of a group of natives, a young person who had all the characteristics of the Albinos. She was, moreover, of a very feeble constitution, as usually happens in such cases, because the condition is bound up with a state of disease.

1793-04-01.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 142-146]
On the morning of the 13th, some islanders having been caught fleeing towards the coast of Tongatapu with articles they had just carried off from our ship, the officer in command had them pursued by our men, when one of them, who had had himself announced as a chief, said that he would punish them himself and would bring us back the stolen articles the very next day; but it seemed to us that he was in league with these rogues, for he took good care not to come back on board.

When we went ashore, *Omalaï* embarked with us and spent a long time admiring the rudder of our longboat; he wished to steer her himself, and did so with great precision. These people use only paddles to steer their canoes.

Coconut oil forms part of the women's toilet, after being perfumed with a small seed which these islanders call *langa kali*, and which they gather on the island of Tongatapu: on examining it we saw that it was mixed with crushed coconut kernels, which they call *mou* in their language. They had spread these out on mats and exposed them to the sun to dry before pressing out the oil, with which the women anoint the upper parts of their bodies, no doubt to keep their skin supple and to prevent perspiration from being too abundant. They keep it in the fruits of the *melodinus scandens*, after removing the seeds. When we bought these little phials (which may be seen in *pl. 31, fig. 14*) we often threw away the oil they held, for fear it might spill into our pockets; but women, seeing with regret that we were wasting this liquid, which they value highly, would usually come forward to receive it on their heads, and then spread it with their hands over their shoulders and arms.

The natives had already sold us a great number of clubs of various shapes, skilfully worked, as may be seen in *pl.* 33. We saw several of them busy carving others with sharks' teeth fixed in the end of a piece of wood *(pl. 32, fig. 23)*. We were astonished to see them cut so quickly into *casuarina* wood with this kind of chisel, in spite of its extreme hardness. Others were already using with great dexterity the iron tools we had procured for them. These workmen all had, in a small bag of matting, pieces of pumice stone with which they polished their work.

I noticed several cotton plants of the species called *gossypium religiosum*, growing in uncultivated places, and I saw with surprise that these people made no use in any of their work of the fine cotton they might obtain from them in abundance.

Towards nine in the evening we perceived a canoe close to the buoy of one of our anchors. Fearing that it might cut the buoy-rope, one of our boats was sent to chase it off: scarcely had it left when someone was heard falling into the water; at once help was hurried to him; but seeing a person swimming away from our frigate without choosing to utter a single word, we no longer doubted that it was a thief making off with some of our belongings. He was pursued immediately, and several times escaped our boatmen by diving; at last they managed to take him only after wounding him in the thighs with a boat-hook which they had used to stop him. As soon as he was on board he was tied up on deck, where he spent the night. He confessed that, having taken several articles from our biscayenne, he had carried them to the canoe which was still waiting for him near our buoy and which soon moved away.
