Half an hour later we thought we saw it again, slowly approaching the stern of our ship to look for the islander we had just seized. At once our yawl pulled hard towards it and, having come up with it, found in it only one native and two paddles; but it was soon perceived that the canoe had brought us another thief; this one had prowled around our ship until the arrival of another canoe, which had come to fetch him and take him ashore. As soon as it was sighted it was given chase, but the natives who manned it paddled so vigorously that it was impossible to overtake them.

1793-04-02.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 146-147]
Citizen Beaupré returned at about three in the morning with *Tonga*, after surveying towards the north-west the passage which that islander had told us of. They had passed very close to Attata, leaving it to larboard as they went away from our anchorage. The chief of that small island, named *Kepa*, had come out to meet them and had given them a very warm welcome. He came to see us in the course of the morning and asked us for news of Captain Cook, who, he told us, was his friend; but he could not hold back his tears on learning of his death, and he drew from his girdle a shark's tooth with which he was about to tear his cheeks to express the violence of his grief, had we not prevented him.

Medicine is practised among these people with an air of mystery. One of the men of our crew who was accompanying us along the beach having hurt his wrist by straining it, a native offered to relieve him and succeeded fairly quickly by massaging the injured part; but at the same time he blew on it several times, no doubt wishing us to attribute to his breath the cure he had just effected.

On the seashore we saw several natives busy squaring large blocks of limestone, which we were told were to serve for the tomb of a chief, one of *Fatafé*'s relations. They lifted them out after detaching them by breaking them with a volcanic pebble, which they had taken the precaution of wrapping round the middle with pieces of matting to prevent splinters of the stone from flying into their eyes. The stones lay almost at the surface of the ground, and were arranged in layers a decimetre thick.

We had already noticed among these people a game played with the hands which they call *léagui*, and which requires great attention. It is played by two, and consists in one trying to repeat instantly the signs made by the other, and the first in turn making signs which the second likewise tries to repeat. In the middle of a group not far from our market we saw two of them putting so much briskness into this kind of exercise that we could hardly follow their movements with our eyes.

Citizen Legrand, who had left the Espérance the day before to try to discover some passages to leeward of our anchorage, returned in the evening after surveying two of them towards the north.

1793-04-03.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 147-159]
I set off early in the morning with all the other naturalists of our expedition to go to the island of Tongatapu. Some natives were willing to take us there in their small canoes, but most of us, not keeping our balance well, capsized these little craft at the moment of setting out; we then decided to embark in their double canoes, which they handled with skill, taking us across under sail fairly quickly. The mast was fixed in the canoe which lay to leeward.

We were obliged to land more than six hundred paces from the shore on account of the shallowness of the water. The natives carried us ashore on their backs, then showed us the dwelling of *Toubau*, the king's brother. We stopped there; the gardener of our expedition presented him with a great many kinds of seeds brought from Europe, chiefly of vegetables; the chief promised us to cultivate them with care. We left him to go deep into woods where the soil was calcareous and where heaps of madrepores could be seen here and there, attesting that the waters of the sea had lain there for a long time. In the trees we saw many large bats of the species named *vespertilio vampyrus*, which the inhabitants told us were very good to eat.

We were about the middle of the wood when an islander who had slipped up behind one of us snatched out of his hands some iron forceps intended for picking up insects: the thief at once took to flight; but he had scarcely gone eighty paces when, feeling himself very hotly and very closely pursued, he placed himself behind a tree, round which he ran several times so as not to be caught; our fellow traveller, however, seized him by his clothing and thought he was on the point of recovering his forceps, imagining that he had the rogue fast; but what was his surprise when the man untied his girdle and left him his clothes, escaping swiftly with the article he had just stolen.

We soon came into fields where we saw each property divided into small plots surrounded by palisades and perfectly cultivated. The Caribbee cabbage, *arum esculentum*, grew vigorously there among many other plants of which I have already spoken and which likewise serve as food for these islanders. The sugar canes growing there were planted at a fairly wide distance from one another, in the shade of the *inocarpus edulis*, whose fruit the inhabitants eat after roasting it; its flavour comes very close to that of chestnuts. In the same ground we also saw several trees of *morinda citrifolia* laden with ripe fruit, which is rather sought after by the natives; they had brought us a great quantity of it during the first days at our anchorage; but its insipid taste had made us reject it.

Having gone on towards the east, we stopped to examine two small huts built within a small enclosure and shaded by fine shaddock trees laden with fruit, and by several trees of *casuarina*. Some islanders told us that the remains of two chiefs of *Toubau*'s family had been laid there. We lifted the mat that closed the entrance of the larger one: the surface of the ground inside was covered with sand, and towards the middle we noticed small rounded pebbles of various colours arranged in an oblong. No doubt out of respect for the dead, none of the inhabitants following us would pick any shaddocks, although we had asked to buy them: they told us they could not sell us any.

We soon returned to *Toubau*'s house, and denounced to him the thief of the forceps. He promised to return them to us the very next day, and he kept his word. The chief urged us to spend the night at his dwelling; but we did not accept his invitation, for fear our absence might cause uneasiness on board.

These people are accustomed to castrate their hogs to make the flesh more delicate. We saw this operation performed on a very young pig, which one islander laid on its back after tying its legs, while another opened the scrotum with the edge of a piece of bamboo and removed the testicles, separating the adhering parts with all the skill of an anatomist.

*Toubau* had us served with fowls grilled on the embers, yams, bananas and bread-fruit baked in the ashes, and we were given coconut milk to drink.

Three of the chief's daughters came to keep us company. They talked a great deal, and although we were pressed by hunger they did not scruple to interrupt us often, obliging us to answer their questions, which turned chiefly on the customs of the French, and in particular on those of the women. As they saw our sailors address themselves to each of them without distinction, they eagerly asked us whether in France the women were not *tabou*, that is to say, whether they enjoyed the same liberty as most of those on their island. The answer by which we tried to acquaint them with our customs pleased them infinitely. They told us that the *egui* of Tongatapu (the chiefs) had several wives, and they asked us how many the French *egui* usually had; but they burst out laughing when they learnt that they had only one. We had great difficulty in persuading them that the same was true of the *egui laï* (the kings) of Europe, which did not give them a high idea of their power.

Of all the articles we offered the women as presents, scented waters were preferred. They appeared to us as passionately fond of perfumes as most of the inhabitants of hot climates, and yet their bodies were partly covered with coconut oil, which gave off a disagreeable smell.

One of the most beautiful girls of this gathering had the little finger of her left hand wrapped in cloth of paper-mulberry bark stained with blood; we asked to see her wound. At once another girl took down from the roof under which we sat a piece of banana leaf, from which she drew the first two joints of this young girl's little finger, which had been cut off fairly recently with the purpose, she told us, of curing her of a serious illness. She showed us the axe of volcanic stone that had been used for the operation, and told us that its edge had first been laid on the end of the third joint of the finger, and that the axe had then been struck hard with the handle of another.

The young person soon went away; but before leaving she gave a kiss to *Toubau*'s daughters after the manner of the inhabitants of the Friendly Islands, which consists in touching with the tip of one's nose the nose of the person one embraces. It is worth noting that these islanders, who rather resemble Europeans, nevertheless have the tip of the nose a little flattened; this slight deformity might well be due to the custom I have just mentioned.

*Toubau*'s daughters exchanged names with us, a custom established among these people as a token of affection; then they played on bamboo flutes an extremely monotonous duet; but we were much amused to see them blowing with the nose through a hole made at the end of these instruments to draw sounds from them. They gave us as presents some combs of a very elegant shape, which may be seen in *pl.* 32, *fig.* 21.

The inhabitants who formed a circle around us having stolen several of our belongings, we complained of it to *Toubau*'s daughters, who shortly afterwards left us without saying anything, probably to go and find their father and beg him to come and put a stop to these thefts; but as we had not time to wait for their return, we soon made our way towards the island of Pangaimotu. The tide being very low, we crossed easily over the shoals that join the islets to the main island. Half-way we stopped at a dwelling where we witnessed the rather amusing way in which a woman was taking her meal. Sitting near a pillar, motionless as a statue, she opened her mouth from time to time to receive the pieces of bread-fruit which another woman put into it. We were told that she was not allowed to touch any kind of food, because she had washed the body of a chief who had died a few days before.

When we reached Pangaimotu, Queen *Tiné*, seated under a shed thatched with coconut leaves and built in the shade of several fine bread-fruit trees, was giving a feast for General Dentrecasteaux. First she ordered some young people of her train to dance, which they at once did with infinite grace; at the same time they sang, while *Fatafé*, who was standing, directed their movements and animated them with voice and gesture *(see plate 27)*.

We then had a grand concert, which differed little from the one we had heard a few days before at the king's; but here the expression of joy was much livelier.

The queen was surrounded by women, while a great number of men stood a short distance away facing her, forming a circle round the musicians.

As soon as the women had stopped dancing, several men rose, each holding in his hand a small club shaped roughly like a paddle, which they brandished in time with the measure with great precision, making various movements with their feet. The musicians, after singing airs whose measure was very slow, sang others in a quick measure, which gave this kind of pyrrhic dance a very spirited action that we admired for a long time. The subject of this dance greatly excited our curiosity; but we soon learnt that its purpose was to celebrate the great deeds of some of their warriors. From time to time the women mingled their voices with those of the men, accompanying their singing with movements full of grace.

One of the armourers of the Espérance was rather surprised to see among these dancers, and at no great distance from *Fatafé*, the islander who had stolen his sabre, the chief having always assured us that he had been unable to discover the thief. It appeared to us, however, that the man was one of his retinue; he withdrew in haste as soon as he perceived that he had been recognised.

Meanwhile some islanders had raised a pyramid of bamboos to which they had tied various fruits, which *Tiné* presented to the General.

We showed a great wish to see some of these people wrestle; but it was pointed out to us that this kind of spectacle was never given in the presence of the queen.

This feast had drawn a great concourse of natives, among whom many thieves had slipped in, whose impudence only increased. They had already taken several articles by force from some of us and had fled with them into the woods.

We were gathered together, more than thirty of us, and were quenching our thirst with the delicious milk of the coconuts that *Tiné* had just given the General, when an islander had the audacity to snatch a knife out of the hands of one of us: indignant at such effrontery, several at once ran after the thief and pursued him as far as the island of Tongatapu; but seeing themselves surrounded by a great number of the inhabitants, they soon came back towards our anchorage; the blacksmith of the Recherche, however, a German by birth, thought fit to show more courage than the others by venturing farther and farther into the midst of the islanders. Soon they turned to face him, pursued him in their turn as soon as they saw him retracing his steps, and even tried to strike him with their clubs, but he held them off for a long time by levelling at the boldest of them a wretched pistol which he tried several times to fire. Being now only about seven hundred metres from our ships, he believed himself entirely safe from any attempt on their part, when one of them split his head open with a blow of a club, while another hurled an assegai into his back; then they fell upon him in great numbers and beat him until they believed him dead. One of them had tried several times to kill him with his pistol, of which he had taken possession; but fortunately the priming had been lost. They were already sharing out his clothes when this was perceived from the Espérance, whence a cannon was at once fired, the ball of which passed very close to the murderers and quickly scattered them. People ran from every side to the help of the unfortunate smith. A man of the crew, having gone forward along the beach to help him, was attacked by an islander who broke two of his teeth with his club; but the islander paid for this outrage with his life, for he was killed on the spot by a musket shot. Our smith was soon lifted up, and although he had a large opening in the left frontal sinus and some other very dangerous wounds, he still had the courage to walk back on board, supported only by the arms.

A few rounds of grape-shot were fired to protect those of us who were ashore. The natives fled in every direction, gathering in very numerous groups at various points of the island; a well-armed detachment was sent to try to disperse them and to bring back the members of our expedition who were still inland.

Several chiefs gathered with some of us close to our market were already rising to go away; but they yielded to the invitations made to them not to leave the spot.

Soon we saw an armed longboat arriving from the Espérance, commanded by Trobriant, first lieutenant of that frigate. Knowing little of the cause of the alarm, and believing that all the natives were ready to fall upon us, he ordered his detachment to seize a double canoe just as it was coming in to the shore, unaware of the events that had just taken place. Most of the natives who manned it at once threw themselves into the sea; but as the chief to whom it belonged remained on the platform, Trobriant sent a man of the crew to seize him. The sailor having tried to strike the native with a club, the native disarmed him and at once took hold of it; they then grappled with each other, and Trobriant thought fit to fire at the islander, whom he killed with a musket shot. We were all exceedingly grieved by this misfortune.

Another inhabitant, a witness of this crime, flung himself into the sea from the top of the canoe's mast, not daring to come down on to the platform. At once a Negro whom we had taken on board at Amboyna pursued him with a pike he held in his hand, but fortunately did not reach him.

The fury of these barbarians was not yet sated. A soldier, a German by birth, whom we had also had with us since leaving Amboyna, catching sight of the unfortunate chief's daughter, who had hidden in the bottom of the canoe, had already raised his sabre to cut her throat when a gunner of the Recherche (Citizen Avignon) stayed the arm of this madman. He placed himself between him and the poor girl, whose mother soon regained the shore, in tears at the loss of her husband. The young girl wept bitterly for her father, and we saw them strike their cheeks and breasts hard with their fists.

We kept as hostages the king's son and *Titifa*, chief of the island of Pangaimotu; but we all noticed with extreme pain the dejection into which this detention threw the king's son, whom we had so often seen commanding his father's subjects with such pride. He repeated to us often that he was our friend and that he wished to follow us to France. *Titifa*, on the contrary, showed not the slightest fear.

These two chiefs spent the night in the great cabin of the Recherche. Each had brought a wooden pillow of the shape of the one shown in *plate* 33, *fig.* 35, on which, after lying down, they rested the back of the head, according to the custom of these people, which is no doubt the cause of the very noticeable flattening to be observed there.

During the night we saw on the north coast of Tongatapu a greater number of fires than we had seen before.

1793-04-04.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 159-162]
The next day, at the first light of dawn, we were woken by the piercing cries of two women who were lamenting as they paddled their canoe round our ship. They cried out by turns, one after the other, no doubt so that their voices might be told apart, and *Titifa* recognized them at once: they were his wife and his daughter, who in their grief were beating their cheeks and breasts with their fists. He immediately ran up on deck, and only succeeded in calming them after telling them of the good treatment he had met with on board; but they were transported with joy when he announced that he would shortly be going ashore. Soon afterwards he embarked in our longboat with the son of King *Toubau*, and we took them both to the island of Pangaimotu. *Titifa*'s wife and daughter were following us in their canoe when, as they passed close by the Espérance, a swivel-gun went off of its own accord and shattered their little craft; they were then obliged to abandon it, for it was going to the bottom. We took them into our longboat and let them see how much we were grieved by this accident; but they very soon forgot the danger they had run. They sat beside *Titifa*, thinking of nothing but the pleasure of seeing him set at liberty again. We made them a present of hardware, among which a hatchet gave them the greatest joy. *Titifa* told us that it would serve him to build another canoe, and that he would not be long in making good the loss he had just suffered.

When we landed on the shore, most of the natives moved away from it and withdrew into the interior of the island; but *Titifa* persuaded them to come back and ordered them to form a circle, which they did at once. The bartering then began again in the best possible order. This chief would not leave us during all that time; but the son of *Toubau* disappeared as soon as he had reached the beach. It seemed to us that the chief who had been killed the day before by Trobriant was much loved by these islanders, for several of them showed great feeling, weeping over his loss.

For fear that they might seek to take reprisals against us, the General ordered everyone in the expedition to remain within the enclosure where the bartering was carried on.

Our ships were sufficiently supplied with all the provisions these islanders could furnish us. As there was no longer anything to fear from the consequences of competition, hardware was distributed among the crews so that they might obtain a few articles for themselves; but the natives then raised their goods to a very high price (often ten times that at which they had sold them before).

We saw in their hands an iron *fish-hook* which they had had the skill to fashion like those they make of bone, pieces of tortoise-shell, mother-of-pearl and other animal substances, the shape of which may be seen in *pl.* 32, *fig.* 27 and 28. The line to the end of which they had fastened it was no doubt intended for fishing at great depths, for they had tied to it a fairly large piece of alabaster cut into a cone *(see pl. 32, fig. 25 and 26)*.

*Titifa* and several other chiefs were not without uneasiness about the hostile designs of some of the islanders towards us. They told us of their fears and urged us to return on board before the end of the day, having no doubt not enough authority over them to hold them in check.

As night drew on, we perceived that the chains of our rudder had been carried off.

1793-04-05.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 162-163]
We noticed on shore a great many young girls who had had their hair cut to the length of a third of a decimetre, except for that round the edge of the head; they had then powdered it with lime, with the intention, we were told, of turning it fair. We saw several others whose hair was already of that colour.

Most of the women never stopped asking us for rings and glass beads, with which they adorned themselves as soon as they had received them. They always accompanied their requests with a gracious smile, at the same time bending the head and laying one hand on the breast, as may be seen in *pl.* 30, *fig.* 1.

*Titifa* brought us some nutmegs whose nuts were fairly round and twice as large as those of the cultivated nutmeg tree, but they were not in the least aromatic; their husk was covered with a rather thick down. The natives, seeing that we had received these with pleasure, were not long in bringing us more.

These people have invented a kind of Pan-pipe which differs from that of Europe only in the proportion of its notes; all the pipes give full tones of small compass, and the highest forms a fourth with the lowest; we bought several of these pipes.

I obtained from the commander of our expedition a place on the larboard quarter-gallery and a large box in which to put young bread-fruit plants, so as to enrich our colonies with so useful a vegetable. Some natives procured me a great number of suckers, which I planted in some very good mould that they brought me, calling it *kelé kelé*. I also took roots and pieces of the stem of this precious tree, which I buried in clay (*oummea* in their language), laying them horizontally. These pieces were so many cuttings, which I intended to plant on our arrival at the Isle of France [Mauritius].

1793-04-06.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 163-168]
Queen *Tiné* came on board at the moment when *Finau* was in the cabin of the General, to whom he had brought as a present a diadem made of the fine feathers of the red-tailed tropic-bird, together with other very small feathers of a brilliant red. When he came out to go home he tried to slip away out of the queen's sight, but as soon as she saw him she made him come near and held out her right foot to him; he at once took it and set it on the back of his head, bowing low, as if to give this queen a token of the respect he owed her. He dared not refuse her these honours, although it seemed to us that he was much mortified by them. The General had just made him a present of several iron tools, and we saw with pleasure that he seemed to know the value of this metal, giving it a very marked preference over the volcanic stones and the bones of which most of these islanders' hatchets are made.

We were then visited by various chiefs, who repeated to us what several others had already explained concerning the reigning family. For this purpose they made use of playing cards with which we supplied them; first they laid them out on a table, then they gave each one the name of one of the members of that family; and it did not appear to us, as Captain Cook supposed, that the family had a particular name (that of *Fatafé*, now borne by the son of *Poulao*), for the father of *Poulao* was called *Taïbouloutou*; he married a woman named *Toubau-Nou*, by whom he had four children, namely two sons, one called *Poulao*, who succeeded his father, and the other *Fatafé*, and two daughters, one named *Tiné* and the other *Nanatchi*. When *Poulao* died he left a very young son named *Fatafé*; the king's brother then took the reins of government, but he died soon afterwards and the sovereignty passed to *Tiné*, his elder sister; she had all its honours without, however, exercising its power, with which it seems that women cannot be invested; the authority passed into the hands of a chief named *Toubau*, the brother of *Tiné*'s mother. This queen had married *Ovea*, one of the chiefs of Tofua, and he had put her away after having had two sons by her, namely *Veaïcou* and *Veatchi*.

It appears, then, that the succession to the throne passes to the brothers and sisters before falling to the children of the princes who have reigned, and that when women are invested with the sovereignty, the exercise of authority is entrusted to one of the nearest relations of their mother, but only for the lifetime of the queen. The family of the *Toubau* will keep the power during the reign of *Tiné*, and *Fatafé*, the son of *Poulao*, will not ascend the throne until after the death of his two aunts. The royal family, though thus stripped of power for the time being, nonetheless enjoyed its honours and received the homage even of those who exercised the authority, as we observed on several occasions.

*Vouacécé*, one of the chiefs of Fiji, had arrived at Tongatapu shortly after we had dropped anchor. We very often received visits from him, and he confirmed what he had told us several times, that it took him three days' sailing in his double canoe, with the winds from the south-east, to reach Fiji, whose position he showed us to lie towards the north-west; we therefore supposed that this island, which is very high and whose fertility he praised to us, was about seventy-two myriametres distant from Tongatapu. This is an immense passage for peoples who, having no instrument of observation, steer only by the sight of the stars once they have lost sight of land; but it is still more difficult to conceive how they can reach Tongatapu from so great a distance when they have to struggle against the south-east winds, and they must be very sure of their landmarks in the sky not to miss their landfall, for they are sometimes obliged to beat to windward for more than a month.

The inhabitants of Tongatapu told us that all the natives of Fiji were cannibals; but *Vouacécé* tried to clear himself of this charge by assuring us that only people of the common class (the *toua*) ate human flesh; nevertheless it appeared to us, from what we learned elsewhere, that the chiefs eat it too: indeed, as these peoples devour only their enemies, and commit this atrocity only to glut their fury, it is to be believed that the natives of Tongatapu were not deceiving us when they assured us that at Fiji even the chiefs were cannibals.

It will no doubt be seen with astonishment that, in spite of this ferocious character, the arts are much further advanced at Fiji than in the Friendly Islands, where the inhabitants never failed to tell us that the finest things they sold us came from Fiji, and they made a point of letting us know that these articles were very markedly superior to those they made themselves.

*Vouacécé* showed us much more desire to learn than any inhabitant of the Friendly Islands, most of whom were drawn to us only by motives of self-interest. He examined every part of our ship with the greatest care. This islander was very tall and finely made, and had a very strongly marked cast of features, *see pl. 29, fig. 2*. The hair on the front of his head was powdered red.

The natives of Fiji are often at war with those of Tongatapu; but as soon as hostilities are over, a very great trade is carried on between them.

The General received from *Fatafé* the present of a small outrigger canoe, newly built, which was at once placed near the main chains. It was three metres long and three decimetres wide, and could carry only two people. Canoes of this kind are decked over for about a fifth of their length at each end, which is enough for sailing safely among the reefs; but their double canoes, being intended to sail on the open sea, are decked over along their whole length, except towards the middle, where a small opening has been left through which to go down and bale them out when water has collected in them. I saw with admiration that these peoples had consulted nature in order to build swift-sailing canoes. The bottom fairly closely imitated the shape of the underside of one of the cetaceans that swim with the greatest speed, leaping in bounds along the surface of the water (the *delphinus delphis*).

1793-04-07.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 168-170]
King *Toubau*, having learned that we were soon to leave his island, came to urge us to put off our departure, and he seemed much grieved by our decision.

The natives no doubt thought that we meant to lay in a large store of bread-fruit, for they brought far more of it to our market than usual; but these fruits would have kept only a very few days without rotting, unless we had dried them after cutting them into slices, or had them fermented in the manner of the natives, much as is done in Europe with various kinds of vegetables. Ever since we had been at the anchorage we had had it in sufficient abundance to supply our daily needs. We ate it with pleasure, and gave up without regret our biscuit and even the small ration of fresh bread that it was customary to serve out to us every day, good though its quality was. We found these fruits much preferable to yams; the natives, however, who came to dine with us ate the one and the other without much distinction. Our cook usually served them to us boiled in water, although they would have been much better if he had taken the trouble to bake them in the oven.

These fruits are of a roughly oval shape, three decimetres long by two thick. The whole of them is eatable, except the extremely thin skin with which they are covered and a very small part situated at the centre, where the cells meet; these contain no seeds, but on the other hand they are filled with a very nourishing pulp, easy to digest, of a rather pleasant taste, which we always ate with fresh pleasure.

For eight months of the year the bread-fruit tree yields fruits which, ripening one after another, thus furnish the islanders every day with food as wholesome as it is plentiful. I shall not give its description here, because it has already been published by able botanists. The failure of the seeds no doubt comes from the practice of propagating it by suckers, and in this respect it differs remarkably from the wild species, whose fruits are much smaller, few in number, and filled with large kernels which are rather hard to digest.

The natives brought us a few pieces of sandalwood, and to make its scent stronger they took care to rub it hard with a rasp of ray-skin, which may be seen in *pl. 32, fig. 24*. They told us that they got it from Fiji, and so they call it *haï-fidgi*. They informed us that they had tried several times, but always in vain, to carry plants of it over to their island.

The canoes that surrounded our ships went back at nightfall towards the nearest shore, as they usually did, and our sailors were always much amused when the young girls who had found means of slipping into the between-decks gave them notice of their departure by calling out to them in a loud voice the following words: *bongui bongui, mitzi mitzi*. I shall not permit myself to give the literal translation of them, but it will be seen from the vocabulary of the language of these peoples, which is to be found towards the end of this volume, that these young girls were not afraid to make known what had passed between them and the men of our crew, by announcing to them that they would begin again the next day.

1793-04-08.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 170-178]
The following day several chiefs came to see us early in the morning and announced to the inhabitants, who were already gathered in their canoes round our ship, that we were about to leave their island; but we were much surprised to see a great number of young women at once burst into tears, uttering piercing cries. Their affliction was no doubt very keen, but it was short-lived; for soon afterwards we saw them making merry with their companions.

*Fatafé* asked us to have two hatchets sharpened for him, which had been given him by Captain Cook and which he had had forged anew on board the Espérance. This chief was accompanied by his wife, who amused herself for a long time playing with a kind of cup-and-ball of these islanders' invention; the object was to pass through a very small half-circle of tortoise-shell a wooden ball which she tossed into the air and which was attached to the instrument by a long string. We were admiring her skill when *Fatafé*, furious with jealousy at seeing in her hands some presents she had just received from an officer of our ship, ill-used her, and although his suspicions were groundless, she had great difficulty in bringing him to see his mistake. This chief was with his father-in-law. We made them a few presents just as the son of King *Toubau* arrived: they instantly hid them in their girdles; but *Toubau* noticed it, and we soon had fresh proof that, if the royal family enjoys the honorific rights of sovereignty, the family of *Toubau* has all the profit of it. *Toubau* searched the girdles of these two chiefs and seized everything they had just received. *Fatafé* had no other means of revenge than to prevent him from eating in his presence, not to let him sit down beside him, and to set his foot on his head; accordingly he held it out to him soon afterwards, and the other paid him the homage due to persons of superior rank.

We had many times seen the chiefs openly seize articles belonging to common people, and we always observed with astonishment that this kind of oppression in no way weakened the unalterable gaiety of their character: when they were gathered together, great bursts of laughter could be heard from them every moment. Their government seemed to us, as it did to Captain Cook, to bear a strong resemblance to the feudal system.

Several natives asked to embark with us and follow us all the way to France. Captain Huon granted a place on the frigate Espérance to *Kové*, one of the queen's sons. This chief, meaning to prove to us that he was drawn only by the pleasure of accompanying us, would accept none of the articles we offered him. The General, whom he came to see, set before him the chief hardships attending long voyages; but he still held to his resolution and went on board the Espérance: at dinner-time, however, several inhabitants came to urge him to go ashore, to see his family at least once more before undertaking so long a voyage. He yielded to their entreaties and never came back on board. Some of the inhabitants told us that he had been unable to resist the tears and prayers of nine wives and a great number of children whom he was about to abandon, perhaps never to see them again. He had just promised them not to leave them. *Kové* had a handsome face, but he had not the gaiety of the other islanders. Perhaps some domestic sorrows had been one of the principal causes of his wish to go far from his native land. Had he carried out his intention, reduced like us to eating worm-eaten biscuit, he would many a time have regretted the delicious fruits of his island.

Towards nightfall we sent up a dozen rockets, and at once we heard the shouts of a great number of inhabitants, echoed from different points along the sea-shore.

Our stay in the Friendly Islands did much towards restoring the health of the crews. We had found an abundance of vegetables there, and we laid in a very large supply of them. The pork there was excellent, which must be attributed in part to the good quality of the roots and fruits on which the inhabitants feed these animals; we shipped as many of them as our pen could hold, and we were afterwards convinced that they could bear a long voyage, although Captain Cook asserts that he found the contrary with those he had obtained in the Friendly Islands at the various calls he made there. During our stay we had bought more than four hundred of them, the greater part of which we had salted. The method recommended by Cook in his third voyage had been followed, which consists in using a strong brine into which is put the quantity of vinegar needed to dissolve the sea-salt. This was all the easier for us because a good part of our wine had turned sour.

Our butcher salted a small quantity of pork using sea-salt alone, and although we were in the torrid zone, it was preserved from corruption just as well as that which had been prepared in the manner indicated by Cook, and we even found it better tasting. The fat bacon kept in the vinegared brine was disgusting from its extreme softness, and it had a very strong taste of vinegar which pleased nobody.

Our coops were full of poultry.

During the whole time of our stay at the anchorage the mercury in the barometer had not risen above 28^p 2^l, and its variation had been about 1^l.

The thermometer, observed in the shade on shore, had not shown more than 25° 4/10, although we had experienced excessive heat there. The winds had blown from south-east to north-east, and had been rather light.

The site of our observatory was in latitude 21° 8' 19" south, and longitude 182° 29' 38" east.

The variation of the compass needle there was 10° east.

The sea rises a metre and a half perpendicular at spring tides, and high water at full and change occurs at about half past six.

The information given us by some very intelligent islanders about the ships that had anchored in this archipelago showed us that La Pérouse had not put in at any of these islands. Moreover, they assured us that no unfortunate accident had befallen the vessels that had stopped there, except Bligh's launch, the incident of which they had related to us without concealment, as I said above. The coolness with which they told us of it proved to us that, if these peoples are not naturally ferocious, at least the feelings of humanity are foreign to them. The blows with sticks and clubs with which the chiefs usually accompanied their orders furnish yet another proof of this. They remembered very well the different times at which they had seen Captain Cook, and to let us know the intervals between them they counted by crops of yams, reckoning two to each year. Several natives, and especially those connected with the royal family, spoke the name of Cook with enthusiasm; but the great severity of that celebrated navigator had prevented many others from keeping so pleasant a memory of him; they spoke of him only to complain of the harsh treatment he had made them suffer. Indeed, although mention is made in his last voyage of only one man wounded in the thigh by a musket-shot, we saw another whose shoulder had been pierced by a ball, and he assured us that he had received this wound during Cook's last stay at Tongatapu.

The inhabitants of the Friendly Islands are in general tall and well made, which they no doubt owe chiefly to the abundance and good quality of their food. The fine shape of these islanders is not spoiled by hard labour. Their muscles being very pronounced, we supposed them to be very robust; but the idle life they lead makes them little capable of great exertions; and so, when they tried their strength against our sailors, they almost always had the worst of it.

Like the women, they have the custom of cutting off one or two joints of the little finger, and sometimes of the ring finger, in the hope of curing themselves of serious illnesses. Most of them are tattooed on every part of the body. We saw a great many whose skin was covered with a scaly eruption; this disease comes perhaps from their not being in the habit of drying themselves, nor of washing in fresh water after bathing in the sea.

We noticed no symptom of venereal disease among these islanders; one of our sailors, however, caught the gonorrhoea there, but from a woman who had had intercourse with a man from the Espérance long infected with that disease. Could these peoples be so fortunate that this contagion, after running rapidly through its stages, had died out of itself among them? for there can be no doubt, from the testimony of Captain Cook, that it once made great ravages there.

The natives of the Friendly Islands have a swarthy skin because they very often expose themselves to the heat of the sun; but the women, who keep fairly constantly within their dwellings or in the shade of the trees, have a very fair complexion. They have, in general, very pleasing and lively features. The good health they enjoy is due in particular to their extreme cleanliness and to the good quality of the food on which they live.

1793-04-09.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 178-179]
## CHAPTER XIII.

*Departure from Tongatapu. View of the southern part of the Archipelago of Espiritu Santo. Discovery of the island of Beaupré. Anchorage at New Caledonia. Meetings with the natives. Description of their huts. These savages are cannibals. Their impudence towards us. They eat large pieces of steatite to appease their hunger. Their attempts to seize our boats. Various excursions into the interior of the island. Death of Captain Huon. New species of spider on which the savages of New Caledonia feed.*

We spread our sails at about seven in the morning and, driven by a fairly fresh east-south-east wind, we steered for an hour north-west by north to north, and then north by east, going out through a passage that had been surveyed to the north of our anchorage by Citizen Legrand.

On this run the lead gave us from eleven to eighteen metres of depth.

Some natives followed us in their canoes, showing us their keen regret at seeing us leave their island; they called out to us from every side *offa, offa Palançois*, giving us tokens of their affection.

We soon passed the canoes that were driven only by paddles, but those under sail were obliged to slacken their pace in order to keep a short distance from us, and we had occasion to observe that their speed was much greater than that of our ships when they chose to make use of the full strength of the wind; they would, however, very quickly have lost this advantage had the wind been stronger and the sea rougher. They stopped following us as soon as we had reached the open sea. We were then more than a myriametre from the anchorage we had just left, and the western end of *Attata* bore south 48° west.

At the same moment a line of forty-five metres gave us a gravel bottom.

1793-04-10.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 179]
The next day, at about five in the evening, we saw Turtle Island to the north-west by north.

1793-04-15.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 179-180]
The Espérance signalled land on the 27th at about seven in the morning, west 18° north, at a distance of about four myriametres. It was Erronan, the most easterly of the islands of the Archipelago of Espiritu Santo, discovered by Quiros in 1606. A little before noon we sighted Annaton south-west by south, five myriametres off.

It was already five in the evening when we saw the island of Tanna, west 16° north. Columns of smoke were issuing from its volcano and spreading far through the air, forming clouds which at first rose to a prodigious height and which, after travelling an immense distance, sank lower as they cooled. During the night we enjoyed the brilliant spectacle of these clouds lit up by the vivid glow of the burning matter hurled out at intervals from the depths of the volcano's abyss.

1793-04-17.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 180-182]
We were running west with a very fresh east wind when, at about half past three in the morning, the officer of the watch (Dumérite) heard the cries of a flock of sea-birds passing very close to our ship. Fearing that we might be in the neighbourhood of the rocks which usually serve them as a retreat, he decided to heave to and wait for daylight before continuing on our course; but at dawn we sighted, a short distance to leeward, a great extent of reefs on which our ship would have been wrecked had not this chance occurrence warned us to stop her way. Indeed it would have been impossible, on an extremely dark night, to make out the breakers soon enough to avoid them; besides, it was blowing a strong gale, and the waves were running so high on every side that those breaking on these reefs could not have been distinguished in time. Beyond the reefs we first saw, to the south 28° west, an island lying nearly a myriametre from them, to which I have given the name of Citizen Beaupré, geographical engineer of our expedition. It lies in latitude 20° 14' south, and longitude 163° 47' east. It is very low and about three kilometres long. We then discovered some rocks to the south 21° east, and soon afterwards we sighted others towards the south.

It is worth noting that the currents set us to the north by about twenty-four minutes a day when we were near the lands of Espiritu Santo and while we were making the passage that separates them from New Caledonia. This no doubt depends on the position of these lands, which, by changing the direction of the currents produced by the prevailing winds, increases their strength.

At about one in the afternoon we sighted to the south-west the high mountains of New Caledonia, and at half past four we were two kilometres from the reefs that border this island. Here the foot of its mountains is washed by the sea, and they are even steeper than in the western part, along which we had sailed a year before.

We could see a fine waterfall whose waters, after disappearing several times into deep ravines, came plunging down into the sea, and we admired the picturesque effect of the torrents we could make out towards the south-west: their foaming white waters made a pleasing contrast with the dark green of these high lands.

We stood off and on all night, trying to hold our own against the currents so as to be in a position to anchor the next day.

1793-04-18.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 182-183]
As soon as day broke we stood in to within a kilometre and a half of the reefs, and ran along them in order to make out the passage by which we were to enter to reach the anchorage; but it was blowing a strong gale from the south-south-east, and we had already fallen to leeward by the time we distinguished the break in the reefs; although we were fairly close to the coast we could not see Observatory Island, which left us uncertain for some time whether we were opposite the anchorage where Captain Cook had dropped anchor in 1774; we therefore went about to work up to the north-east. But towards the middle of the day our observations left us no further doubt that we were near Observatory Island, and we soon sighted it, although it is extremely low; we then made sail for the anchorage. The lead gave us from twenty to twenty-five metres of depth in the gap between the reefs, and once we were between them and the coast we found no more than from thirteen to sixteen metres.

A double canoe at once made sail and headed towards us. It was manned by eleven natives, who handled it in a way that did not give us a high opinion of their knowledge of the art of navigation. They called out to us and showed us some pieces of white cloth, which they waved, keeping all the while more than two hundred metres from our ship. Soon afterwards they went back towards the coast.

The Espérance, which was a little to windward of us, ran aground on a shoal; we immediately manoeuvred so as to avoid the same danger, and anchored shortly afterwards in order to give assistance to that frigate. General Dentrecasteaux at once sent our longboat to her, and by eight in the evening we had the welcome news that she had suffered no damage and was afloat again.

1793-04-19.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 183-204]
The next day, at sunrise, four canoes were under sail and making towards our ships: they showed some fear when they were very close to them. However, one of the savages who manned them yielded to our invitations and came on board, and was followed by almost all the others. We were surprised that they set more store by our cloth than by nails and even hatchets, which they called *togui*, much as the inhabitants of the Friendly Islands do, although they did not speak the same language, as may be seen from the vocabulary of the language of these peoples, which is to be found towards the end of this volume. We could not doubt, however, that they knew iron, which they called by the name of *pitiou*; but the very hard stones they use make it less useful to them than to many other islanders of the South Sea.

We showed them coconuts and yams, urging them to bring us some; but far from going to fetch us any, they wanted to buy ours, and offered us their spears and clubs in exchange, letting us know that they were very hungry by pointing with the hand to their bellies, which were extremely flat. They showed fear at the sight of the pigs we had on board, which led us to suppose that they did not possess this quadruped, although Captain Cook had left two of them (a male and a female) with one of their chiefs; but as soon as they caught sight of our poultry, they imitated the crowing of the cock well enough to leave us no doubt that they had fowls on their island.

None of the women who were in these canoes would consent to come on board our ship, and when we wished to make them a present of any articles, the men undertook to carry them to them.

These savages had come in double canoes of the shape of the one represented in *plate* 44, *fig.* 1. Their mast was fixed at an equal distance from the two canoes, towards the fore end of the platform by which they are joined to each other. They are not built with so much art as those of the Friendly Islands, and they are very far from sailing so fast. There was one of them one side of which, striking hard against our ship, was so badly damaged that it sank in a very short time. The savages who manned it at once took refuge on the other hull and let themselves drift with the current, which carried them towards the land. The other canoes left us soon afterwards and made for this one to help it.

Very early in the morning we hove round the capstan to warp ourselves towards Observatory Island by means of several hawsers fastened end to end; but they parted several times and obliged us to let the anchor go again.

We were surrounded by canoes paddled by natives, who came up on our ship and sold us several of their articles, which may be seen in *plates* 37 and 38. Some of them had brought a small number of coconuts and sugar-canes, which they would never part with, although we offered them a high price.

These savages were quite naked, but they had the penis wrapped, some in pieces of coarse cloth made of bark, others in large leaves of trees. Their hair is woolly. The black colour of their skin is almost as dark as that of the natives of the cap de Diemen, whose cast of features closely resembles theirs *(see pl. 35)*. Several had their heads bound round with a small net of wide mesh. We saw with surprise a great many who, no doubt wishing to appear to have very long hair, had fastened to it two or three tresses made of the leaves of grasses covered with the fur of the bat called *vespertilio vampyrus*, which hung down to the middle of their backs.

Most of these islanders, armed with spears and clubs, carried at the girdle a little bag filled with stones cut into an oval shape, which they hurl with their slings *(see plates* 35 and 38, *fig.* 16, 17 and 18*)*. The lower lobe of their ears, pierced with a very large hole, came down to their shoulders; some had put leaves into it, others a piece of wood to enlarge it still further. Several had this same lobe cut into strips; it had probably been torn in this way in fighting or in running through the forests.

We noticed behind the ears of one of these savages some swellings of the shape of a calf's sweetbread, and as large as half a fist. He seemed very pleased to see us examine this ornament. He had made it grow by means of a caustic which had no doubt caused him great irritation for a long time.

The women had no other clothing than a fringe of strands of bark which served them as a girdle, going several times round the body *(see pl. 36)*.

The canoes kept close alongside our ship by means of various ropes we had thrown them. Each of them, however, had for an anchor a very large stone tied to a long rope; but none of them let it go.

The following day we weighed anchor at six in the morning and made several boards to draw nearer to Observatory Island, which the inhabitants know by the name of *Pudyoua*. It was no more than a kilometre from us, east 3° 15' south, when we anchored at about half past

ten. We could see the lands of New Caledonia from east 19° 30' south to west 12° north, the nearest shore being eleven and a half hectometres from our ship. The inhabitants no longer had any need of their canoes to come and see us. Most of them swam out, laden with the articles they wished to sell us.

I think I ought to relate here an act of malice which nearly caused the loss of the young bread-fruit plants I had taken at the Friendly Islands. I had watered them the day before; but seeing early in the morning drops of water falling from the box in which they were planted, I had no doubt that someone had also watered them long after me. I was convinced of it when I tasted the water that was filtering through the earth; it was sea-water. The inquiries I made to discover the culprit were fruitless.

We went ashore at about one in the afternoon, and we were soon surrounded by a great number of inhabitants who had just come out of the woods, into which we made our way several times without going far from the sea-shore. We soon came upon a few isolated huts, three or four hundred paces apart and shaded by a small number of coconut palms. Some time afterwards we found four that formed a small hamlet in one of the darkest spots of the forest; they all had roughly the shape of beehives, three metres high and as many wide *(see in pl.* 38 *fig.* 28, 29 *and* 30*)*.

*Figure* 28 represents one of these huts surrounded by a palisade a metre and a half high, made of the stalks of coconut leaves set very close together and driven into the ground eleven decimetres from the sides of the hut; they also served to form a little alley in front of the door.

We next noticed many huts that were not surrounded by palisades *(see fig.* 29*)*. The door, which was a metre high by half a metre wide, was sometimes closed by means of a piece of coconut leaf with its leaflets interlaced. Several of these doors had two uprights made of planks, at the top of which a man's head had been rather roughly carved. The lower part of the dwellings, raised perpendicularly to the height of a metre, was surmounted by a fairly regular cone ending in the top of a post that rose from the centre of their floor.

*Figure* 30 represents the interior. The framework was made of poles resting on the top of the post which is seen planted in the centre of the floor, and whose base is two thirds of a decimetre thick. A few pieces of wood bent into arches make these little lodges fairly solid. Their covering is of thatch and is about two thirds of a decimetre thick. Mats covered the ground, on which the natives are perfectly sheltered from the inclemency of the weather; but the mosquitoes there are so troublesome that they are obliged to light a fire to drive them away when they wish to sleep; and as the smoke has no outlet but the door, which is very low, they must be extremely inconvenienced by it.

Inside there was usually a plank placed horizontally and tied with cords at a height of nearly a metre against one of the sides of the hut. Only fairly light articles could be laid on it, for its fastenings were very weak.

Near some of these dwellings we observed little mounds of earth three to four decimetres high, surmounted towards the middle by a very open trellis-work two to three metres high; the savages called it *nbouet*, and let us know that it was a burial place: they leaned their heads to one side, supporting them with the hand, then shut their eyes, to express the rest enjoyed by the remains of those who had been laid there.

On returning towards our landing place we found more than seven hundred natives who had come running from all sides. They asked us for cloth and iron in exchange for their articles, and some of them soon proved to us that they were very barefaced thieves. Among their various tricks I shall mention one that two of these rogues played on me. One of them offered to sell me a little bag, containing stones cut into an oval shape, which he wore at his girdle. He at once untied it and pretended to be giving it to me with one hand, while with the other he received the price we had agreed upon; but at that very moment another savage, who had placed himself behind me, gave a loud shout to make me turn my head his way, and the rogue immediately ran off with his bag and my goods, trying to hide himself in the crowd. We did not choose to punish him, although most of us were armed with muskets. It was to be feared, however, that this act of leniency might be regarded by these peoples as a mark of weakness and make them still more insolent. What happened shortly afterwards seems to confirm this. Several of them were bold enough to throw stones at an officer who was only two hundred paces from us. We still did not choose to take severe measures against them; for Forster's account had prejudiced us so favourably towards them that we needed yet further facts to destroy the good opinion we had of the gentleness of their character; but we soon had incontestable proofs of their

ferocity. One of them, holding in his hand a freshly broiled bone and devouring a remnant of flesh still clinging to it, came up to Citizen Piron and invited him to share his meal; Piron, thinking the savage was offering him a piece of some quadruped, accepted the bone, which was now covered only with tendinous parts; and when he showed it to me, I recognized that it belonged to the pelvis of a child of fourteen or fifteen. The natives around us pointed out on a child the position of this bone; they admitted without difficulty that the flesh with which it had been covered had served for some islander's meal, and they even let us know that it was a very dainty dish for them.

This discovery threw us into great anxiety about the fate of the men of the crew who were still in the woods; soon afterwards, however, we had the pleasure of finding ourselves all gathered in the same place, and we no longer feared that any of our people would fall victim to the barbarity of these islanders.

As we were surprised, on reaching our ship, to see no savage on board, we were told that they had come in great numbers, but had been driven off because they had stolen a great many articles. Most of them had fled in their canoes and the others had jumped into the sea to swim for the shore; two of them, however, had come back on board, having been unable to swim fast enough to rejoin the others, either because of some infirmity or because they had thrown themselves into the sea too long after the departure of their canoes to be able to take refuge in them. As the sun had already set and they were cold, they went to warm themselves at our galley fire.

Most of those of our expedition who had stayed on board would not believe the account we gave them of the barbarous taste of these islanders, for they could not persuade themselves that these peoples, of whom Captain Cook and Forster had drawn so favourable a picture, were degraded by so horrible a vice; but it was not difficult to convince the most incredulous. I had brought back the already gnawed bone, which our surgeon-major recognized as that of a child; I held it out to the two inhabitants we had on board; instantly one of these cannibals seized it greedily and tore off with his teeth the ligaments and cartilages still attached to it; I then passed it to his companion, who also found something on it to gnaw.

The various signs that were clumsily made to them in order to get them to admit that they ate their fellow men were the cause of a very great misunderstanding. At once an extreme consternation was painted on all their features; they no doubt believed that we too were cannibals and, imagining that their last hour had come, they began to weep. We did not succeed in reassuring them entirely, in spite of all our efforts to repel this insulting notion. One of them rushed out through a port and held on to one of the chains of the foremast shrouds, ready to throw himself into the sea; the other jumped in and swam off to take refuge in the farthest of the boats we had astern of our ship; they soon, however, recovered from their fright and came back to us.

The stream at which Captain Cook had taken in water on this land was dry at the season when we were there: we found, however, to the south-west of our ship a watering place about three hundred paces from the sea-shore; its water was very pure, but it was not easy to fill, and the pool from which it was drawn yielded only enough to fill, once a day, the casks that the longboat of each ship could carry. We had to wait until the next day for enough to collect to fill them again.

Close by this watering place was found the foot of an iron candlestick eaten away by rust, which had probably been there since 1774, the time when Captain Cook anchored in this roadstead.

The following day we went ashore early in the morning on the nearest part of the coast, where we found some savages already taking their meal; they offered us some freshly broiled meat to eat with them, which we recognized as human flesh; the skin still attached to it kept its shape and even its colour in several places. They showed us that they had cut this slice from the middle of the arm, and they let us know by very expressive signs that, after piercing with their spears the man whose remains we saw in their hands, they had beaten him to death with their clubs. No doubt they meant to give us to understand that they devoured only their enemies; and indeed, how could we have met with so many inhabitants on this land if hunger were the only cause that led them to eat one another?

We made our way to the south-south-west and soon crossed a fairly low tract of ground, where we saw some plantations of yams and sweet potatoes; we then came to the foot of the mountains, where we found ten inhabitants who went along with us. We soon saw them climb trees of the species known by the name of *Hybiscus tiliaceus*, from which they tore the youngest shoots, which they chewed on the spot to press out the mucilage contained in their bark. Others gathered the fruits of the *cordia sebestena*, of which they ate even the stones. We had not expected to see cannibals content themselves with so frugal a meal.

The heat was excessive and we had not yet found any water. We followed a ravine in which we noticed the traces of the torrent that rushes down it in the rainy season; the green of the shrubs we could see farther on along its banks gave us hope of finding there a spring at which to quench our thirst; and indeed, as soon as we had reached it, we saw very clear water welling up at the foot of an enormous sandstone rock, from which it went on to fill a large hollow worn in a block of the same kind of stone. We halted at this spot, and the natives who were with us came and sat down beside us. We gave them some biscuit, which they ate willingly although it was for the most part worm-eaten; but they would not taste our cheese; yet we had no other food to offer them. They preferred the water of the pool to brandy and wine, and drank it in a rather amusing way. With their heads bent seven or eight decimetres above the water, they threw it several times with the hand against their faces, each time opening their mouths wide to catch whatever came to the opening; they had soon quenched their thirst. It will readily be believed that even the most skilful of these drinkers could not help wetting a great part of their bodies. As they were muddying our water, we urged them to go and drink lower down, which they at once did.

Some of them came up to the most robust among us and felt, again and again, the most muscular parts of their arms and legs, uttering *kapareck* with an air of admiration and even of desire, which was not too reassuring for us; they gave us, however, no cause for displeasure.

In these parts I noticed many plants belonging to the same genera as a great number of others I had already collected in New Holland, although the distance separating these two lands is very considerable.

We saw with surprise, about a third of the way up the mountain, little walls built by the natives one above another to stop the slipping of the soil they cultivate. I have found this practice extremely widespread among the inhabitants of the mountains of Asia Minor.

It is not a general custom among the savages of New Caledonia to make an incision in the prepuce; however, among six of them who were willing to satisfy our curiosity, we noticed one who had it slit lengthwise in its upper part.

As soon as we had reached the middle of the mountain, the natives who were following us urged us to go no farther, and warned us that the inhabitants of the other side of this range would eat us. We nevertheless went on climbing to the summit, for we were well enough armed not to fear these cannibals. No doubt those who were with us were at war with them, for they would not follow us any farther.

The mountains we climbed rise in an amphitheatre and are a continuation of the great chain that runs through the island along its whole length. Their perpendicular height is about eight hundred metres above sea level. We could see them rising gradually towards the east-south-east and stretching as far as a very high mountain about six myriametres from our anchorage.

The chief components of these great masses are quartz, mica, a steatite of greater or lesser hardness, green schorl, garnets, specular iron ore, etc.

On returning to the foot of these mountains, we halted among some families of savages gathered near their huts, and we showed several of them that we were very eager to quench our thirst with coconut water; but as these fruits are few in this part of their island, they held a council for a fairly long time before making up their minds to sell us any. At length one of them went to pick a few from the top of one of the tallest coconut palms and bring them to us; we were extremely surprised at the speed with which he climbed. Holding the trunk of the tree with his hands, he ran up its whole length almost as easily and as quickly as if he had been walking on level ground. I had never had occasion to admire such agility among the other islanders we had visited until then.

The sea often washed the foot of the coconut palm whose fruits we had just received, and so they were full of a rather acrid liquid, which we drank nonetheless, for we were very thirsty. The children of these savages watched for the moment when we had emptied the coconuts of their water to ask us for them, still finding a way of making use of them. They tore off with their teeth the fibrous husk of these young fruits, whose nut was not yet formed, and then ate the tender part it enclosed, which was too harsh for us to put up with.

We learned on reaching the ship that in the morning two islanders had carried off a forage cap and a sword from an officer of our ship (Bonvouloir) while he was busy on the beach making astronomical observations. The men of the crew who had gone ashore with him had, however, traced a very large circle in the sand around the place of observation, and had forbidden these savages to enter it. But two thieves, having concerted their scheme, rushed up behind this officer, who had just put his sword under him after sitting down; at once one of them seized his cap, and the moment he got up to chase him, the other carried off his sword. This bold trick was no doubt not their first attempt.

Night was coming on, all our boats were already alongside, and yet two officers (Dewelle and Willaumez) were still ashore with two men of the crew; but they soon arrived on the sea-shore, followed by a great number of inhabitants. The General's boat was sent at once and brought them back on board. They told us that the savages, who had gathered round them to the number of more than three hundred, seeing that all our boats had left the shore, had behaved towards them with the greatest effrontery. One of them having snatched Dewelle's sword, Dewelle tried to pursue him, but the others at once raised their clubs to defend the thief. All of them were robbed with the greatest impudence. However, when our boat arrived to help them, two chiefs, who had probably prevented the other savages from going to still greater lengths, asked to embark in it. They brought two small bundles of sugar-cane and some coconuts to the General, who made them a present of a hatchet and various pieces of cloth. These chiefs, whom they call *theabouma* in their language, wore on their heads a cylindrical cap adorned with feathers, shells, etc. *(see pl.* 37, *fig.* 2 *and* 3*)*. It could not serve to protect them from the rain, for it was open at the top.

A double canoe set out from the shore and soon came to carry these chiefs to land. It was already night when it left us; the savages had lit a small fire on a bed of sand towards the middle of the platform to warm themselves.

We went ashore with the men of the crew who were to work at laying in our supply of wood. They cut it half a kilometre from the place where the water was being taken in.

We did not go far from our woodcutters, for we were few in number and the intentions of the natives towards us were very suspect to us. At about nine in the morning they seized our pinnace, which, anchored close to the shore, was guarded by one man only, and they were already hauling it towards the beach so as to carry off the more easily the articles it contained, when another boat fortunately came to its help. The thieves gave up their attempt only when we were on the point of firing on them.

Lasseny, having gone ashore to make astronomical observations, had been forced to re-embark almost at once, for he had been unable to keep off a group of savages who seemed intent on seizing his instruments, although he was armed and accompanied by two assistants and several boatmen.

The master gunner of the Espérance, while shooting in the forest, caught sight towards noon, in a large clearing not far from the place where wood was being cut, of more than two hundred natives practising the throwing of the spear and performing various evolutions. He withdrew without having been discovered and hurried to us to tell us what he had just witnessed; an officer of our ship at once set out with four musketeers to observe the movements of these savages; but they advanced upon them as soon as they had caught sight of them, and forced them to hurry back towards our woodcutters. The savages soon reached the same spot, and let us glimpse the design they had formed of seizing the axes that had just been laid down in the midst of our workmen, who were gathered for their meal; the officer in command at once gave orders to carry these tools to the longboat, but the sailor who took charge of them was set upon by the islanders, and they were on the point of snatching them from him when several musket-shots were fired at them. One of the boldest, having been brought to the ground, still had strength enough to drag himself into the woods. All the others withdrew there at once, and with their slings they hurled at us a hail of the oval-cut stones they carried in little bags hanging from their girdles; but they wounded no one dangerously, for they kept at a great distance; besides, most of the stones they threw were stopped by the branches of the trees behind which they had withdrawn. It does not always turn out so when they fight among themselves, since they are no doubt not afraid to come closer; and so they sometimes put out one another's eyes in this way in their battles, as several of these inhabitants who were missing an eye had told us. When they throw stones with their slings, they swing them only half a turn above the head, which is as quick as if they threw them with the hand. These stones, cut from a fairly hard steatite, are very slippery; that is why they take the precaution of moistening them with their spittle, so that they may hold on the two small cords that form the bottom of their slings.

The various movements of these savages having been observed from on board the Recherche, the General had two cannon fired at them, which at once scattered them through the woods; but soon afterwards one of their chiefs came towards us alone and unarmed, holding in his hand a piece of white cloth made of tree bark, which the officer in command received as a pledge of the good understanding that was henceforth to remain undisturbed between these savages and us. Four other natives soon came and sat down among us with as much confidence as their chief, behind whom they placed themselves; but he seemed very angry with several others who came afterwards to rest in the shade of the neighbouring trees, and he called them thieves *(kaya)* several times over.

We re-embarked at four in the afternoon, and we were already heading for our ships when we saw a troop of savages running towards us along the beach, laden with various kinds of fruit which they wished to give us as a present. Several times they plunged into the water to bring them to us, but we were being carried to the west by a very rapid current, and we could not stop to receive these tokens of reconciliation.

1793-04-24.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 204-208]
The next day I went ashore quite close to our watering-place, at the moment when the General was making his way there. The guard was stronger than on the day before, the better to overawe the islanders. It was feared, after what had passed between them and us the previous day, that, knowing perhaps the effects of some poison, they might have tainted the water with which our casks were about to be filled; it was therefore thought proper, on the advice of our surgeon-major, to try it first on a goose, and the bird suffered no harm from it; but several of the sailors, unwilling to wait for the result of this trial before quenching their thirst, had already drunk of it before it was even begun.

Some of the inhabitants having come near our landing-place, two lines were traced in the sand beyond which they were forbidden to pass, and we had the satisfaction of seeing that they submitted very readily to these orders. We gave most of them pieces of biscuit, which they asked of us by holding out one hand towards us, while with the other they showed us their belly, naturally very flat, but whose muscles they contracted with all their strength to draw it in still further. I saw one arrive, however, whose stomach was already well filled, and who nevertheless ate in our presence a piece of a very soft steatite, of a greenish colour and as large as two fists. We afterwards saw many others eat freely of this same earth; it serves to deaden the sense of hunger by filling their stomach and so supporting the viscera attached to the diaphragm, and although this substance yields no nourishing juice, it is nevertheless very useful to these people, who must very often be exposed to long privations of food, since they give very little attention to the cultivation of their lands, which are in any case very barren.

It is worth noting that the inhabitants of New Caledonia have no doubt chosen the steatite I have just mentioned only because, being very friable, it does not remain long in their stomach and intestines. One would never have imagined that cannibals would have recourse to such an expedient when pressed by hunger.

Three women, who had come to join the other savages gathered around us, gave us a rather poor idea of their music; they sang a trio, keeping time very well, but the harshness and the dissonant harmonies of their voices produced in us very disagreeable sensations; the savages, however, seemed to listen to them with great pleasure.

The gardener Lahaie and I ventured into the midst of the woods, accompanied by only two men of the crew. We chose to go where we had hopes of meeting few of the natives; these took care to crouch behind thickets when they caught sight of us; at other times they kept behind large trees, round which they moved as we advanced a few steps; one old man, however, seeing us come forward on both sides of the tree behind which he was hidden, and being unable to avoid being seen, came up to us with the air of a man giving himself up to our mercy; but he seemed much reassured when we offered him a few pieces of biscuit. The gardener had just scattered in the woods various kinds of seeds brought from Europe; he had a few left, which he gave to this savage, urging him to sow them.

We soon came upon several huts, all standing apart from one another, in which we were surprised to find no inhabitant. They were built in the same manner as the one I described towards the beginning of this chapter. Further on we noticed a heap of ashes; probably one of these dwellings had been burnt fairly recently by the fire which these savages kindle in them to drive out the mosquitoes. Its floor had been raised by about two decimetres to protect it from flooding.

Two tombs which stood not far from it had suffered no damage. I saw there two human bones, each hung by a cord from a long stick driven into the ground; one was a tibia, and the other a thigh-bone.

On the hills I crossed on my way back to our landing-place I noticed the tree known by the name of *commersonia echinata*, which grows very abundantly in the Moluccas. Among the new species of shrubs I gathered was a jasmine remarkable for its simple leaves and for its marigold-coloured flowers, which have no scent.
