Some fires lit very near the summit of the neighbouring mountain showed us that it served as a retreat for natives.

On reaching our landing-place we found a great number of savages who had gathered there since our departure. They told us that several of the inhabitants had been wounded in the affair they had had with us the day before, and that one of them had already died of his wounds. As for themselves, they showed us no hostile intentions; but a longboat of the Espérance, which had been some distance from there towards the east, had been attacked a few hours before our return by a band of other savages, who had thought themselves strong enough to take possession of it; happily their attempt had not succeeded.

On arriving on board we were told that no canoe had come near our ships, which we thought should be put down rather to a strong wind that had blown all day than to fear of our resentment for the hostilities they had committed the day before.

1793-04-25.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 208-215]
Several of us from the two ships had planned to go and visit the far side of the mountains lying to the south of our anchorage; we gathered on the shore early in the morning, twenty-eight in number. We had agreed to go there all armed, so as to be able to help one another should the savages dare to attack us.

We walked a long time along well-trodden paths; we were accompanied by a few of the inhabitants. Several of us, following their example, chewed young shoots of *hybiscus tiliaceus*, and spat them out almost at once; but what was our surprise to see these savages pick them up eagerly and chew them again without disgust.

When we had got about half-way up the mountain, we found very large blocks of mica in which we noticed garnets that had lost their transparency, most of them bigger than a thumb. Further on we found some in sandstone rocks which were very small, but had kept all their lustre.

The smoke that rose at intervals from the depths of a grove which we saw a short distance off to the south-south-west led us to turn our steps that way. There I came upon two men and a child busy roasting over the coals the roots of a species of bean known to botanists by the name of *dolichos tuberosus*, which these islanders call *yalé*. They had not long pulled them out of the ground, for they were still attached to the stem, which was laden with flowers and fruit. They bore the marks of the dryness of the soil in which they had grown; their fibres were almost woody, and they were no more than two centimetres thick and three to four decimetres long.

Quite close by we met a small family who seemed alarmed at our approach. We at once gave presents to all of them in the hope of reassuring them, which succeeded with the husband and the two children; but one of us having offered a pair of scissors to the mother, and wishing to show her their use by cutting off a few of her hairs, the poor woman instantly burst into tears; no doubt she imagined that her last hour had come; she grew calm, however, as soon as the instrument had been put into her hands.

The inhabitants of these mountains appeared to us to live in the greatest wretchedness; they were all extremely lean. They sleep in the open air without, however, being tormented by mosquitoes, for these insects are driven from the heights by the east-south-east winds which blow there fairly constantly. These same winds so check the growth of plants that the trees which lower down reach a great height are found there only in the form of shrubs. The *melaleuca latifolia*, for example, scarcely reaches four decimetres in height there, whereas on the hills it grows to a height of nine or ten metres. Yet among the plants peculiar to the summits of these mountains, several seem perfectly suited to the great agitation of the air to which they are exposed there. I shall give the description of one of the most remarkable; it forms a new genus, which I designate by the name of *dracophyllum*.

The calyx is composed of six small, ovate, acute leaves.

The corolla, which is of a single piece, is slightly divided at its margins into six equal parts. It is surrounded by six small scales placed at its base.

The stamens, six in number, are attached to the corolla by rather slender filaments, of about the same length as the anthers.

The ovary is superior, rounded, and surmounted by a style with a simple stigma.

The capsule has six cells, each containing several seeds, most of which are abortive.

I must observe that very often one of the parts of the fructification is wanting.

I have given this plant the name of *dracophyllum verticillatum* because its flowers are arranged in rings.

Its leaves are leathery and slightly toothed at the margins. They leave their marks on the stem as they fall from it, as happens with all the species of *dracaena*, to which this plant bears a close affinity, even in the texture of its wood. It therefore belongs to the division of the monocotyledons, although it has a calyx and a corolla, and it falls naturally next to the family of the asparagus.

Looking out from the summit of these mountains over an immense stretch of reefs which guard the approach to this land, we discovered another passage a little to the west of the one by which we had reached the anchorage where our ships lay. To the south our gaze fell upon a fine valley surrounded by large plantations of coconut palms, from which we saw the smoke of fires lit by the savages rising in columns. Wide tracts of land, which appeared to us to be cultivated, in the lowest parts, betokened a large population. This valley was crossed by a channel full of water, which we took for a river, and whose several branches ran out from the foot of the eastern mountains; but we afterwards found that this channel was filled with stagnant sea water. Towards the south-west we could see the reefs along which we had coasted the year before, and we noticed there the same gap which winds that were too strong had prevented us from sounding. It seemed to us likely to offer a safe passage to ships wishing to anchor under the shelter of these reefs.

We were now followed by only three natives, who had no doubt seen us a year earlier coasting along the western shore of their island, for before leaving us they spoke to us of two ships they had seen on that side.

We walked for some time to the south-west along the crest of the mountain, then went down into a ravine, where we found two men and a child who, quite reassured as to our intentions towards them, did not stir from the rock on which they were sitting. When we were quite near them they showed us a basket *(see pl. 38, fig. 24)* filled with tubers resembling those of the roots of the species of sunflower called *helianthus tuberosus*. They told us they were called *paoua*, saying that they were good to eat, and they were willing to sell us a small quantity of them.

Seeing, thirty paces further on, a thick smoke coming out from among great heaped-up rocks which offered very good shelter from the wind, we made our way there and saw a young savage busy roasting roots, among which I recognised those of the *dolichos tuberosus*. He did not seem surprised at our visit, and smiled at us from the depths of his grotto, which was full of a very black smoke by which, however, he seemed hardly troubled.

Soon the flank of the mountain, split open by the torrents that rush down it in the rainy season, showed us bundles of fine needles of green schorl in a fairly soft steatite, and lower down small fragments of very transparent rock crystal.

On our way back to our ships we passed through a small hamlet, whose inhabitants came out of their huts unarmed. They let us examine the inside of them, and one of them made no difficulty about selling us the human bones that hung above one of their tombs.

We soon reached the seashore, where we found a group of natives who followed us, asking us for something to eat; but as all our provisions were used up, I treated them to pieces of a greenish and very soft steatite which I had brought from the summit of the mountains. Some of them ate as much as a kilogramme of it.

When we re-embarked to return on board, one of the crew, having fired into the air to discharge his musket, struck terror into most of the islanders on the shore, who suddenly took flight and went to hide in the woods; but a few, not mistaking our intentions towards them, showed not the least fear and called back the fugitives, who soon returned to join them.

1793-04-26.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 215-217]
On the 8th I was obliged to stay on board all day to describe and prepare the collection I had gathered the day before.

We received a visit from several natives who came out swimming. They took great care to assure us that they were not among those who had committed acts of hostility against us, and they told us that they had eaten two of those thieves, or *kaya*, one of whom had had his thigh and the other his belly pierced by a ball in the affair that had taken place between them and us; but we did not wholly believe this story, because we thought they had told it to their own advantage, so as not to appear suspect to us.

They had brought an instrument which they call *nbouet*, a name they also give to their tombs. It was made of a fine flattened piece of serpentine, sharp at the edges, cut roughly into an oval, perfectly polished, and two decimetres long. It was pierced with two holes, through each of which passed two very flexible rods which fixed it to a wooden handle, to which they were bound with braids of bat's hair; this instrument stood on a foot made from a coconut shell, which was also fastened with braids of the same kind, some of them thicker *(see pl. 38, fig. 19)*. Until then we had been unable to learn the use of this instrument; these savages told us that it served to cut off the limbs of their enemies, which they share out after the fight. One of them demonstrated it for us on one of the crew, who lay down on his back at his invitation. First he acted out a fight, in which he showed us the enemy falling under the blows of his spear and of his club, which he brandished violently; then he performed a sort of Pyrrhic dance, holding this instrument of slaughter in his hand, and showed us that they began by opening the belly of the vanquished man with the *nbouet*, and that they threw the intestines far away after tearing them out by means of the instrument shown in *pl.* 38, *fig.* 20, which is made of two human ulnae, shaped, well polished, and set in a very strong web of braids. He showed us that the organs of generation were then cut off and became the share of the victor; that the legs and arms were cut off at the joints and distributed, as were the other parts, to each of the combatants, who carried them to his family. It is hard to depict the ferocious greed with which he conveyed to us that the flesh of this unhappy victim was devoured by them after being roasted over the coals.

This cannibal gave us to understand at the same time that the flesh of the arms and legs was cut into slices seven to eight centimetres thick, and that the most muscular parts were a very pleasing dish to these people. It was then easy for us to explain why they often felt our arms and legs while showing a violent desire; at such times they made a slight whistling sound, which they produced by clenching their teeth and pressing the tip of the tongue against them, and then, opening their mouths, they made several clicking noises in succession.

1793-04-27.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 217]
We went ashore on the 9th, but we were too few in number to venture far from our watering-place. We no longer saw in the neighbourhood the numerous groups of inhabitants we had seen in the first days of our stay at the anchorage, which led us to think that they had gone back to their dwellings, which were no doubt fairly distant from this spot; indeed, how could so great a number of men have found the means of subsistence on this extremely barren coast.

1793-04-28.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 217-223]
The next day we set out early, eighteen in number, all well armed, with the intention of crossing a very high mountain lying to the south-south-east, and then, if the weather were favourable, of going down into a fine valley which we had already glimpsed from a great distance behind this mountain.

We first walked eastwards along the shore, and soon entered a large wood where, among the various birds we shot, there was a fine species of magpie, which I have named the *New Caledonia magpie*; it is entirely black, except for the upper part of the belly and of the back, and the neck, which are white: the bill is slightly toothed at the tip of each mandible; it is of a dull black for two-thirds of its length from the base, the rest being yellowish. The tail feathers are arranged two by two in tiers, the upper ones being much longer than the others *(see pl.* 39 *where this bird is shown natural size)*.

We had already gone more than two kilometres when we came to a village made up of a small number of huts, set far enough apart from one another that fire could not spread should one of them unhappily fall a prey to the flames. Two of them had been burnt fairly recently. There we saw women preparing their meal by cooking the bark of trees and various roots, among which I recognised those of the *hypoxis* I have already mentioned. These different foods were cooking dry in a large earthen pot held above the fire by three large stones which served it as a trivet. Quite close to the entrance of one of these huts could be seen a great heap of human bones, on which we noticed very recent traces of fire. It was probably an inhabitant of this hamlet who had stolen Bonvouloir's sword, as I related above, for we found its scabbard and sword-belt hung like a kind of trophy above one of their tombs.

On leaving this village we followed a path running to the south-east, and before long we saw a few Caribbean cabbages *(arum esculentum)* planted near a stream whose waters the inhabitants had led, lower down, towards a plantation of *arum macrorrhizon*. Further on we noticed young banana plants set five to six metres apart from one another, and several stools of sugar cane.

We were soon surrounded by at least forty natives, who came out of the neighbouring huts and of a few cabins scattered over a wide plain covered with herbaceous plants, above which rose a small number of coconut palms; but we were astonished to see among these savages only a very few men, and even these were all old or infirm and most of them crippled; the rest were women and children, who showed great joy on receiving the presents of glass beads we gave them. We supposed that the able-bodied men were busy far away, on some expedition against their neighbours.

We were about two kilometres from the first village when we came upon another, twice as large, standing on the banks of a small river, which we followed upstream, climbing towards the south. More than thirty natives came out of their huts to meet us, and followed us for some time. Soon we saw three others coming down from the mountains, among whom we recognised one who had visited us many times on board the Recherche. Several of them pointed him out to us as a chief of great distinction, whom they knew by the name of *Aliki*.

We rested on the bank of the small river to take our meal; but wishing to guard against any surprise on the part of these savages, we invited them to sit down. The *Aliki* at once complied with our invitation, and all the others followed his example. As the water was a few paces below us, some of the savages took care to go and fill our bottles as fast as we emptied them.

After breakfast we climbed to the south, accompanied by the *Aliki* and three other inhabitants who had shown a great wish to follow us. Coconut palms and banana plants set on the less steep sides of the ravine hollowed out by the waters of the small river told us that some natives lived there. We found there a hut exactly like those we had come across before. The *Aliki* told us it belonged to him. It was surrounded by a few trees of a new species of fig, whose fruit these people eat after exposing it to the fire for some time in earthen vessels to take away its corrosive quality.

Towards ten in the morning, clouds brought up by a fresh south-east wind wrapped the summits of the mountains and gave us for some time a heavy rain, to which the savages seemed hardly sensible. They sought no shelter from it, while we had withdrawn under very leafy trees. As soon as it had stopped we continued on our way, and they followed us, showing us many marks of affection. One of them, wishing to relieve one of our sailors who was burdened with a large tin box already full of various objects of natural history, agreed to carry it for more than four hours.

Soon we crossed the small river, on whose banks I noticed the *acanthus ilicifolius*. We then climbed for some time over very steep rocks, and we had nothing but praise for these savages, who hastened to hold us up by the arms to keep us from falling.

Each of them carried a serpentine axe, and one of them, wishing to show us how they used it to cut wood, cut down a branch of *melaleuca latifolia* about a decimetre thick. Only after a great many blows did he manage to make a slight notch in it, and then he broke it by bearing down hard on its end; they all showed the greatest surprise on seeing us fell in a very short time, with a battle-axe, some of the largest trees of the forest.

We had just reached one of the highest summits of these mountains when one of us let the savages know that he wished for some water. Two of them immediately offered to fetch some from the bottom of a ravine which seemed to us more than a thousand paces away. They set off, and we soon lost sight of them. As they were a very long time in returning, we feared that they had made off with the bottles we had entrusted to them; but at last they came back, and seemed pleased to be able to offer us very clear water to quench our thirst.

We then went down towards the south-east and crossed a fine valley, where I made a very plentiful harvest of plants, among which were the *acrostichum australe* and several new species of *limodorum*.

A very heavy rain obliged us to seek shelter in hollows in the rocks, where we stayed for some time. We invited the savages who were with us to share our meal, but we were very surprised to see these cannibals disdain the salt pork we offered them.

The bad weather having dissuaded us from spending the night in the mountains, we went back towards our ships, bearing to the west so as to follow the slope of a large valley parallel to the one we had just crossed. There I noticed several new species of *passiflora*. Ginger, *amomum zingiber*, grew there fairly abundantly, but the natives told us that they made no use of it; they left us, going off towards the east, as soon as we had reached the shore, where we found longboats to take us back to our ships.

1793-04-29.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 223]
I spent the whole of the 11th describing and preparing the large collection of objects of natural history I had made the day before.

1793-04-30.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 223-225]
The next day we made our way to the south-east, and after going fairly deep into the woods we came to a hut surrounded by palisades, behind which were a woman and two children, who seemed frightened at our approach; but they were reassured when we gave them pieces of cloth and glass beads.

We then walked towards two large fires lit by some savages in one of the darkest parts of the forest. They fled as soon as they saw us, leaving behind two baskets filled with the bark of trees.

We soon reached the edge of some marshes, where we shot a few charming birds of the genus *muscicapa*; they were drawn to these places by clouds of mosquitoes, on which they fed. Further on we found two young girls who had just lit a fire; they were roasting for their meal various sorts of roots, among which I recognised several belonging to plants I had come across in the shade of the great trees of the forest. They abandoned their provisions for a time and kept moving away as we approached them.

On coming out of the woods we met several inhabitants, who went with us towards our anchorage. They were much amused to see Citizen Riche's dog run after some other savages, whom he very quickly overtook, although they were a long way off and running with all their might. As he did them no harm, those who were beside us urged us to set him on some women who came out of the forest, and they were already delighting in their fright; but we would not yield to the wish of these natives.

On reaching the seashore we witnessed a thing which points to a great corruption of morals among this cannibal people. Two girls, the elder of whom was about eighteen, were showing to some of our sailors what they are accustomed to veil with the fringed girdle I have already mentioned, and which forms their whole clothing. They had fixed the price of their compliance at the value of a nail or of some other object of like importance, and they required each of the curious to pay them in advance.

On arriving on board our ship I found a chief who had dined there at the officers' table. He had come in a canoe with his wife, whom he had never been willing to allow to come on board, despite the repeated requests made to him.

1793-05-01.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 225]
On the 13th we went shooting in the great woods that lay to the south-east of us, and a prodigious number of birds were killed there. We stopped in a small hamlet, where we saw roughly carved boards on two tombs; the inhabitants warned us that it was forbidden to go near them; but they very readily agreed to sell us, for a few pieces of cloth, a human skull that hung above another tomb, and whose frontal bone was broken on the left side. They gave us to understand that this warrior had been killed with blows of a club in a fight.

1793-05-02.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 225-231]
The following day we set out very early in the morning, twenty in number, having resolved to cross the mountains and then go down into the great valley where, on one of our excursions, we had seen from a great distance much cultivated land. It was likely that we should meet a great many inhabitants there; but we were all well enough armed to drive them off should they dare to attack us.

At first we followed the shore, advancing westwards, and, going now and then into the woods, we saw some inhabitants move away from their huts at our approach and abandon a net they had spread out to dry. It appears that this fishing implement, which is commonly eight metres long and one and a half wide, is very rare among these people. They showed us very few of them during the whole time we stayed on their island, and none of them would ever part with one at any price.

Near there we noticed the remains of a great quantity of shellfish which had served the islanders as food; among them were several of the species known by the name of holy-water stoup, whose length was three to four decimetres. On them could be seen the traces of the fire that had been used to cook the animal they contained.

It is chiefly the women who go to gather shellfish. From time to time we saw some of them, opposite our anchorage, wade into the sea up to the waist and gather great quantities, which they found in the sand by means of a pointed stick that they drove into it.

We had already covered more than a myriametre along the coast without finding a stream, when three young savages came to meet us and urged us to follow them towards their cabin, not far from the path we were following. There we found a spring, below which they had cut channels to lead its waters towards a few plants of *arum macrorrhizon*, whose roots they eat.

We were on the slope of a hill in the shade of some coconut palms. One of the savages, whom I asked to pick us some of the fruit, climbed to the top of these trees with extreme agility.

We soon continued on our way to the west. The air was calm; we felt an excessive heat, and we were assailed by a cloud of mosquitoes, which caused us great suffering, stinging us all over the body, even in the eyes and ears. Happily a breeze sprang up a little while afterwards and rid us of them by scattering them far and wide.

We soon reached the edge of a deep channel which ran inland as far as the foot of a very steep mountain. It served the islanders as a harbour, and we saw three of them enter it in a double canoe, which they at once made fast with a line tied to the foot of a tree on the side where we were; then they went off at a slow pace towards the hills to the south-east, pretending not to see us. Their canoe was the only one in this harbour. We used it to cross to the other side, where we found a small cabin whose neighbouring plantations had been laid waste very recently; a few remains of Caribbean cabbages and sugar canes could still be seen there, and all the coconut palms had been cut off at the top; perhaps its unhappy inhabitants had fallen victim to the voracity of the barbarians who had thus stripped them.

Until then we had come upon the tombs of these savages only very near their huts; but this time we saw one, far from any dwelling, beside the path we were following. It differed from the others in being built of stone from its base up to half its height.

Towards the middle of the day we halted in the shade of several *casuarina equisetifolia* and of various new species of *cerbera* which grew on the banks of a stream, where we quenched our thirst and where I found a few fragments of hornstone rolled by the waters. We had just caught two sea snakes *(coluber laticaudatus)*, which we ate after roasting them over the coals; but we found their flesh very tough and of a rather bad taste.

We were more than two myriametres from our ships when fresh traces of devastation once more made us lament the fate of these wretched inhabitants, whom revenge often drives to the most horrible excesses. They had destroyed the principal dwelling and topped all the coconut palms around it; only they had spared two small sheds roofed with the spongy bark of *melaleuca latifolia*.

Soon a forest of coconut palms, whose tops we could see half a myriametre to the west, and the smoke rising in columns from various points within it, betokened a large population. We made towards this place for some time; but some marshes which had to be crossed before reaching it made us give up our plan; besides, the day was drawing to its close. We therefore went on towards the south, looking for a convenient spot to spend the night, and soon settled on a rise whose difficult approach protected us from any surprise on the part of the savages. We lit a fire, for on these heights there was a sharp cold, which we felt all the more keenly for having experienced very great heat on the plain during the day. I handed over to the men of the crew who were with us all the birds whose skins I did not intend to keep, and among those they roasted on the spot for our supper were several *corvus caledonicus*, and some very large pigeons of a new species which I had already met with in the first days of our stay at the anchorage.

Everyone had supper and then gave himself up to sleep, while two of us watched by turns and kept a good guard, for it was to be feared that the light of our fire might draw some islanders towards us. We were soon warned that the light of several torches could be seen towards the foot of the mountains, with which some savages were advancing eastwards and drawing near our retreat. In an instant everyone was on his feet to watch their movements, and we prepared to receive them as was fitting, should they take it into their heads to come and attack us; but after crossing several hills they went down towards the shore, marching eastwards and moving away from us. Perhaps these cannibals were about to undertake some expedition against their enemies. As it did not seem that we were the object of their search, we went back to sleep at once, trusting to the vigilance of our sentries.

1793-05-03.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 231-235]
The next day, at first light, we climbed towards the south-east and soon reached the crest of the mountain, from which we saw to the west-south-west, on the seashore, the wide mouth of the channel that crosses the plain we meant to visit.

We soon went down into a small valley, towards the middle of which rose a charming grove standing by itself, which seemed to have been planted by the hand of man; but the shrubs grew there so vigorously only because they stood in fairly good soil, moistened moreover by the waters that fell from the neighbouring mountains. There I made a large harvest of plants, among which was a new species of fern of the genus *myriotheca*, the largest plants of which rose to a height of four metres, although their trunk was no more than a decimetre in circumference.

On leaving this grove we saw, three hundred paces below us, two natives making their way to the plain, the whole extent of which now lay open to us. They looked at us, but kept on their way nevertheless, despite our invitations to come to us. One of them carried on his shoulder, at the end of a stick, a basket filled, no doubt, with roots.

We had only a few more hills to cross to reach the plain when several of our party, fearing that they would run short of food if they went further, and perhaps meet numerous bands of savages, left us to return that very day on board our ships. This desertion reduced our number to fifteen; but we continued on our way none the less. Soon, beside a path much used by the savages, we found a few cabbage palms; we feasted on the tender leaves at the top of these trees, then went down into a ravine where several fine *aleurites* added to our meal a good supply of fruit, whose kernels we found of a very pleasant taste.

Quartz and mica, spread over a large area, formed in this place a very glittering foliated rock, laid down in fairly thin beds.

At last we entered the plain, and soon the sad sight of a dwelling entirely destroyed and of several coconut palms cut down at the foot bore witness once more to the barbarity of the inhabitants.

Further on we saw plantations of yams, sweet potatoes, etc. We walked for some time to the south, and were wondering at not meeting any savage, when I caught sight of an old man busy pulling up roots of *dolichos tuberosus*, which he handed to a child to clean. He did not seem in the least intimidated on seeing us come towards him; but every feature of the child betrayed the greatest fear. The old man had lost an eye, which he told us had been put out by the blow of a stone. We thought we recognised him as one of the inhabitants who had come several times to visit us on our ships.

He went with us along a path running south-east across the plain; but he had great difficulty in keeping up with us, for he had been wounded in one leg, on which could be seen two large scars opposite each other, as if it had been pierced through by a spear.

On both sides of the path could be seen huts surrounded by coconut palms, scattered at great distances from one another; only a few savages appeared in the distance in the midst of this vast plain. On our left rose a dense forest of coconut palms which stretched to the foot of the mountains, and in whose shade we could see a great number of huts.

We had gone about two kilometres with this savage when he invited us to stop near a dwelling which probably belonged to him, for he urged us to pick for ourselves the fruit of the coconut palms around it, excusing himself on the ground that his wounds prevented him from climbing to the top of these trees. I gave him pieces of cloth of various colours and some nails, which he seemed to value highly. Soon another savage came up to us, and the two of them followed us as far as the bank of a branch of the great channel that crossed the plain; it was filled with stagnant water, as salt as that of the sea.

We could see women and children in the distance when our two savages left us, pointing out to us a path which led us into the mountains.

At the same moment some other natives set fire to dry grass a long way ahead of us beside the path we were following, and then disappeared into the woods.

After walking for half an hour to the north-east I came to a very pleasant hillside, where the inhabitants had built three sheds two metres high to enjoy the cool air there; they were hemispherical in shape and open at the bottom all round to a height of three decimetres, so as to let the air circulate freely. We found no savages in either of the two neighbouring huts, which were built quite close to a pool surrounded by *hybiscus tiliaceus*; but we saw round about a large piece of cultivated ground covered with sweet potatoes, yams, and the species of *hypoxis* whose roots these people eat, and which grows wild in their forests.

It had been dark for an hour when at last we reached the summit of the mountains, from which, looking towards the north-east, we saw the lights of our ships. Six to eight hundred paces below us shone several fires lit by the savages. The cold obliged us too to light one, a very large one, round which we took our meal; then we lay down to sleep, while two of us guarded two passes by which the islanders might have come to surprise us; none of them, however, sought to disturb our rest; only, at daybreak, the sentry posted to the north-east signalled three who were advancing towards us rather slowly, but they turned back at the cry he gave to warn us of their approach.

1793-05-04.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 235-238]
All our provisions being by then used up, we felt keenly the need to return on board. I could not, however, resist the wish to give a few hours to visiting a charming grove on the far side of the mountain, a short distance from the place where we had spent the night. There I observed a great number of plants which I had not yet found on any of the excursions I had made on this island. Most of them belonged to the family of the proteas and to that of the bignonias.

I shall give the description of one of the finest shrubs that grew on these heights. It forms a new genus, which I name *antholoma*, and which should be placed in the family of the date-plums. The calyx, composed of two to four ovate leaves, often falls off when the flower opens.

The corolla is of a single piece, cup-shaped, and unevenly crenate at the margins.

The stamens, very numerous (about a hundred), are attached to a fleshy receptacle. The anthers end above in a point, below which they open at the tip of their cells.

The ovary, pyramidal and four-sided in shape, slightly sunk in the receptacle, is surmounted by a style ending in an acute stigma.

The fruit has four cells filled with a great number of seeds; it was not yet ripe; but I believe it becomes a capsule.

I designate by the name of *antholoma montana* this shrub, of which I saw several plants as much as five metres high. Its leaves are alternate, very leathery, and are found only at the ends of the branches, as are the flowers.
