One of the geographers of our party, having meanwhile gone off a kilometre from us to determine the position of the reefs he could make out from the top of a fairly high peak, received a visit from a savage who came up to him with a threatening air; he was armed with a spear and a club, and we feared that he meant to attack our companion, but he was content to examine the instruments he was using, without giving him the least cause for complaint.

We reached the ship towards the middle of the day. I noticed alongside a double canoe carrying two sails. It was built like those of the islanders of New Caledonia; but the natives who manned it spoke the language of the inhabitants of the Friendly Islands. There were eight of them, seven men and one woman, all very powerfully muscled *(see pl. 34)*. They told us that the island they came from lay to the east, a day's distance from our anchorage, and that it was called *Aouvea*. It was no doubt the island of Beaupré that they meant.

These islanders, who were quite naked, had the end of the foreskin fastened against the lower belly with a cord of coconut fibre which went twice round it. They knew the use of iron, and seemed to us much more intelligent than the savages of New Caledonia.

I was rather surprised to see one of the planks of their canoe coated with a layer of varnish. It seemed to have belonged to some European ship, and I could no longer doubt it once I had found that calx of lead entered in very large quantity into the composition of this varnish. This plank no doubt came from a ship of some civilised nation which had been wrecked on their coasts. I urged these savages to tell us what they knew on this subject; they at once made sail to the west, promising to come back the next day to bring us information; but they did not keep their word, and we had no further opportunity of seeing them.

We were told on our return that on the day we had left the ship to make the excursion we had just completed, some savages had tried to carry off the axes of our woodcutters and had assailed them with stones; but that two musket shots had been enough to disperse them.

1793-05-05.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 238]
I spent the whole of the 17th describing and preparing the numerous collection of natural history objects I had brought back from the mountains.

1793-05-06.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 238-242]
The next day the news of the death of Captain Huon, which we learned at daybreak, spread great sorrow among all the members of the expedition. This able seaman had died at about one in the morning of a hectic fever which had been consuming him for several months. He had borne the approach of death with the greatest composure. In accordance with his last wishes he was buried towards the middle of the island of Pudyoua, under cover of night. He had asked that no monument be raised to him, for fear that the inhabitants of New Caledonia might discover the place of his burial.

Shortly after sunrise eight of us went ashore and struck west-south-west into the woods. We soon came to a hut, from which a native emerged holding a mask, which he agreed to sell me for two joiner's chisels. This mask was carved from a piece of coconut wood *(see pl. 37, fig. 1)*, but much better sculpted than the various figures we had seen elsewhere on planks at the entrance of their dwellings. He covered his face with it several times, and looked out through the holes pierced in its upper part. There was no opening at the eyes, but there was one at the mouth. No doubt they use these masks so as not to be recognised by their enemies when they undertake some hostile enterprise against them.

We then walked towards two fires lit close to some huts, where we found a man and a woman busy cooking figs of a new species, which they had put on the fire in a large earthen pot without water, to rid them of their corrosive quality. They told us these figs were called *ouyou*.

Around the other hearth I noticed two children feasting on spiders of a new species which I had very often observed in the woods, where they spin threads so strong that they frequently offered us a most troublesome resistance. First they killed them by shutting them up in a large earthen vessel which they heated over a good fire, then they grilled them on the embers to eat them. They swallowed at least a hundred of them in our presence. Later, on this same island, we found several other inhabitants who eagerly sought out this kind of food. So odd a taste, and one so widespread among these large tribes, caused us much surprise, although some Europeans are known to eat spiders, especially those of cellars, in which they find a taste of hazelnut.

The inhabitants of New Caledonia call this species of spider *nougui*; I designate it by the name of *aranea edulis* (the spider eaten by the Caledonians). It is shown at natural size in *pl.* 12 *fig.* 4. The arrangement of its eyes *(see fig. 5 and 6)*, which are eight in number, two of them towards the middle of the corselet and very far from the others, leads me to place it in a new section. They are black in colour. The corselet, greyish above, is covered with silvery hairs; between the eyes four brown spots can be seen on it. It is black beneath. The abdomen, coloured above like the upper part of the corselet, is marked with eight to ten brown depressions. On the sides there are five or six oblique greyish bands, and beneath several tawny spots. The legs, which are also tawny and covered with silvery-grey hairs, are blackish at their tips.

One of the soldiers who accompanied us had lost one of his pistols; we told the inhabitants of these huts, and promised them a reward if they brought it to us. Half an hour after we had left them, we were pleased to see a savage running towards us to hand back this weapon, which he had found, he told us, on the sand. Indeed the soldier remembered that he had left it at the spot where we had dined. A piece of cloth and a jacket were an extremely welcome reward for this islander. He followed us for some time with another Caledonian, then took his leave of us, saying *alaoué* after slightly bowing his head, and went off looking very satisfied.

When we had reached the shore, one of us fired a musket to alert the crew of our frigate and ask that a longboat be sent for us, and the noise of the report brought more than eighty natives gathering around us; we urged them to sit down as they arrived, so that they should not come too close to us, and despite the disproportion in numbers, for there were only eight of us, they all complied with our request. One of these savages had some fairly sweet oranges, which he was willing to sell me for a pair of scissors.

On arriving on board we learned that several people from the Espérance, being in a boat, had been greeted in the morning with a hail of stones by some savages, on whom several musket shots had had to be fired to force them to fall back into the woods. It must be admitted that the fight had been started by the imprudence of a member of the crew who, wishing to make the Caledonians withdraw, had taken aim at them with his musket, which he had been clumsy enough to let go off.

1793-05-07.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 242-243]
General Dentrecasteaux gave the command of the Espérance to Dauribeau.

I was very busy on board for a great part of the day with work indispensable for the preservation of my collections; I went ashore in the afternoon, and immediately afterwards I saw some inhabitants falling upon our fishermen to snatch their net from them together with the fish they had just caught. At least twenty musket shots had to be fired at them before they could be entirely dispersed. All that time they stood firm on the shore, replying with their slings, and with a stone they badly wounded the master gunner of the Espérance in the arm; then they gave ground, and after a few moments they returned once more to the charge; but when they saw two of their men struck down by a shot, and so wounded that they could drag themselves only with great difficulty as far as the woods, the terror was general; they fled, and none of them thought of attacking us any more.

At the moment this affair was beginning, the commander of our expedition was leaving his ship to go on board the Espérance; he at once had his boat steered towards the coast, but the savages were entirely dispersed by the time he got there.

Before being disturbed by the islanders, our fishermen had caught several species of *scorpaena*, among which the one known by the name of *scorpaena digitata* stung one of the boatmen in the hand so sharply that for some hours he felt a very violent pain along the whole length of his arm.

1793-05-08.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 243-250]
The next day, at the first light of dawn, we landed on the shore nearest our ship, then six of us, all well armed, struck into the woods and walked for a long time to the south-south-west. On this excursion I found many plants which I had not yet collected.

I soon noticed a large breadfruit tree growing towards the middle of the mountain, the second I had come across on this island. I took three suckers from it, which I placed in a box where I was growing those I had taken at the Friendly Islands. The leaves were less deeply divided than those of the latter. Perhaps these trees do not produce such excellent fruit; but from the care the inhabitants took of the one I had noticed in a village to the south-east of our ships, I could not doubt that they set great store by this plant; it was planted in very good soil and surrounded by very solid palisades. Neither of these two trees was then bearing fruit; they carried only a great many male flowers.

We had already climbed to a great height in the mountains when some of our crew who were on the coast took it into their heads to fire their muskets into the air to unload them before returning on board. The sound of this musketry made us resolve to turn our steps towards them at once, for fear that they might be engaged in some affray with the savages. Night was coming on; we embarked to make for our ship, but the east-south-east wind blew so hard and the current was so strong that we were violently carried to the west. We even had great difficulty in reaching the Espérance, which we left half an hour later, when the weather had become more favourable, to go on board the Recherche.

The inhabitants of New Caledonia are, in general, of middling stature; we did, however, see one who was nearly two metres tall, but he was very ill-made. Their hair is woolly. The custom of plucking out the hair is fairly widespread among these peoples; yet a few could be seen who let their beards grow. The colour of their skin is as black as that of the savages of cap de Diemen; they do not, like them, cover themselves with charcoal dust; we noticed only a few who had blackened part of their chest with it, drawing broad oblique bands called *poun* in their language. Several were adorned with necklaces of the shape of the one shown in *plate* 37, *fig.* 4; these necklaces were made of braids; from them they usually wore, hanging on a cord, a small, rather crudely carved piece of bone which appeared to be a human bone. Their arms were sometimes decorated with bracelets cut, some from shells, others from quartz and other very hard stones *(see pl. 37, fig. 5 and 6).*

These warlike peoples take the greatest care in making their weapons; they polish them to perfection. Their clubs are of very varied shapes; some of them can be seen in *plate* 37.

I was rather surprised that they did not know the use of the bow.

Their spears, which are usually five metres long, are no more than six centimetres in circumference towards the middle. I admired the ingenious method they have devised for increasing the speed of these javelins when they throw them. For this purpose they use a short length of very elastic cord made of coconut fibre and the hair of the flying fox; they fix one end of it to the tip of the forefinger, while the other, which ends in a sort of globular knob, is wound round the spear in such a way that it releases it as soon as the weapon is thrown *(see plate 35).*

Among these inhabitants I observed no well-marked symptom of venereal disease; several, however, had a rather considerable swelling of the organs of generation, and others had swollen inguinal glands.

The voracity of which the Caledonians had given us proof prevented the General from giving them the he-goat and the she-goat he had intended for them. No doubt they will have eaten the two pigs and the two dogs which Cook had presented to one of their chiefs before letting them multiply. They scarcely took the slightest care of their fowls; I saw only three hens and one cock during our stay on their island.

We saw in their hands none of the objects that had been given to them by Captain Cook. Perhaps these riches brought misfortune upon the inhabitants of this coast by inciting their neighbours to come and plunder them.

I noticed with astonishment that the authority of the chiefs had always seemed almost nil in the various affairs we had had with these savages; but I was no less surprised to see them exercise rather great power when their own interests were concerned; for most of the time they seized the articles their subjects had received from us.

During our stay in New Caledonia we enjoyed fairly fine skies.

The winds varied from north-east to south, and the freshest were those that blew from the east and the south-east.

Our anchorage lay in latitude 20° 17' 29" south, and longitude 162° 16' 28" east.

The variation of the magnetic needle there was 9° 30' east. The mercury in the barometer did not rise above 28p 2l 2/10, and did not fall below 28p 1l 4/10.

Despite the excessive heat we experienced on the coast, the thermometer taken there did not exceed 25°, and on board it never rose beyond 21°.

The tides were felt at our anchorage only once a day. High water at full and change occurred at half past six in the evening, and the waters rose sixteen decimetres perpendicular.

During our stay in New Caledonia we were unable to gather any information about the fate of the unfortunate navigators who were the object of our search. It is not, however, beyond likelihood to believe that this dangerous and almost unapproachable land proved fatal to them. It is known that La Pérouse was to survey its western coast, and one cannot but shudder with horror at the thought of the fate that awaits the unhappy voyagers whom a shipwreck shall force to take refuge among the cannibals who inhabit it.

1793-05-12.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 250]
## CHAPTER XIV.

*Departure from New Caledonia. Meetings with the inhabitants of the island of Santa Cruz. Their bad faith. One of these savages slightly pierced the forehead of one of our sailors with an arrow; the sailor died of the consequences of this wound. Singular construction of their canoes. View of the southern part of the Solomon archipelago. Meetings with its inhabitants. Their treachery. Survey of the northern coasts of the Louisiade. Meetings with its inhabitants. Danger of this navigation. We pass through Dampier Strait to survey the northern coast of New Britain. Death of General Dentrecasteaux. Scurvy makes great ravages on our two ships. Death of the baker of the Recherche. Anchorage at Waigeo.*

ON the 21st we set sail from New Caledonia very early in the morning; but when we had reached the open sea we were held by a calm near a great chain of reefs which we could see to the west, and against which the sea broke in a frightening manner; however, we managed to get away from them with the help of a light south-east wind which rose during the night; we ran along them the following days, and on the 24th we discovered, beyond this chain to the west, the island of Moulin at more than three myriametres' distance, and then the Huon Islands.

1793-05-13.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 250]
The next day our ship was on the point of being wrecked on the reefs by which these islands are surrounded, when the light of dawn showed us the full danger of our position; at once we went about and stood away from them. A few hours before the end of the day we observed that these reefs joined those we had run along the previous year.

1793-05-19.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 250]
We soon steered for the island of Santa Cruz, which we sighted very early in the morning on the 1st of Prairial, to the north-west, at a distance of about four myriametres.

1793-05-20.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 250-251]
The next day, at about four in the afternoon, being half a myriametre from the shore, we saw two natives coming towards us in an outrigger canoe. At first they stopped a long way off until five other canoes had joined them, then they came closer to our ship. Only one of these canoes was manned by three savages; the others carried only two. They spoke to us and invited us by signs to land on their island; but none would agree to come on board despite our repeated invitations. The most trusting came no nearer to it than about fifty metres. For weapons they had bows and arrows, and for ornament necklaces and bracelets decorated with shells.

As night was approaching, we manoeuvred to stand off and on; they then left us and returned towards the coast; but a few hours later, despite the darkness of the night, we were visited by another canoe whose savages no doubt believed that we had a perfect command of their language, for they talked to us for a long time in a very loud voice; getting no answer, they at last went back to their island.

1793-05-21.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 251-258]
As soon as day began to break we drew in towards the coast, and soon we saw twelve canoes making for us. They were not long in coming alongside our ship. Most of them were laden with various kinds of fruit, among which I noticed breadfruit much smaller and less good than that we had eaten at the Friendly Islands; it was not, however, of the wild species, for it contained only a very small number of seeds. We were rather surprised that these islanders set little value on the iron we offered them; yet we could not doubt that they knew its use, for one of them owned the end of a joiner's chisel hafted on a piece of wood in the same manner as their stone axes; but when we had shown them pieces of red cloth, the cries of admiration they uttered, saying *youli*, *youli*, gave us hope of turning these articles to much better account with them than our hardware. And indeed they agreed to sell us some of their weapons, but, no doubt fearing that we might turn them against them, they took the precaution of not parting with their bows, and even of blunting all the arrows they let us have.

Several of them soon gave us proof of their bad faith. In order to have our trade goods for nothing, they would first offer a fairly good price for them and insist that they be handed over in advance; then they would keep them and refuse to hand over their value.

At about eight in the morning the General sent two boats to sound an inlet which we could see two kilometres away to the north-west. Suddenly we lost sight of them, and we were not without anxiety about their fate when they reappeared towards noon at the mouth of the channel they had just examined; several musket shots fired from these same boats had let us know that they had been attacked by the savages. At the sound the canoes that surrounded us had fled in haste. Our boats soon arrived and informed us that the inlet we had taken for a bay was one of the ends of a channel separating the island of Santa Cruz from that of New Jersey. This channel runs north-east by east over its whole length, which is only half a myriametre, and it is about two kilometres across at its widest. It was sounded with great accuracy, and a line of sixty-six metres found no bottom anywhere, not even at a hundred metres from the shores.

A great many canoes had followed our boats, while numerous groups of savages posted on the coast tried to lure them in by showing them coconuts, bananas and various other fruits; some at last had made up their minds to bring these productions of their island to them in person, swimming out to receive the pieces of cloth of different colours intended for them.

Our boats, having returned to the entrance of the channel a short distance from a small village built on the coast of New Jersey, were on the point of leaving these savages when one of them was seen to rise in the middle of his canoe and make ready to shoot an arrow at a man in the Espérance's boat. Everyone stood on guard; nevertheless the islander repeated his hostile gestures; then one of our men levelled his musket at him; but the savage, not at all frightened by this threat, slowly drew his bow and loosed an arrow which struck one of our oarsmen in the forehead, although he was at a distance of more than eighty metres. He was at once answered with a musket shot and a blunderbuss shot. The latter weapon covered the canoe from which the arrow had come with a hail of balls, and immediately the three islanders who manned it threw themselves into the sea; soon afterwards they climbed back into their canoe and paddled briskly towards the coast, but the aggressor was at last hit by a ball; then all three jumped into the water again, abandoning their little craft with some bows and arrows, which the men in our boats took possession of.

These canoes all have outriggers and are built as shown in *pl.* 44, *fig.* 3. It is on the platform to be seen between the canoe and the outrigger, which is made of a fairly close latticework, that they place their bows. The hull of the canoe is commonly five metres long by five decimetres wide. It is of a single piece cut from the trunk of an extremely light tree, almost as soft as mapou wood. Along its whole length it has a hollow a decimetre and a half wide. It is there that the paddlers sit, their legs one in front of the other, sunk in up to the calf. They are seated on the upper part, which is flattened. At the two ends, which are heart-shaped, can be seen two T's one above the other, carved shallowly, and sometimes in relief. The underside of the canoe is fairly well shaped to help its speed. The outrigger is always on the paddlers' left.

These islanders are in the habit of chewing betel; they carried the leaves, with areca nuts, in small bags of matting or coconut fibre. The lime they mix with it was kept in lengths of bamboo or in gourds.

These peoples are, in general, of a rather dark olive colour, and the character of their features indicates a close resemblance between them and most of the inhabitants of the Moluccas; only a few were to be seen who had very black skin, thick lips, and a broad flat nose, and who appeared to be of a quite different race; but in all these islanders the hair was frizzy and the forehead very broad. They are, in general, fairly tall; their thighs and legs are not very muscular, which is probably due in great part to the idle life they lead and to the long time they spend in their canoes.

Most of them had the nose and ears pierced with holes through which they had passed rings of tortoiseshell.

Almost all were tattooed, particularly on the back.

I noticed with surprise that the fashion of wearing fair hair was very widespread among these savages, which contrasted strikingly with the colour of their skin. No doubt these fops used lime to produce this effect, as I had seen done at the Friendly Islands. They are in the habit of plucking out their hair. Such notions of modesty as they have have not taught these peoples to wear clothing. They commonly have the belly bound with a cord passed two or three times round it. Their bracelets are made of woven matting and decorated with worn shells; they wear them on various parts of the arm, even above the elbow.

The sailor who had been hit by the arrow felt only a slight pain. He could have had his wound dressed at once by the surgeon of the Recherche, but he wished to wait until he was back on board the Espérance. We were at that time very far from supposing that so slight a wound could one day prove fatal to him.

As soon as the boats had been hoisted aboard the ships, we steered south-west by west, running along the coast of the island of Santa Cruz at a kilometre and a half's distance, where we could see a great many savages calling to us and inviting us to land. Several launched their canoes to come out to us; but we were sailing too fast for them to be able to reach us.

We could make out mountains, the highest of which were at least three hundred metres in perpendicular height. They were all covered with tall trees, between which a very white earth could be seen here and there, which appeared to be laid down in beds.

From there, after running along a myriametre and a half of coast, we came abreast of a large bay where good holding ground would no doubt be found, but it is open to the south-east winds, which were then blowing.

Soon we saw, out to sea towards the south, some canoes making for the island of Santa Cruz; others appeared at a greater distance and seemed to us to be fishing on a shoal; at the same moment we discovered towards the south another reef fairly close to us, which stretched a long way to the west.

We had just made out Volcano Island when a great number of canoes came out of Graciosa Bay and headed towards us. As we then had only a breath of wind, they had ample time to approach. Seventy-four of them had already been counted, which had stopped at a distance of eight to nine hundred metres from the ship, when clouds piling up over the mountains made the savages who manned these frail craft fear the danger of being swamped if they kept the sea any longer. At once they paddled towards the coast, and they had not yet reached it when a violent wind arose, accompanied by heavy rain, which hampered their progress a good deal.

We stood off and on during the night. The General intended to anchor the next day in Graciosa Bay.

Several fires were shining on the shore, which we were close enough to for us to make out the voices of the inhabitants, who seemed to be calling to us. A few rockets were let off with the intention of giving them a pleasant surprise, and suddenly cries of admiration rose from various points of the coast; but the deepest silence followed these demonstrations of joy, although several more rockets were fired.

1793-05-22.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 258-259]
During the night we saw no sign on Volcano Island to show that it still harboured subterranean fires. This small island could not contain within it a large enough quantity of combustible matter to feed without cease the volcanic flames which Captain Carteret had observed there twenty-six years before.

1793-05-23.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 259-261]
The south-east wind continued all day, and even the next day, to bar us from the entrance of the bay, a short distance from which stood a great many huts built in the shade of coconut palms planted along a sandy beach.

The natives soon appeared on the shore; the General then sent two boats towards them, and our frigates drew near enough to be able to protect them in case of attack by the inhabitants. The swell was too heavy for anyone to venture a landing, yet several natives swam out and brought us coconuts in exchange for pieces of red cloth, which they preferred to all the other articles we offered them. Some came in their canoes, and all showed fairly good faith in the exchanges they made with us. Perhaps they acted thus only because they had heard of the affair that had taken place between us and some inhabitants of the eastern part of their island; nevertheless they offered us only the worst of what they had. Most of the coconuts they brought us had sprouted; it was only after some time that they sold us bows and arrows; but for fear that we might turn these weapons against them, they took the precaution of carrying the bows to one of the boats and the arrows to the other. The arrows had not been blunted. Fixed to their tips by means of a reddish mastic could be seen a small, well-sharpened piece of bone or tortoiseshell, one centimetre long. Other arrows had points of the same material two to three decimetres long. Several more were armed with the bone found at the root of the tail in the species of ray called *raia pastinaca*.

Several pigs could be seen on the coast, which they would not bring us whatever price was offered; but they promised to sell them to us if we came ashore.

I noticed in their hands a necklace of glass beads, some red, others green, which seemed to me to be of English manufacture. They agreed to exchange them.

We bought from these inhabitants a piece of cloth which did not give us a favourable idea of their skill. It was made of very coarse tree bark, rather badly stuck one layer on another.

One of them wore on his chest a small piece of alabaster, flattened and cut into a circle, which he parted with to please us.

This meeting had already lasted nearly two hours when all the savages withdrew at a signal given them by one of their chiefs; but when they saw our boats preparing to leave their coast, the women came right down to the shore to try to persuade us to land there; we nevertheless continued our manoeuvre; we were soon back on board the ships, and shortly afterwards we made sail for the lands of the Arsacides.

1793-05-25.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 261]
On the 7th, at ten in the morning, we sighted the îles de la Délivrance in the west.

Towards noon we took the bearing of the more southerly of them from west 13° south to west 19° south, at two myriametres' distance, and of the other at west 27° south. We had just found 10° 48' for our ship's south latitude, and 160° 18' for her east longitude. These two small islands are very steep along almost their whole circuit, although they are rather low. We saw inhabitants on them and large plantations of coconut palms.

We soon crowded sail to close the lands of the Arsacides, whose high mountains we could see to the west-south-west.

1793-05-26.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 261-263]
The next day we ran along their coasts; at about ten in the morning we had just weathered a shoal which stretched more than three kilometres out to sea, when through the carelessness of the lookouts the ship passed over another shoal, on which there was fortunately enough water for her to suffer no damage.

At noon we had had 10° 54' south latitude and 159° 41' east longitude, when we took the bearings of the lands of the Arsacides from east 21° north to west 29° north; we were then half a myriametre south of the nearest shore. These coasts, broken by hills running out into the sea, form small inlets which offer shelter from the east winds. Most of these little capes each end in a rather tall pyramidal rock crowned with a tuft of very green shrubs. Farther inland we could see these same hills backed by mountains of moderate height which presented a very picturesque appearance.

It is chiefly at the head of these little coves that the inhabitants have settled. Several came down to the shore to enjoy the spectacle our ships offered them. Their huts were built in the shade of numerous plantations of coconut palms.

We had not yet seen any canoes along this coast when, at about four in the afternoon, one came out towards our ship. We were much astonished that the islanders who manned it had dared to venture on an extremely rough sea in so frail a craft, whose greatest width did not exceed two-thirds of a metre; accordingly they had seated themselves in the deepest part so as to keep their balance well *(see pl. 43, fig. 2)*.

Having come within about two hundred and fifty metres of our frigate, they addressed a few words to us in a very loud voice, pointing to their island and inviting us to land on it; then they came nearer still; but a very violent squall forced them to make for the land again.

These islanders were no more clothed than the inhabitants of the island of Santa Cruz, whom they closely resemble.

1793-05-27.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 263-270]
The next day, at daybreak, we found that the currents had carried us 18' to the east during the night. Our surprise was all the greater because the east winds then prevailing ought to have produced currents in the opposite direction. Could the tides be the cause of this singular set of the waters of the sea in these parts?

At about ten in the morning four canoes left the coast and came within about four hundred metres of our ship; but we could not wait for them to come nearer, for we were obliged to keep on our course to weather a cape which, in the position we were in, would have interfered with the nautical observations we intended to make.

At noon we were in latitude 10° 33' south and longitude 158° 57' east, and we could see the sea breaking with great violence a short distance away against Cape Phillip, which is very steep. We weathered it at about four in the afternoon, and immediately afterwards we saw a large bay whose shores appeared very populous; we noticed there several sheds under which the inhabitants had put their canoes to shelter them from the weather, and on every side huts could be seen, even up towards the summits of the highest mountains.

The savages soon launched five canoes and came towards us. They all kept within hail, except one of them who, mounted on a catamaran, came much closer to the stern of our ship to receive the pieces of red cloth we were throwing into the sea. His manner showed the greatest mistrust. He kept his eyes fixed on us, none of our movements escaped him, and yet he had the skill to catch every object thrown to him. Soon, at his call, the canoes drew near. The spectacle presented by this native seated on a few planks tossed by the waves amused us for a few moments. Our fiddler wished to entertain these islanders with a few tunes on the violin; but just as he was tuning his instrument they went off towards the Espérance.

Shortly afterwards five other canoes came alongside, showing us the greatest confidence. The natives who manned them no doubt knew the use of iron, for they showed much joy on receiving the nails we offered them. We could not find out whether these peoples are accustomed to barter; what is certain is that it was impossible for us to obtain anything from them in that way, although they had spears, clubs, bows and arrows; yet they were very eager to receive everything we gave them; they made us very obliging offers if we would land on their coasts, and, giving free rein to their natural gaiety, they repeated several times the Malay word *sousou* (the breast), accompanying their talk with very expressive gestures which singularly diverted our sailors.

At sunset these savages went back to the coast and lit three large fires.

During the night the currents had carried us into a great channel along this eastern island of the Arsacides, otherwise called the island of San Cristobal, which forms part of the Solomon archipelago discovered by Mendaña. It already lay to the north of us, and soon afterwards we saw Contrariety Island, which was set towards the middle of the day from east 14° north to east 30° north at a distance of one myriametre; we had just had 9° 53' south latitude and 159° 8' east longitude. This small island is somewhat hilly and very wooded.

We were soon running very close along the islets called the Three Sisters; then we beat to windward to make southing and get out of the strait that separates the island named Guadalcanal by Mendaña from that of San Cristobal.

At about eight in the evening the Espérance came within hail of us to tell us of an act of treachery she had just suffered at the hands of the islanders. During the previous night she had been surrounded by a great number of canoes, from which only two natives had come on board. They had praised the various fruits of their island to them in extravagant terms and had promised to procure a great quantity of them if they would come ashore; at last they had gone away towards the middle of the night; but among many canoes that had remained near the Espérance, one was noticed, much larger than the others, which, as day was approaching, went round the ship several times; it stopped for a moment, and at once at least a dozen arrows were shot from it, by which one of the crew (Desert) was wounded in the arm; fortunately most of the other arrows had stuck in the planking. After this volley the traitors fled in haste, and they were already a long way off when a musket was fired at them; they were not hit, but a rocket aimed with great precision, which burst very close to their canoe, gave them a great fright. The other canoes had also taken flight, but they had not been slow to return.

This cowardly treachery, and the conduct these same savages had shown towards Captain Surville, led us to believe that they had been guided by nothing but treacherous designs when they had used every means to try to persuade us to land on their coasts.

The little wind that blew at intervals from north-west to west-north-west scarcely allowed us to steer our ship, and the currents were carrying us very perceptibly towards Contrariety Island. We observed it under a clear sky, and the engraving of it that Surville published represents it with great accuracy. We were three kilometres from it when a canoe put off from the coast to come alongside. It was manned by four natives, who were grateful for the presents of cloth and hardware we made them, for immediately afterwards they gave us in return several coconuts, which they called *niou*, like most of the other inhabitants of the South Sea.

They showed very lively joy at the sight of the nails we offered them; they never stopped asking us for more, very often repeating *maté* (dead) and brandishing those they had just received, as if they wished to give us to understand that they would use them against their enemies. Shortly afterwards eight other canoes joined this one and came up to our ship without showing the least fear. We admired the elegant shape of these craft, which exactly resembled those we had seen on the preceding days along the eastern lands of the Arsacides *(see plate 43, fig. 2).* They were about seven metres long by two-thirds of a metre wide and five decimetres deep. Their bottom was of a single piece cut from a tree trunk; and to raise the sides they had fixed, on struts set at some distance from one another on each side of the craft, a plank running its whole length, and at the two ends they had fastened others above the first. On the outer surface of these last could be seen figures of birds, fishes, etc., roughly carved. Most of the canoes ended forward in a bird's head, below which could be seen a large tuft of fringes dyed red, which seemed to me to be made of vacoua leaves; there were others at the stern, likewise red, and towards that end, inside several canoes, a carved dog could be seen, separate from the craft, which made me think that these savages possess this animal; but I noticed with surprise that they had given it roughly the shape of a bloodhound; yet it is probable that they do not have this variety, and that the carving we saw was merely a roughly made representation of the kind of dog found in most of the islands of the South Sea.

These savages were obliged to stay constantly in the bottom of their craft to prevent them from being overturned by the waves, and they suffered the discomfort of sitting in the water that the sea shipped into them; but they took care to bail them out from time to time.

Among the objects we were able to obtain from them was a large line fixed to the end of a long rod, which seemed to me rather remarkable, because most of the other savages we had visited are accustomed to hold in the hand the line with which they fish. Their hooks were of tortoiseshell.

For ornament these peoples had bracelets made of various shells, among which was the sea-ear, which I easily recognised; others, made of coconut fibre, were decorated with a great quantity of Job's-tears seeds fastened all round them.

It does not appear that these peoples chew betel; at least I saw no sign of it. These canoes had spent several hours around us when one of the chiefs gave a signal to leave, and at once they paddled towards the coast with great speed; one canoe, however, stayed a few moments longer to receive some pieces of red cloth that we were offering it just as the others were leaving us; but soon these islanders, seeing their companions already far off, paddled with all their might to try to catch them up. It was then that we saw with surprise their canoe cut through the waves so fast that it could make at least a myriametre and a half an hour.

1793-05-31.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 270-271]
Early in the morning of the 13th we began to run along the southern coast of Guadalcanal, which slopes down fairly gently, and in the interior of the island we could make out a great chain of very high mountains running in the same direction. Among them we soon recognised Shortland's Mount Lama. The shore was lined with coconut palms, in whose shade we could see a great many huts. Shoals barred access to this coast over a great extent, and along it we were singularly thwarted by currents which set us towards the east. This unexpected course of the waters of the sea astonished us all the more because it seemed that the winds that had prevailed since we had been in these parts ought to have driven them towards the west.

1793-06-03.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 271]
On the morning of the 16th we weathered Cape Hunter, discovered by Shortland.

Towards ten o'clock we passed very close to an islet joined to the coast by some reefs, on which we saw several groups of savages squatting in the shade of fine plantations of coconut palms and banana trees, which gave this little island an extremely picturesque appearance. A great many canoes lay on the sand, and we expected to see some of them launched to come out to us; but we were singularly astonished at the indifference of the islanders; they did not stir from their places, and did not even take the trouble to stand up to enjoy the spectacle of our ships the better.

This little island lies in latitude 9° 31' south, and longitude 157° 19' east.

We soon sighted the westernmost point of Guadalcanal.

1793-06-06.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 271-272]
On the 19th, towards noon, we could see the largest of the Hammond Islands from north 4° west to east 6° north, at a myriametre's distance, when we were in latitude 8° 49' south and longitude 155° 9' east. We then left this archipelago and made sail for the northern coasts of the Louisiade.

The survey we had just made of the lands of the Arsacides left us in no doubt that they were the Solomon archipelago discovered by Mendaña, as Citizen Fleurieu had so soundly surmised in his excellent work on the discoveries of the French.

1793-06-08.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 272]
On the 21st the Espérance informed us of the death of the unfortunate man of her crew (Mahot) who, seventeen days before, had been wounded in the forehead by an arrow shot by a savage of the island of Santa Cruz. The wound had nevertheless healed well, and fourteen days had passed without his experiencing the slightest untoward symptom; but all at once he was seized with a very violent tetanus, of which he died at the end of three days.

Several persons supposed that the arrow by which he had been struck had been poisoned; but this conjecture seemed to me all the less well founded as the wound had healed perfectly and the wounded man had kept in fairly good health for fourteen days; besides, it was ascertained that the arrows which had been found in the canoe abandoned by the offender, and which the men of our crew had seized, were not tainted with poison, for several fowls were pricked with them and suffered no ill effects; but it is not rare in burning climates to see the slightest puncture followed by a general spasm, which is almost always a sign of death.

1793-06-11.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 272-273]
On the 24th, towards ten in the morning, we sighted the coasts of the Louisiade, and at first we took the easternmost lands for Cape Deliverance; but we soon recognised that they lay 25' further north.

We were astonished at the rapidity of the currents, which had carried us 44' to the north in the space of twenty-four hours. The observations made on board the Espérance also gave the same result.

From there we steered to the west, running along fairly high lands which we could only coast at a distance, on account of the prodigious number of shoals which, scattered very far out to sea, made our navigation extremely dangerous.

1793-06-13.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 273-274]
On the 26th, as soon as day broke, we found ourselves surrounded by low lands and reefs, among which very rapid currents from the west-north-west had carried us during the night; in vain did we make tacks, with a fairly good south-east wind, to try to extricate ourselves from this dangerous position; the currents always prevented us from working up beyond an islet lying to the north-east at a distance of half a myriametre, towards which there appeared to be a passage leading to the open sea. We were then in latitude 10° 58' south, and longitude 151° 18' east. The space in which we could beat about, growing narrower, increased the danger as we were carried to the westward; moreover, no bottom was found anywhere: we had at last to resolve to venture between some low lands which lay to the north-west, in the hope of finding an outlet there for our ships; but this course was not taken until towards the end of the day. It was already night when, having reached a rather narrow pass, a calm came on, and we then found ourselves at the mercy of a rapid current which might at any moment have caused our loss by throwing us upon the reefs; yet when day broke we had the satisfaction of seeing ourselves in the open sea and delivered from these dangers. Our position had doubtless been very perilous; but since we had been sailing through seas strewn with reefs we had grown so accustomed to danger that I and several others went to bed at our usual hour and slept as peacefully as if we had been in the greatest safety.

1793-06-16.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 274-276]
The coasts which we had so far run along to the north of these lands were cut up by a great number of channels. This numerous archipelago had shown us many dwellings, without, however, affording us the sight of a single islander; but on the 29th, having reached latitude 10° 8' south, and longitude 149° 37' east, and rounding very close a group of islets which lay to the south of us, we saw fifteen natives come out of their huts. Three of them at once embarked in an outrigger canoe and made towards us; but we were sailing far too fast for them to be able to overtake us.

Soon another canoe appeared near the westernmost islet; it was much larger than the first; it carried a nearly square sail, which it spread at once, and it was not long in coming up near our ship; but it was in vain that we urged it to come alongside. Shortly afterwards it went off towards the Espérance, and as soon as it was a short distance from that frigate it lay with its sail shivering in the wind, unwilling to draw any nearer. Our two ships were hove to. Citizen Legrand, wishing to see these islanders at close quarters, jumped into the water and quickly swam out to their canoe. We were told in the evening that this officer had not seen any weapons in their hands, and that, although there were twelve of them, they had shown some fear when they saw him coming towards them.

It appears that they did not know the use of iron, for they set little value on what he offered them.

These islanders were entirely naked and of a black colour not very deep. Their woolly hair was adorned with tufts of feathers; their bellies were bound with a cord wound several times round them, doubtless in order to give support to the muscles of the lower abdomen. Several wore bracelets plaited from coconut fibre.

We admired their skill in sailing close to the wind when they returned towards the coast.

1793-06-17.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 276-279]
On the 30th, in the morning, two outrigger canoes under sail, each manned by twelve savages, went rapidly round our ship, watching us with great attention, but from a great distance; then they kept to windward of us for a fairly long time. We were then in latitude 9° 53' south, and longitude 149° 10' east. Everything pointed to a numerous population on the southern coast, and above all towards the head of a large bay which stretched to the south-south-west. Soon we saw coming towards us some canoes, each manned by ten or eleven natives, who kept about a hundred metres from our ship; but the pieces of cloth which we threw into the sea for them persuaded them to come nearer. They seemed greatly surprised to see on our ship a young black whom we had had with us since our departure from Amboyna; it was in vain that this negro spoke Malay to them; they did not understand that language. These inhabitants all had woolly hair and olive skin; yet I noticed one as black as the negroes of Mozambique, whom he closely resembled. Like them, his lower lip projected considerably beyond the upper. All of them chewed betel. None wore any clothing. They were adorned with bracelets to which they had fastened various shells. Several wore a small bone in a hole pierced through the septum of the nose. Others wore, slung across the shoulder like a bandolier, shells tied to cords.

These inhabitants gave us yams which they had baked in the ashes and had peeled with great care.

We saw no other weapons in their hands than rather short spears, sharpened at one end only.

Their huts could be made out; like those of the Papuans, they were raised on posts two to three metres above the ground.

These savages invited us to land on their island, but seeing that we were drawing away from it very perceptibly, for rapid currents were carrying us to the west, they left us and made back for their coasts.

Two canoes were still quite close to the Espérance at about half past three, when we saw three musket shots fired from that frigate, and the savages at once fleeing, paddling with all their might. We soon learnt that one of the canoes had assailed the men of the crew with stones, without the slightest provocation having given occasion for this attack. Happily these traitors had wounded no one, and they had been fired upon only to frighten them.

Shortly afterwards two longboats were sent to sound, along the coast, several inlets where good anchorages were hoped for. The hope was disappointed: it was necessary to come within a hundred metres of the coast to find bottom with a line seventy metres long, and a hundred metres further out it was reached only with a line of a hundred and sixteen metres.

In spite of the terror which the musket shots fired at their comrades must have spread among these inhabitants, some of them nevertheless came alongside us, having set out from the very place where the others had taken refuge. They showed us great bad faith, agreeing to any price for us to hand over our articles of trade, and, as soon as they had them in their hands, refusing to give us anything more; one of them, however, consented to part in our favour with a flute and a necklace, which are represented in *pl.* 38, *fig.* 26 and 27.

I noticed one of these savages who, like the inhabitants of New Zealand, wore tied round his neck with a very thin cord a piece of human bone cut off towards the middle of the ulna. Could this be a sort of trophy proclaiming the defeat of an enemy, and are these inhabitants to be added to the number of the cannibals?

Several had smeared their faces with charcoal dust. It is their custom to cover their private parts with long leaves of vacoua, which they pass between the thighs and fasten to the waist in front and behind by means of a tightly drawn cord.

We saw in their hands fairly large fishing nets, to the lower edge of which they had tied various kinds of shells. They also had shells in small cylindrical baskets lined inside with fibres which seemed intended to keep them from breaking.

They had combs with three diverging teeth, some of bamboo, others of tortoiseshell.

These savages left us as night came on, which we spent making tacks.

1793-06-18.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 279]
We had made barely two myriametres to the north-west since the day before when we found ourselves surrounded by low lands linked by breakers, among which we were forced to beat about even during the night. We passed several times over shoals, which were made out by the light of a very faint moon, and we often found ourselves in less than ten metres of water.

The calm which came on towards midnight left us at the mercy of currents which carried us towards the coast, on which several fires lit by the savages were shining.

1793-06-19.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 279-283]
As soon as day broke we saw in the distance the Espérance, which was still much nearer the land than we were, and which was having herself towed by her boats.

Soon savages came in great numbers alongside our ship; nevertheless we could not get a single one of them to come on board; an old man had already left his canoe in answer to our invitation when he was turned from his purpose by the others, who eagerly drew him back to them, as if they thought he was exposing himself to very great danger.

We thought we recognised among these islanders some of those whom we had seen two days before. They were very curious to learn the names of the objects we gave them; but what rather surprised us was that they asked them of us in these words, *poé nama*, an expression which differs little from the Malay *apa nama* (what is that called)? They did not, however, understand the persons on board who addressed them in the Malay tongue.

These savages had brought a kind of pudding in which we recognised yams and lobster meat well mixed together. They offered us some, and all of us who ate of it found it very good to the taste.

A human ulna, hollowed into a groove at one end, served most of these inhabitants for drawing out of the bottom of a gourd the lime which they mixed with their betel. They sold us an axe of the shape of the one represented in *plate* 12, *fig.* 9. It was made of a piece of fairly well-polished serpentine, hafted on a handle of wood all of one piece; it is remarkable that the edge of the stone lay in the direction of the length of the handle, as with our axes.

These peoples are very fond of scents. Most of the objects which they gave us were perfumed. They had various very aromatic barks of trees, one of which seemed to me to come from the species of laurel known under the name of *laurus culilaban*, which is very common in the Moluccas. Meanwhile the calm still continued, and towards one in the afternoon the General sent the large cutter to help tow the Espérance, whose crew must already have been very tired. At last, towards half past four, a light south-east breeze sprang up, which allowed that frigate to draw away from the reefs. Soon afterwards our cutter returned on board and told us that the Espérance had been surrounded for a very long time by a great number of islanders; that towards noon most of them had pointed out to the crew of that frigate two canoes which were setting out from two small islands and going to meet each other; that they had given them to understand that the savages who manned them would soon engage in combat, and that the prize of victory would be to eat the vanquished. During this account a ferocious joy had been seen to show on their faces, as though they were to take part in that horrible meal. After this conversation almost all those in our ship who had eaten in the morning of the pudding prepared by the savages, of which I have just spoken, were seized with nausea, fearing that human flesh might have gone into the making of this dish, of which these islanders had seemed to think highly.

Soon the two canoes were near enough to each other to join battle, and the warriors had been seen to climb onto a wooden platform supported by the outrigger and the canoe, and then hurl stones at one another with their slings, while each, carrying a shield on his left arm, tried to ward off the blows of his adversary; however, they had separated at the end of half a quarter of an hour, none appearing dangerously wounded, and they had made back for their coasts.

The commander of the Espérance sent General Dentrecasteaux a club and a shield which he had obtained from these savages.

The club was rather broad and flattened at one of its ends.

The shield was the first defensive weapon that we had noticed among the savage peoples we had so far visited. It was of a very hard wood and of the shape that may be seen in *pl.* 12, *fig.* 7 and 8. It was nearly a metre high, five and a half decimetres wide, and a centimetre and a half thick. The outer side was slightly convex. Towards the middle of *figure* 8, which represents its inner side, may be seen three short pieces of rattan by means of which the inhabitants fasten this weapon to the left arm.

These islanders, although very numerous alongside the Espérance, had committed no act of hostility; only one of them had seemed about to hurl a spear at a man of the crew who was standing on the wale, but on seeing a musket levelled at him he had at once left off his threatening gestures, and the canoe in which he was had withdrawn in haste.

On the following days we ran along some very low islets, beyond which we saw at first, to the south, some very high lands. The prodigious number of shoals which we met with at every moment prevented us from coasting them closely.

1793-06-24.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 283]
On the 7th, having reached latitude 8° 7' south, and longitude 146° 39' east, very high lands of New Guinea were sighted from the south-west to the north-west; after following them in their trend towards the north-west, we arrived on the 9th at a gulf about eight myriametres deep, enclosed between very great mountains, the highest of which were to the north, where they joined the one which forms Cape King William.

1793-06-26.journal_labillardiere: (Labillardière's account for this day is given under 1793-06-24.)

1793-06-28.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 284]
The calm kept us there until the 11th: we then made sail, steering towards Dampier Strait.

1793-06-29.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 284-286]
The next day, at daybreak, we discovered to the north-west by west a very high mountain, furrowed towards the summit by very deep lengthwise hollows. It was Cape King William. We then saw rising the western coast of New Britain, towards which we steered under all sail, so as to be north of Dampier Strait before nightfall. The sun being full in our faces, the look-out could not see in time a shoal over which we passed towards eight in the morning, meeting with extremely heavy waves. Once clear of it, we believed ourselves out of all danger, when three quarters of an hour later we found ourselves between two shoals lying very close together, forming ahead of us a blind alley from which it was impossible for us to get out with the south-south-east winds, which drove us ever further into it. The commander at once ordered the ship to go about; but there was not time to trim the sails so that the manoeuvre could succeed: our ship then drifted towards the shoals which lay to the north of us, and on which we expected soon to see her go to pieces, when Citizen Gicquel called out from high in one of the main shrouds that he had just discovered between these rocks a gap, very narrow indeed, but through which our frigate could nevertheless pass. We at once steered for this passage, and at last came out of that peril, one of the most dreadful we had run in this campaign; yet we were not yet out of danger; for some time we were surrounded by other shoals which forced us to change course several times, but we had the good fortune to find a passage through the small intervals which separated them.

Towards noon we were already well advanced in the strait, when we were in latitude 5° 38' south, and longitude 146° 24' east.

The coasts of New Britain then bore from east 37° south to east 61° north; we were half a myriametre from the shore.

The island on which Dampier had seen a volcano bore west 38° north, at a distance of a myriametre and a half. This volcano was then extinct; but we saw, a myriametre off to the west 28° north, a small cone-shaped island which had offered Dampier no sign of subterranean fires. A thick smoke rose from its summit at intervals, and towards half past three there issued from the depths of the volcano's chasms a quantity of burning matter which, falling on the eastern side of the mountain, flowed down to its base; there it met the sea, whose waters it set boiling, and they at once rose in the form of clouds of a dazzling whiteness. At the moment of the explosion a thick smoke tinged with various colours, among which the colour of copper predominated, had shot up beyond the highest clouds.

Along the coast of New Britain we saw many inhabitants and a great number of huts raised on posts like those of the Papuans.

We came out of the strait before nightfall.

We then ran along the northern coast of New Britain, to the north of which we discovered several small, very mountainous islands, unknown until then. The currents on this passage were hardly perceptible, except on the meridian of Port Montague, where they carried us rapidly to the north, which led us to presume that we were opposite a channel dividing the lands of New Britain.

1793-07-08.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 286-287]
We left them on the 21st, after having been thwarted in the survey we had just made of them by south-east winds and very frequent calms.

For a long time we had been reduced to living on worm-eaten biscuit and salt meat which had greatly deteriorated; and so the scurvy was already making great ravages. Most of us were forced to give up drinking coffee, because it caused us extremely troublesome spasms.

1793-07-10.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 287]
On the 23rd we ran fairly close along the Portland Islands.

1793-07-11.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 287]
In the afternoon of the 24th we sighted the easternmost of the Admiralty Islands.

1793-07-17.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 287]
On the 30th, towards sunset, the Anchorites were discovered to the south-west by west.

1793-07-20.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 287]
Towards seven in the evening of the 3rd of Thermidor we lost General Dentrecasteaux. He succumbed to the violence of dreadful colics which he suffered for two days. He had lately had a few rather slight symptoms of scurvy, but we were very far from believing ourselves threatened with so great a loss.

1793-08-01.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 287]
On the 15th the Traitors' Islands were sighted, and towards noon they bore from south 35° west to south 42° west, at a distance of four myriametres; we were then in latitude 6' south, and longitude 134° 3' east.

1793-08-07.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 287]
On the 21st our baker died of scurvy, his whole body affected by an emphysema which the heat of the equator had increased with astonishing rapidity.

1793-08-10.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 287-294]
On the 24th we doubled the Cape of Good Hope of New Guinea, and on the 29th we anchored at Waygiou.

## CHAPTER XV.

*Stay at Waygiou. Our scurvy patients find prompt relief. Meetings with the natives. Anchorage at Buru. We pass through the Strait of Buton. Ravages of dysentery. Anchorage at Surabaya. Stay at Semarang. My detention in the fort of Anké near Batavia. Stay at the Isle of France [Mauritius]. Return to France.*

During our stay at Waygiou we were often visited by the natives, who brought us turtles, several of which weighed from ten to twelve myriagrammes, and which they had taken for the most part on the Ayu Islands. The broth made from them brought great relief to our scurvy patients. The inhabitants, having perceived how much we needed them, made us pay ten times their value. These turtles, after their heads had been cut off, still went on walking for several hours. The inhabitants also sold us turtle eggs, cooked and dried in pigs' guts, smoked turtle flesh, fowls, pigs, of which they told us there were great numbers in the woods, shaddocks, coconuts, papayas, gourds of different kinds, rice, purslane *(portulaca quadrifida)*, sugar canes, yams, sweet potatoes, bananas, lemons, capsicum, ears of maize still green which they had roasted, and young stems of the papaya tree. They assured us that the young stems and the fruit of this tree before it ripens were very pleasant to eat when cooked. They also brought us sago, of which they had made a kind of rather flat cake a decimetre wide by two long; they ate them without any other preparation. Some also offered us sago in the form of a sourish paste which they had caused to ferment.

Most of the islanders go with the whole body naked, except for the private parts, which they cover with a coarse cloth that seemed to me to be made from the bark of a fig tree. The heat of the climate does not let them feel any need of clothing. Their chiefs alone are dressed in very wide trousers and a jacket of stuffs which they buy from the Chinese, who come from time to time, they told us, to anchor at the place where we were. Some were adorned with silver bracelets which the Chinese had also procured for them. Almost all the chiefs of these savages had travelled in the Moluccas and spoke the Malay tongue. Some wore a hat of vacoua leaves, of a conical shape much like those of the Chinese; others had their heads bound with a sort of turban. They all have frizzy hair, very thick and fairly long. The colour of their skin is not very black. Some let their moustaches grow; they have the septum of the nose and the ears pierced. Several showed us great skill in archery, aiming several times in succession at a mark more than forty paces away, which their arrows always came extremely close to. Others were armed with very long lances tipped with points of iron or bone. These islanders doubtless know how to work iron, for they set great value on the bars of that metal which we gave them; they also sought after tin-plate, but they showed a very marked preference for our cloths, above all those of a red colour.

The island of Waygiou, which the inhabitants call *Ouarido*, is covered with very large trees and everywhere presents mountainous ground, fairly high even at a short distance from the shore. Huts of bamboo were to be seen there, raised on posts about three metres above the ground and roofed with latania leaves.

A very remarkable fact is that at the moment we went ashore, those of our seamen who were least affected by scurvy, and even those who showed no sign of it at all, experienced a considerable swelling in every part of the body; but this symptom, by which some of us had been alarmed, entirely disappeared after three or four hours of walking.

During our stay on this island I ranged its forests unceasingly; I gathered there a rich collection of new plants, and I killed many rare birds, among others the species of promerops which Buffon calls the promerops of New Guinea, a large, very black cockatoo *(psittacus aterrimus)*, and a new species of hornbill to which I have given the name of the hornbill of the island of Waygiou. Its bill, which is curved and of a dirty white, is two decimetres long. Each mandible is unevenly toothed; the upper mandible is surmounted by a sort of yellowish casque, flattened and fluted. The wings and body are black, the tail is white, and the neck of a fairly bright rufous *(see plate 11)*. This fine bird measures eight decimetres in length from the tip of the bill to the ends of the feet.

In the midst of the woods I saw many wild cocks. The hen which the natives brought us was hardly larger than a partridge, and yet she laid eggs twice as large as those of our hens. This species of wild fowl is black, whereas the one which I killed in the forests of Java is grey in colour.

The crowned pheasant of the Indies *(columba coronata)* is very common in these thick forests, where we came upon wild orange trees here and there, whose fruit furnished our scurvy patients with a very wholesome lemonade.

The natives who came on board told us that the roadstead where we had cast anchor was infested with caymans; this did not, however, prevent several men of the crew from bathing in it; having gone deep into the mangrove forests, we noticed their tracks printed on the mud. It is chiefly during the night that the caymans are most to be feared.

During our stay at the anchorage we received visits from several chiefs. The chief of Ravak had supped and slept on board the Espérance on the eve of our departure, but as soon as he saw that preparations were being made to weigh anchor he jumped into the water, fearing that we meant to carry him off. His fright would have astonished us had we not learnt that the Dutch, five months before, had carried off his brother in the midst of an entertainment which they had given him on board their ship. This chief was dressed in trousers and a very full gown of printed calico, with a satin waistcoat, and the earrings he wore were of gold.

The peoples of this island had declared war on the Dutch, and most of the men, headed by the most powerful of their chiefs, to whom they give the title of sultan, had gone to join the inhabitants of Ceram in order to attack the governor of Amboyna, who was to pass that way while making his tour of the Moluccas. The inhabitants of the huts built on the shores of the roadstead where our ships lay at anchor had, before their departure, provided for the safety of their wives and children by taking them to villages in the interior of the island. This roadstead, called *Boni-Sainé* by the natives, and lying about a myriametre to the east of Ravak, is formed by the coast of Waygiou and a very small island which the inhabitants call *Boni*, which lay to the east of us. There we were almost on the equator, our latitude having been found to be 38″ south. We had there 128° 53' for our longitude east.

We took in our water towards the head of this roadstead, from a fairly large river which our longboats could ascend for more than a kilometre from its mouth at low tide, and twice as far at high tide.

The thermometer observed on board did not rise above 24°, doubtless owing to the abundance of the rains.

The barometer varied only from 28ᵖ 1ˡ to 28ᵖ 1ˡ ½.

The variation of the magnetic needle was 1° 14' to the east.

The winds were rather light and varied only from south-south-east to south-west.
