1793-08-27.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 294]
On the 11th of Fructidor we left Waygiou, following its north coast and standing to the west in order to double its western point. There we met with a shoal which is not marked on the charts, where the soundings varied from eight to sixteen metres over a space of about six hundred metres which we had to cross. Here and there we noticed points of rock rising almost to the surface of the water; we were fortunate enough to avoid them. The greatest extent of this shoal is about two kilometres from north to south.

1793-09-03.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 294-298]
We anchored in the roadstead of Buru on the 18th of Fructidor, two kilometres to the north 28° east of the Dutch settlement, in forty metres of water on a bottom of muddy sand. The commander of this post at once dispatched a corporal to us to offer all the refreshments we needed. After a few minutes we saw muskets fired into a herd of buffaloes grazing on the beach, and the corporal told us that the Resident had ordered the two fattest to be killed for our ships. Knowing the needs of navigators, he sent us a quantity of fruit, some bottles of a pleasant liquor drawn from the sagwire palm *(saguerus, Rumph. vol. 1, fig. 13)*, and young leaves of a species of fern of the genus *asplenium*, which grows in the shade in damp places; they are eaten as a salad; they are very tender and of a pleasant flavour.

This Resident, whose name was Henri Commans, was a good man and of great simplicity of manners; he was much loved by the inhabitants; it was he whose happiness the Dutch of Amboyna had extolled to us, telling us that he could sleep as much as he liked. At his house we met several natives who had seen General Bougainville when he stayed at Buru, and who recalled with enthusiasm the name of that celebrated navigator.

That day and the following ones were spent in ranging over the various districts of the island, which everywhere presents a varied and very picturesque appearance. The sago palm is very abundant here; it forms the chief food of the inhabitants; it is even an article of export. Great plantations of it were to be seen close to the Dutch settlement, in marshes which make this place very unhealthy, above all as the spring comes on.

Nowhere had I seen teak grow so tall. Two long avenues of it have been planted behind the town, whose trees are nearly forty metres high. In the Moluccas the Dutch build ships of this wood, the most durable of all those known. The *cayou pouti* of the Malays *(melaleuca latifolia)* grows abundantly on the hills. The Resident showed us a large still which he used for distilling the leaves of this tree, from which he drew a great deal of cajeput oil every year.

The island of Buru furnishes several woods for marquetry which are much sought after by the Chinese, and some others fit for dyeing. Two Chinese junks were then lying aground on the mud to the north-west of the Dutch fort. The village near which this fort is built is called *Cayeli* in the Malay tongue. Those of the natives who follow the Mahometan religion have a mosque there, whose roofs, diminishing by stages as they rise, present a very pleasing sight, as may be seen in *plate 42*, which represents part of this village.

The coast to the east of the village is watered only by very small rivers; but half a myriametre to the north-west we went up a very large one, which the inhabitants call *Aer-Bessar*, and which also discharges into the roadstead; this very deep river was more than eighty metres wide over the three or four kilometres of it that we covered. The island of Buru doubtless owes so considerable a river to the great height of its mountains. Its banks several times showed me the handsome shrub known under the name of *portlandia grandiflora*.

The pebbles rolled down from the summits of these mountains, which I found on the banks of different rivers, were fragments of quartzose rock mixed with mica, and often of a sandstone whose elements are also quartz.

Birds, above all parrots, are so abundant on this island that it very probably takes its name from them, the word meaning bird in Malay.

Deer, goats and wild boars are so plentiful in the woods that the natives supply the Resident with as many as he wants for two charges of powder and shot a head. The species of wild boar called *babi-roussa (sus babyrussa)* is also found there.

The natives appeared to us to dread exceedingly several species of snakes which they told us were very numerous on their island; but I did not come upon any of these reptiles during our stay, which I nevertheless spent in ranging the forests fairly constantly.

We were not yet in the rainy season; nevertheless the high mountains gathered storms almost every evening, which broke with a great crash during the night.

The bay having been sounded, there was found at its entrance, a little short of the eastern point called Point Rouba, a bank of rock on which only one to two metres of water were found over an extent of about two kilometres towards the west-north-west; but the rest of this wide entrance is very deep, even at a short distance from the western point or Point Lessatello, which the inhabitants call *Tanguiou-Corbau* (Buffalo Point).

The astronomical observations made at the village of Cayeli gave 3° 21' 54" for its latitude south, and 125° 1' 6" for its longitude east.

The dip of the magnetic needle was 20° 30'.

Its variation, observed on board the ship, was 0° 54' east.

The highest point shown by the thermometer on board was 23°, and on shore 25° 3/10.

The mercury in the barometer varied only from 28ᵖ 1ˡ to 28ᵖ 2ˡ.

At the syzygies the establishment of the tides is at about a quarter to twelve; the waters then rise two metres perpendicular.

1793-09-15.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 298]
On the 30th of Fructidor we set sail from Buru, steering for the Strait of Buton, which we entered on the 1ˢᵗ of Vendémiaire in the afternoon.

1793-09-21.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 298-299]
The next day, towards sunset, we anchored a kilometre from the coast, opposite the entrance of the channel which separates Pangesani from Celebes.

1793-09-22.journal_labillardiere: (Labillardière's account for this day is given under 1793-09-21.)

1793-09-23.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 299]
Dauribeau being ill, Rossel was given the command of the expedition, and formed the plan of going out by this channel. Early on the 3rd he sent off a longboat, which explored more than three myriametres of it, strewn with a great number of islets, particularly towards the coast of Celebes; it had found both shores bordered almost everywhere by marshes and covered with mangroves.

1793-09-24.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 299]
From this report several seamen thought it was to be feared that there might not be enough water along the whole length of this channel for our ships to pass through; nevertheless we entered it the very next day, and after having gone two myriametres into it, we let go the anchor as night came on.

1793-09-25.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 299]
The following day another longboat was sent to finish sounding this passage.

1793-09-28.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 299]
It arrived on the 8th in the afternoon, and told us that the passage was strewn with a great number of sandbanks, and that many shoals were met with there which were very hard to make out on account of their blackish colour, which made this outlet extremely dangerous; it was therefore decided to go back into the Strait of Buton, and after having been forced to cast anchor there, often several times a day, we arrived at last on the 16th at its southern end, where we anchored near the village of Buton, two kilometres north of the nearest coast.

1793-10-06.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 299-302]
We had taken a long time to get through this strait, because we had had to lie at anchor every night, and almost always to wait during the day, before making sail, until the tides had set up currents favourable to the course we wished to hold.

The natives had come out to bring us various kinds of fruit common in the Moluccas, among which I noticed pumpkins of very varied shapes. They had also loaded their canoes with wild breadfruit, of which all those who ate found the kernels very hard to digest, although they had been roasted. They also procured for us a great number of fowls, goats, smoked fish in great quantity, and from time to time fresh fish. Most of these inhabitants did not allow themselves to trade with us before having asked leave of the commander of our ship, to whom they made a present. They told us that within the past year they had seen four European ships pass through this strait, namely two coming from Ternate, and the others from Banda and Amboyna. These peoples trade with the Dutch; they preferred money to almost all the other articles we offered them; most of them, however, eagerly asked us for powder and shot, but, obtaining none, one of them offered us two slaves in exchange for a rather small quantity of ammunition, and he appeared much astonished when he saw that we did not accept the offer he had just made us.

These inhabitants brought us a great number of parrots of the species called *psittacus alexandri*, and the white-crested cockatoo *(psittacus cristatus)*.

We were rather surprised to see in their hands cloths of cotton and of the thread of the *agave vivipara*, which they told us they had made themselves.

I took advantage of the stops made in this strait to go ashore. I found there a great quantity of plants which I had not yet met with elsewhere, among which I must mention the grape-shaped nutmeg tree, already described by Citizen Lamarck; its fruit is not aromatic. I also gathered there the *cynometra ramiflora*, the *gyrinocarpus* of Goertner, and various species of rattans *(calamus)*, which, after climbing to the tops of the tallest trees, came down again to the ground and then climbed up others no less tall, often presenting stems several hundred metres long.

The fruits of the silk-cotton tree, *bombax ceiba*, and of several new species of the same genus which are very common in the forests, provided abundant food for numerous troops of pithecus monkeys *(simia sylvanus)*; we killed a few of them in order to preserve their skins. Almost everywhere on the damp ground we noticed tracks of deer, wild boars and buffaloes. We often came upon large herds of the last lying in miry places, but they always took flight as soon as they caught sight of us, and it was impossible to pursue them through the mud.

On the island of Pangesani I several times crossed thick forests of the palm known under the name of *corypha umbraculifera*, where I saw squirrels of the species called *sciurus palmarum*, which fled in every direction at our approach.

Near the shore the inhabitants had put up some sheds, under which had been placed bamboo lattices on which they lay the fish when drying it over the fire to preserve it.

The natives, knowing the danger of living near the marshes which make the northern coast of Pangesani very unhealthy, have built no village there. It was in the midst of these same marshes that we caught the seeds of an extremely contagious dysentery, which made all the greater ravages on our ships as we were already prodigiously weakened by long living on food of poor quality, which had deteriorated still further during the voyage. I too was attacked by this disease, which carried off many of our people.

1793-10-07.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 302-307]
The next day, at sunrise, four chiefs bearing the title of *oran-kaïa* came on board to tell us that we were not permitted to go ashore without first informing the sultan, who resided at the village of Buton and was an ally of the Dutch company. We told them of our wish to visit this end of the island, and one of them at once went to inform that petty sovereign of it.

Soon we received a visit from two Dutch soldiers, who offered to procure us an interview with the sultan, assuring us that the natives would not dare, without his having given leave, to sell us the refreshments we needed. First they took us to their own dwelling, where we were told that the sultan would not be visible until very late in the afternoon. Upon this, a fairly large party of us went on into the interior of the island, heading east. The natives we met did not appear at all surprised to see us, and showed no wish to follow us.

After walking for more than two hours along a small river covered with a great number of boats, some of which were coming from the strait laden with fish, we forded it in order to climb towards the north. We followed steep paths, on the edges of which I gathered many plants, among others the *barleria prionitis*

*nitis*, and several new species of *croton*.

Most of the dwellings were built on the tops of the charming hills by which this part of the island is broken up. We were received with cordiality by the natives, who offered us different kinds of fruit. One of them in particular, having gone to pick coconuts for us, rapidly reached the top of one of the tallest trees by a means which seems to me remarkable. First he bound his legs together near their lower end with a piece of cloth, thus forming a point of support which helped him to grip the trunk of the tree with his feet strongly enough to bear the whole weight of his body; and as the trunk of this palm was not very thick, by clinging alternately with his arms and his feet along the tree he very quickly reached its top.

On the summits of the steepest parts of some of the hills could be seen forts, in which the inhabitants take refuge when the enemy approaches their dwellings. These bastions of a sort consist of fairly thick stone walls, three to four metres high, enclosing a square piece of ground twenty to thirty metres across.

The natives who a few days before had sold us cloths had not deceived us in telling us that they had been made on the island of Buton.

That day we saw in some houses several looms on which such cloths were being made, in much the same way as our weavers go about it when they make linen. These islanders used cotton threads dyed in various colours; it seemed to me that red and blue were their favourite colours.

Towards four in the afternoon we went to the village of Buton to see the sultan; we did not know that one had to bring him some presents in order to gain access to him. As we had nothing to offer him, he was not to be seen. Only his son and his nephew received us near the fort in which he resides. They took great pains to repeat to us that the whole island was under his rule; that he was the ally of the Dutch company, and that its enemies were his. They told us that the inhabitants of Ceram having lately made an incursion on their coasts, four had been taken and delivered up to the king, who had immediately had them beheaded. Directly after this account they invited us to step forward a few paces, and showed us with an air of satisfaction the heads of these unfortunates, displayed on the walls of the fort on the ends of very long pikes.

The village of Buton is built on a rise which is very steep towards the north-east and surrounded by thick walls which shelter the inhabitants from the incursions of their enemies. The houses, made of bamboo, are roofed with palm leaves like those of the other inhabitants of the Moluccas. The streets are very narrow, for the aim has been to make the most of this rather small piece of ground. The market was supplied with a great variety of fruit and fish.

The sultan lives in a fort built of stone. It appeared to us that this chief lived in rather marked distrust of the agents of the Dutch company, although he is its ally; for the three Dutch soldiers, who were the only occupants of the company's factory, did not have leave to live in the village where he resides. They were relegated more than two kilometres from there, to a wretched isolated dwelling. They were soon to leave it and go to Macassar; but they had been held back for some time by the fear of meeting the boats of the inhabitants of Ceram, their enemies, which had been cruising for some time in those waters.

It was already night when we went down to the shore to return on board. It was the hour of low tide. Most of us had been suffering from the dysentery for several days, and nevertheless we had to go into the water up to our waists to reach the longboat, which greatly aggravated our illness.

In the course of that day the natives had supplied our ships with rice, maize, sugar canes, yams, fowls, eggs, ducks and goats. They had been offered hardware in return for these provisions, but they had preferred the money which is current in the Moluccas, and particularly the small silvered coin which they call *koupan pera*, and which the Dutch bring from Europe.

At the syzygies the establishment of the tides is at about one in the afternoon in the bay where we were, the waters rising two metres perpendicular.

We had anchored in latitude 5° 27' 18" south, and longitude 120° 27' east.

1793-10-08.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 307]
On the 18th, in the afternoon, we spread all our sails to clear Buton Strait, and we soon gained the open sea.

1793-10-10.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 307]
On the 20th, in the morning, we passed through Selayar Strait. A great number of canoes and natives were scattered along the shore; others were sailing towards Celebes.

1793-10-18.journal_labillardiere:
[t. II, p. 307-308]
We anchored several times along the coast of Madura, and on the 28th, in the afternoon, we cast anchor in ten metres of water, on a bottom of reddish mud, at a short distance from the north-west point of that island and at the entrance of the channel leading to Surabaya, one of the principal settlements which the Dutch occupy on the island of Java. It was our intention to anchor there, and as early as nine o'clock in the morning the Espérance had dispatched a longboat to the village of Gresik, to ask for a pilot who might guide our ships through the passage leading to it.

Five days went by without our receiving the least news of our longboat.

1793-10-20.journal_labillardiere:
— Continuation and end of the narrative: captivity in Java and return to France (1793-1796) —

[t. II, p. 308-309]
It was feared that she had fallen in with pirates; and on the 2nd of Brumaire another was dispatched, in the belief that the first had not reached its destination; for no one could imagine that she had been detained by Dutchmen who knew the object of our mission, when on the 4th we received a letter from the officer commanding that longboat, and learned that he was being held prisoner by the Dutch, who were then at war with France; a short time afterwards, however, the council of Surabaya sent us word that, in accordance with instructions it had just received from Batavia, it offered us every assistance at its disposal, and on the 5th two pilots were sent to us. We were obliged to cast anchor a great many times before reaching the roadstead of Surabaya, where we anchored on the 7th, two kilometres to the north of the mouth of the river which runs through the town; the flagstaff of the fort bore south 2° east, and the village of Gresik west 30° north.

Dysentery had already carried off six men of the crew since our departure from Buton.

[t. II, p. 308-311]
We were soon given leave to stay in the town of Surabaya, where I lodged on the 10th with Messrs Bawer and Hogh, who received me with the greatest cordiality.

Ten days later the council of Surabaya revoked the permission it had given us, and all were at once obliged to return on board, except the sick, among whom I was still numbered, for the dysentery had left me in a state of extreme weakness; being separated from those of the crew who were suffering from this contagious disease, purgatives and the use of sago and whey brought me great relief, and I was soon entirely cured.

It was high time that this captivity should end, for the number of sick was increasing on board our ships with frightening rapidity; nearly half of the crews were already attacked by dysentery and malignant fevers, and the number of the sick diminished only through the death of some of them. At last, however, the council restored the permission it had revoked a few days before, and we had the satisfaction of seeing ourselves all together again in the town.

The heat was excessive during the first days we spent at Surabaya. I was astonished to see Réaumur's thermometer rise there as high as 27°; but this heat was of short duration, for the change of monsoon, which took place about the middle of Brumaire, brought for a long time, especially in the afternoon, heavy rains which cooled the atmosphere so much that the thermometer showed no more than 22° to 23° in the greatest heat of the day.

As soon as I had recovered a little, I made very frequent excursions into the neighbourhood of the town, and as far as my strength allowed. I had the pleasure of seeing my natural history collections enriched with a great number of objects which I had not yet found elsewhere.

Most of the roads, for a good distance from Surabaya, were shaded by hedges of bamboo. Elsewhere there were long avenues of *mimusops elengi*, *guillandina moringa*, *nauclea orientalis*, *hybiscus tiliaceus*, etc., which gave a most wholesome shade in these burning climates. I was rather surprised to see the trunks of these last trees covered with branches right down to the ground along their whole length, so different in habit were they from all those of the same species I had met with elsewhere; but I soon saw some Javanese making, with a large chopper, a number of notches in the bark, fairly close to one another, and I learned that this practice had been in use among them from time immemorial, in order to bring forth young shoots at the places so cut. They take care to choose the rainy season, so that the operation may succeed more surely. Vegetation is then so rapid in this climate that, a short time after the operation, I saw buds breaking out in great numbers from the middle of the bark cut in the manner I have just described. These peoples are, however, in general but little skilled in agriculture.

[t. II, p. 311]
On the 21st of Frimaire the governor of Surabaya granted the naturalists leave to visit the mountains of Prau, which lie about six myriametres to the west-south-west of the town.

[t. II, p. 311-313]
We set out the very next day for the village of Poron, which is built near the foot of these mountains. Some Javanese took charge of our baggage, which they carried slung from long bamboos, the ends of which rested on the shoulder of each of them.

After travelling nearly four myriametres, we reached Souda-Kari, where we dined in the Javanese manner at the house of the chief of that village, who had had a great meal prepared for us. It consisted of various dishes of smoked fish, and of horse's and buffalo's flesh which, we were told, had been kept for more than six months after being cut into very thin strips and dried in the sun. All these dishes were seasoned with pepper, capsicum and ginger, spread with profusion. Rice served us in place of bread. To end this feast we had a great quantity of delicious fruit.

We soon set off again, and a short time afterwards there came on a heavy rain which troubled us exceedingly. We were accompanied by a sergeant of the Dutch troops. He was not long in giving us proofs of his authority over some Javanese who were on their way to the village we had just left; he had the umbrellas they were carrying snatched from their hands, and not one of them dared refuse. We did not know what he meant to do with them, when he came up to us to offer them to us, saying that he found it strange that these people should dare to shelter themselves thus from the rain while they saw us exposed to the inclemency of the weather; but what surprised him greatly was that not one of us would make use of these umbrellas, which we urged him to return to those to whom they belonged.

At length we arrived at the village of Poron, where we were received by the chief, who bears the title of Deman. His principal duty is to fix the share of labour of the natives in the corvées.

The tract we had just crossed from Surabaya is a very extensive plain where rice is the principal crop. The fields were already covered with two to three decimetres of water, held in by the earthen dikes surrounding them.

Before reaching the village of Souda-Kari we had noticed large plantations of indigo. In the island of Java it is usually the Chinese who work this commodity, because they have a far wider knowledge of the arts than the natives.

We had also seen the castor-oil plant *(ricinus communis)* cultivated in several fields; the Javanese extract from its seeds an oil for burning.

In this fine plain there were also to be found, though in small quantity, crops of maize, sugar-cane, and yellow sorghum *(holcus sorghum)*.

We spent the night in a bamboo dwelling where the greatest cleanliness prevailed. It was built quite close to that of the Deman.

[t. II, p. 313-314]
The following day we settled at the western end of this same village, on lands belonging to the Tomogon of Banguil, who had his residence more than a myriametre and a half from where we were, and who nevertheless arrived in the course of the morning to order the inhabitants to watch over our safety and to supply us with whatever provisions we might need.

This Tomogon was a man of great wit, who spoke Dutch well and was very well informed of the news from Europe. Of Chinese origin, he had been obliged to embrace the Mahometan religion in order to obtain the title of Tomogon.

We were dreadfully tired from the journey we had made the day before on horses that were very small, like all those of this island.

[t. II, p. 313-318]
Their extremely rough trot had distressed us all the more because the saddles we had been obliged to use were not padded: they were of a very hard wood, covered only with a thin skin glued on to it. Besides, the stirrups used by the Javanese were too short for us, and could not be let down, which had put us in a very uncomfortable posture; so on that day we went only a short way from our dwelling; but the next day we crossed a stretch of half a myriametre over a plain already for the most part flooded, and then came to the mountains of Prau. The Tomogon of Banguil went there on horseback, followed by more than a hundred horsemen, fairly well mounted. We found him in the forest, where he was waiting for us; but, knowing little, no doubt, of the simple way in which naturalists travel, he had had chairs brought for us to sit on at the top of a mountain, from which we could see through the trees a wide expanse of country which he told us was under his authority; this chief, wishing us to see it still better, had a great many teak trees topped on the spot, and we saw with regret that this moment's pleasure cost him more than a hundred stems of so fine a tree.

Peacocks were very common in this forest, which we ranged in every direction; we killed several. Among the collection of plants that I gathered were several fine species of *uvaria*, *helicteres* and *bauhinia*.

The inhabitants were busy clearing, towards the foot of the eastern mountains, an excellent piece of ground covered with trees, the smallest of which they felled with the axe, while they merely stripped the bark from the largest near the foot to make them die.

In the afternoon thunder rumbling in the distance announced rain, which soon fell with violence, as usually happens in this season; and so we were forced to return to our dwelling. The Tomogon, before going back to Banguil, had repeated to the inhabitants his order that our wants and our safety should be provided for.

On the following days we visited the mountains of Panangounan, advancing into the lands of the Emperor of Solo through great forests of teak, in the shade of which the *pancratium amboinense* grew in abundance. Our guides often told us of their fear of meeting tigers, and said that these were very common in the thickets near the streams, where they lay hidden to surprise the quadrupeds when they come to drink. We did not, however, see any of these wild beasts.

The Javanese who accompanied us were almost always on horseback, and did not dismount even in places where it was rather difficult to make one's way; but as soon as they caught sight of the plant called in their language *kadiar-ankri*, they instantly dismounted and ran, vying with one another, to gather it. So much eagerness on their part aroused our curiosity, and they soon told us that the tubers of its roots, dried and reduced to powder, are a powerful aphrodisiac. The ardour they showed in obtaining it proved to us that they set great store by remedies of this auxiliary sort, which are moreover much sought after by most of the peoples living in hot climates. This parasitic plant was found only on large tree-trunks. It was not yet in fruit; it appeared to me, however, to be a new species of *pothos*.

In the course of these various excursions I shot several wild cocks, whose plumage, varied with very brilliant colours, I admired. Their crowing, which we had often heard in the midst of the woods, had at first made us think that we were near some dwelling, but in a short time we learned to distinguish it perfectly from that of the domestic cock. The comb of the wild cock is not red, but whitish, mixed with a very faint tint of violet which grows somewhat deeper towards the edges.

Most of the marshes near our dwelling were covered with the very broad leaves of the nelumbo *(nymphea nelumbo)*, on which we very often saw a new species of jacana differing little from the one called *parra sinensis*, and we admired the lightness with which this bird, whose feet are very long, walked from leaf to leaf, thus keeping itself on the surface of the water.

At a short distance to the west of the village of Poron could be seen two colossal statues, which the Javanese call *retcio*, and for which they have great veneration. They told us that they invoked them in their greatest needs. Each was carved from a block of stone twenty-two decimetres high. Very ample garments had been represented, and the two heads had the same cast of features as the Moors; it seems to me very probable that these statues were raised in honour of some of those conquerors of the Moluccas, although the inhabitants could tell us nothing on the subject.

The Dutch sergeant who accompanied us was passionately fond of the music of the Javanese. From the first days after our arrival at Poron he had sent for a woman singer, whose shrill voice was accompanied by two musicians; every evening one of them played a kind of dulcimer and the other a sort of mandolin. While we were at work describing and preparing our collections, we had to listen for several hours to this discordant music, which nevertheless never failed to draw a great crowd of natives.

All the airs were sung in Javanese. They generally turned on love, as our sergeant, who understood the language of these people perfectly, explained to us. He told us that these airs had been improvised, according to the custom of the singers of Java. This one accompanied her voice with various gestures suited to the subject, and above all with movements of the fingers that were very difficult to perform and won her the applause of the islanders. If report is to be believed, these singers do not pride themselves on very strict morals.

[t. II, p. 318-319]
On the 29th we returned to Surabaya.

Citizen Riche and I had formed the plan of going to spend some time in the mountains of Passervan, which we had come very close to in our last excursion. They are very high, and we had very often heard their fertility praised. Wheat is grown there with great success. Several kinds of fruit trees brought from Europe thrive perfectly on these heights, because their temperature is very mild. We needed a fresh permission from the governor to make this journey; but Dauribeau, who undertook to ask it of him on our behalf, told us that the governor had just received new instructions from the council of Batavia, according to which he could no longer allow us to go very far from the town, but only to a distance of three to four hours' walk. I went several times to see a spring which is only a myriametre and a half from it towards the west. Its waters become covered with petroleum oil, which is carefully collected to be mixed with tar. A great quantity of pumice stones is met with in its neighbourhood.

[t. II, p. 318-321]
Citizen Riche and I lived in the same house. We usually went out together to make our researches, and every evening we returned to Surabaya laden with a number of objects we had not found before. We always saw with regret the coming of night, which put a stop to our labours. But on the 1st of Ventôse, as early as four o'clock in the morning, the commandant of the place (Châteauvieux), followed by some thirty armed Dutch soldiers, came to inform us, on behalf of Dauribeau and the principal officers of our expedition, that we were under arrest. Shortly afterwards we learned that several of our fellow-voyagers shared the same fate, and we could not guess what might have given rise to so arbitrary an act of authority; we soon learned that news arrived from Europe had determined Dauribeau to hoist the white flag and to place himself under the protection of the Dutch, who were then at war with France. No doubt he had already formed at that time the plan, which he afterwards carried out, of selling the ships of the expedition. To succeed the more surely, he had to rid himself of all those whom he well knew would loudly disapprove of such conduct. And so we were handed over to the Dutch as prisoners of war, seven in number, namely Legrand, Laignel, Willaumez, Riche, Ventenat, Piron and myself; and we were taken to Semarang, obliged to travel nearly forty myriametres over dreadful roads in the rainy season. We had to cross in boats several great plains flooded by torrents coming down from the high mountains which lay to the south of us, and which form part of the great chain that runs from east to west through the whole length of the island of Java.

Michel Sirot and Pierre Creno, both servants on board the Espérance, followed us into our banishment.

Dauribeau had stripped me of all my collections. On leaving Surabaya I entrusted to the gardener Lahaie eleven bread-fruit trees, and an equal number of roots and cuttings of that precious plant, which had kept perfectly in clay and could yield as many young plants. He promised me to take the greatest care of them and gave me a receipt for them.

Most of the crew were thrown into the prisons of the tomogon of Surabaya, from which they came out some time afterwards, some to be transferred to those of Batavia, and the others to remain with Dauribeau.

[t. II, p. 321]
As for us, we had left Surabaya on the 6th of Ventôse.

This town lies in latitude 7° 14' 28" south, and longitude 110° 35' 43" east.

The variation of the magnetic needle there was 2° 31' 14" west, and the dip 25°.

[t. II, p. 321-323]
It was only after enduring a great deal of fatigue that we at last arrived at Semarang on the morning of the 21st.

The officer commanding the place at once took us to Governor Overstraaten. He told us that the chief surgeon of the hospital (Mr Abbegg) had had lodgings prepared for us, and he urged us to go and take possession of them; but what was our surprise when, on reaching this surgeon's house, he showed us into one of the wards of his hospital, where he pointed out seven beds which, he said, had just been put up for us. There was neither table nor chair in the place. In vain did we represent to him that we were not ill, and had no wish to become so in a hospital: his answer was always that, by the Governor's orders, he could offer us no other lodging.

We were therefore obliged to have recourse to the governor, to make him feel, if it were possible, all the harshness of such treatment towards men who, on returning from a long and arduous voyage undertaken for the advancement of the sciences and the arts, believed they deserved a different reception among a civilised people. It was not, however, until we had parleyed for several hours that the order for our confinement in a hospital was changed. We lived near the centre of the town, and had it for our prison.

A short time afterwards we were allowed to go as far as half a myriametre from Semarang, but with the restriction that we were not to go towards the seashore.

In travelling from Surabaya to Semarang I had been surprised to see, in the markets of several villages, stalls filled with little square, flattened cakes of a reddish clay which the inhabitants call *tana ampo*. I had at first supposed that they might use it to scour their cloth; but I had soon seen them chewing small quantities of it, and they assured me that they put it to no other use.

While crossing the great rice-fields we had found at the foot of the mountains, the natives had several times pointed out to us fields of rice on slopes too steep for the water to remain on them; a species of rice was grown there which does not need to be in flooded ground to thrive perfectly; but great care is taken to grow it only in the season when it is watered every day by heavy rains.

I had already noticed in the island of Java, on various heights, a great number of coconut palms which, stripped of their leaves, had died where they stood. It had seemed to me rather astonishing to see so many of them within so limited a space, and I had not been able to guess the cause; but at last I learned from several inhabitants of the hills lying a short distance to the north-west of Semarang, where I saw many of these coconut palms, that they had been struck by lightning; these inhabitants had witnessed it, and they told me that the same happened on many other heights of the island. Indeed, these tall trees, standing thus alone, are peculiarly exposed to the terrible effects of lightning; besides, the abundant sap with which they are filled does not a little to attract the matter of the thunder.

[t. II, p. 323]
On the 16th of Germinal we learned that a packet-boat was shortly to sail from Batavia for Europe. The governor of Semarang was good enough to allow two of us to go to the regency of Batavia to ask for a passage in that vessel. We were all equally burning with the desire to see our country again; but the matter had to be decided by lot. It fell in favour of Citizens Riche and Legrand, and on the 17th of Floréal they left for Batavia.

[t. II, p. 323-325]
Twelve days later the governor of Semarang ordered us to go to the same place, where we were to wait until there should be some opportunity of returning to France other than the packet-boat I have just mentioned, for it was even very uncertain whether Riche and Legrand would find a place in her.

Several Dutchmen who took an interest in us informed us that the fleet in which we still had hopes of sailing for Europe was not to sail for six or seven months, and they assured us that it was not likely there would be any other opportunity before then of returning to our country. The dysentery I had caught in the marshes of Buton Strait made me fear a return of it amid the marshes of Batavia, whose exhalations are more unwholesome still. Besides, residence at Batavia is so pernicious to most Europeans, especially in the first year they live there, that of a hundred soldiers arrived from Europe ninety usually die in the first year, and the rest, having become somewhat seasoned, drag out a languishing existence there. Other Europeans, who live there in great comfort, do not perish in so frightful a proportion; but with the meagre allowance granted us as prisoners of war, we could not hope to procure anything there beyond the barest necessities.

Citizen Piron and I obtained leave not to go to Batavia until the moment of the departure of the Dutch fleet. Our companions in misfortune, Laignel, Ventenat and Willaumez, set out for that place, and as soon as they had arrived they were sent to the fort of Tangaran, more than two myriametres from the town. Riche and Legrand, instead of obtaining their passage in the packet-boat, which was soon to sail, had been relegated to the fort of Anké. About two months later, however, they had the good fortune to sail for the Isle of France [Mauritius] in a ship which was carrying there prisoners taken from our privateers.

[t. II, p. 323-325]
Dauribeau, not yet satisfied with having stripped me of my collections, asked the governor of Semarang to have the manuscript taken from me which contained the observations I had made during the voyage in search of La Pérouse. In vain did I protest against this violation of the most sacred of all property; nevertheless on the 10th of Thermidor Governor Overstraaten ordered a search to be made of my effects, which he had had placed under seal for a month past; but fortunately my journal was not found.

[t. II, p. 323-325]
Dauribeau, who had arrived at Semarang a short time before to negotiate with the governor the sale of the ships of our expedition, died on the 5th of Fructidor.

[t. II, p. 323-327]
The time for the departure of the Dutch fleet was drawing near. Citizen Piron and I set out for Batavia on the 14th of Fructidor. We had on board the vessel which carried us there several Javanese, one of whom was in irons. His poor wife was seated beside him; she had chosen to follow him into exile. We were heartbroken to learn from the lips of this unfortunate man the cause of his ruin; his name, he told us, was Piromongolo; he came from the village of Calibongou, in the government of Semarang; he had paid three hundred and fifty rixdollars to be one of the mantris of that village, but another inhabitant had supplanted him by giving a larger sum, and those who had received his money, instead of returning it to him, were ridding themselves of him by exiling him to Ceylon, where he was to be confined like many other inhabitants of the Moluccas whom the Dutch sacrifice to their vengeance or to their pretended political interests. Among the charges heaped upon his head, he was accused, he told us, of being a sorcerer; the poor man confessed to us with great simplicity that he himself knew nothing of it; but that, in any case, he could assure us that those who had stolen his three hundred and fifty rixdollars were far more dangerous sorcerers than he.

The Dutch Company has fixed at a modest sum the salary it allows the various governors of the island of Java; but it tolerates the abuses arising from the very ample compensation which most of them contrive to procure for themselves by levying on the natives contributions much heavier than those which are to be paid into the Company's warehouses, and turning the surplus to their own profit.

The Chinese are, so to speak, the only people who work at the making of sugar. They make scarcely anything but sugar-candy, and they are permitted to sell it only to the governor; he buys it on account of the Dutch Company; but he often forces these unfortunate Chinese to deliver it to him at half the price he makes the Company pay for it; the Company nevertheless still obtains it very cheaply (about twenty centimes the half-kilogramme).

The contributions which the governors receive in money bring them a very considerable gain when, keeping the money, they repay the Company in paper currency. In this way they could make 20 per 100 at the time of my stay in the island of Java.

The appointment of natives to various posts is yet another means of fortune, from which many Governors and Residents know how to draw very great advantage.

[t. II, p. 327]
On the 16th we dropped anchor in the roadstead of Batavia.

[t. II, p. 327-331]
After we had remained two days on board, the commander of the roadstead took us ashore, and we were at once transferred to the fort of Anké, which is only about half a myriametre to the west of the town. We were given the room which our companions in misfortune, Riche and Legrand, had occupied.

On every side we were surrounded by marshes, which make this place very unhealthy; it is, however, much less so than the town, where the low tides lay bare in a great number of canals a blackish mud from which the heat of the sun draws exceedingly pernicious emanations. The marshes of Anké, on the contrary, were covered with various plants growing so close together that they resembled fine meadows in full growth. From the bottom of the stagnant waters rose a great number of grasses, sedges, nelumbos, etc., and the spaces these different plants left between them were filled with great quantities of *pitsia stratiotes*, which, keeping itself on the surface of the water by means of the air-vesicles with which its leaves are furnished at the base, absorbed in great quantity the noxious miasmas as they rose from the mire, and changed them, as is well known, into respirable air with the help of the sun's rays; and this transmutation is due especially to the *pitsia*, for experience has shown that it so powerfully prevents the decomposition of stagnant water that fish kept in a small quantity of water, in which they die at the end of a few days, live in it a very long time if its surface is covered with this singular plant, each plant of which occupies about a square decimetre.

These marshes serve as a lair for enormous serpents of the species called *boa constrictor*. One of them used to come fairly regularly every five or six days to carry off some fowl from the poultry-house of an innkeeper near the fort of Anké, at whose house we had been allowed to take our meals. This innkeeper was an extremely hard man. Whenever a fowl was missing, he at once charged with dishonesty an old slave to whom the care of his poultry-house was entrusted, and, without pity for the unhappy man, had him given fifty strokes of the rattan each time a hen disappeared; but one day the thief (it was a *boa constrictor* serpent which had swallowed one of the largest) found itself so swollen that it could not get out through the opening by which it had entered the poultry-house; whereupon the slave avenged himself for the blows he had received and cut it into several pieces. The hen that was taken from its stomach had gone in head first. It had undergone no alteration. The serpent was of middling size, for it was only four metres long; but a few days later some Javanese killed another, not far from there, which was ten metres long. This one, it seems, did not trouble itself much with eating fowls. In its stomach was found a kid weighing a myriagramme and a half.

The river which flows past the foot of the fort of Anké is frequented by caimans. One day I saw one of the largest advance into the midst of a band of children who were swimming in the river. It instantly seized one of them and disappeared beneath the water; nevertheless, a few days afterwards other children came back to bathe at the same spot.

During the last months of our stay at Anké, four officers of the French privateer the *Modeste* came to lodge in the fortress where we were held. Their presence softened our captivity a little. They had been made prisoners of war aboard a Dutch ship, a few days after having taken her as a prize.

The major of the place, who came to see us very often, told us of the death of the victualling clerk of the Recherche, named Girardin. It was found to be a woman, as had been suspected since the beginning of our voyage, although she had all the features of a man. It seems that the desire to satisfy her curiosity had been in great part what had led her to undertake this voyage. She had left a very young child in France.

The corvette *Nathalie*, with Citizen Riche on board, had been dispatched from the Isle of France to claim our ships from the regency at Batavia; but on arriving in the roadstead this corvette was held for five months under the guns of two Dutch ships of war, and could obtain nothing more than leave to carry away those members of our expedition who were in prison, and a few other Frenchmen who were prisoners of war.

[t. II, p. 331]
At length, on the 9th of Germinal, we set sail for the Isle of France.

It was high time that I left the marshes amid which the fort of Anké is built; for more than a month I had been suffering from a dysentery which was making very rapid progress. But as soon as I breathed a pure air, my illness abated from day to day.

[t. II, p. 331]
On the 18th of Floréal I arrived at the Isle of France. I very often ranged over its high mountains, and observed their productions, which are extremely varied.

Until then there had been no opportunity I could take advantage of to return to my country, when General Malartic sent the *Minerve* to France, giving the command of her to Citizen Laignel, one of my companions in misfortune. I embarked in this ship, which sailed from the Isle of France on the 30th of Brumaire.

[t. II, p. 331-332]
It is worth noting that, while steering north-north-west from the 25th degree of north latitude and the 31st degree of west longitude, we saw, over a space of more than one hundred and forty myriametres, the sea covered with a prodigious quantity of seaweed of the species called *fucus natans*; it points to very extensive banks where it has its origin. This inquiry well deserves the attention of navigators.

[t. II, p. 332]
On the 22nd of Ventôse we anchored at the Île de Batz, and soon afterwards I went on to Paris.

I was not long in learning that my natural history collections had been carried to England. The French government at once claimed them; the President of the Royal Society of London, Mr Banks, supported this request with all the energy that might be expected from his love of the sciences, and some time afterwards I had the happiness, on receiving them, of finding myself in a position to make known the natural productions I observed in the various lands at which we touched in the course of this voyage.

The bread-fruit trees I had entrusted to the gardener Lahaie were carried to the Isle of France, together with others which this gardener was cultivating; some have been sent to Cayenne, and others deposited in Paris in the hothouses of the Jardin des Plantes.

END OF THE SECOND AND LAST VOLUME.
